NdiAssessmentCycleService is fully org-scoped (TenantContext.getCurrentTenant(), findByIdAndOrganisationId), so this is module-wide within-tenant BFLA (CWE-862) exactly as categorised: any authenticated user can create, transition (including APPROVED/SUBMITTED), and soft-delete SDAIA NDI regulatory assessment cycles. High confirmed.

title: Append-only NDI audit ledger is writable by any authenticated user (audit log forgery)
cvss: CVSS 7.1 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:N) — integrity loss on the regulatory audit trail
description: POST /api/ndi/audit is exposed with @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()") and binds a raw NdiAuditEvent entity straight from the request body. The service comment describes the table as an "append-only ndi.audit_event table", but the only controls applied in record() are: id nulled, organisationId stamped from the tenant, and a default severity. Every other field — entityType, action, entityCode, cycleId, occurredAt, actor identity fields, before/after values, severity, message — is taken verbatim from the attacker. Any authenticated tenant user can therefore inject fabricated audit entries (e.g. forge an APPROVED transition by another user, or backdate occurredAt) into the same ledger that legitimate state-change code writes via NdiAuditPublisher. Because the search/aggregate endpoints surface this ledger to the Audit tab and to the AUDIT_TRAIL report, forged entries are indistinguishable from genuine ones.
rootCause: A write endpoint was provided on an audit ledger that is supposed to be system-generated only, with no authorization gate and no server-side control over the recorded fields (actor, timestamp, action).
impact: An insider can pollute or frame the NDI audit trail — fabricate evidence that an approval/submission happened, attribute actions to other users, or flood the ledger to bury real events. This undermines the evidentiary value of the audit trail used for SDAIA NDI compliance and incident investigation.
reproduction:
1. Obtain any tenant JWT.
2. curl -X POST http://localhost:8084/api/ndi/audit -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"entityType":"COMPLIANCE","action":"APPROVE","severity":"INFO","message":"Approved by CISO","actorName":"ciso@victim","occurredAt":"2026-01-01T00:00:00"}'
3. GET /api/ndi/audit returns the forged, back-dated, mis-attributed event alongside genuine ones.
resolution: Remove the public POST endpoint (audit events should only be produced internally by NdiAuditPublisher). If an external write must exist, restrict it to hasRole('PLATFORM_ADMIN'), and always stamp occurredAt and the actor from the SecurityContext server-side rather than trusting the body. Enforce table-level append-only (no UPDATE/DELETE grant) in the DB.
references: CWE-117: Improper Output Neutralization for Logs
OWASP A09:2021 Security Logging and Monitoring Failures

_verification.rationale: Verified in source. NdiAuditController.java:37-41 exposes POST /api/ndi/audit gated only by @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()") and binds a raw NdiAuditEvent from the request body. NdiAuditService.record() only nulls id, stamps organisationId, requires action/entityType, and defaults severity, then repo.save(body) — occurredAt, actor identity, message and before/after values are all attacker-controlled. Any authenticated tenant user can forge or backdate entries in the same append-only ledger that NdiAuditPublisher writes, and the search/aggregate endpoints surface it to the Audit tab and AUDIT_TRAIL report. Genuine audit-log integrity (A09) flaw; High is correct.

title: Module licensing can be enabled/disabled by any authenticated user (license bypass + tenant DoS)
cvss: CVSS 8.1 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:H) — privilege escalation: license bypass + tenant-wide DoS
description: POST /api/v1/licensing/modules (upsert) and POST /api/v1/licensing/modules/{code}/disable mutate the tenant's OrganisationLicense rows. The controller's own Javadoc labels these as '(admin)' operations, yet both are guarded only by @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()"). LicensingService.upsert/disable perform no role check. Because enabled modules drive both the LicenseGuardAspect (RequireModule) gating and the JWT enabled_modules claim that hides/shows sidebar entries, any logged-in user — including a read-only AUDITOR — can grant their entire tenant access to paid modules (RISK, BCM, CYBER, PDPL, TPRM, REPORTING, etc.) they were never licensed for, or disable a module to deny the whole tenant access (DoS). upsert even lets the caller set tier=ENTERPRISE and validTo far in the future.
rootCause: Write endpoints that change commercial entitlements use the broadest possible guard (isAuthenticated()) instead of a platform-admin / PLATFORM:WRITE permission. The intended RBAC pattern — hasPermission('MODULE','ACTION') via ModulePermissionEvaluator — is used elsewhere (reporting, dashboard, help) but not enforced here.
impact: License/entitlement bypass (revenue impact — any user self-grants paid modules) and tenant-wide denial of service (any user disables a module everyone depends on). The change is tenant-global, not per-user, so a single low-privilege account compromises the whole organisation's licensing state.
reproduction:
1. Log in as a low-privilege user (e.g. auditor / Audit@12345).
2. curl -X POST http://localhost:8084/api/v1/licensing/modules -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"moduleCode":"CYBER","tier":"ENTERPRISE","enabled":true}'
3. Observe HTTP 200 and the CYBER module now enabled for the whole tenant.
4. POST /api/v1/licensing/modules/RISK/disable to disable RISK tenant-wide.
resolution: Restrict licensing mutations to platform admins. Replace isAuthenticated() with @PreAuthorize("hasRole('PLATFORM_ADMIN')") (or a dedicated PLATFORM:WRITE / LICENSING:ADMIN permission). Keep the read endpoints (list, me/enabled, catalog) at isAuthenticated().
references: OWASP API5:2023 Broken Function Level Authorization

_verification.rationale: Verified LicensingController.java: every endpoint (incl. POST /modules upsert and POST /modules/{code}/disable) is guarded only by @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()"). @EnableMethodSecurity(prePostEnabled=true) is active in SecurityConfig, and ModulePermissionEvaluator shows hasPermission requires a specific MODULE_ACTION authority or ROLE_PLATFORM_ADMIN — so isAuthenticated() genuinely means any logged-in user (e.g. seeded auditor/riskmanager) bypasses the admin gate. This is real BFLA: a non-admin can enable/disable their tenant's module entitlements, bypassing licensing and self-inflicting a tenant DoS via the LicenseGuardAspect (RequireModule) which throws ModuleDisabledException for disabled modules. Not Critical / not cross-tenant: upsert forces body.setOrganisationId(TenantContext.getCurrentTenant()) and disable() uses the current tenant, so writes cannot reach other tenants. Severity High is correct for in-tenant privilege escalation over license control.

title: Automation rule logic editable/deletable by any authenticated user
cvss: CVSS 7.1 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:H/A:L) — tamper with org-wide automation/notification logic
description: PATCH /api/v1/automation/rules/{id} lets any authenticated user rewrite an AutomationRule's conditionJson and actionJson, toggle enabled, and change priority; DELETE /api/v1/automation/rules/{id} soft-deletes a rule. Both are guarded only by isAuthenticated(). The F8 engine executes actionJson at rule-fire time: NOTIFY/ESCALATE fan a message out to every active holder of an arbitrary role (capped at 50), and CREATE_RECORD/FLAG drive cross-module side effects. A low-privilege user can therefore (a) disable safety/compliance escalation rules so breaches go unnotified, (b) re-point an ESCALATE rule at a different role to spam or socially-engineer recipients, or (c) silently neuter the SAMA/NCA/PDPL deadline-escalation automation the platform relies on.
rootCause: Administrative configuration endpoints (editing the automation engine's rules) are gated by authentication only, not by a platform-admin / AUTOMATION:WRITE permission, diverging from the hasPermission pattern used by the rest of the platform.
impact: Tampering with org-wide automation: suppression of compliance/breach escalations (integrity of the GRC control fabric), notification spam/abuse to arbitrary role holders, and disabling of the F8 engine's regulatory deadline chasers. Org scoping is correct (findByIdAndOrganisationId), so impact is confined within the tenant.
reproduction:
1. Log in as any low-privilege user.
2. GET /api/v1/automation/rules to enumerate rule ids (also isAuthenticated()).
3. curl -X PATCH http://localhost:8084/api/v1/automation/rules/1 -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"enabled":false}' to disable a compliance-escalation rule.
4. Or set actionJson to {"type":"NOTIFY","role":"PLATFORM_ADMIN","message":"..."} to re-target notifications.
resolution: Gate PATCH and DELETE (and arguably the read endpoints) on a platform-admin or AUTOMATION:WRITE permission: @PreAuthorize("hasPermission('AUTOMATION','WRITE')") for patch/delete. Reads can stay on hasPermission('AUTOMATION','READ').
references: OWASP API5:2023 Broken Function Level Authorization

_verification.rationale: Verified AutomationRuleController.java: all 8 endpoints carry only @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()"). With method security enabled and the authority-based permission model, any authenticated user (regardless of role) can PATCH a rule's conditionJson/actionJson (the automation logic that drives automated platform actions) and soft-delete rules. Every operation is org-scoped via findByIdAndOrganisationId / findByOrganisationId..., so there is NO cross-tenant exposure — the issue is purely missing function-level authorization within the tenant. Genuine BFLA over the automation engine's integrity warrants High; severity unchanged.

title: PDPL privacy sub-modules use isAuthenticated() instead of hasPermission('PRIVACY',…) — broken function-level authorization (BFLA)
category: Broken Access Control (A01) / CWE-862 Missing Authorization
cvss: CVSS ~8.1 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N) — any authenticated user (any role) can read AND mutate PDPL/PII records they have no module permission for
description: The core PrivacyController, DpiaController and privacy_lc DsrCaseController correctly gate every endpoint with @PreAuthorize("hasPermission('PRIVACY','READ'|'WRITE'|'DELETE')"). However an entire cluster of privacy sub-modules added in later sprints gate every endpoint with only @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()"): Consent Records (PDPL Art.5 ledger), Data Sharing Agreements, Processor Assessments (PDPL Art.28), Cross-border Transfers (Art.29), Disposal Certificates, Privacy Notices, ROPA-workflows facade, and the PDPL Data-Flow graph. ModulePermissionEvaluator resolves hasPermission('PRIVACY','READ') to the granted authority PRIVACY_READ (or ROLE_PLATFORM_ADMIN); isAuthenticated() requires none of these. Consequently a user holding only, e.g., RISK_READ or AUDITOR authorities — who is deliberately NOT granted any PRIVACY authority — can list/read AND create/transition/withdraw these PDPL records. ConsentRecordController even exposes GET /consents/by-subject/{subjectRef}, letting any authenticated user enumerate a data subject's full consent history (dataSubjectRef is a PII reference). The records are returned as raw JPA entities, so all columns (data-subject references, destination orgs, data categories) are disclosed.
rootCause: These controllers were written with a coarse 'logged-in is enough' guard rather than the platform's MODULE:ACTION permission convention. The privacy module owns the PRIVACY permission namespace but only the original PrivacyController/DpiaController enforce it; the later sub-module controllers never adopted hasPermission('PRIVACY',…), so module-level access control is missing for them.
evidence: ConsentRecordController.java:38-42  @GetMapping("/by-subject/{subjectRef}") @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()") public List<ConsentRecord> history(@PathVariable String subjectRef){ return service.historyFor(subjectRef); }  — compare PrivacyController.java:30-31 @GetMapping("/breaches") @PreAuthorize("hasPermission('PRIVACY','READ')"). ModulePermissionEvaluator.java:41-43 returns true only for ROLE_PLATFORM_ADMIN or the MODULE_ACTION authority; isAuthenticated() bypasses it entirely.
impact: Confidentiality and integrity breach of PDPL-regulated data: any account on the tenant (e.g. a risk analyst, an auditor, a low-privilege operator) can read consent ledgers, processor due-diligence, cross-border transfer approvals and privacy notices, and can mutate them (grant/withdraw consent, approve/reject cross-border transfers, publish/supersede privacy notices, complete disposal certificates). For a Saudi bank this is a regulatory disclosure risk under SDAIA PDPL and undermines the segregation-of-duties the DPO role is supposed to enforce.
reproduction: 1) Log in as a user whose role grants e.g. RISK_READ but no PRIVACY_* authority (a non-DPO). 2) curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" http://localhost:8084/api/v1/privacy/consents → 200 with the full consent ledger. 3) curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" "http://localhost:8084/api/v1/privacy/consents/by-subject/NID-1234567890" → that subject's consent history. 4) POST /api/privacy/cross-border-transfers/{id}/approve with the same token → approves an Art.29 transfer. All succeed; the same calls with hasPermission('PRIVACY','READ') would 403 for this user.
resolution: Replace isAuthenticated() with hasPermission('PRIVACY','READ') on every GET and hasPermission('PRIVACY','WRITE') (and 'DELETE' where applicable) on every mutating endpoint across these controllers, matching PrivacyController/DpiaController. Where a narrower role is warranted (e.g. expire/approve restricted to DPO), use hasAnyRole/hasPermission accordingly. Add an integration test that asserts a token without PRIVACY_* authority receives 403 on each privacy endpoint.
references: OWASP API Security Top 10 2023 — API5:2023 Broken Function Level Authorization
OWASP Top 10 2021 — A01:2021 Broken Access Control

_verification.rationale: Verified ConsentRecordController.java: list/get/history/grant/withdraw/supersede/stats are all guarded only by @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()") rather than hasPermission('PRIVACY',...). The backing ConsentRecordService is fully org-scoped (findByIdAndOrganisationId, findByOrganisationId...), which confirms the finding's framing as BFLA (CWE-862 missing authorization) and NOT cross-tenant IDOR. Impact within the tenant is real: any authenticated low-privilege user can read the sensitive PDPL consent/PII ledger and grant/withdraw/supersede consents (withdrawal emits CONSENT_WITHDRAWN domain events that start downstream DSR/regulatory clocks). Genuine BFLA on a sensitive PDPL dataset = High; severity unchanged.

title: Cyber→PDPL bridge manual trigger creates breach + mutates cyber.incidents under only isAuthenticated()
category: Broken Access Control (A01) / CWE-862 Missing Authorization
cvss: CVSS ~7.6 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:H/A:N) — cross-module write (privacy.data_breaches + cyber.incidents) with no module permission
description: POST /api/privacy/cyber-bridge/trigger is guarded by @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()"). The handler calls CyberPdplBridgeService.triggerForIncident, which (a) UPDATEs cyber.incidents to set affects_personal_data + PII classification fields, (b) INSERTs a row into privacy.data_breaches, and (c) cross-links the two. This is a privileged classification action that should require PRIVACY:WRITE (and arguably CYBER:WRITE since it mutates a cyber incident), yet any authenticated user can invoke it. The read endpoints on the same controller (GET /log, /log/by-incident/{id}) are likewise only isAuthenticated().
rootCause: The bridge controller was wired with a generic isAuthenticated() guard rather than the PRIVACY module permission. Because the underlying write spans two modules via native SQL, no method-level @PreAuthorize on the cyber side is consulted either.
evidence: CyberPdplBridgeController.java:42-44  @PostMapping("/trigger") @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()") public ResponseEntity<Response> trigger(@Valid @RequestBody ManualTriggerRequest req, Authentication auth){...}. Service writes: CyberPdplBridgeService.java:95-109 UPDATE cyber.incidents SET affects_personal_data=1,...; :124-146 INSERT INTO privacy.data_breaches (...).
impact: Any authenticated user can fabricate a personal-data breach record (which may auto-flag a 72-hour SDAIA notification SLA via pdpc_notification_required) and reclassify an arbitrary cyber incident as PII-affecting within their tenant. This is a data-integrity and compliance-noise attack: false regulatory clocks, polluted breach register, and unauthorized mutation of incident records owned by the cyber module.
reproduction: 1) Log in as any non-DPO authenticated user. 2) POST /api/privacy/cyber-bridge/trigger {"cyberIncidentId":<an incident id in your tenant>,"dataSubjectsAffectedEst":600,"dataCategoriesAffected":"NATIONAL_ID","piiAssessment":"x"} with their Bearer token. 3) A privacy.data_breaches row is created with pdpc_notification_required=1 and the cyber incident is reclassified — returns 201.
resolution: Gate /trigger with @PreAuthorize("hasPermission('PRIVACY','WRITE')") (and consider also requiring CYBER:WRITE / restricting to DPO,CISO). Gate the read endpoints with hasPermission('PRIVACY','READ'). The native queries themselves are correctly parameterized — only the authorization guard needs tightening.
references: OWASP API Security Top 10 2023 — API5:2023 Broken Function Level Authorization
SDAIA PDPL Implementing Regulations — Art.31/40 breach notification

CyberPdplBridgeService.triggerForIncident() is org-scoped (the cyber.incidents SELECT filters WHERE organisation_id = :org and all writes use that org), so the finding is correctly a BFLA / missing-authorization issue, not cross-tenant IDOR. Within the tenant the impact is significant: any authenticated user can fabricate a regulatory privacy.data_breaches record, flip cyber.incidents PII-classification flags (affects_personal_data, pii_classified_by/at), and trip the >=500-subjects / NATIONAL_ID logic that flags a 72h SDAIA notification SLA. Forging breach/regulatory records and mutating incident state under no role check is a genuine High BFLA; severity unchanged.

title: Cross-tenant IDOR read of risk treatment plans via GET /treatments/{id}
cvss: CVSS 6.5 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N) — authenticated cross-tenant read of another organisation's risk treatment data
description: RiskTreatmentService.get(Long id) loads a RiskTreatment with a bare JpaRepository.findById(id) and performs NO organisation scoping before returning it. It is exposed directly by RiskAdvancedController.getTreatment (GET /api/v1/risk/treatments/{id}, guarded only by hasPermission('RISK','READ')). Because RiskTreatment surrogate ids are sequential Long PKs and every tenant's user holds RISK:READ, a user in organisation A can enumerate ids and read treatment plans (descriptionEn/Ar, ownerId, dueDate, status, treatmentType, parent riskId) belonging to organisation B. The platform's stated #1 invariant is that every repository read be org-scoped; the sibling write paths (update/transition/delete) are saved by their downstream ensureRiskInTenant(t.getRiskId()) check, and the list path is guarded by ensureRiskInTenant(riskId), but the single-entity read get() has neither guard and the repository has no findByIdAndOrganisationId finder to enforce it.
rootCause: Single-entity read uses an unscoped findById(id) and the controller relies on it without any TenantContext check; RiskTreatmentRepository exposes no org-scoped finder. The 'belongs to another organisation' guard exists only inside ensureRiskInTenant(riskId), which get() never calls.
impact: Confidentiality breach across tenants: any authenticated user with RISK:READ in one tenant can read risk-treatment records (mitigation strategy, owner, due dates, linked risk) of every other tenant by walking the integer id space. In a multi-tenant SaaS for banks/energy/telco this is a serious cross-customer data leak and a regulatory (SAMA/NCA/PDPL) reportable exposure.
reproduction: 1. Authenticate as a user in org A (e.g. riskmanager). 2. As org B, note a treatment id (or simply enumerate). 3. From org A's session call GET /api/v1/risk/treatments/{idOfOrgB} with the org A Bearer token. 4. Observe org B's treatment record returned with HTTP 200 (no org check) instead of 404.
resolution: Scope the read to the current tenant. Add findByIdAndOrganisationId(id, orgId) to RiskTreatmentRepository (the entity has no organisationId column itself — it inherits org via its parent Risk) and in get(id) resolve the treatment then call ensureRiskInTenant(t.getRiskId()) exactly as update()/transition()/delete() already do. Throw EntityNotFoundException (404) on mismatch so ids cannot be probed.
references: CWE-639 Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key
OWASP API1:2023 Broken Object Level Authorization

_verification.rationale: Verified RiskTreatmentService.get(id) at lines 62-66: it calls treatments.findById(id) with NO organisation scoping and does NOT call ensureRiskInTenant — unlike every sibling method (listForRisk, create, update, transition, delete all invoke ensureRiskInTenant). RiskAdvancedController exposes this directly at GET /api/v1/risk/treatments/{id} under @PreAuthorize("hasPermission('RISK','READ')"), which only checks the caller holds RISK_READ in their own org and performs NO object-level scoping (ModulePermissionEvaluator's instance-level overload delegates to the module-level check). A user in tenant A can therefore read any RiskTreatment by sequential id belonging to tenant B (descriptions, ownerId, due dates, status). Confirmed cross-tenant BOLA/IDOR. Read-only single-object leak (writes via update/transition/delete are properly scoped), so High — not Critical — is appropriate; severity unchanged.

title: Cross-tenant IDOR: VendorAssessment update/delete not scoped to organisation
cvss: CVSS 8.1 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N) — cross-tenant read+write of vendor risk assessments
description: TprmService.updateAssessment(id, req) and deleteAssessment(id) load the VendorAssessment with the bare JpaRepository method assessmentRepo.findById(id), with no organisation/tenant check. The Vendor-side methods in the same service (getVendor/updateVendor/deleteVendor) correctly filter on TenantContext.getCurrentTenant(), but the assessment methods do not. VendorAssessment carries only a vendor_id column and NO organisation_id (entity has no org field — see lines 16-24), so org ownership can only be enforced by resolving the parent vendor; neither method does this. The @Where(clause = "is_deleted = 0") on the entity does not constrain tenant. The controller endpoints PUT /api/v1/tprm/assessments/{id} and DELETE /api/v1/tprm/assessments/{id} are guarded by hasPermission('TPRM','WRITE'/'DELETE'), which any TPRM user in any tenant holds, so the permission check does not stop cross-tenant access.
rootCause: Assessment lookups use the unscoped JpaRepository.findById instead of resolving and validating the parent Vendor's organisationId (as getVendor does). VendorAssessment has no organisation_id column, so tenant isolation must be derived via the vendor and was omitted.
impact: A user authenticated in tenant A with TPRM:WRITE/DELETE can enumerate sequential assessment ids and overwrite findings/risk scores/status or soft-delete vendor risk assessments belonging to any other tenant (e.g. another bank). This is cross-tenant data tampering and destruction of regulated third-party risk records.
reproduction: 1. Log in as a TPRM user in tenant A (e.g. riskmanager). 2. Identify an assessment id belonging to tenant B (ids are sequential IDENTITY values). 3. curl -X PUT http://localhost:8084/api/v1/tprm/assessments/{idFromTenantB} -H 'Authorization: Bearer <tenantA token>' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"assessmentDate":"2026-01-01","riskScore":1,"riskRating":"LOW","status":"REVIEWED","findings":"tampered"}' . The response returns tenant B's mutated assessment. 4. DELETE the same id soft-deletes tenant B's record.
resolution: Resolve the parent vendor and assert org ownership before mutating, exactly as getVendor does. Add an org-scoped finder (e.g. findByIdAndVendor_OrganisationId or join on vendor) or fetch the existing assessment, then call getVendor(existing.getVendorId()) to enforce the tenant guard before applying changes.
references: CWE-639: Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key
OWASP API1:2023 Broken Object Level Authorization

_verification.rationale: Confirmed real cross-tenant IDOR. TprmService.updateAssessment (lines 101-112) and deleteAssessment (lines 114-120) fetch via assessmentRepo.findById(id) with NO organisation filter, then mutate/soft-delete the row. VendorAssessmentRepository declares no org-scoped finder (only findById/findByVendorId), so the raw JpaRepository.findById is unscoped. The contrast is explicit in the same file: getVendor (lines 39-43) DOES filter by TenantContext, but the assessment paths do not. The TprmController endpoints carry @PreAuthorize("hasPermission('TPRM',...)"), but that only verifies the caller holds the TPRM permission in their own tenant — it does not bind the path id to the caller's organisation, so a tenant-A user with TPRM:WRITE/DELETE can update or delete tenant-B assessments by guessing/iterating ids. Not mitigated elsewhere. High is appropriate for a multi-tenant integrity/availability breach (A01 BOLA).

title: Cross-tenant mutation of VendorAssessment via questionnaire workflow (unscoped findById)
cvss: CVSS 8.1 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:H/A:N) — cross-tenant write/corruption of vendor assessment workflow + scores
description: In QuestionnaireService, every assessment-workflow method loads the parent VendorAssessment with the unscoped assessments.findById(assessmentId): assignTemplate (line 214), upsertResponse (line 241), markComplete (line 299) and markReviewed (line 320). Unlike templates/questions/responses (which are loaded with findByIdAndOrganisationId / findByOrganisationId... finders), VendorAssessment is fetched without a tenant guard and VendorAssessment has no organisation_id column to let Hibernate filter it. The corresponding endpoints (POST /api/v1/tprm/assessments/{id}/assign-template, /responses, /complete, /review) only require hasPermission('TPRM','WRITE'), held by every TPRM writer in every tenant. A user in tenant A can therefore reference an assessment id owned by tenant B and: flip its workflow_status to IN_PROGRESS/COMPLETED/REVIEWED, overwrite its templateId/totalQuestions/answeredCount, and (when the foreign assessment has no template, so the template-mismatch guard at line 246 is skipped) write a response row and trigger recomputeAssessment, which saves a recomputed computedScorePct/riskScore/riskRating onto tenant B's assessment.
rootCause: VendorAssessment is loaded by id alone with no derivation of the owning organisation (it has no organisation_id and no parent-vendor org check), so tenant isolation is not enforced on the assessment object even though the questionnaire child entities are correctly org-scoped.
impact: Cross-tenant integrity violation: an attacker in one tenant can corrupt the workflow state and computed risk scores of another tenant's third-party risk assessments, and prematurely mark them COMPLETED/REVIEWED — undermining the integrity of regulated vendor-risk records and audit trails.
reproduction: 1. Authenticate as a TPRM writer in tenant A. 2. Pick an assessment id belonging to tenant B. 3. curl -X POST http://localhost:8084/api/v1/tprm/assessments/{idFromTenantB}/review -H 'Authorization: Bearer <tenantA token>' . If tenant B's assessment is COMPLETED, its workflow_status flips to REVIEWED under tenant A's action. The /complete and /assign-template endpoints similarly mutate it.
resolution: Resolve the assessment through a tenant-aware path. Either add organisation_id to vendor_assessments and load via findByIdAndOrganisationId, or add a private helper that loads the assessment, then validates the owning vendor's org (vendorRepo.findById(va.getVendorId()).filter org == current). Apply it in assignTemplate, upsertResponse, markComplete, markReviewed and recomputeAssessment.
patchBefore:
VendorAssessment va = assessments.findById(assessmentId)
    .orElseThrow(() -> new EntityNotFoundException("VendorAssessment not found: " + assessmentId));
references: CWE-639: Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key
OWASP API1:2023 Broken Object Level Authorization

_verification.rationale: Confirmed real cross-tenant mutation. QuestionnaireService.assignTemplate (line 214), markComplete (line 299) and markReviewed (lines 320-321) all resolve the parent VendorAssessment via assessments.findById(assessmentId) with no organisation scoping (repository has no org-scoped finder), then write to it (assignTemplate sets templateId/totalQuestions/workflowStatus/score; markComplete/markReviewed flip workflowStatus). @PreAuthorize('TPRM','WRITE') on the controller does not scope by tenant, so a tenant-A user can advance/overwrite tenant-B assessment workflow state. Nuance: upsertResponse (lines 238-293) is partially constrained — q is fetched org-scoped (findByIdAndOrganisationId) and line 246 rejects when the victim assessment's templateId mismatches the attacker-scoped question's templateId — so the response-write path is only fully exploitable when va.templateId is null; but assignTemplate/markComplete/markReviewed are cleanly cross-tenant. The core claim (unscoped findById enabling cross-tenant mutation) holds. High is correct.

title: Weak password policy — minimum length 8, no complexity, no breach check
cvss: CVSS ~5.3 — weak passwords accepted, amplifies the lack of lockout in SEC-AUTH-001
description: Passwords are validated only by Jakarta `@Size(min = 8, max = 100)` on UserRequest.password. There is no complexity requirement (no required mix of upper/lower/digit/symbol), no check against common/breached passwords, no maximum-repeat / dictionary check, and no dedicated change-password endpoint with re-validation (password is simply re-encoded in UserService.create/update). The field is also nullable (not @NotBlank), so passwords are set wherever provided with no policy beyond length. For a regulated GRC platform targeting SAMA/NCA controls, an 8-char minimum with no complexity is below typical baselines. (Note: PasswordPolicyRunner referencing minLength 14 is a STUB control-test for external AD systems, not enforcement of this application's own user passwords.)
rootCause: Password strength is enforced only by a bean-validation length annotation; no PasswordPolicy/validator component exists for the application's own user store.
evidence: public record UserRequest( @NotBlank @Size(min = 3, max = 100) String username, ..., @Size(min = 8, max = 100) String password, ...)  // only length, password not even @NotBlank
impact: Users (and admins creating users) can set trivially guessable passwords such as 'password' or 'aaaaaaaa'. Combined with the absence of lockout/throttling (SEC-AUTH-001), this materially increases the success probability of online guessing and credential stuffing.
reproduction: 1. As an admin, POST /api/v1/iam/users with password "password" (8 chars, all lowercase). 2. The request passes validation and the account is created with that password. 3. No complexity or breach-list rejection occurs.
resolution: Introduce a password-policy validator (custom @StrongPassword constraint or a service-layer check) enforcing length >= 12, at least three of four character classes, rejection of the username/email substrings, and ideally a breached-password (k-anonymity HaveIBeenPwned) or local common-password blocklist. Apply it on create, update, and a dedicated self-service change-password endpoint that also requires the current password.
patchBefore: @Size(min = 8, max = 100) String password,
references: OWASP A07:2021 Identification and Authentication Failures

title: Function-level authorization too broad: ~30 BCM cycle/DRP endpoints gated only by isAuthenticated()
cvss: CVSS 6.5 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:H/A:L) — any authenticated user of any role can mutate BCM crisis/plan/risk state
description: Across the bcm/cycle and bcm/drp subtrees, roughly 30 write and read endpoints are annotated `@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")` instead of the platform's documented `hasPermission('BCM','READ|WRITE|DELETE')` model (per CLAUDE.md and as correctly used by BcmController and bcm_lc/InvocationController). Because method security is enabled (SecurityConfig: @EnableMethodSecurity(prePostEnabled = true)), these annotations ARE enforced — but only to the level of 'has a valid JWT'. Any authenticated principal — including a read-only AUDITOR, or a user whose role grants no BCM module permission at all — can therefore create/update/transition/delete crisis events, BCP/DRP plans, BCM risks, gaps/CAPAs, assessment cycles, BIA assessments, and management reviews, and can fire the SIEM webhook that auto-escalates to a CrisisEvent (BcmAuditCompletionController.ingestSiem, severity>=3). Tenant isolation still holds (services scope by TenantContext), so this is intra-tenant privilege escalation / BFLA, not cross-tenant exposure.
rootCause: These controllers were built ahead of the BCM permission wiring and used isAuthenticated() as a placeholder; the TODO is even acknowledged inline on the SIEM webhook ('accepts any authenticated caller for now'). The module's own correct pattern (hasPermission) was never back-filled here.
evidence: CrisisEventController create: `@PostMapping  @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")  public ResponseEntity<CrisisEvent> create(@Valid @RequestBody CrisisEvent body)`. CrisisEventController delete-equivalent transition and activate-bcp/drp all `@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")`. BcmAuditCompletionController.ingestSiem (line 91-95) `@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")` with comment 'Webhook ingest — accepts any authenticated caller for now.' grep over the package found 30+ isAuthenticated() occurrences on mapped methods.
impact: A low-privilege or read-only user (e.g. AUDITOR, or any tenant employee with a JWT) can tamper with live crisis management: open or close crisis events, activate/deactivate BCP/DRP plans, alter risk scores, delete remediation gaps/CAPAs, or inject a fake high-severity SIEM alert that spins up a real crisis event — undermining segregation of duties required by ISO 22301 / SAMA BCF governance.
reproduction: 1. Log in as an AUDITOR (read-only seeded role) or any user lacking BCM:WRITE. 2. POST /api/v1/bcm/crisis-events with a minimal valid body → 200 Created. 3. POST /api/v1/bcm/crisis-events/{id}/transition {to:'CANCELLED'} → succeeds. 4. POST /api/v1/bcm/siem-events {severity:5,title:'x'} → auto-creates a CrisisEvent. None of these should be permitted for a read-only role.
resolution: Replace `isAuthenticated()` with the module permission expressions: `hasPermission('BCM','READ')` on GET endpoints, `hasPermission('BCM','WRITE')` on POST/PUT/PATCH/transition, `hasPermission('BCM','DELETE')` on delete/archive. For the SIEM webhook, require a dedicated permission (e.g. BCM:INGEST) or a shared-secret integration credential rather than a user JWT.
references: OWASP API5:2023 Broken Function Level Authorization

title: Read-only AUDITOR role granted write/approve/delete on BIA, ROI and crisis-comms endpoints
cvss: CVSS 5.4 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:L) — segregation-of-duties violation, write granted to read role
description: BiaQuantitativeController applies a single CLASS-level `@PreAuthorize("hasAnyRole('BCM_MANAGER','CISO','PLATFORM_ADMIN','RISK_MANAGER','AUDITOR','CFO')")` to ALL nine endpoints, including create, update, submit, cfo-approve, board-approve and DELETE/archive. The same broad role set therefore lets an AUDITOR (a read-only assurance role) and a RISK_MANAGER create and mutate quantitative BIAs and even archive them — there is no per-method narrowing that restricts write/approval verbs to the appropriate roles. The same pattern (read roles permitted to mutate) appears on the crisis-comms template controller. This breaks segregation of duties: an auditor signing off on a control they themselves can edit is a governance integrity failure even though tenant isolation is intact (the service scopes by TenantContext.requireOrganisationId via loadOrThrow).
rootCause: Authorization expressed once at class level with the union of every role that needs ANY access, instead of per-method role sets that separate read from write/approve. The class-level grant is the lowest common denominator and over-grants the write verbs.
evidence: Class annotation: `@PreAuthorize("hasAnyRole('BCM_MANAGER','CISO','PLATFORM_ADMIN','RISK_MANAGER','AUDITOR','CFO')")`. Methods create()/update()/cfoApprove()/boardApprove()/archive() carry NO method-level @PreAuthorize, so all inherit the class grant — AUDITOR can POST/PUT/DELETE.
impact: An auditor can fabricate or alter the financial avoidable-loss inputs that feed StrategyRoiService board recommendations, or archive a quantitative BIA, defeating the four-eyes / SoD controls expected by SAMA and an external ISO 22301 auditor.
reproduction: 1. Log in as AUDITOR. 2. POST /api/v1/bcm/bia/quantitative with a valid body → 201 Created (should be 403). 3. DELETE /api/v1/bcm/bia/quantitative/{externalId} → 200 archived.
resolution: Keep the broad read grant at class level but add method-level `@PreAuthorize` that restricts writes/approvals: create/update to BCM_MANAGER/CISO/PLATFORM_ADMIN; cfo-approve to CFO/PLATFORM_ADMIN; board-approve to BOARD_MEMBER/PLATFORM_ADMIN; archive to BCM_MANAGER/PLATFORM_ADMIN. Remove AUDITOR/RISK_MANAGER from any mutating verb.

title: Global exception handler leaks exception class name and root-cause message in all profiles (including prod)
category: Sensitive Information Disclosure (A05:2021 — Security Misconfiguration / CWE-209)
cvss: CVSS ~5.3 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:N/A:N) — information disclosure of internal exception types, SQL object names, and stack-trace-derived messages to any caller
description: The catch-all @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class) builds the client-facing ProblemDetail 'detail' from the exception's simple class name plus its root-cause message, and additionally serialises the fully-qualified exception class name into an 'exception' property and the raw root message into a 'rootCause' property. This is returned to the HTTP client for ANY unhandled server error. The same root-message exposure occurs in missingObjectResponse() (line 249, 'rootCause' carries SQL Server's 'Invalid object name schema.table' verbatim). There is no profile gate — application-prod.yml contains no server.error override and no branch on the active profile, so production responses disclose the same internal detail as dev. For a multi-tenant GRC platform handling SAMA/NCA-regulated data, exposing internal class names (revealing framework versions and package structure), SQL object/schema names, and exception messages aids reconnaissance and can leak data-layer structure.
rootCause: The handler was intentionally designed to surface developer-friendly diagnostics in the toast/response body ('Real bugs surface clearly instead of hiding behind "An unexpected error occurred."' — comment at lines 368-369). This design was never gated to dev-only, so it ships in prod.
impact: An unauthenticated or low-privilege attacker who triggers any unhandled exception (malformed input down an unguarded path, a NullPointerException, a constraint failure) receives the internal exception type, package path, and root-cause text. SQL-layer messages disclose schema and table names (e.g. 'platform.users', 'admin.committee_*'). This accelerates targeted attacks (SQLi probing, dependency-CVE matching) and violates least-disclosure expectations for a regulated platform.
reproduction: 1. Authenticate (or hit any endpoint that can throw before auth). 2. Send input that triggers an unhandled RuntimeException, e.g. a payload that causes a downstream NPE or an uncategorised DataAccessException. 3. Observe the JSON ProblemDetail response contains 'detail' = '<ExceptionSimpleName>: <root message>', plus 'exception' = fully-qualified class name and 'rootCause' = raw message. Confirm identical behaviour with --spring.profiles.active=prod.
resolution: Gate verbose diagnostics to non-prod only. In prod, return a generic detail ('An unexpected error occurred. Reference: <correlationId>') and omit the 'exception' and 'rootCause' properties; log full details server-side keyed by a correlation id returned to the client. Inject the active Environment/profile (or a @Value flag) into the handler and branch on it. Apply the same treatment to missingObjectResponse() so SQL object names are not echoed in prod.
references: CWE-209: Generation of Error Message Containing Sensitive Information
CWE-211: Externally-Generated Error Message Containing Sensitive Information

title: Token-as-credential public portal endpoints are permitAll with acknowledged-incomplete hardening (no rate limit / brute-force protection)
category: Broken Access Control / Identification & Authentication Failures (A01/A07:2021 / CWE-307)
cvss: CVSS ~5.3 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:N) — unauthenticated, token-guessing / enumeration risk on public token endpoints without rate limiting
description: A set of public, unauthenticated endpoints are permitAll where a per-record token IS the only credential: TPRM vendor BCP attestation (/api/v1/tprm/bcp-attestations/by-token/** GET+POST), whistleblower portal (status/reply by token), customer-complaints tracking (/api/v1/complaints/public/track/**), case-intake tracking (/api/v1/intake/track/**), and PDPL public sub-processor list. The code comment at lines 95-96 explicitly acknowledges the control gap: 'Full vendor portal hardening (rate-limit, MFA bind, full audit) is a follow-up.' With no rate limiting, IP throttling, or lockout at this layer (and dev sets max-failed-login-attempts=99 which governs only login, not these token lookups), the token space is exposed to online brute-force / enumeration. If any token is short, sequential, timestamp-derived, or otherwise low-entropy (must be verified in the service/token-generator code), an attacker can enumerate other vendors'/reporters'/customers' confidential records — a serious confidentiality breach for whistleblower (SAMA CG Art.28 / CMA CG Art.87) and complaint PII data. The HTTP layer correctly permits these by design; the finding is the absence of compensating brute-force controls behind that permit, by the authors' own admission.
rootCause: Public token-keyed endpoints were shipped before the compensating controls (rate limiting, audit, token-entropy guarantees) that a credential-bearing public surface requires. Authorization is delegated entirely to token possession with no throttle.
impact: An unauthenticated attacker can attempt to guess/enumerate per-record tokens at full request speed to read or submit against other tenants' vendor attestations, whistleblower cases, and customer complaints (which include PII per the comments). For a regulated GRC platform this risks exposure of confidential whistleblower identities and complaint PII, with regulatory consequences under PDPL and SAMA/CMA conduct rules.
reproduction: 1. Without authenticating, GET /api/v1/complaints/public/track/<guess> or /api/v1/tprm/bcp-attestations/by-token/<guess> in a loop. 2. Observe no rate limiting / lockout from the HTTP/security layer. 3. If tokens are sequential/low-entropy, valid records are discoverable; confirm token entropy by reviewing the token generator in the corresponding service.
resolution: Add per-IP and per-token-prefix rate limiting / exponential backoff on all public token endpoints (e.g. bucket4j filter or gateway throttle). Enforce cryptographically-random, sufficiently-long tokens (>=128-bit). Audit-log access attempts (without logging reporter IP where policy forbids). Consider short token TTLs and single-use submission tokens. Track and close the acknowledged 'follow-up' hardening items before production exposure.
references: CWE-307: Improper Restriction of Excessive Authentication Attempts
CWE-639: Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key (IDOR)
OWASP A07:2021 Identification and Authentication Failures

title: TenantWriteGuard mass-assignment / cross-tenant write interceptor defaults OFF
category: Broken Access Control / Multi-tenant isolation (A01:2021 / CWE-639)
cvss: CVSS ~6.5 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:H/A:N) — cross-tenant write integrity risk if any service forgets the per-call setId(null)/org-scoping defense, with the platform-wide backstop disabled by default
description: TenantWriteGuardInterceptor is the platform-wide Hibernate-level backstop that throws SecurityException on cross-tenant writes performed without TenantContext.allowCrossTenantWrite(). It is gated by grc.security.tenant-write-guard.enabled which defaults to false (line 52-53) and is NOT set to true in any committed profile (neither application.yml, application-dev.yml, nor application-prod.yml define grc.security.tenant-write-guard). The code itself documents that with the guard off, 'Per-service setId(null) defense is the only mass-assignment guard active' (lines 92-93). Given the platform's stated #1 risk is org-scoping/tenant isolation, shipping the only centralized, defense-in-depth control for cross-tenant writes in a default-disabled state means a single missed per-service guard (a forgotten setId(null) or an unscoped repository save) results in an unguarded cross-tenant write with no backstop. The feature-flag rationale (soak in staging first) is reasonable for rollout but the committed prod profile never flips it on, so production likely runs without the backstop.
rootCause: New defensive interceptor was intentionally shipped default-off to allow staged activation (lines 26-45), but no profile (notably application-prod.yml) ever enables it, leaving the centralized cross-tenant write guard inactive in production by default.
impact: If any one of the many module services omits or mis-implements its per-call tenant/id scoping (mass-assignment of organisation_id, or a save that crosses tenants), the write proceeds and corrupts or injects data into another tenant's records, with no platform-level interceptor to block it. For a multi-tenant SAMA/NCA GRC platform this is a high-integrity, cross-tenant data-isolation breach.
reproduction: 1. Inspect committed profiles: grep grc.security.tenant-write-guard across application*.yml -> no enabled:true. 2. Start with profile prod -> log shows '[TenantWriteGuard] interceptor NOT wired'. 3. Exercise any service path that saves an entity with an attacker-supplied organisation_id where that service lacks the setId(null)/scope check -> write succeeds cross-tenant (no SecurityException).
resolution: Enable grc.security.tenant-write-guard.enabled=true in application-prod.yml (after the documented staging soak) so the platform-wide backstop is active in production. Keep the per-service defenses as primary; treat the interceptor as defense-in-depth that should be ON by default in any real deployment. Add a startup assertion/health indicator that fails or warns loudly if the guard is disabled in prod.
patchBefore:
# application-prod.yml — no grc.security.tenant-write-guard block (defaults to false)
grc:
  security:
    session-timeout-minutes: 30
    max-login-attempts: 5
    lockout-duration-minutes: 30
patchAfter:
# application-prod.yml
grc:
  security:
    session-timeout-minutes: 30
    max-login-attempts: 5
    lockout-duration-minutes: 30
    tenant-write-guard:
      enabled: true   # platform-wide cross-tenant write backstop ON in prod
references: CWE-639: Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key
CWE-915: Improperly Controlled Modification of Dynamically-Determined Object Attributes (Mass Assignment)
OWASP A08:2021 Software and Data Integrity Failures

title: Control-mapping endpoints have no @PreAuthorize — any authenticated user can read and replace an entity's control links (BFLA)
cvss: CVSS 7.1 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:H/A:N) — no function-level authz on a write endpoint
description: None of the three ControlMapController endpoints (GET /{entityType}/{entityId}, GET .../evidence, and PUT /{entityType}/{entityId}) declare any @PreAuthorize. With @EnableMethodSecurity(prePostEnabled=true) and SecurityConfig's terminal rule anyRequest().authenticated(), the only gate is that a valid JWT is present. Every other controller in the compliance/regulatory domain enforces a module permission (hasPermission('COMPLIANCE',...)) or a role list. The PUT performs a destructive replace-set: it deletes ALL existing control links for the (org, entityType, entityId) tuple and re-inserts the supplied set. Any authenticated user of any role (e.g. a read-only AUDITOR, or a low-privilege operator) can wipe and rewrite the control-to-evidence mapping for any risk/control/policy in their own tenant.
rootCause: The controller relies solely on the global authenticated() floor and omits the method-level @PreAuthorize the rest of the platform uses, so authorization collapses from 'right module+action' down to 'any logged-in user'.
impact: Within a tenant, an under-privileged user can silently destroy and forge the manual control-mapping layer that feeds evidence-readiness and framework-coverage rollups, degrading the integrity of compliance reporting. There is no cross-tenant exposure (service is org-scoped via TenantContext), but the missing function-level check is a clear privilege gap relative to the platform's own conventions.
reproduction: 1. Log in as any low-privilege user (e.g. AUDITOR). 2. PUT /api/v1/control-links/RISK/123 with body {"subControlIds": []}. 3. The response is 200 and all control links for RISK 123 in the tenant are deleted — no COMPLIANCE:WRITE or admin role was required.
resolution: Add method-level authorization to all three endpoints: COMPLIANCE:READ (or CONTROLMAP:READ) on the GETs and COMPLIANCE:WRITE on the PUT, matching the convention used by ControlController and FrameworkAnchorController.
references: OWASP API Top 10 2023: API5 Broken Function Level Authorization
OWASP Top 10 2021: A01 Broken Access Control

_verification.rationale: CONFIRMED that ControlMapController (tss-grc-backend/.../controlmap/controller/ControlMapController.java) carries NO @PreAuthorize on any of its three endpoints (GET list, GET evidence, PUT replace-set). With SecurityConfig's default rule .anyRequest().authenticated() and @EnableMethodSecurity NOT denying by default, any authenticated user — including read-only roles like AUDITOR — can replace an entity's control links via PUT /api/v1/control-links/{type}/{id}. This is a genuine BFLA, and the surrounding compliance/risk controllers all use the hasPermission('MODULE','ACTION') pattern, so this is a real deviation. However, the audit title also claims 'in-tenant IDOR': I REFUTE that aspect — ControlMapService is fully org-scoped (every method calls TenantContext.getCurrentTenant() and queries findByOrganisationIdAndEntityTypeAndEntityId / deleteForEntity(orgId,...)), so there is NO cross-tenant exposure and the data altered is the caller's own tenant. The exposed data is internal control-to-evidence mapping metadata (not PII/credentials), and the actor on writes is correctly taken from @AuthenticationPrincipal. Real authorization gap but the impact (in-tenant integrity of non-sensitive mapping data, no cross-tenant reach) is below the other High BFLA findings here; adjusting to Medium.

title: Policy attestation can be completed (attest/decline) by any user, not the assigned attester — repudiation / attestation fraud
category: Broken Object Level Authorization / Improper Authorization (A01)
cvss: CVSS 6.5 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:N) — integrity of attestation-of-record
description: PolicyService.attest(id, evidenceRef) and decline(id, reason) load the attestation by (id, org) and flip its status to ATTESTED/DECLINED, but they never verify that the authenticated caller is the user named in PolicyAttestation.userUsername (the assignee). Combined with the controller's isAuthenticated()-only gate, any logged-in user in the tenant can complete or decline an attestation that was assigned to a different employee. The attested record (who confirmed they read and accepted the policy, with attestedAt timestamp and evidence) is then attributed to the original assignee, not the actor who actually pressed the button.
rootCause: No identity binding between the authenticated principal and the attestation's assignee (userUsername); authorization is reduced to 'authenticated + same tenant'.
impact: Attestation-of-record is a compliance artefact (proof an employee read/accepted a policy). A user can falsely complete attestations on behalf of colleagues, producing fraudulent acceptance records and false coverage in the policy aggregate KPIs — a repudiation and audit-integrity problem for SAMA/NCA policy governance.
reproduction: 1. Admin assigns attestation A to user 'alice' (PENDING). 2. User 'bob' (any role) calls POST /api/policy/attestations/{A}/attest. 3. Response 200; the record shows ATTESTED with userUsername='alice' and attestedAt=now, even though bob acted.
resolution: Bind the action to the assignee: compare the authenticated principal's username/id to a.getUserUsername() and reject (403) when they differ, unless the caller holds an explicit compliance-admin override. Record the actual actor separately (updatedBy) for forensics.
references: CWE-639: Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key
OWASP API Top 10 2023: API1 Broken Object Level Authorization

title: Spring Security Web 6.5.5 — HTTP response headers may not be written (security policy bypass & information disclosure)
cvss: 9.1 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N) — CVE-2026-22732

locations.note: spring-boot-starter-parent BOM manages the Spring Security version
spring-boot-starter-security pulls in spring-security-web transitively

description: spring-security-web 6.5.5 is affected by CVE-2026-22732 (CWE-425, CVSS 9.1): when servlet applications specify HTTP response headers via Spring Security and rely on the default lazy header-writing, there is a possibility that security-relevant HTTP headers are never written to the response, leading to a security policy bypass and information disclosure.
rootCause: Spring Security version is managed by the spring-boot-starter-parent BOM (pom.xml lines 8-15, Boot 3.5.6 pins Spring Security 6.5.5), which predates the 6.5.9 fix.
evidence: Trivy: {"VulnerabilityID": "CVE-2026-22732", "PkgName": "org.springframework.security:spring-security-web", "InstalledVersion": "6.5.5", "FixedVersion": "6.5.9, 7.0.4", "Severity": "CRITICAL"}.
impact: Security headers (e.g. cache-control, frame options, CSP) configured through Spring Security may silently fail to be written, bypassing the application's intended security policy and disclosing protected information — high risk for a security platform whose own headers harden the bilingual GRC UI and API.
reproduction: Run `trivy fs --scanners vuln tss-grc-backend/pom.xml`; CVE-2026-22732 reports CRITICAL against spring-security-web 6.5.5. `mvn dependency:tree` confirms spring-security-web:6.5.5 is pulled by spring-boot-starter-security.
resolution: Upgrade spring-boot-starter-parent to 3.5.14 (which pins Spring Security >= 6.5.9/6.5.10) or override <spring-security.version>6.5.10</spring-security.version> in <properties>. Re-scan to confirm spring-security-web and spring-security-core resolve to >= 6.5.10.
patchBefore:
<parent>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
    <version>3.5.6</version>
</parent>
patchAfter:
<parent>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
    <version>3.5.14</version>
</parent>
<!-- or in <properties>: -->
<!-- <spring-security.version>6.5.10</spring-security.version> -->

_verification.rationale: Version confirmed: built jar bundles spring-security-web-6.5.5.jar (and spring-security-config-6.5.5.jar), managed by Spring Boot parent 3.5.6. The cited advisory class — 'HTTP response (security) headers may not be written' — is a real documented Spring Security issue. But VMware/Broadcom rate this class Moderate, and the practical impact is weakened security headers (e.g. CSP/HSTS occasionally not emitted) leading to defence-in-depth degradation / minor information disclosure, not a direct 'security policy bypass' enabling compromise. Marking Critical is unjustified. 6.5.5 is also a recent release. Real but Medium.

title: Microsoft SQL Server JDBC Driver 12.8.1.jre11 — improper input validation enables spoofing (CVE-2025-59250)
cvss: 8.1 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N) — CVE-2025-59250

locations.note: <mssql.version>12.8.1.jre11</mssql.version> property
direct mssql-jdbc dependency declaration

description: The directly declared mssql-jdbc 12.8.1.jre11 driver is affected by CVE-2025-59250 (CWE-20, CVSS 8.1): improper input validation in the JDBC Driver for SQL Server allows an unauthorized attacker to perform spoofing over a network.
rootCause: Explicitly pinned to 12.8.1.jre11 via the <mssql.version> property (pom.xml line 32) and consumed at lines 112-116; the 12.8.2.jre11 patch on the 12.8.x line was not applied.
evidence: Trivy: {"VulnerabilityID": "CVE-2025-59250", "PkgName": "com.microsoft.sqlserver:mssql-jdbc", "InstalledVersion": "12.8.1.jre11", "FixedVersion": "10.2.4.jre11, 11.2.4.jre11, 12.2.1.jre11, 12.6.5.jre11, 12.8.2.jre11, 12.10.2.jre11, 13.2.1.jre11", "Severity": "HIGH"}. pom.xml line 32: <mssql.version>12.8.1.jre11</mssql.version>.

_verification.rationale: PARTIALLY CONFIRMED. pom.xml line 32 declares mssql.version = 12.8.1.jre11 and lines 112-116 use it, so the vulnerable version claim is accurate; CVE-2025-59250 is a real Microsoft mssql-jdbc improper-input-validation/spoofing issue affecting this version (fixed in 12.10.1/13.2.1). It is a legitimate Vulnerable-&-Outdated-Components (A06) hygiene finding and the dependency should be bumped. However, the exploit precondition is a malicious or MITM SQL Server endpoint: the JDBC URL, host and credentials are server-side and operator-controlled (application-dev.yml/prod externalised secrets), not attacker-influenceable, so there is no direct user-facing attack surface. The CVSS for this class of spoofing CVE sits in the medium band and real-world exploitability in this single-trusted-DB deployment is low. Downgrading from High to Medium — valid patch obligation, limited practical risk.
