title: Separation-of-duties controls (CAPA verifier ≠ owner, evidence approver) are enforced against client-supplied name strings, not the authenticated principal
category: Broken Access Control / Business Logic (A01) — CWE-639 / CWE-602
cvss: CVSS 6.5 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:N) — bypass of segregation-of-duties / self-approval
description: The corrective-action 'Rule A' separation-of-duties control rejects verification only when the supplied verifier name equals the stored ownerName. Both the verifier identity and the owner identity are free-text strings supplied by the client (the verify endpoint reads body.get("verifiedBy"); ownerName came from an earlier client-supplied create/update body). The check is a case-insensitive string compare, never tied to the authenticated user (GrcUserDetails). The same pattern applies to evidence approval, which records approvedBy from body.get("approvedBy") rather than the principal. An actor can therefore self-verify their own corrective action simply by passing any verifier string that differs from ownerName (e.g. add a space, change case differently, or supply an arbitrary colleague's name), and can attribute an approval to anyone. Combined with SEC-ESG-001 (no role enforcement), the 'four-eyes' guarantee these endpoints advertise is cosmetic.
rootCause: Actor identity for SoD-sensitive actions is taken from the request body instead of the authenticated SecurityContext / GrcUserDetails. The control compares two attacker-controllable values.
impact: Self-approval / self-verification of sustainability corrective actions and evidence, defeating the segregation-of-duties control that regulators (CMA, SAMA) expect on remediation sign-off. Approval/verification audit attribution is forgeable, breaking non-repudiation.
reproduction: 1. As any authenticated user, create a CAPA with ownerName="Alice" and attach evidenceRef. 2. POST /{id}/start, /{id}/complete. 3. POST /{id}/verify with body {"verifiedBy":"Alice "} (trailing space) or {"verifiedBy":"Bob"} — the same person verifies their own action; the row records VERIFIED by the supplied name with no link to the real caller.
resolution: Derive the actor from the authenticated principal: inject @AuthenticationPrincipal GrcUserDetails and set verifiedBy/approvedBy from its user id/name. Enforce Rule A against the principal's user id versus the stored owner user id (store owner as a user id, not a display string). Reject the action if the principal equals the owner. Remove verifiedBy/approvedBy from the request body so attribution cannot be forged.
references: CWE-639: Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key
CWE-602: Client-Side Enforcement of Server-Side Security
OWASP Top 10 2021 — A04:2021 Insecure Design (segregation of duties)

title: Sustainability write endpoints bind raw JPA @Entity request bodies with no @Valid — mass-assignment of workflow/audit fields
category: Mass Assignment / Improper Input Validation (A08/A04) — CWE-915 / CWE-20
cvss: CVSS 5.3 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:N) — caller can set server-controlled lifecycle/attribution fields at create
description: Every create/update endpoint in the Sustainability slices binds the persistent JPA @Entity directly as the @RequestBody (e.g. SustainabilityEvidence, GhgEmissionRecord, CmaDisclosure, MaterialTopic, SgiCommitment, CorrectiveAction) with no DTO and no @Valid. The services reset id and organisationId server-side (good — so tenant/identity cannot be forged), but they do NOT scrub the remaining server-controlled lifecycle and attribution columns. On create, the caller can pre-set approvalStatus/status (e.g. submit an evidence row directly as APPROVED, or a GHG record as APPROVED), approvedBy/approvedAt/reviewerName/verified/verificationDate, createdBy/createdAt, supersedesId, etc., bypassing the intended state machine and approval gates. Unlike the AI governance and climate sub-packages, which use dedicated request DTOs (MlModelRequest, FinancedEmissionsRequest) with @Valid + @NotBlank/@Size constraints and an explicit applyFields() whitelist, the Sustainability slices have no such boundary.
rootCause: Controllers expose the JPA entity as the API contract and rely on the service to selectively copy fields on UPDATE only; CREATE persists the inbound entity almost verbatim (after id/org reset), so any column the entity exposes is mass-assignable on creation.
impact: A caller can create records that skip the review/approval workflow (e.g. evidence born APPROVED with an arbitrary approvedBy, or a GHG/CMA record born APPROVED), forging approval attribution and defeating the lifecycle gates the module enforces on transitions. Audit columns (createdBy) are also client-settable. This compounds SEC-ESG-001 and SEC-ESG-002.
reproduction: POST /api/sustainability/evidence with body {"titleEn":"x","approvalStatus":"APPROVED","approvedBy":"CFO","confidentiality":"PUBLIC"} → 201, row persisted APPROVED/approvedBy=CFO without ever passing through the approve() workflow or any approver check.
resolution: Introduce request DTOs for each create/update (as the climate and AI sub-packages already do) carrying only client-settable fields, annotate the controller params with @Valid and the DTO fields with Jakarta constraints (@NotBlank/@Size/@Min). In the service, force initial lifecycle status and null out approval/attribution/audit fields on create regardless of input; set approvedBy/createdBy from the authenticated principal. Never accept the entity as the wire contract.
references: CWE-915: Improperly Controlled Modification of Dynamically-Determined Object Attributes (Mass Assignment)
OWASP API Security Top 10 2023 — API6:2023 / API3:2023
OWASP Top 10 2021 — A04:2021 Insecure Design, A08:2021

title: Evidence item create accepts arbitrary client-supplied status — four-eyes Segregation-of-Duties and review workflow can be fully bypassed
cvss: CVSS 7.1 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:N) — a single user with EVIDENCE:WRITE self-approves compliance evidence, defeating the SoD control
description: `EvidenceItemService.create()` calls `applyRequest()`, which blindly copies the client-supplied `status` onto a new entity: `if (req.status() != null) item.setStatus(req.status());` (line 383). There is no validation against `ITEM_STATUSES` and no transition-guard. The system deliberately enforces Segregation of Duties only on the `approve()` transition (lines 194-199: the creator may not approve their own evidence). Because `create` lets the caller set `status` directly, a user can `POST /api/v1/evidence/items` with `{"status":"APPROVED"}` and obtain an APPROVED evidence item without ever passing through submit -> review -> approve, never triggering the SoD check or producing an `EVIDENCE_APPROVED` review trail. The same hole lets the create path also seed EXPIRED/REJECTED or any free-text status. `update()` shares the same `applyRequest` and can re-set status on an existing item, again skipping `validateTransition`.
rootCause: Mass-assignment of a workflow-controlling field (`status`) on create/update, with the state-machine guard (`validateTransition`) and the SoD guard living only on the dedicated transition methods (`submitForReview`/`approve`/`reject`). The DTO exposes `status` as a freely settable input field.
impact: Defeats the regulatory four-eyes / SoD control (ECC 2-3, ISO 27001 A.5.3, SAMA) the platform advertises for evidence approval. A single insider with EVIDENCE:WRITE can manufacture self-approved compliance evidence, which fulfils linked evidence-requests (`fulfilRequest`) and feeds coverage rollups, audit packs and attestations — directly enabling compliance fraud and undermining the integrity of every downstream assurance artefact.
reproduction:
1. Authenticate as a user with EVIDENCE:WRITE (e.g. `riskmanager`).
2. `curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
   -d '{"titleEn":"Self-approved control evidence","evidenceType":"DOCUMENT","status":"APPROVED"}' \
   http://localhost:8084/api/v1/evidence/items`
3. Response shows the item created directly in status APPROVED; no EvidenceReview row, no SoD check, no EVIDENCE_APPROVED transition event — yet the item now counts as approved evidence in the matrix and stats.
resolution: On create, ignore any client `status` and force the canonical initial state (`DRAFT`); only allow an explicit non-DRAFT seed for trusted system/import flows behind a separate permission. On update, never mutate `status` via `applyRequest` — route all status changes exclusively through `transitionStatus`/`approve`/`reject` so `validateTransition` and the SoD guard always run. Validate any accepted status against `ITEM_STATUSES`.
references: CWE-915: Improperly Controlled Modification of Dynamically-Determined Object Attributes (Mass Assignment)
CWE-841: Improper Enforcement of Behavioral Workflow

_verification.rationale: Real but severity overstated. EvidenceItemCreateRequest has a status field and create()→applyRequest() does `if (req.status() != null) item.setStatus(req.status())` with no validation that the value is a legal starting state, so an EVIDENCE:WRITE user can mint an item directly in APPROVED, bypassing the DRAFT→PENDING_REVIEW→APPROVED state machine and the EvidenceReviewController review record. However the 'four-eyes Segregation-of-Duties' framing is weak: the legitimate approve path (EvidenceItemController /approve) is itself only @PreAuthorize(hasPermission('EVIDENCE','WRITE')) — the same permission as create — so a single WRITE user can already approve their own evidence through the normal flow. The status-injection therefore adds an integrity/validation gap (skips the review row and transition guards) but not a fundamentally new privilege, and it still requires EVIDENCE:WRITE and is org-scoped. Net incremental impact is Medium, not High.

title: Evidence chain-of-custody endpoints guarded only by isAuthenticated() — any user can read and mutate WORM chain status (BFLA)
cvss: CVSS 5.4 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:N) — any authenticated user reads chain reports and triggers chain-status writes without EVIDENCE permission
description: Every endpoint of the evidence chain-of-custody controller uses `@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")` rather than the module guard `hasPermission('EVIDENCE','READ')`/`'WRITE'` used by the rest of the evidence module. The sibling `EvidenceItemController`/`EvidenceMatrixController` correctly gate reads on EVIDENCE:READ. More importantly, `POST /api/evidence/chain/{evidenceId}/verify` is a state-mutating operation: `verifyChain` runs `UPDATE evidence.evidence_versions ... SET chain_status, chain_verified_by, chain_break_reason` and `UPDATE evidence.evidence_items SET chain_status, chain_last_verified_by ...` (service lines 138-168). So any authenticated principal — including users with zero evidence permissions — can trigger verification writes and stamp themselves as `chain_verified_by`/`chain_last_verified_by` on tamper-evidence integrity records. The head queries ARE org-scoped (`WHERE id=:id AND organisation_id=:org`), so this is in-tenant BFLA, not cross-tenant; native queries are fully parameterised (no SQLi).
rootCause: Authorization for this sub-package was written to a weaker standard (presence of authentication) than the module convention (permission on EVIDENCE), and a write endpoint was placed behind the same weak guard as reads.
impact: A user with no evidence rights can read chain-of-custody reports (which version content hashes are valid/broken) for any evidence in their tenant and can write to the integrity ledger (chain_status, verified_by). This pollutes the tamper-evidence audit trail and lets a low-privileged actor overwrite the recorded verifier identity on regulated WORM records.
reproduction:
1. Authenticate as a user with NO evidence permission.
2. Read: `curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" http://localhost:8084/api/evidence/chain/15` — returns the full chain report.
3. Mutate: `curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" http://localhost:8084/api/evidence/chain/15/verify` — the chain_status/chain_verified_by columns are updated and the caller is stamped as verifier.
resolution: Replace `isAuthenticated()` with `hasPermission('EVIDENCE','READ')` on the two GET endpoints and `hasPermission('EVIDENCE','WRITE')` (or a dedicated EVIDENCE:VERIFY) on the verify endpoint, matching the rest of the evidence module.
references: OWASP API5:2023 Broken Function Level Authorization

title: Board pack read endpoints guarded only by isAuthenticated() — sensitive board-level reports exposed to any authenticated user
cvss: CVSS 6.5 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N) — confidential board/risk/audit/incident summaries readable by any authenticated principal
description: `GET /api/board-pack/packs` (list) and `GET /api/board-pack/packs/{id}` (get) are annotated only `@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")`, while the write endpoints correctly require `PLATFORM_ADMIN`/`CRO`/`REPORTING_WRITE`. A BoardPack aggregates the most sensitive material in the platform — `riskSummaryJson`, `appetiteBreachesJson`, `auditEngagementsJson`, `incidentsJson`, `pdplSummaryJson`, `ccmSummaryJson`, `slaSummaryJson`, plus board audience and review comments (see `BoardPackService.create`, lines 67-75). The service is correctly tenant-scoped (`findByOrganisationId...`), so this is in-tenant over-exposure: any authenticated user — including roles with no reporting/governance rights — can enumerate and read every board pack in their organisation.
rootCause: Read authorization was set to bare authentication instead of a reporting/governance role or REPORTING:READ permission, inconsistent with the write-side guards on the same controller and with the read guards used by the audit-committee and pivot controllers.
impact: Confidential board-level governance reporting (consolidated risk posture, appetite breaches, open audit engagements, incidents, privacy and SLA summaries) leaks to any logged-in user, breaching need-to-know and the confidentiality expectations of SAMA/CMA corporate-governance reporting.
reproduction:
1. Authenticate as a low-privilege user (e.g. `auditor`).
2. `curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" http://localhost:8084/api/board-pack/packs` — returns the list of board packs for the tenant.
3. `curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" http://localhost:8084/api/board-pack/packs/BP-2026-XYZ` — returns the full board pack including all sensitive *_Json sections.
resolution: Gate the read endpoints with a board/governance-appropriate guard mirroring the write side and the audit-committee controller, e.g. `@PreAuthorize("hasAnyRole('PLATFORM_ADMIN','CRO','BOARD_MEMBER','AUDIT_COMMITTEE_CHAIR','AUDIT_COMMITTEE_MEMBER','COMPANY_SECRETARY') or hasAuthority('REPORTING_READ')")`.
references: CWE-200: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor
OWASP API5:2023 Broken Function Level Authorization

title: JWT access token stored in sessionStorage (JS-readable) in both v1 and v2 frontends
cvss: CVSS 5.4 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N) — no direct exploit by itself; severity is the multiplier it gives to any XSS (SEC-FE-001)
description: Both frontends persist the bearer access token in Web Storage (`sessionStorage`), which is fully readable by any JavaScript running on the origin. v2: auth.ts stores under key `grc.accessToken` (getAccessToken reads `sessionStorage.getItem(TOKEN_KEY)`); api.ts:53 also writes the refreshed token straight to sessionStorage. v1: auth.js stores under `grc_jwt`; login.html:287 does the same. The refresh token is correctly kept in an HttpOnly cookie (good), but the access token is not. Any successful XSS (e.g. SEC-FE-001) can read the access token with a single `sessionStorage.getItem(...)` call and replay it against the API as a full bearer credential (1h lifetime in dev / 15m prod). This is the standard sessionStorage-vs-memory trade-off; it is acceptable only when XSS is otherwise fully controlled, which is not the case for the legacy UI.
rootCause: Design choice to persist the access token in Web Storage for convenience across reloads, rather than holding it only in a JS closure / in-memory variable and relying on the HttpOnly refresh cookie to re-mint it on reload.
evidence: auth.ts:15 `return sessionStorage.getItem(TOKEN_KEY);` ; auth.ts:25 `sessionStorage.setItem(TOKEN_KEY, accessToken);` ; api.ts:53 `sessionStorage.setItem('grc.accessToken', newToken);` ; auth.js:13 `return sessionStorage.getItem(this._TOKEN_KEY);`
impact: Turns any XSS from a nuisance into a full session/account takeover and (because the JWT carries the `org` tenant claim) a cross-tenant compromise vector. The token can be exfiltrated and replayed from anywhere until it expires.
reproduction: With any XSS foothold (see SEC-FE-001), execute `sessionStorage.getItem('grc.accessToken')` (v2) or `sessionStorage.getItem('grc_jwt')` (v1) and POST it to an attacker endpoint; then call any `/api/v1/...` endpoint with `Authorization: Bearer <stolen>`.
resolution: Hold the access token only in a module-scoped in-memory variable (JS closure), and rely on the existing HttpOnly refresh cookie + `/api/auth/refresh` to silently re-mint it on page reload (the v2 api.ts already has the refresh plumbing). This removes the token from any persistent JS-readable store, dramatically shrinking the XSS blast radius. If reload-survival is required, prefer a non-extractable approach (e.g. short-lived token in memory, refresh-on-load). Pair with strict CSP and the SEC-FE-001 fix.
references: CWE-922: Insecure Storage of Sensitive Information
OWASP A07:2021 Identification and Authentication Failures
OWASP JWT / Token Storage guidance (avoid localStorage/sessionStorage for tokens)

title: Open redirect via unvalidated `redirect` parameter on legacy login page
category: URL Redirection to Untrusted Site / Open Redirect (A01:2021)
cvss: CVSS 4.7 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N) — phishing / token-relay aid; not direct code execution
description: The legacy login page reads the `redirect` query parameter and passes it directly to `window.location.replace(redirect)` with no validation that it is a same-origin relative path. This happens in two places: the already-logged-in fast path (line 183-184) and the post-login success path (line 290-291). An attacker can craft `https://app/login.html?redirect=https://evil.example/login` (or the scheme-relative `redirect=//evil.example`) so that after a victim authenticates they are silently bounced to an attacker-controlled look-alike page. The v2 React login (tss-grc-ui-v2/src/pages/LoginPage.tsx:22-24) does this correctly — it only honours `next` if it `startsWith('/')` and not `'//'` — which confirms the team knows the mitigation but did not apply it to the legacy page. `javascript:` payloads are generally neutralised by `location.replace`, so this is an open-redirect (phishing) issue rather than direct XSS.
rootCause: User-controlled redirect target used in a navigation sink without an allowlist / same-origin check.
evidence: login.html:183-184 `const redirect = new URLSearchParams(location.search).get('redirect') || '/dashboard.html'; window.location.replace(redirect);` (identical at 290-291).
impact: Enables convincing credential-phishing: a link to the legitimate, trusted login origin redirects the user to an attacker page immediately after they log in, where session/credentials can be harvested. Also useful in OAuth/token-relay chains.
reproduction: 1. Send victim `https://<app-host>/login.html?redirect=https://evil.example/`. 2. Victim logs in on the genuine site. 3. login.html:291 runs `window.location.replace('https://evil.example/')` and the victim lands on the attacker site still trusting the flow.
resolution: Validate the redirect target is a same-origin relative path before navigating — exactly as the v2 LoginPage already does. Reject anything not starting with a single `/` (and not `//`).
patchBefore:
const redirect = new URLSearchParams(location.search).get('redirect') || '/dashboard.html';
window.location.replace(redirect);
references: CWE-601: URL Redirection to Untrusted Site (Open Redirect)
OWASP Unvalidated Redirects and Forwards Cheat Sheet

title: Tenant AML officer can inject/poison platform-global sanctions lists (OFAC/UN/EU) consumed by every tenant
category: Broken Access Control / Improper Authorization (A01, CWE-639)
cvss: CVSS ~6.5 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:N/I:H/A:N) — cross-tenant data-integrity poisoning of shared screening lists
description: Platform-global sanctions lists are stored with organisation_id IS NULL and are visible to (and screened by) every tenant via findVisibleTo / findActiveVisibleTo. SanctionsListService.update() deliberately blocks edits to global lists from a tenant context ('Cannot edit platform-global list ... from tenant context'). However bulkImportEntries() and refresh() use the same loadOrThrow()->findByIdVisibleTo() lookup, which returns global lists to any tenant, and neither method applies the same org-NULL guard. A tenant AML_OFFICER (the role required by POST /lists/{id}/entries/bulk-import) can therefore append arbitrary entries to a global OFAC/UN/EU list. Imported rows take row.setOrganisationId(l.getOrganisationId()) = NULL, so they become globally visible. This lets one tenant inject false sanctions entries (causing false-positive hits and operational blocking for all other tenants) — or, if combined with future delete/refresh-overwrite logic, suppress entries.
rootCause: Inconsistent authorization across write paths: the org-NULL global-list guard exists only in update(), not in bulkImportEntries() or refresh(). findByIdVisibleTo intentionally returns shared global lists, so 'visible' is wrongly treated as 'writable'.
evidence: update(): `if (l.getOrganisationId() == null) { throw new IllegalArgumentException("Cannot edit platform-global list ..."); }`. bulkImportEntries(): `SanctionsList l = loadOrThrow(req.listId()); ... row.setOrganisationId(l.getOrganisationId()); entryRepo.save(row);` with NO org-NULL check. loadOrThrow -> `listRepo.findByIdVisibleTo(id, org())` which matches `l.organisationId IS NULL OR l.organisationId = :orgId`.
impact: Cross-tenant integrity compromise of a financial-crime control: a single tenant can degrade sanctions-screening accuracy for all tenants (mass false positives blocking onboarding, or noise masking true hits), violating SAMA AML/CFT obligations.
reproduction: 1) As AML_OFFICER in tenant 2, GET /api/v1/aml/sanctions/lists, note a global list id (organisationId null, e.g. OFAC). 2) POST /api/v1/aml/sanctions/lists/{id}/entries/bulk-import with listId={id} and fabricated entries. 3) The entries persist with organisation_id NULL. 4) As any user in tenant 3, POST /checks against that list — fabricated entries now produce hits.
resolution: Apply the same org-NULL guard in bulkImportEntries() and refresh(): only the platform admin (cross-tenant scope) may write to organisation_id IS NULL lists; tenant officers may write only to lists they own (l.getOrganisationId() != null && equals(org())).
references: CWE-639: Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key
OWASP API1:2023 Broken Object Level Authorization

title: Mass assignment via raw JPA-entity request bodies on create (FourthPartyExposure, SupplierResilienceTest); persistence-layer org guard not wired in
category: Mass Assignment / Improper Input Handling (A08, CWE-915)
cvss: CVSS ~5.4 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:H/A:L) — workflow/state-field tampering and soft-delete via unfiltered create
description: Several endpoints bind the JPA @Entity directly as the @RequestBody and persist it. FourthPartyExposureController.create(@RequestBody FourthPartyExposure req) and SupplierResilienceTestController.create(@RequestBody SupplierResilienceTest req) pass the client-supplied entity to repo.save() after only overriding organisationId and nulling id. The FourthPartyExposure entity exposes writable setters for workflow/state and audit columns — status, concentrationRisk, isDeleted, isActive, lastValidatedBy, validatorName, createdBy, updatedBy, rowVersion. A caller can therefore POST a record pre-set to status=VALIDATED with an arbitrary validatorName (bypassing the validate() workflow step), or set isDeleted=1 / isActive=0 at creation. The validate() invariant check only constrains dependencyType/downstreamCriticality/status enum membership — it does not stop status=VALIDATED or audit-field spoofing. organisationId itself is overridden so cross-tenant create is not possible, and update() copies a field whitelist so update is safe; the exposure is on create. Note also that the documented platform backstop (TenantWriteGuardInterceptor / TenantContext.allowCrossTenantWrite) is explicitly NOT wired in yet (see TenantContext lines 74-81), so there is no persistence-layer net catching entity mass-assignment.
rootCause: Controllers accept and persist mutable persistence entities instead of constrained request DTOs; no @Valid; the create path does repo.save(req) on the attacker-controlled object graph.
evidence: FourthPartyExposureService.create: `validate(req); req.setOrganisationId(TenantContext.getCurrentTenant()); req.setId(null); FourthPartyExposure saved = repo.save(req);`. Entity has `private String status = "DISCOVERED"; private String validatorName; private Short isDeleted = 0;` all with Lombok @Setter. Controller: `public ResponseEntity<FourthPartyExposure> create(@RequestBody FourthPartyExposure req)`.
impact: Integrity tampering of third-party-risk records: fabricated validation status/validator attribution, immediate soft-deletion or deactivation at create, and forged created_by/row_version audit metadata — eroding the auditability the GRC platform exists to provide.
reproduction: 1) POST /api/scm/fourth-party with body {"primaryVendorName":"x","fourthPartyName":"y","dependencyType":"SOFTWARE","downstreamCriticality":"HIGH","serviceDescriptionEn":"z","status":"VALIDATED","validatorName":"CISO","isDeleted":0,"createdBy":999}. 2) The persisted row reflects the attacker-chosen status/validatorName/createdBy.
resolution: Bind a constrained request DTO (only client-settable fields) for create/update and map server-side; never expose status/concentrationRisk/isDeleted/isActive/createdBy/validatorName as inbound fields. Add @Valid. Wire the documented Hibernate TenantWriteGuardInterceptor as defence-in-depth.
references: CWE-915: Improperly Controlled Modification of Dynamically-Determined Object Attributes
OWASP A08:2021 Software and Data Integrity Failures

title: Workflow-submission review (APPROVE/REJECT/CLOSE) allowed for any authenticated user; create body not validated
cvss: CVSS ~5.4 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:N) — same-tenant approval integrity
description: POST /api/v1/workflow-submissions/{id}/review transitions a submission to APPROVED/REJECTED/CLOSED/UNDER_REVIEW but is guarded only by @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()"). There is no role gate (e.g. reviewer/approver) and no check the caller is distinct from the submitter, so a user can approve their own submission. Reads/writes ARE org-scoped (repo.findByOrganisationIdAndId), so this is a same-tenant segregation-of-duties / BFLA issue rather than cross-tenant. Separately, the create endpoint (line 36-38) binds @RequestBody CreateBody with no @Valid; only manual null/blank checks in the service exist and payloadJson is stored unbounded/unparsed.
rootCause: Authorization for a state-changing review action is only 'authenticated'; no segregation-of-duties or approver role is enforced.
evidence: @PostMapping("/{id}/review") @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()") public WorkflowSubmission review(@PathVariable Long id, @RequestBody ReviewBody body) { return service.review(id, body); }
impact: Any authenticated tenant user can approve, reject or close any workflow submission in their organisation — including ones they themselves submitted — bypassing the reviewer/maker-checker control these submissions are meant to enforce (V127 seed rules route PDPL breaches, NCA incidents, above-appetite risk acceptances through this flow).
reproduction: 1. As any user, POST /api/v1/workflow-submissions to create a submission. 2. POST /api/v1/workflow-submissions/{id}/review with {"decision":"APPROVE"}. 3. Submission is APPROVED by its own author with no reviewer role required.
resolution: Restrict /review to an approver/reviewer permission (e.g. hasPermission('WORKFLOW','APPROVE') or per-module reviewer roles), and reject self-review by comparing the submitter to the caller. Add @Valid + Jakarta constraints to CreateBody (size caps on titleEn/payloadJson, required fields) instead of relying on manual checks.
references: CWE-841: Improper Enforcement of Behavioral Workflow
OWASP API5:2023 Broken Function Level Authorization

title: Committee lifecycle mutations (create/dissolve/approve-minutes) gated only by isAuthenticated() — governance BFLA, inconsistent with rest of module
cvss: CVSS ~5.4 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:H/A:N) — same-tenant governance integrity
description: Every endpoint in CommitteeController (the primary committee + meeting CRUD, including createCommittee, updateCommittee, dissolveCommittee, createMeeting, completeMeeting, approveMinutes, cancelMeeting) is guarded only by @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()"). This is markedly weaker than — and inconsistent with — the sibling committee controllers (CommitteeResolutionController, CommitteeMeetingPapersController, CommitteeMemberRegistryController, CommitteeActionItemController, CommitteeCalendarController) which all require hasPermission('ADMIN','READ'|'WRITE'). The service layer IS tenant-scoped (TenantContext throughout CommitteeService), so this is a same-tenant function-level authorization gap, not cross-tenant. approveMinutes correctly derives the approver from the Authentication object (good), but any authenticated user can still trigger it.
rootCause: The controller was not brought in line with the module's ADMIN:WRITE authorization convention; 'isAuthenticated()' grants every logged-in user (auditors, risk analysts, viewers) full write access to board/committee governance records.
evidence: @PostMapping("/{id}/dissolve") @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()") public CommitteeResponse dissolveCommittee(...) ; @PostMapping("/meetings/{id}/approve-minutes") @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()") public MeetingResponse approveMinutes(...)
impact: A low-privilege but authenticated user can create or dissolve committees and approve official meeting minutes for the organisation — high-integrity governance records (board/audit-committee minutes feed CMA/SAMA corporate-governance attestations). This is a controls-integrity and segregation-of-duties failure even though data stays within the tenant.
reproduction: 1. Log in as a non-admin role (e.g. AUDITOR). 2. POST /api/admin/committees/{id}/dissolve with {"reason":"x"} — succeeds. 3. POST /api/admin/committees/meetings/{id}/approve-minutes — succeeds, minutes marked MINUTES_APPROVED.
resolution: Align CommitteeController with the rest of the module: require hasPermission('ADMIN','READ') on GETs and hasPermission('ADMIN','WRITE') (or a dedicated COMMITTEE permission) on the create/update/dissolve/meeting-mutation endpoints. Consider a narrower role for approve-minutes (committee secretary/chair).
references: CWE-1220: Insufficient Granularity of Access Control
OWASP API5:2023 Broken Function Level Authorization

title: Outbound EDR/VM actions accept arbitrary host/asset IDs with no tenant-ownership check (cross-tenant containment / risk-acceptance)
cvss: CVSS 6.5 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:H) — applicable when one platform instance serves multiple tenants against one shared Falcon/Tenable
description: containHost(hostId)/liftContainment(hostId)/hideHost(hostId) and Tenable recastSeverity/acceptRisk/removeRecast(pluginId, assetUuid) take the target identifier straight from the URL path/body and forward it to the single, globally-configured Falcon/Tenable instance. The services require a non-null TenantContext but never verify that the supplied hostId/assetUuid actually belongs to the calling tenant (there is no lookup against this tenant's known assets/detections). The integration credentials are platform-global config (one baseUrl + one credential pair), so when a single deployment serves more than one tenant they all share one upstream EDR/VM tenant. A SOC operator in tenant A can therefore isolate (network-quarantine) or un-isolate a host, or recast/accept-risk a finding, that belongs to tenant B simply by supplying B's host/asset id. Containment is a destructive, availability-impacting action.
rootCause: No binding between the tenant scope and the external object identifier. Authorization is purely functional (role can contain) with no object-level check that the host/asset is in the caller's tenant inventory; the upstream integration is shared across tenants.
impact: In a multi-tenant deployment sharing one Falcon/Tenable backend, a user can quarantine another tenant's production hosts (denial of service) or downgrade/accept-risk another tenant's vulnerabilities (integrity / compliance evasion). If each tenant maps 1:1 to its own integration instance the exposure is limited to intra-tenant BFLA; the audit trail records userId, which mitigates non-repudiation but not the action itself.
reproduction:
1. In a deployment where tenants A and B share one configured CrowdStrike instance, authenticate as tenant A SOC_TIER_2.
2. POST /api/v1/integrations/crowdstrike/contain/{hostId} with hostId = a Falcon device id owned by tenant B and any reason >0 chars.
3. The action is dispatched to the shared Falcon tenant and host B is isolated; no check confirmed host B belongs to tenant A.
resolution: Before dispatching, resolve the target id against the calling tenant's own inventory (e.g. crowdstrike_detection_log / tenable_finding_log scoped by organisation_id, or an asset registry) and reject ids not owned by TenantContext. For genuinely multi-tenant deployments, also segregate upstream credentials per tenant so one tenant cannot act on another's upstream objects.
references: CWE-639: Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key
OWASP API1:2023 Broken Object Level Authorization

title: Tenable plugin/asset id interpolated into outbound API URL path without validation (path injection / SSRF-adjacent)
category: Improper Neutralization in URL / SSRF (A10 / A03)
cvss: CVSS 5.4 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:N) — authenticated request-path manipulation against the configured Tenable host
description: recastSeverity/acceptRisk/removeRecast build the request path with IO_RECAST_PATH_FMT.formatted(assetUuid, pluginId) and pass the resulting string to RestClient .uri(url(path)). pluginId comes from the @PathVariable with no @Pattern (validatePluginId only checks non-blank), and assetUuid from the body has only @Size(max=80) with no character constraint (the /remove-recast RemoveRecastBody.assetUuid has no constraint at all). Because the values are concatenated raw into the URL path, a value such as a/../../session or one containing %2f / query-delimiter characters can traverse to a different Tenable API path or alter query semantics on the configured Tenable host. The base host is fixed by config so this is host-bounded path manipulation, not full SSRF, but it lets an authorized user reach Tenable endpoints other than the intended recast/accept-risk routes (e.g. read or mutate other workbench resources the API key can reach).
rootCause: Untrusted identifiers are placed into a URL path via String.format and a raw .uri(String) template instead of being validated against a strict format and passed as encoded URI variables.
impact: An authorized CISO/RISK_MANAGER can craft pluginId/assetUuid to redirect the outbound call to unintended Tenable API paths under the same host, using the platform's privileged API key — expanding the effective surface of the integration credential beyond recast/accept-risk and bypassing the justification/audit semantics those routes assume.
reproduction:
1. Authenticate as RISK_MANAGER.
2. POST /api/v1/integrations/tenable/recast/{pluginId} where pluginId = '1/../../scans' (URL-encoded as needed) with a valid body and a 30+ char justification.
3. Observe the outbound request path resolves to a non-recast Tenable endpoint (visible in stub recorded-calls or via the audit log/ruleId mismatch). Constrain pluginId to digits to confirm the fix blocks it.
resolution: Validate pluginId (Tenable plugin ids are numeric) with @Pattern("\\d+") and assetUuid with a UUID @Pattern on both RecastRequest, AcceptRiskRequest and RemoveRecastBody; re-validate in the service. Pass identifiers as RestClient URI variables (uri(template, vars)) so they are percent-encoded, rather than pre-formatting them into the path string.
references: CWE-88: Improper Neutralization of Argument Delimiters (Argument Injection)

title: Splunk webhook HMAC verification has a body-mismatch fallback that allows signature bypass
cvss: CVSS 5.3 (AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:N) — forged alert ingestion when raw body is not cached
description: The HMAC check computes the digest over the request body, but when the raw body was not cached as the 'RAW_BODY' request attribute it falls back to req.getReader().lines().reduce("", (a,b) -> a+b). By the time the handler runs, Spring's @RequestBody Map binder has already consumed the servlet input stream, so getReader() typically yields an empty string. The HMAC is then computed over "" — a value the attacker can also compute — while the actual JSON payload that gets ingested is the already-parsed Map. This decouples the signed bytes from the processed content: an attacker who knows the shared secret-over-empty-string (or who can force the empty-body path) can present a valid-looking signature for an arbitrary alert body. There is no servlet filter in this package that sets RAW_BODY, so the fragile fallback path is the default. Additionally the comparison uses a non-constant-time length check before the constant-time loop, and the whole verification is silently skipped when no shared secret is configured (role guard only).
rootCause: Signature is verified against a best-effort re-read of an already-consumed request stream rather than against the exact bytes that produced the parsed payload. No ContentCachingRequestWrapper / filter guarantees the signed bytes equal the processed bytes.
impact: The HMAC control intended to authenticate Splunk's outbound webhook can be defeated when the raw body is not cached (the default), letting a party that reaches the endpoint inject forged SIEM alerts into socops.security_event with attacker-chosen severity/host, polluting the SOC triage queue and SLA timers and triggering downstream automation. Combined with SEC-INT-002's missing tenant scoping, forged events are written under the caller's tenant.
reproduction:
1. Configure grc.integrations.splunk.webhook-shared-secret.
2. POST a JSON alert to /api/v1/integrations/splunk/webhook with X-Splunk-Signature = HMAC-SHA256('', secret).
3. Because @RequestBody already drained the stream, verifySignature computes HMAC over "" and matches the header, so the forged alert with attacker-controlled severity is accepted and stored.
resolution: Register a ContentCachingRequestWrapper (or a filter that stores the exact raw bytes in RAW_BODY) for this route and verify the HMAC over those bytes; fail closed if the raw body is unavailable instead of hashing an empty string. Keep the constant-time compare but drop the early length-based exit only after confirming both inputs are fixed-length hex. Consider making the shared secret mandatory in non-dev profiles so verification is never silently skipped.
patchBefore:
if (req.getAttribute("RAW_BODY") instanceof String cached) { body = cached; }
else { body = req.getReader().lines().reduce("", (a, b) -> a + b); }
references: CWE-347: Improper Verification of Cryptographic Signature
CWE-345: Insufficient Verification of Data Authenticity
OWASP A08:2021 Software and Data Integrity Failures

title: Workflow approval / submission state changes have no segregation-of-duties control
cvss: CVSS 6.5 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:N) — any user can self-approve and submit regulatory packages
description: The compliance, evidence, and submission-package workflows implement a maker/checker lifecycle (DRAFT -> SUBMITTED -> UNDER_REVIEW -> APPROVED; submission DRAFT -> READY -> SUBMITTED -> ACKNOWLEDGED). The state machine is enforced (illegal transitions throw), but the *authorization* on the privileged steps (approve, submit, acknowledge, reject) is only isAuthenticated(). The approver/submitter identity is also taken from a free-text body field (approverName, submitterName) rather than the authenticated principal. Consequently a single low-privilege user can drive an item all the way to APPROVED and submit the package to the regulator, and can name any person as the approver. There is no enforced separation between the user who prepares/submits and the user who approves.
rootCause: Same isAuthenticated() gap as SEC-NDI-001, compounded by attribution (approverName/submitterName) coming from the request body instead of the SecurityContext, so the recorded approver cannot be trusted.
evidence:
NdiSubmissionPackageController.approve(): @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()") ... service.approve(id, body.get("approverName"));
NdiComplianceAssessmentService.approve(): cur.setApproverName(approverName);  // free-text, from body
impact: Defeats the maker/checker control intended for NDI submissions. A single account compromise or a malicious insider can fabricate an approved, attested submission package and mark it SUBMITTED/ACKNOWLEDGED with an arbitrary named approver, producing a false regulatory record.
reproduction:
1. As any tenant user, create a compliance assessment, set status COMPLIANT with evidence, submit, mark-under-review, then approve — all with the same token.
2. POST /api/ndi/submission-package/{id}/approve with body {"approverName":"Some CISO"} succeeds; the package shows an approver who never acted.
resolution: Gate approve/submit/acknowledge with a distinct permission (e.g. hasPermission('NDI','APPROVE') / hasRole) separate from WRITE, and derive approverName/submitterName from the authenticated principal, not the body. Optionally enforce that the approver != the last editor/submitter.
references: CWE-639: Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key
OWASP API5:2023 Broken Function Level Authorization

title: Cross-tenant soft-FK references stored without ownership validation (dataclass / data_officer)
cvss: CVSS 4.3 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:N) — bounded cross-tenant linkage / referential integrity violation
description: Several create paths persist caller-supplied foreign-key ids onto new rows without verifying those ids belong to the caller's organisation. In DataOfficerService: createLineage() stores sourceEntryId/targetEntryId, scheduleDisposal() stores retentionRuleId, createQualityRule() stores catalogEntryId, and recordQualityRun() stores qualityRuleId — none re-load the referenced row with a findByOrganisationIdAndId check. In DataclassService.createException() the request's dataAssetId/dataFlowId are written directly to the exception (unlike createFlow(), which loads the asset via the org-scoped loadAsset()). Because the dependent listing endpoints (e.g. listLineage(sourceId), listQualityRuns(ruleId)) are themselves org-scoped, these do not directly leak another tenant's data, but they let one tenant create rows that point at another tenant's entity ids, corrupting referential integrity and producing misleading lineage/quality/exception linkages. The NDI module, by contrast, validates cross-module risk_id ownership via NdiCrossLinkService.validateRiskExists() — the data modules lack the equivalent.
rootCause: FK ids are trusted from the request DTO and set directly on the entity; no companion findByOrganisationIdAndId existence/ownership check is performed before persisting the link.
impact: A tenant can plant lineage edges, quality runs, disposal jobs, or data-classification exceptions that reference identifiers belonging to other tenants or to non-existent rows, polluting NDMO/PDPL records and dashboards and undermining data trustworthiness. Direct cross-tenant data disclosure is not achieved because read paths are org-filtered, hence Medium rather than High.
reproduction:
1. As tenant A user, POST /api/v1/data-officer/lineage with {"sourceEntryId": <a catalog id owned by tenant B>, "targetEntryId": <another tenant B id>}.
2. The lineage row is created under tenant A pointing at tenant B's ids; integrity of both tenants' catalogs is now questionable.
resolution: For every caller-supplied FK, load the referenced row with the org-scoped finder (findByOrganisationIdAndId) and reject if absent, exactly as createFlow() already does with loadAsset() and as NdiCrossLinkService.validateRiskExists() does for NDI.
references: CWE-639: Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key
CWE-1220: Insufficient Granularity of Access Control
OWASP API1:2023 Broken Object Level Authorization

title: Vite dev server — server.fs.deny bypass + path traversal + LAN exposure (high)
cvss: CVSS 7.5 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N) — GHSA-fx2h-pf6j-xcff rated High by npm; arbitrary file read off the dev host. Network-exploitable here because vite.config.ts sets host:true + allowedHosts:true (binds 0.0.0.0/LAN). Rated High (not Critical): read-only, dev/build-time tooling, not the production artifact.
description: tss-grc-ui-v2 pins vite ^5.4.10 and resolves to vite 5.4.21 (package-lock.json line 2359). npm audit flags three vite advisories against the installed version: (1) GHSA-fx2h-pf6j-xcff (HIGH) — server.fs.deny bypass on Windows alternate paths lets a request read files the deny-list was meant to protect; (2) GHSA-4w7w-66w2-5vf9 (moderate) — path traversal in optimized-deps `.map` handling (CWE-22/200); (3) GHSA-v6wh-96g9-6wx3 (moderate) — launch-editor NTLMv2 hash disclosure via UNC path handling on Windows (CWE-73/522). All three apply because 5.4.21 falls in the vulnerable range <=6.4.2. Crucially, vite.config.ts (lines 20-42) configures the dev server with `host: true` and `allowedHosts: true`, binding to 0.0.0.0 and accepting arbitrary Host headers, so the dev server is reachable from any machine on the LAN rather than localhost-only. This converts a localhost-only weakness into a LAN-reachable one. The platform runs on Windows (env: Windows 11), where the server.fs.deny bypass and the launch-editor NTLM disclosure are specifically Windows-path issues.
rootCause: Outdated vite (5.4.21) carrying multiple unpatched dev-server file-serving flaws, combined with a hardened-down dev-server config (host:true / allowedHosts:true) that exposes the server beyond localhost on a Windows host where the Windows-specific bypasses apply.
evidence:
package.json:32  "vite": "^5.4.10"  -> resolved 5.4.21 (package-lock.json:2359 "version": "5.4.21"). vite.config.ts:20-27
  server: {
    port: 5173,
    strictPort: false,
    host: true,
    allowedHosts: true,
impact: An attacker on the same LAN (or anyone who can lure a developer's browser to a malicious page while the dev server is up) can read files outside the project root from the developer's workstation (source, .env.local with VITE_API_BASE and any secrets, SSH keys) and, via the launch-editor UNC path issue on Windows, trigger an SMB authentication that leaks the developer's NTLMv2 hash to an attacker-controlled host for offline cracking. Dev/build-time only — this tooling is not part of the shipped production bundle — but the LAN binding makes it a realistic internal-network exposure.
reproduction: 1. Start the dev server: cd tss-grc-ui-v2 && npm run dev (listens on 0.0.0.0:5173 due to host:true). 2. From another host on the LAN, request a file via the optimized-deps `.map` traversal (GHSA-4w7w-66w2-5vf9) or a server.fs.deny alternate-path bypass (GHSA-fx2h-pf6j-xcff) using a Windows alternate path form to read a file the deny list should block. 3. For the NTLM leak, induce a UNC path (\\attacker-host\share) through the launch-editor flow and capture the SMB auth with responder. npm audit --json confirms: vite range <=6.4.2, fixAvailable vite@8.0.16 (isSemVerMajor).
resolution: Upgrade vite to a patched release. npm audit reports the fix as vite@8.0.16 (major). Validate the build/plugin compatibility (vite 8 requires @vitejs/plugin-react bump and Node version check), or as an interim mitigation set the dev server back to localhost-only (host: 'localhost' or host: false, drop allowedHosts:true) so the flaws are not LAN-reachable. Re-run `npm audit` after the bump.

_verification.rationale: All cited facts verified: package-lock.json:2359 resolves vite 5.4.21 (in the vulnerable <=6.4.2 range for the three GHSA advisories) and vite.config.ts:20-27 sets host:true + allowedHosts:true, exposing the dev server on 0.0.0.0/LAN on a Windows host. However every one of these advisories targets the Vite DEV SERVER only; production ships a static `vite build` output with no dev server running, so the exposure exists solely on developer machines on a trusted LAN. Real but dev-only attack surface — High overstates production impact; Medium.

title: esbuild dev server allows any website to read dev-server responses (CORS, moderate)
cvss: CVSS 5.3 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N) — GHSA-67mh-4wv8-2f99. Browser-mediated cross-origin read of dev-server responses. Dev-only tooling; requires a developer to visit a malicious page while the server runs.
description: esbuild 0.21.5 (package-lock.json line 1715) is pulled in transitively as a dependency of vite 5.4.21 (vite declares esbuild ^0.21.3 at package-lock.json line 2365). GHSA-67mh-4wv8-2f99 (CWE-346, Origin Validation Error) reports that esbuild's dev server sets a permissive CORS policy (Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *) and does not validate the request origin, so any website the developer visits can send cross-origin requests to the running dev server and read the responses — including bundled source. The installed 0.21.5 is within the vulnerable range <=0.24.2. Combined with the LAN-exposed vite dev server (host:true, vite.config.ts:26), the attack surface is broadened beyond a single developer's loopback.
rootCause: Transitive esbuild 0.21.5 (via vite 5.4.21) ships a dev server with wildcard CORS and no origin validation; vite 5.x has not bumped to a patched esbuild.
impact: While a developer runs `npm run dev` and browses the web, a malicious site can read the responses served by the esbuild/vite dev server cross-origin — leaking application source, route maps, and any inline config/secrets present in the served modules. Confidentiality only; dev/build-time, not the production artifact.
reproduction: 1. cd tss-grc-ui-v2 && npm run dev. 2. In the same browser, open an attacker page that issues fetch('http://localhost:5173/src/main.tsx') (or the LAN IP, since host:true). 3. Because esbuild replies with permissive CORS, the attacker page reads the body. npm audit --json: esbuild range <=0.24.2, fix delivered by bumping vite.
resolution: esbuild is transitive — fix by upgrading vite to a release that depends on a patched esbuild (>=0.25.0). npm audit reports the fix path as vite@8.0.16 (isSemVerMajor:true). After the vite bump, confirm node_modules/esbuild resolves to >=0.25.0 and re-run `npm audit`. Interim: bind the dev server to localhost only (see SEC-NPM-001).
patchBefore:
// transitive via vite ^5.4.10
node_modules/esbuild  -> 0.21.5

title: react-router open redirect via protocol-relative (//) URL reinterpretation (moderate)
cvss: CVSS 6.1 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:C/C:L/I:L/A:N) — GHSA-2j2x-hqr9-3h42, npm-rated moderate. Open redirect; ships in the production bundle (runtime dependency).
description: react-router-dom is a DIRECT runtime dependency (package.json line 21, ^6.28.0) and resolves to 6.30.3, which transitively pins react-router 6.30.3 (package-lock.json lines 2048-2071). GHSA-2j2x-hqr9-3h42 (CWE-601) describes that react-router's same-origin redirect handling treats a path beginning with `//` as same-origin, but the browser reinterprets `//evil.com` as a protocol-relative URL pointing to an external host — yielding an open redirect. The installed 6.30.3 is the top of the vulnerable range (>=6.7.0 <6.30.4); the fix landed in 6.30.4. Unlike the vite/esbuild/babel findings, react-router ships in the deployed production bundle, so this is a genuine runtime exposure, not a dev-tooling-only one.
rootCause: react-router 6.30.3 (and react-router-dom 6.30.3) classifies redirect targets starting with `//` as same-origin, ignoring that protocol-relative URLs resolve to an external authority in the browser.
evidence:
package.json:21  "react-router-dom": "^6.28.0"
package-lock.json:2048-2051
    "node_modules/react-router": {
      "version": "6.30.3",
...
package-lock.json:2069-2070 (react-router-dom deps) "react-router": "6.30.3"
impact: If any redirect target in the app is derived from user-controllable input (e.g. a ?redirect= / ?next= / returnUrl query param after login), an attacker can craft a link to the trusted GRC app that bounces the authenticated user to //evil.com — enabling phishing and OAuth/token-forwarding attacks against high-value users (PLATFORM_ADMIN, AUDITOR). Impact is conditional on whether the app actually feeds external input into a router redirect; rated Medium accordingly.
reproduction: 1. Identify any redirect that passes a value to navigate()/redirect() from a query param. 2. Visit https://<grc-app>/login?redirect=//evil.com and authenticate. 3. Observe the browser navigate to https://evil.com (protocol-relative). If no user-controlled redirect path exists in the codebase, exploitability drops to theoretical.
resolution: Upgrade react-router-dom (and the transitive react-router) to >=6.30.4, which fixes the same-origin check to reject protocol-relative `//` targets. npm audit reports fixAvailable:true (non-major) for both. Additionally, allowlist redirect targets to known internal paths rather than trusting incoming values.
patchBefore:
// tss-grc-ui-v2/package.json
"react-router-dom": "^6.28.0"   // resolved 6.30.3 (vulnerable)
patchAfter:
// tss-grc-ui-v2/package.json
"react-router-dom": "^6.30.4"   // resolves react-router 6.30.4+ (patched)
references: OWASP A01:2021 Broken Access Control (Unvalidated Redirects and Forwards)

title: react-router-dom inherits open redirect from react-router (direct dep, moderate)
cvss: CVSS 6.1 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:C/C:L/I:L/A:N) — same advisory as react-router (GHSA-2j2x-hqr9-3h42), exposed through the direct dependency react-router-dom@6.30.3.
description: react-router-dom is the DIRECT dependency the app declares (package.json line 21). npm audit lists it as a separate vulnerable package (isDirect:true, range 6.6.3-pre.0 - 6.30.3) whose vulnerability is `via: [react-router]` — i.e. it re-exports the vulnerable react-router 6.30.3 open redirect (GHSA-2j2x-hqr9-3h42, CWE-601). The installed react-router-dom is 6.30.3 (package-lock.json line 2064), which depends on react-router 6.30.3 (line 2070). This entry is the developer-facing handle for the fix: bumping react-router-dom is what actually pulls in the patched react-router. Reported as its own finding because npm audit tracks it as a distinct advisory entry, but it is the same underlying CWE-601 defect as SEC-NPM-003.
rootCause: Direct dependency react-router-dom 6.30.3 pins the vulnerable react-router 6.30.3, propagating the protocol-relative `//` open-redirect flaw into the application.
evidence:
package.json:21  "react-router-dom": "^6.28.0"
package-lock.json:2063-2070
    "node_modules/react-router-dom": {
      "version": "6.30.3",
...      "react-router": "6.30.3"
impact: Same as SEC-NPM-003 — open redirect reachable in the shipped production bundle if user input drives a router redirect. Because react-router-dom is the declared direct dependency, this is the single line to change to remediate both audit entries.
reproduction: Same as SEC-NPM-003: authenticate to the app with a crafted ?redirect=//evil.com and observe external navigation, provided a user-controlled redirect path exists.
resolution: Bump the direct dependency react-router-dom to >=6.30.4 (npm audit fixAvailable:true, non-major). This transitively upgrades react-router to the patched version, closing both SEC-NPM-003 and SEC-NPM-004. Combine with a server/client-side redirect-target allowlist.

// tss-grc-ui-v2/package.json
"react-router-dom": "^6.28.0"   // -> 6.30.3 (depends on react-router 6.30.3)
patchAfter:
// tss-grc-ui-v2/package.json
"react-router-dom": "^6.30.4"   // -> react-router 6.30.4+ patched
references: OWASP A01:2021 Broken Access Control (Unvalidated Redirects and Forwards)

title: Control Library and Authority-Document write operations gated only by isAuthenticated()
cvss: CVSS 6.5 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:N) — unauthorized creation/modification/deletion of GRC control & regulatory data
description: Every mutating endpoint of the unified Control Library (POST/PUT/DELETE /controls, /control-objectives, /control-mappings, /risk-control-links, /control-assessments and their /transition actions) and of the Authority Documents catalog (POST/PUT/DELETE /authority-documents, /citations, /transition) is annotated @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()"). These are the system-of-record for the GRC spine (NCA ECC / SAMA / PDPL controls, citations, control-to-citation mappings, risk-control matrix, effectiveness assessments). Any authenticated user — regardless of role — can create, edit, retire, supersede or soft-delete this regulated content, and walk workflow state machines (e.g. transition a control DRAFT->ACTIVE or an authority document to SUPERSEDED). Data is correctly tenant-scoped, so this is BFLA within the tenant, not cross-tenant.
rootCause: Controllers in the platform F1/F2 slices were written with a uniform isAuthenticated() guard instead of the hasPermission('CONTROL_LIB'/'REGULATORY','WRITE'|'DELETE') checks the project's RBAC model (ModulePermissionEvaluator + the CONTROL_LIB/REGULATORY/POSTURE module codes in LicensingService.KNOWN_MODULES) clearly intends.
impact: Integrity loss of the control library and regulatory catalog: a non-privileged user can fabricate or retire controls, alter control-to-citation coverage (which directly feeds the F5/F6 compliance-posture heatmaps shown to examiners), or delete mappings — undermining the audit-defensibility the platform sells. No confidentiality/cross-tenant break.
reproduction:
1. Log in as a read-only role (auditor).
2. curl -X DELETE http://localhost:8084/api/v1/control-mappings/5 -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" — observe 204 and the mapping disappears from the posture heatmap.
3. curl -X POST http://localhost:8084/api/v1/controls -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"controlCode":"X-1","titleEn":"fake","domain":"CYBER"}'.
resolution: Apply module-scoped permissions: reads -> hasPermission('CONTROL_LIB','READ') / hasPermission('REGULATORY','READ'); writes -> ...'WRITE'; deletes -> ...'DELETE'. The transition endpoints should require WRITE.
references: OWASP API5:2023 Broken Function Level Authorization

title: Platform-wide audit log readable by any authenticated user
cvss: CVSS 5.3 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N) — disclosure of the tenant security/audit trail to all users
description: All four read endpoints of the F7 audit log (GET /api/v1/audit-log, /stats, /history, /trace/{correlationId}) are guarded only by isAuthenticated(). The audit log is the tenant's security ledger: it records who did what (usernames, roles, IP addresses, source endpoints, old/new value JSON diffs, workflow transitions, license changes, rule fires). Exposing it to every authenticated user — including the lowest-privilege role — lets any user reconstruct other users' and admins' activity, harvest internal entity ids, and read change diffs that may contain sensitive field values. Queries are tenant-scoped (findByOrganisationId...), so this is intra-tenant over-exposure, not cross-tenant.
rootCause: An inherently administrative/forensic data set is exposed at the authentication tier rather than behind an AUDIT_LOG:READ or platform-admin permission (the AUDIT_LOG module code already exists in LicensingService.KNOWN_MODULES).
impact: Information disclosure: any user can read the full tenant audit trail, including admin actions, value diffs, and source IPs — useful for reconnaissance and for an insider to monitor whether their own activity is being investigated. No data is mutated.
reproduction:
1. Log in as a low-privilege user.
2. curl http://localhost:8084/api/v1/audit-log -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" — returns the tenant-wide audit ledger including other users' actions and value diffs.
resolution: Gate all audit-log reads on a dedicated permission: @PreAuthorize("hasPermission('AUDIT_LOG','READ')") (or hasRole('PLATFORM_ADMIN')). Consider that /history is sometimes used inline on detail pages — if so, expose a narrower, entity-scoped history under the owning module's READ permission instead.
references: CWE-200: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor
OWASP A09:2021 Security Logging and Monitoring Failures

title: Generic persistence append endpoint has no authorization guard
cvss: CVSS 5.4 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:L) — unauthorized writes to arbitrary tenant key/value stores
description: PersistenceController is a generic key/value store backing the frontend's persistence adapter. PUT and DELETE correctly require hasPermission('PLATFORM','WRITE'), but POST /api/v1/persistence/{key} (append) carries NO @PreAuthorize at all. It is therefore covered only by the global SecurityConfig rule .anyRequest().authenticated(), meaning any authenticated user can append arbitrary JSON rows to any store key in their tenant. The body is @RequestBody Object serialized verbatim with no schema, size, or row-count validation, so a user can also write unbounded volumes. This is inconsistent with the bulk-write endpoints on the same controller, which are PLATFORM:WRITE.
rootCause: Missing method-level authorization annotation on the append handler; the author relied on the global authenticated() default while protecting the sibling PUT/DELETE with PLATFORM:WRITE, creating an inconsistent privilege boundary.
impact: Any authenticated user (including read-only roles) can write/pollute arbitrary tenant persistence stores and inflate storage. Org scoping is enforced, so the write stays within the tenant; integrity/availability of frontend-persisted data is the concern.
reproduction:
1. Log in as an auditor.
2. curl -X POST http://localhost:8084/api/v1/persistence/anyKey -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"injected":true}' — returns 200 with a new rowSeq even though the role has no PLATFORM:WRITE.
resolution: Add @PreAuthorize("hasPermission('PLATFORM','WRITE')") to the append handler to match PUT/DELETE, and add a payload-size / row-count bound.
references: OWASP API5:2023 Broken Function Level Authorization

title: File upload/list/get endpoints lack authorization annotations and content controls
category: Broken Function Level Authorization (A01) / Unrestricted Upload
cvss: CVSS 5.4 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:L) — unauthorized upload + enumeration of tenant file metadata
description: FileUploadController.list (GET), upload (POST) and get (GET /{id}) have no @PreAuthorize (only the global authenticated() applies); only delete requires PLATFORM:WRITE. Consequences: (1) any authenticated user can upload files and can list metadata for any attachedTo key in their tenant (e.g. attachedTo='dsr/DSR-2026-013' or 'evidence/EV-1078'), enumerating which sensitive records have attachments and reading filename/uploadedBy/crNumber/residency — there is no per-record ownership or owning-module READ check, so a user with no privilege on the privacy/evidence module can still browse those files' metadata. (2) The upload performs only a stub virus scan (EICAR string + extension blocklist) and enforces no max file size, MIME allowlist, or filename sanitisation in code (file.getOriginalFilename() is stored and used to build the storage key verbatim).
rootCause: Missing method-level authorization on read/upload handlers, and reliance on a documented-but-unimplemented storage/scan backend. Access is scoped only by tenant + a free-text attachedTo string the caller supplies, with no link back to the owning record's module permission.
impact: Intra-tenant: enumeration/disclosure of file metadata attached to sensitive records (DSR/evidence/incident) by users lacking those modules' permissions, plus unauthorized uploads. The virus-scan/size gaps are latent risks until the real storage backend is wired, but the stored unsanitised originalFilename flows into the S3 key and into responses.
reproduction:
1. Log in as a low-privilege user.
2. curl 'http://localhost:8084/api/v1/files?attachedTo=dsr/DSR-2026-013' -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" — returns the file list/metadata for that DSR without any privacy-module permission.
3. curl -F file=@x.bin -F attachedTo=evidence/EV-1 http://localhost:8084/api/v1/files -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" — uploads successfully.
resolution: Add @PreAuthorize to list/upload/get (at minimum hasPermission('PLATFORM','READ')/('PLATFORM','WRITE')); ideally derive the owning module from attachedTo and check that module's permission. Enforce a configured max-file-size (spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size + an in-code check), a MIME allowlist, and sanitise originalFilename before using it in the storage key.
references: CWE-434: Unrestricted Upload of File with Dangerous Type

title: Cross-module write endpoints (departments, issues, calendar, buyer-gap risk/privacy actions) gated only by isAuthenticated()
cvss: CVSS 5.4 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:H/A:L) — unauthorized writes across multiple modules
description: Several platform/cross-module write surfaces are guarded only by isAuthenticated(): BuyerGapController exposes POST risk-control links, POST risk attestations, and POST sweeps that mutate privacy DSR/breach state and emit domain events under /api/v1/risk/** and /api/v1/privacy/** without RISK:WRITE / PRIVACY:WRITE; DepartmentController create/update/archive; IssueController create/update/transition; CalendarController create/update/delete. None of these enforce a module permission, so any authenticated user can create or change this data. Tenant scoping is correctly enforced in every backing service (BuyerGapService explicitly validates risk.organisationId == current tenant), so there is no cross-tenant break — the issue is missing function-level RBAC, plus inconsistency with the well-guarded reporting/dashboard controllers.
rootCause: These controllers (and the buyer-gap bundle that spans risk/privacy/evidence) were shipped with a blanket isAuthenticated() guard rather than the module-action permissions the platform's RBAC model defines.
impact: Within a tenant, any role can mutate risk-control linkage, file risk attestations in another user's name, trigger PDPL/DSR breach sweeps (which flip DsrCase/CrisisEvent state and fire events), and create/edit departments, issues, and calendar events — eroding data integrity and segregation of duties that SAMA/NCA expect. No cross-tenant or unauthenticated exposure.
reproduction:
1. Log in as a low-privilege user.
2. curl -X POST http://localhost:8084/api/v1/risk/risks/1/attestations -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"decision":"CONFIRMED","attestedByName":"spoofed"}' — creates an attestation with no RISK:WRITE.
3. curl -X POST http://localhost:8084/api/v1/privacy/dsr/sla/sweep -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" — mutates DSR SLA-breach state.
resolution: Apply the owning module's WRITE/DELETE permission to each handler: RISK:WRITE on the risk-control/attestation endpoints, PRIVACY:WRITE on the DSR/breach sweeps, EVIDENCE:WRITE on the evidence freshness/connector endpoints, PLATFORM:WRITE (or a Departments/Issues permission) on departments/issues/calendar mutations.
references: OWASP API5:2023 Broken Function Level Authorization

title: Unauthenticated public sub-processor list allows cross-tenant enumeration via attacker-controlled org parameter
cvss: CVSS ~5.3 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:N/A:N) — unauthenticated cross-tenant read of (intentionally public) vendor list for arbitrary orgs
description: GET /api/v1/privacy/subprocessors/public is permitAll in SecurityConfig and takes a caller-supplied ?org=<id> query parameter that is passed straight into SubprocessorPublicListService.publicList(orgId) → repo.findByOrganisationIdAndLifecycleStageAndIsDeletedFalse(orgId,"APPROVED"). Because there is no JWT and thus no TenantContext, the org id is whatever the caller sends (defaulting to 1). An unauthenticated attacker can iterate org=1,2,3,… and harvest the APPROVED sub-processor list (legal name EN/AR, country, region, processing purpose, cross-border safeguard) for every tenant, not just the one whose public privacy notice references the endpoint. While PDPL Art.12 intends this list to be public, exposing every tenant's vendor map through one un-scoped, enumerable parameter is a tenant-isolation weakness and a competitive-intelligence leak.
rootCause: The endpoint is org-agnostic by design (no tenant context for anonymous callers) but trusts a client-supplied org id with no host-to-tenant binding, rate limiting, or allow-list of organisations that have opted into public disclosure.
evidence: SubprocessorController.java:157-162  @GetMapping("/public") public List<PublicSubprocessorResponse> publicList(@RequestParam(name="org",required=false) Long orgId){ return publicListService.publicList(orgId == null ? 1L : orgId); }  ;  SecurityConfig.java:101 .requestMatchers(HttpMethod.GET, "/api/v1/privacy/subprocessors/public").permitAll().
impact: Anonymous enumeration of every tenant's approved sub-processor / vendor relationships and cross-border destinations. For multi-tenant SaaS this leaks one customer's supply chain to anyone, including competitors, and lets an attacker map which banks use which processors and in which countries.
reproduction: 1) Without any auth: for i in 1..50; curl "http://localhost:8084/api/v1/privacy/subprocessors/public?org=$i". 2) Each call returns the APPROVED sub-processors for tenant i, regardless of whether tenant i intended a public list.
resolution: Bind the public list to a host-based tenant resolver (the planned ethics.<bank>.sa style) instead of a client-supplied org id, OR gate disclosure behind a per-org 'public_transparency_enabled' flag and return 404 for orgs that have not opted in. Add rate limiting to the permitAll path to blunt enumeration. At minimum, do not default to org 1 and reject requests where org cannot be resolved from the request context.
references: CWE-639: Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key
OWASP API Security Top 10 2023 — API1:2023 BOLA

title: Hardcoded database credentials and plaintext user passwords in Python scripts
cvss: Risk rationale: dev-only secret (the documented sa/tss.123 dev DB password) hardcoded in ~78 scripts, plus 5 plaintext application user passwords in a password-reset helper. Not a network-exploitable bug, but a real secrets-management hygiene failure: if any of these files reach a shared/public repo or the dev password is ever reused in a non-dev environment, it grants full sa access. Bandit did not emit B105/B106 here because the literals are inside ODBC connection strings / dict values rather than tracked password kwargs; reported per explicit scope to cover hardcoded creds.
description: The SQL Server sa credential is hardcoded as 'UID=sa;PWD=tss.123' in 78 Python files at the repo root and under .tools/ (verified by grep: 78 occurrences across 78 files). Separately, .tmp/reset_pw.py embeds five plaintext application-user passwords (Audit@12345, Risk@12345, Compliance@12345, Analyst@12345, Viewer@12345) and then builds UPDATE iam.users SET password_hash = '{h}' ... WHERE username = '{user}' by string interpolation, writing the result to reset_pw.sql. While tss.123 is the documented dev password (CLAUDE.md / application-dev.yml), embedding it and the app passwords in source-controlled scripts spreads the secret widely and couples every utility to one privileged login.
rootCause: No centralised secrets/connection configuration for the Python tooling. Each script copy-pastes the same sa connection string literal, and the password-reset helper hardcodes the credential scheme instead of reading it from the environment or prompting.
evidence:
.tmp/reset_pw.py:4-10
creds = {
    "auditor":    "Audit@12345",
    "rmanager":   "Risk@12345",
    "compliance": "Compliance@12345",
    "ranalyst":   "Analyst@12345",
    "viewer":     "Viewer@12345",
}

seed_real_data.py:39
    'UID=sa;PWD=tss.123;Unicode_Results=Yes;'

.tools/forensic_final.py:26-27
CONN=("DRIVER={ODBC Driver 17 for SQL Server};SERVER=localhost;DATABASE=TSS_GRC;"
      "UID=sa;PWD=tss.123;TrustServerCertificate=yes")
impact: Anyone with read access to the repo obtains the dev sa password and the standard app-user password scheme. If the dev DB is reachable (it binds localhost:1433 with sa enabled) this is full administrative DB access. The plaintext app passwords reveal the org-wide credential convention (<Role>@12345), which likely matches seeded accounts and is trivially guessable for other roles. Risk escalates sharply if the same literal is ever reused outside dev or if .tmp/ scripts are committed.
reproduction:
1. grep -rn 'PWD=tss.123' *.py .tools/*.py -> 78 files.
2. Open .tmp/reset_pw.py -> five plaintext passwords in the creds dict.
3. With the dev DB up: sqlcmd -S localhost -U sa -P tss.123 -Q "SELECT 1" authenticates as sa.
resolution: Read the connection string / password from environment variables (e.g. os.environ['DB_PASSWORD'], os.environ.get('GRC_DB_DSN')) — matching the backend's existing DB_PASSWORD convention — with no default that contains a real secret. Provide a single shared db_connect() helper imported by every script so the literal exists in zero places. For reset_pw.py, prompt for the password (getpass) or read from env, and never write plaintext passwords into source. Add the dev password to a .env (git-ignored) and rotate it. Add a secret-scanner (gitleaks/trufflehog) and bandit B105/B106 to CI.
patchAfter:
import os, getpass
DB_PASSWORD = os.environ["DB_PASSWORD"]  # no hardcoded default
CONN = f"...UID=sa;PWD={DB_PASSWORD};..."
# reset_pw.py: take the new password interactively, never store it
new_pw = getpass.getpass(f"New password for {user}: ")
references: OWASP A07:2021 Identification and Authentication Failures

title: Raw JPA entities bound as @RequestBody on assessment/treatment/KRI/appetite write endpoints (mass assignment, no @Valid)
cvss: CVSS 5.3 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:N) — client can set server-managed fields and bypass DTO validation
description: Several write endpoints bind the persistence @Entity directly as the request body with no DTO and no @Valid: RiskAdvancedController.recordAssessment(@RequestBody RiskAssessment body), createTreatment/updateTreatment(@RequestBody RiskTreatment body), and KriAppetiteController.createKri/updateKri(@RequestBody KriDefinition body), createAppetite/updateAppetite(@RequestBody RiskAppetiteStatement body). This lets a client populate any settable column on the entity — e.g. RiskAssessment.assessorId (attribution can be forged to any user id), externalId, assessmentDate; RiskTreatment.completedAt/status on update(); KriDefinition / RiskAppetiteStatement.organisationId could be supplied in JSON. Create paths partly mitigate by overwriting organisationId server-side and calling body.setId(null), but updateTreatment() binds the entity straight onto the managed row with no field allow-list and no validation, and recordAssessment() trusts the body's assessorId. None of these endpoints declare @Valid, so the only constraints are the manual checks inside the service (1..5 scale on assessment; enum sets on treatment/KRI) — fields without a manual check are accepted unvalidated.
rootCause: Controllers expose JPA entities as the API contract instead of purpose-built request DTOs with @Valid constraints and an explicit field allow-list; create methods scrub id/org but update methods and child-attribution fields are not protected.
impact: Integrity / non-repudiation: an authenticated RISK:WRITE user can forge the assessor of a risk re-assessment (assessorId set from the body, not from the JWT principal), backdate assessmentDate, and set entity fields the API never intended to expose. Forged attribution undermines the audit/attestation trail that the ERM module is built to provide to regulators. Missing @Valid also means malformed values reach the persistence layer where only some are caught.
reproduction: 1. As any RISK:WRITE user, POST /api/v1/risk/risks/{riskId}/assessments with body {"likelihood":3,"impact":3,"assessorId":999,"assessmentDate":"2020-01-01"}. 2. Observe the saved assessment is attributed to user 999 with a backdated date — neither was taken from the authenticated principal.
resolution: Introduce request DTOs (e.g. RiskAssessmentRequest, RiskTreatmentRequest) carrying only client-writable fields, annotate with Jakarta constraints, and bind with @Valid. Derive assessorId from the authenticated principal (Authentication / GrcUserDetails) rather than the body. On update, copy only the allow-listed fields onto the managed entity. Apply the same DTO pattern to the KRI/appetite create/update endpoints.
references: CWE-915 Improperly Controlled Modification of Dynamically-Determined Object Attributes (Mass Assignment)
OWASP A08:2021 Software and Data Integrity Failures

title: Unbounded client-controlled page size on Emerging-Risk and Scenario list endpoints
cvss: CVSS 5.3 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:L) — memory/DB pressure from arbitrarily large page requests
description: EmergingRiskController.list and RiskScenarioController.list accept a raw int 'size' query parameter and pass it straight into PageRequest.of(page, size) with no upper bound. There is no global spring.data.web.pageable.max-page-size configured (grep of src/main/resources returned no match), so a request such as ?size=100000000 instructs Hibernate to fetch and materialise that many rows for the tenant in one query, plus map each to a Response record. RiskController/KriAppetiteController use @PageableDefault which Spring caps at the default max (2000), but these two controllers build the Pageable by hand and bypass that protection.
rootCause: Manual PageRequest.of(page, size) with an unvalidated, unbounded size parameter and no global max-page-size guard.
impact: An authenticated user can drive large result-set fetches that spike heap and DB load, degrading or denying service for the tenant (and, on a shared node, neighbours). Low data-integrity impact but a cheap availability lever.
reproduction: 1. Authenticate. 2. GET /api/risk/emerging?size=100000000 (or /api/risk/scenarios?size=100000000). 3. Observe a single large query / large allocation; repeat to sustain pressure.
resolution: Clamp size to a sane maximum (e.g. Math.min(size, 200)) and floor page at 0, or switch these endpoints to @PageableDefault/@PageableDefault(size=…) Pageable injection, and set spring.data.web.pageable.max-page-size globally in application.yml as defence in depth.
references: CWE-770 Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling
