1. Log in as any user.
2. curl 'http://localhost:8084/api/v1/issues?page=0&size=100000000' -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" and observe the server attempting to load an unbounded page.
resolution: Clamp the page size, e.g. PageRequest.of(page, Math.min(Math.max(size,1), 200)) in IssueService.list (mirroring AuditLogService). Prefer @PageableDefault/Pageable with a configured max page size for consistency.
references: CWE-770: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling

title: Audit-log source IP taken from unvalidated X-Forwarded-For (audit-trail spoofing)
cvss: CVSS 3.7 (AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N) — forgeable source IP in the security audit trail
description: AuditLogService.extractIp reads the X-Forwarded-For request header and stores the first value as the audit row's ip_address whenever the header is present, with no allowlist of trusted proxies. Any authenticated user can set an arbitrary X-Forwarded-For on their requests, so every audited action they perform can be attributed to a forged source IP in the F7 audit ledger. This weakens the evidentiary value of the audit trail that SAMA/NCA examinations rely on.
rootCause: The forwarded-header is trusted unconditionally instead of only when the request arrives from a known/trusted reverse proxy (or via Spring's ForwardedHeaderFilter configured for the deployment topology).
impact: Forensic/repudiation risk: audit entries can be made to point at an attacker-chosen IP, frustrating incident investigation and undermining non-repudiation. Low severity — it does not grant access, only degrades log integrity, and the username/role fields remain trustworthy (derived from the JWT).
reproduction:
1. Log in as any user.
2. Perform any audited action with header: -H 'X-Forwarded-For: 8.8.8.8'.
3. GET /api/v1/audit-log and observe the new entry's ip_address recorded as 8.8.8.8 rather than the real client address.
resolution: Only honour X-Forwarded-For when the immediate peer (req.getRemoteAddr()) is a configured trusted proxy; otherwise use req.getRemoteAddr(). Better, configure Spring's ForwardedHeaderFilter / server.forward-headers-strategy per deployment and read the resolved remote address.
references: CWE-348: Use of Less Trusted Source
OWASP A09:2021 Security Logging and Monitoring Failures

title: SDAIA breach-submission and DSR-extend endpoints accept unbounded/untyped Map<String,Object> bodies (no DTO validation)
cvss: CVSS ~3.1 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N) — weak input typing/validation on privileged workflow mutations
description: Several privileged mutation endpoints accept raw @RequestBody Map<String,Object> or unvalidated entity bodies instead of @Valid DTOs with Jakarta constraints. Examples: PrivacyController.extendDsr reads body.get("days") as a Number with no bounds (a caller can pass days=2_000_000 to push the PDPL SLA arbitrarily far out); recordSdaiaSubmission takes a record with no @Valid/@NotBlank; DpiaController.approve/reject and the Ethics AML/EthicsCase transition handlers accept untyped maps. The CRUD create/update endpoints on PrivacyController (createBreach/createDsr/createRopa) and the ethics controllers bind the JPA entity directly via @RequestBody with no @Valid, so client-supplied audit/server-managed fields are accepted from the wire (mass-assignment surface), though the services re-stamp organisationId and (for DPIA) null the id.
rootCause: Workflow endpoints were implemented with ad-hoc Map parsing rather than typed, validated request DTOs. No @Valid is applied and no @Min/@Max/@NotBlank constraints bound the values.
evidence: PrivacyController.java:200-205  @PostMapping("/dsrs/{id}/extend") public DataSubjectRequest extendDsr(@PathVariable Long id, @RequestBody Map<String,Object> body){ Integer days = body.get("days") instanceof Number n ? n.intValue() : null; return privacyService.extendDsr(id, days);} — PrivacyService.extendDsr only floors at 30 when null/<=0; no upper bound. createBreach(@RequestBody DataBreach req) at lines 45-47 has no @Valid.
impact: Weak typing allows out-of-range or unexpected values to drive regulated SLA clocks (DSR due date, breach states) and produces inconsistent validation behaviour. Direct entity binding without @Valid widens the mass-assignment surface and bypasses the bean-validation messages the platform ships. No direct confidentiality breach, hence Low.
reproduction: 1) As a PRIVACY_WRITE user: POST /api/v1/privacy/dsrs/{id}/extend {"days":3650}. 2) The DSR due date is pushed out 10 years with no rejection, defeating the PDPL 30/60-day SLA model.
resolution: Introduce typed request records with Jakarta constraints (e.g. ExtendDsrRequest(@Min(1) @Max(60) int days)), annotate every mutating handler body with @Valid, and replace Map<String,Object> transition bodies with explicit DTOs. For create/update, bind a request DTO (not the JPA entity) and map server-managed fields server-side.
references: CWE-915: Improperly Controlled Modification of Dynamically-Determined Object Attributes (Mass Assignment)

title: Sensitive PII written into audit-log/business-event messages (consent subject refs, KYC names/IDs, whistleblower actors)
category: Sensitive Data Exposure (A09/A02) / CWE-532 Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File
cvss: CVSS ~3.5 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:N/A:N) — PII persisted into audit ledger / event payloads readable by lower-privileged log/automation consumers
description: Multiple services embed personal data directly into audit-log free-text messages and DomainEvent payloads. ConsentRecordService logs 'Consent granted: subject=<dataSubjectRef> purpose=… basis=…' and emits the dataSubjectRef in every CONSENT_* event payload and as the event correlation id ('consent:'+dataSubjectRef+':'+purposeCode). CoiService logs the declarant's full name and employee number into COI_DECLARATION_* audit rows and event payloads. WhistleblowerRetaliationService logs the named claimed actor. These audit rows and F8 event payloads are consumed by separate audit/automation subsystems whose access control is broader than the privacy/ethics module permission — so PII leaks to viewers who should not see the underlying record.
rootCause: Audit/event messages were built by string-concatenating the human-readable record including PII identifiers, instead of referencing the entity by surrogate id and keeping PII in the tenant-scoped entity tables only.
evidence: ConsentRecordService.java:124-127 audit.log("CREATE","ConsentRecord", saved.getId(), "Consent granted: subject=" + saved.getDataSubjectRef() + " purpose=" + saved.getPurposeCode() + " basis=" + saved.getLegalBasis()); and emit(...) payload includes m.put("dataSubjectRef", nullSafeStr(c.getDataSubjectRef())) (lines 66-67, 86-87). CoiService.java:260-263 logs finalDecl.getFullNameEn() + employeeNo.
impact: Personal data (PDPL-regulated subject references, employee names/IDs, named subjects of whistleblower retaliation claims) is duplicated into the audit ledger and the automation event bus. Anyone with audit-log read or rule-engine visibility — a broader population than the data owner — can recover PII, contradicting data-minimisation (PDPL Art.4) and the module's own access scoping.
reproduction: 1) Grant a consent via POST /api/v1/privacy/consents. 2) Read the audit log (audit-log module) as a user with audit read but no PRIVACY permission → the row text contains the data subject reference. 3) Inspect the CONSENT_GRANTED DomainEvent payload in the automation subsystem → dataSubjectRef present.
resolution: Reference records in audit/event text by surrogate id only (e.g. 'ConsentRecord#<id>') and keep PII identifiers out of free-text messages and event payloads, or hash/tokenise the subject reference for correlation. If a subject correlation key is genuinely required for rule matching, use a non-reversible token rather than the raw reference, and ensure audit/event consumers enforce the same data-classification controls as the source module.
references: CWE-532: Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File
OWASP Top 10 2021 — A09:2021 Security Logging and Monitoring Failures

title: SQL built by Python string/f-string interpolation in DB bootstrap & seed scripts (B608 x56)
cvss: Risk rationale: Bandit rates B608 MEDIUM, but exploitability here is LOW. The interpolated tokens are trusted internal constants (integers such as days_ago/hours_ago, or schema/index names read from the live dev DB) while all external/business data is passed via parameterised '?' placeholders. No untrusted-input path reaches the string-built portion, and the scripts are dev-only DB bootstrap utilities run by an operator with the sa account. Reported as a pattern-hygiene/defence-in-depth issue per scope.
description: Bandit flagged 56 B608 'Possible SQL injection via string-based query construction' occurrences across the repo-root Python DB scripts. The two largest concentrations are seed_real_data.py (19) and seed_socops_data.py (12); the rest are spread across ~19 other setup_*/seed_*/.tools scripts. Verified two representative cases. In seed_real_data.py the SQL is an f-string, but business data (email, name, status, org_id) is bound through '?' placeholders; the only interpolated value is the integer day-offset {days_ago} taken from a hardcoded Python constant list, used inside DATEADD(day, -{days_ago}, ...). Same shape in seed_socops_data.py (interpolated {-hours_ago}/{sla_offset} integers). The genuinely string-built case is .tools/introspect_schema.py, a DDL generator that interpolates schema/table/index names (e.g. CREATE {unique_kw}INDEX [{ix['name']}] ON {schema}.{table}) — but those identifiers come from the live dev DB's own sys.schemas/sys.indexes catalog, not from any external input. Confidence breakdown from the scan: 36 LOW / 20 MEDIUM, 0 HIGH.
rootCause: Convenience pattern of assembling SQL with Python f-strings/concatenation instead of fully parameterising every value. Integers and schema identifiers cannot be bound the same way as values, so authors inlined them. None of the inlined tokens originate from untrusted input, but the pattern is brittle: a future edit that interpolates an attacker-influenced field would silently become injectable.
evidence:
seed_real_data.py:305-319
for rtype, rname, remail, status, days_ago in DSRS:
    run(
        f"""
        IF NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM privacy.data_subject_requests
                       WHERE requester_email = ? AND organisation_id = ? AND request_type = ?)
        INSERT INTO privacy.data_subject_requests (...)
        VALUES (NEWID(), ?, ?, ?, ?, DATEADD(day, -{days_ago}, GETDATE()),
            DATEADD(day, -{days_ago} + 30, CAST(GETDATE() AS DATE)), ?, 0, ...)
        """,
        remail, ORG_TSS, rtype, ORG_TSS, rtype, rname, remail, status, ...)

.tools/introspect_schema.py:208
out.append(f"IF NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM sys.indexes WHERE name = '{ix['name']}' AND object_id = OBJECT_ID('{schema}.{table}'))")
impact: In the current code there is no exploitable injection: the inlined tokens are trusted constants/catalog names and these scripts never accept network/user input. The real impact is maintenance risk and a poor pattern that scanners (and auditors) will keep flagging, plus the chance of a regression if someone later inlines a user/business field. If any of these scripts were ever repurposed to accept caller-supplied parameters, the string-built portions would become first-order SQL injection against the dev/prod database under the sa login.
reproduction:
1. bandit -r . -f json | jq '.results[] | select(.test_id=="B608")' — yields 56 hits.
2. Open seed_real_data.py:307 and confirm DATEADD(day, -{days_ago}, ...) is f-string-interpolated while data uses '?'.
3. Trace DSRS (line ~289) — days_ago is a hardcoded int literal, not input. No injection reachable as written.
4. Open .tools/introspect_schema.py:208 — confirm identifiers come from sys.indexes/sys.schemas, not external input.
resolution: For integer day/hour offsets, bind them as parameters too (pyodbc supports binding the DATEADD operand: DATEADD(day, -?, GETDATE()) with the int passed in the args tuple) rather than f-string interpolation. For the DDL generator, validate identifiers against an allowlist regex (^[A-Za-z0-9_]+$) before interpolation and/or use QUOTENAME() in the emitted T-SQL. Add a repo lint gate (bandit B608) so new string-built SQL is caught in review. Because these are dev-only, the priority is low — but standardising on a single parameterised run() helper across all setup_*/seed_* scripts removes the whole class.
patchBefore:
run(
    f"""
    ... VALUES (NEWID(), ?, ?, ?, ?, DATEADD(day, -{days_ago}, GETDATE()),
        DATEADD(day, -{days_ago} + 30, CAST(GETDATE() AS DATE)), ?, 0, ...)
    """,
    remail, ORG_TSS, rtype, ORG_TSS, rtype, rname, remail, status)
patchAfter:
run(
    """
    ... VALUES (NEWID(), ?, ?, ?, ?, DATEADD(day, -?, GETDATE()),
        DATEADD(day, -? + 30, CAST(GETDATE() AS DATE)), ?, 0, ...)
    """,
    remail, ORG_TSS, rtype, ORG_TSS, rtype, rname, remail,
    days_ago, days_ago, status)

# introspect_schema.py — validate identifiers before interpolation
import re
assert re.fullmatch(r'[A-Za-z0-9_]+', ix['name']), f"unsafe index name {ix['name']!r}"
references: CWE-89: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command

title: Silent exception suppression: try/except/pass and try/except/continue (B110 x8, B112 x6)
cvss: Risk rationale: dev-tooling robustness/observability issue, not a vulnerability. Broad except: pass / except: continue blocks swallow all errors (including KeyboardInterrupt-adjacent and unexpected failures), which can mask data-corruption or partial-failure bugs in the bootstrap/seed scripts but has no direct exploit path.
description: Bandit raised 8 B110 (try/except/pass, CWE-703) and 6 B112 (try/except/continue) hits across dev tooling under .tools/ and .tmp/. Verified .tools/forensic_final.py:22-25 (try: sys.stdout.reconfigure(...) except Exception: pass) and .tmp/dump_edit.py:13-14 (try: rec = json.loads(line) except: continue). These suppress errors during stdout reconfiguration and per-line JSON parsing.
rootCause: Quick scripts that intentionally skip malformed lines / optional setup steps, using a catch-all that discards the exception instead of catching the specific expected type and logging it.
impact: Operational, not security. Swallowed exceptions can hide partial seed/bootstrap failures (a script reports success while having skipped rows), complicating audit reproducibility. A bare 'except:' (dump_edit.py:14) also catches SystemExit/KeyboardInterrupt, which is poor practice.
reproduction:
1. bandit -r . | grep -E 'B110|B112' -> 14 hits.
2. Open .tmp/dump_edit.py:14 -> bare 'except: continue'.
resolution: Catch the specific expected exception (json.JSONDecodeError, AttributeError) and at minimum log/count the skipped item. Replace bare 'except:' with 'except Exception:' (or the precise type) so control-flow signals propagate. Low priority given dev-only scope.
patchBefore:
try: rec = json.loads(line)
        except: continue
references: CWE-703: Improper Check or Handling of Exceptional Conditions

title: Unchecked casts on free-form Map body in correctAssessment / KRI reading / appetite exposure
cvss: CVSS 3.1 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:L) — malformed JSON triggers 500/ClassCastException
description: Several endpoints accept an untyped Map<String,Object> body and perform unchecked casts: correctAssessment casts ((Number) body.get("likelihood")) and (String) body.get("assessmentNotesEn"); recordReading/updateExposure dereference body.get("value").toString() (NPE if 'value' absent) and parse it with new BigDecimal(...) (NumberFormatException on non-numeric); acknowledgeBreach reads userId from the body. A client sending the wrong JSON type or omitting a required key triggers an uncaught ClassCastException / NullPointerException / NumberFormatException surfacing as a 500. These are not typed, validated DTOs, so no Jakarta constraints apply and error handling is inconsistent. There is no injection or privilege impact (values are numeric/notes only), but it is poor input hygiene and a minor availability/robustness issue, and acknowledgeBreach trusts a body-supplied userId for attribution rather than the principal.
rootCause: Use of weakly-typed Map<String,Object> request bodies with manual casting/parsing instead of validated request DTOs; missing null/type checks.
evidence:
Integer likelihood = body.get("likelihood") == null ? null : ((Number) body.get("likelihood")).intValue();
        ...
        BigDecimal value = body.get("value") instanceof Number n
            ? new BigDecimal(n.toString())
            : new BigDecimal(body.get("value").toString()); // NPE if 'value' missing
impact: Authenticated clients can trigger 500 responses (and noisy stack traces in non-prod) with malformed payloads; breach acknowledgement is attributed to a caller-supplied userId rather than the authenticated user, weakening the acknowledgement audit trail.
reproduction: 1. As a RISK:WRITE user, PUT /api/v1/risk/assessments/{id} with body {"likelihood":"abc"} -> ClassCastException 500. 2. POST /api/v1/risk/kris/{id}/readings with body {} -> NPE on body.get("value") 500.
resolution: Replace the Map bodies with typed DTOs (e.g. AssessmentCorrectionRequest, KriReadingRequest, ExposureUpdateRequest) carrying @NotNull/@DecimalMin constraints validated with @Valid; derive acknowledger userId from the authenticated principal instead of the body.
references: CWE-704 Incorrect Type Conversion or Cast

title: TLS certificate validation disabled in DB connections (TrustServerCertificate / Encrypt=No)
cvss: CVSS 3.7 (AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:N) — MITM exposure on the DB channel; localhost-only in practice for the dev scripts, but the prod JDBC default also trusts any cert
description: The base/dev JDBC URL uses `encrypt=true;trustServerCertificate=true`, which encrypts the channel but disables certificate validation, defeating MITM protection. The ~14 Python scripts that connect via ODBC use `TrustServerCertificate=yes` or `Encrypt=No`, which similarly disable validation (or encryption entirely). For the localhost dev scripts the practical exposure is negligible, but the same `trustServerCertificate=true` pattern is carried in the base `application.yml` datasource URL that the prod profile's documented `DB_URL` comment also references — meaning an operator copying the example connects to the production database over a channel that trusts any presented certificate.
rootCause: Certificate trust was disabled to avoid configuring a CA/trust store during local development, and the insecure setting was left in the base configuration and the prod URL example rather than scoped strictly to dev.
evidence: application.yml:15 — "url: ${DB_URL:jdbc:sqlserver://localhost:1433;databaseName=TSS_GRC;encrypt=true;trustServerCertificate=true;sendStringParametersAsUnicode=true}"
impact: An attacker positioned between the application (or a script) and the SQL Server can present a forged certificate and transparently intercept/modify all database traffic, including the `sa` login and every tenant's data. Risk is high only on untrusted networks; on localhost it is informational.
reproduction: 1. Inspect application.yml:15 and the prod DB_URL example comment (application-prod.yml:9). 2. Note `trustServerCertificate=true` (Java) and `TrustServerCertificate=yes`/`Encrypt=No` (Python). 3. On a non-localhost link, an ARP/DNS-spoof MITM with a self-signed cert is accepted without error.
resolution: For non-dev environments set `encrypt=true;trustServerCertificate=false;hostNameInCertificate=<cn>` and provision the SQL Server CA into the JVM trust store (the prod example URL already hints at this — make it the enforced default, not a comment). For the dev scripts, gate trust-disabling behind an explicit env flag so it cannot leak into shared instances.
patchBefore: url: ${DB_URL:jdbc:sqlserver://localhost:1433;databaseName=TSS_GRC;encrypt=true;trustServerCertificate=true;sendStringParametersAsUnicode=true}
patchAfter:
url: ${DB_URL:jdbc:sqlserver://localhost:1433;databaseName=TSS_GRC;encrypt=true;trustServerCertificate=true;sendStringParametersAsUnicode=true}
# NOTE: trustServerCertificate=true is the LOCAL-DEV default only. Non-dev DB_URL
# MUST use trustServerCertificate=false;hostNameInCertificate=<cn> with the SQL
# Server CA in the JVM trust store. application-prod.yml has no default for DB_URL,
# so prod is forced to supply a validated URL.
references: Microsoft JDBC: Connecting with SSL encryption

title: Production CORS allow-list not overridden; falls back to permissive credentialed pattern matching
cvss: CVSS 4.2 (AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:N) — contingent on CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS being mis-set in prod; default fallback is localhost-only so direct exploitability is limited
description: The base config comment states "In production, set to empty list (same-origin via Nginx reverse proxy)" and CorsConfig.java repeats that the prod profile sets `grc.cors.allowed-origins` empty. In reality `application-prod.yml` contains NO `grc.cors` block (verified — grep for cors/allowed-origins in application-prod.yml returns no matches), so prod inherits the base default `${CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS:http://localhost:3000}`. Combined with `CorsConfig` using `setAllowedOriginPatterns(...)` + `setAllowCredentials(true)`, this is a documentation-vs-reality gap: the security relies entirely on the operator remembering to export `CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS` correctly. Because `setAllowedOriginPatterns` treats entries as wildcard patterns (the dev profile uses `http://192.168.*:[*]`, `http://10.*:[*]`, `http://172.*:[*]` together with credentials), any over-broad value supplied via the env var in prod would allow credentialed cross-origin reads from a wide range of origins.
rootCause: Prod relies on an env var the YAML never asserts, and the comment claiming an explicit empty prod list was never implemented. The pattern-matching CORS source plus allowCredentials=true makes any wildcard origin value dangerous.
evidence: application-prod.yml has no `grc.cors:` key (grep returns 'No matches found'); base default at application.yml:145 — "allowed-origins: ${CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS:http://localhost:3000}"; CorsConfig.java:39,43 — "config.setAllowedOriginPatterns(allowedOrigins); ... config.setAllowCredentials(true);"
impact: If CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS is left unset or set to a broad pattern in production, browsers will attach the HttpOnly refresh cookie / Authorization responses for cross-origin requests from attacker-controlled origins matching the pattern, enabling session-riding data theft. With the documented intent (empty list) unimplemented, this depends on operator discipline rather than a safe default.
reproduction: 1. Deploy with `--spring.profiles.active=prod` and no CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS exported. 2. Observe Access-Control-Allow-Origin: http://localhost:3000 with Allow-Credentials: true on /api/** preflights. 3. Set CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS to a wildcard pattern and any matching origin can make credentialed cross-origin calls.
resolution: Make prod fail-closed: add an explicit `grc.cors.allowed-origins: ${CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS:}` (empty) to application-prod.yml so an unset value yields no allowed origins, and document that wildcard patterns must never be used in prod. Consider rejecting wildcard patterns when allowCredentials is true.
patchBefore: # application-prod.yml — (no grc.cors block; inherits base default http://localhost:3000)
patchAfter:
grc:
  cors:
    # Same-origin behind Nginx in prod -> no cross-origin allowed by default.
    # Wildcard patterns are forbidden here (allowCredentials=true is on).
    allowed-origins: ${CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS:}
references: CWE-942: Permissive Cross-domain Policy with Untrusted Domains

title: Dev profile ships broad LAN CORS wildcards with credentials enabled and lockout effectively disabled
cvss: Risk rationale: dev-only profile, but the allowed-origin set (entire 192.168/10/172 RFC1918 space, any port) plus allowCredentials=true and 99-attempt/1-min lockout creates real exposure on shared developer LANs
description: The dev profile sets `grc.cors.allowed-origins` to include `http://192.168.*:[*]`, `http://10.*:[*]`, and `http://172.*:[*]` — effectively the entire RFC1918 private address space on any port — while `CorsConfig` enables `setAllowCredentials(true)`. It also sets `max-failed-login-attempts: 99` and `lockout-duration-minutes: 1`, which disables brute-force protection. These are intentional dev conveniences (documented in CLAUDE.md and the LAN-access commits), so the rating is Low. However, when a developer runs the dev stack on a shared corporate/coffee-shop LAN with real seeded credentials (admin/Admin@12345 etc.), any other host on the subnet can host a page that makes credentialed cross-origin requests to the dev API, and the near-disabled lockout permits unlimited password guessing.
rootCause: Developer-experience trade-offs (zero-config LAN access, no lockout friction) were encoded as profile defaults; they are safe only under the assumption that the dev machine is never on an untrusted network with real data.
evidence: application-dev.yml:71 — "...,http://192.168.*:[*],http://10.*:[*],http://172.*:[*]" ; application-dev.yml:72-74 — "max-failed-login-attempts: 99 / lockout-duration-minutes: 1"
impact: On a shared LAN, a co-located attacker can (a) ride a developer's authenticated session via credentialed CORS from any RFC1918 origin, and (b) brute-force the well-known seeded passwords with no lockout. Confined to dev with throwaway data, impact is low; with production-like seed data on a laptop in public, it is meaningfully higher.
reproduction: 1. Start backend with profile=dev on a machine at 192.168.1.50. 2. From 192.168.1.99, host JS that POSTs to http://192.168.1.50:8084/api/v1/... with credentials:'include' — preflight is allowed. 3. Script 200 login attempts/min against /api/v1/auth/login without triggering lockout.
resolution: Keep the broad wildcards strictly behind the dev profile (already the case) and document the 'untrusted network' caveat. Prefer enumerating the developer's actual LAN IP via env var over the whole RFC1918 range, and raise the dev lockout to a non-trivial value (e.g. 20/5min) so brute-force is still slowed in dev.
patchBefore:
cors:
    allowed-origins: "...,http://192.168.*:[*],http://10.*:[*],http://172.*:[*]"
  security:
    max-failed-login-attempts: 99
    lockout-duration-minutes: 1
patchAfter:
cors:
    # Set DEV_LAN_ORIGIN to your machine's LAN URL instead of the whole RFC1918 space.
    allowed-origins: "http://localhost:3000,http://127.0.0.1:3000,${DEV_LAN_ORIGIN:}"
  security:
    max-failed-login-attempts: 20
    lockout-duration-minutes: 5
references: CWE-307: Improper Restriction of Excessive Authentication Attempts

title: Mass assignment and missing input validation: JPA entities bound directly as request bodies
cvss: CVSS 4.3 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N) — client-controlled internal fields + unvalidated input
description: The legacy TprmController binds the persistence @Entity types directly as @RequestBody (createVendor(@RequestBody Vendor), updateVendor(@RequestBody Vendor), createAssessment(@RequestBody VendorAssessment), updateAssessment(@RequestBody VendorAssessment)) with no @Valid and no DTO layer. This is inconsistent with the rest of the audited modules (cpty, openbanking, outsourcing, bcp_attestation) which all use validated request DTOs. Two concrete weaknesses follow: (1) Mass assignment — a client can supply id, externalId, isDeleted, createdAt (Vendor) or id, externalId, isDeleted, workflowStatus, computedScorePct (VendorAssessment) in the JSON body; createVendor saves the entity as-is (only organisationId is overwritten server-side). A client could, for example, POST a vendor with isDeleted=true or seed arbitrary externalId/createdAt. (2) No bean validation — vendorName, riskRating, status, emails, etc. are persisted with no @NotBlank/@Size/@Email/enum checks, so malformed or oversized values reach the database and the bilingual/workflow invariants are not enforced at the boundary.
rootCause: No DTO/validation layer for the original vendors/assessments endpoints; the JPA entity doubles as the API contract, exposing internal/managed columns to client binding.
impact: Lower than the IDOR findings because organisationId is forced server-side, but a client can set internal-state fields (e.g. isDeleted, workflowStatus, computedScorePct) and inject unvalidated/oversized data, leading to inconsistent records and bypass of workflow/scoring invariants. Combined with SEC-TPRM-001, the lack of validation widens the tampering surface.
reproduction: 1. As a TPRM writer, POST /api/v1/tprm/vendors with body {"vendorName":"x","isDeleted":true} — the row is created already soft-deleted. 2. POST /api/v1/tprm/assessments with {"vendorId":<own>,"assessmentDate":"2026-01-01","workflowStatus":"REVIEWED","computedScorePct":0} — workflow/score fields are accepted directly, bypassing the questionnaire engine that is supposed to own them.
resolution: Introduce VendorCreate/Update and AssessmentCreate/Update DTOs with Jakarta constraints (@NotBlank, @Size, @Email, allowed-value checks) and @Valid on the controller params; map only whitelisted fields in the service. Never bind JPA entities directly to request bodies.
references: CWE-915: Improperly Controlled Modification of Dynamically-Determined Object Attributes (Mass Assignment)

title: Public token-authenticated vendor-portal endpoints lack expiry, rate-limiting, and leak PII
cvss: CVSS 4.3 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:N) — unauthenticated endpoints; bounded by 122-bit unguessable token
description: GET /api/v1/tprm/bcp-attestations/by-token/{token} and POST /api/v1/tprm/bcp-attestations/by-token/{token}/submit are @PreAuthorize("permitAll()") — fully unauthenticated. The opaque token is the only credential. Mitigating factors: the token is a random UUIDv4 (submissionToken = UUID.randomUUID(), ~122 bits of entropy, not enumerable) and getByToken/submitByToken/doSubmit resolve the row by token and enforce a state guard (guardSubmit allows only INVITED/REMINDED/OVERDUE/REJECTED). Residual weaknesses: (1) the token never expires and is not single-use/rotated after submission, so a leaked URL (referrer logs, email forwarding, browser history, proxy logs) is replayable indefinitely; (2) the permitAll() submit endpoint has no rate-limiting or abuse audit (the controller Javadoc itself defers rate-limit/audit/MFA-bind to a follow-up); (3) the AttestationResponse returned by the public getByToken includes submitted-by contact name/email (PII), evidence file path/name, and the submissionToken itself, so anyone with the token reads vendor contact PII and internal evidence paths.
rootCause: v1 vendor-portal design intentionally treats the bearer token as the sole credential without expiry, single-use semantics, rate-limiting, or response field minimization for the unauthenticated path.
impact: If a submission URL leaks, an outsider can read the vendor's contact PII and evidence file path and (while the row is in a submittable state) overwrite the attested RTO/MTPD/BCP test data. Brute force is impractical due to the 122-bit token, so this is defense-in-depth rather than a directly exploitable break, hence Low.
reproduction: 1. Obtain a submission token (e.g. from a forwarded vendor email or logs). 2. curl http://localhost:8084/api/v1/tprm/bcp-attestations/by-token/<uuid> with no Authorization header — returns the attestation incl. submittedByContactEmail, evidenceFilePath and the token. 3. curl -X POST .../by-token/<uuid>/submit with a JSON body overwrites the attestation while it is INVITED/REMINDED/OVERDUE/REJECTED.
resolution: Add an expiry (token_expires_at) and reject expired tokens; make the token single-use (rotate/invalidate after SUBMITTED); add rate-limiting + audit on the permitAll() submit path; and minimize the by-token response (omit submissionToken and trim contact PII / internal evidence paths for the unauthenticated view).
references: CWE-307: Improper Restriction of Excessive Authentication Attempts
OWASP A07:2021 Identification and Authentication Failures

title: Unbounded client-controlled page size on list endpoints (resource exhaustion)
cvss: CVSS 3.7 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:L) — authenticated DoS via large page size
description: Several list endpoints accept a client-supplied size request param with a default but no upper bound, passing it straight into PageRequest.of(page, size): ObController.listApiCalls/listTpps/listConsents/listIncidents, CptyController.list, and ThirdPartyCyberAssessmentController.list (size default 100, no @Max). A caller can request size=1000000 and force the backend to materialize and serialize an arbitrarily large result set in one query. The TprmController vendor list uses @PageableDefault(size=20) but also has no max-page-size cap configured. These are authenticated endpoints, so impact is limited to authorized users, but a single tenant user can degrade the service for the shared backend.
rootCause: No maximum page-size clamp on raw int size params (and no global spring.data.web.pageable.max-page-size), so the client fully controls fetch size.
impact: An authenticated user can issue size=1000000 against api-calls (an append-only high-volume table) and similar endpoints, causing large heap allocation, slow queries, and potential OOM/GC pressure affecting all tenants on the shared instance.
reproduction: curl 'http://localhost:8084/api/v1/openbanking/api-calls?page=0&size=1000000' -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' — the server attempts to fetch and serialize up to a million rows.
resolution: Clamp the page size to a sane maximum (e.g. Math.min(size, 200)) in each controller/service, or set spring.data.web.pageable.max-page-size globally and prefer Pageable params with @PageableDefault plus a configured max.
references: CWE-770: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling

title: Refresh-token cookie scoped to /api/auth/refresh but logout/login path mismatch and absent on non-cookie clients
cvss: Informational — defense-in-depth observation; no direct exploit
description: The refresh cookie is set with HttpOnly; Secure; Path=/api/auth/refresh; SameSite=Strict — a strong attribute set that correctly limits cookie exposure and gives CSRF protection on the refresh endpoint. Two minor observations: (1) the cookie Path is /api/auth/refresh, which means the browser will NOT send it to /api/auth/logout (a different path); logout therefore relies on the client also clearing it and on the server's best-effort revoke, and the server-side revoke in logout() only runs if the cookie happens to be presented. (2) The bulk-revoke query revokeAllByUserId intentionally omits organisation_id (documented), which is acceptable for the self-service path (caller passes their own userId) but means an admin revoke flushes a user's sessions across all tenants — fine by design but worth noting in tenant-isolation reviews. These are noted for completeness; the cookie hardening itself (single fully-attributed Set-Cookie, no duplicate cookie without SameSite) is correctly implemented.
rootCause: Cookie Path is scoped narrowly to the refresh endpoint; logout lives on a sibling path so it cannot rely on automatic cookie transmission for server-side revocation in all clients.
evidence:
response.addHeader("Set-Cookie", String.format("grc_refresh=%s; HttpOnly; Secure; Path=/api/auth/refresh; SameSite=Strict; Max-Age=%d", refreshToken, refreshTokenExpiryMs / 1000));
// logout writes: grc_refresh=; ... Path=/api/auth/refresh; ... Max-Age=0
impact: Low: if a browser does not include the refresh cookie on the POST /api/auth/logout call (because the cookie Path is /api/auth/refresh), the server's revoke-on-logout is skipped and only the client-side cookie clear (Max-Age=0) happens, so a previously captured refresh token remains valid until rolled or expired. Rolling-refresh revocation and admin revoke still mitigate stolen tokens on the next refresh.
reproduction: 1. Log in, capture the grc_refresh cookie. 2. Call POST /api/auth/logout; because the cookie Path is /api/auth/refresh, some clients will not attach the cookie, so the server cannot read the jti to revoke. 3. The refresh-token row stays active in platform.refresh_token until its next use triggers rolling revocation or it expires.
resolution: Either widen the cookie Path to /api/auth (covering both /refresh and /logout) so logout can read and revoke it server-side, or have the frontend always include credentials on logout and confirm the cookie is transmitted; keep SameSite=Strict and HttpOnly/Secure unchanged. Optionally consider whether cross-tenant bulk revoke should require an explicit org scope for non-platform-admin callers.
patchBefore: Path=/api/auth/refresh   // set on login, logout, and clear
patchAfter: Path=/api/auth          // covers /api/auth/refresh and /api/auth/logout so logout can revoke server-side
references: OWASP A07:2021 Identification and Authentication Failures

title: Mass-assignment cross-tenant write backstop (TenantWriteGuardInterceptor) is stubbed and not wired
category: Broken Access Control / Mass Assignment (A01/A08) — CWE-915
cvss: Defense-in-depth gap — relies entirely on per-service req.setId(null); no platform backstop
description: Several BCM write endpoints bind raw JPA entities directly via @RequestBody (BcmController.createPlan/updatePlan/createProcess/updateProcess/createBia/createExercise take BcmPlan/CriticalProcess/BiaRecord/BcmExercise, not validated DTOs). The cross-tenant mass-assignment defense for these is purely the per-service convention of calling req.setId(null) and req.setOrganisationId(currentTenant) before save. The documented platform-wide backstop, TenantWriteGuardInterceptor, is explicitly NOT ACTIVE (its own Javadoc: 'Wiring status — NOT YET ACTIVE ... This bean exists as a stub'). For SEC-BCM-001 (createBia) the per-service defense is itself missing (no setOrganisationId). The create* paths that DO call setId(null)+setOrganisationId are presently safe, and the update* paths re-load an org-scoped entity and copy only whitelisted fields, so this is a defense-in-depth/info-level observation that amplifies the impact of any future endpoint that forgets the convention.
rootCause: Tenant-write integrity depends on a hand-applied per-method convention with no enforced backstop; the interceptor designed to catch omissions has never been wired into the Hibernate SessionFactory.
evidence: TenantWriteGuardInterceptor Javadoc lines 36-48: 'Wiring status — NOT YET ACTIVE. This bean exists as a stub so it can be code-reviewed and unit-tested before being wired into the EntityManager / SessionFactory.' BcmController.createPlan: `public BcmPlan createPlan(@RequestBody BcmPlan req)` — raw entity, no @Valid; defense is BcmService.createPlan `req.setId(null); req.setOrganisationId(TenantContext.getCurrentTenant());`.
impact: No direct exploit today on the create/update paths that follow the convention, but the platform has no enforced guard against a future (or already-missed, see SEC-BCM-001) write path that omits the id-null / org-stamp step, which would allow cross-tenant overwrite via JPA merge of an id-bearing body.
reproduction: N/A (defense-in-depth). Confirmable by code review: the interceptor is never registered via HibernatePropertiesCustomizer or hibernate.session_factory.interceptor.
resolution: Complete the interceptor wiring per its own pre-activation checklist (register via a HibernatePropertiesCustomizer bean, wrap legitimate cross-tenant sweeps in TenantContext.allowCrossTenantWrite(), add the attack-simulation tests), and migrate raw-entity @RequestBody write endpoints to validated request DTOs so organisationId/id can never be bound from the client.
references: CWE-915: Improperly Controlled Modification of Dynamically-Determined Object Attributes (Mass Assignment)
OWASP A08:2021 Software and Data Integrity Failures
OWASP API6:2023 Unrestricted Access to Sensitive Business Flows

title: Stale/incorrect LocaleConfig uses HTTP-session locale resolver in a declared-stateless API
cvss: Risk rationale: SessionLocaleResolver would create HttpSessions, contradicting the STATELESS design; minor session-fixation surface and dead-config confusion. Info.
description: LocaleConfig registers a SessionLocaleResolver and a LocaleChangeInterceptor (?lang=) — a server-side, session-backed i18n mechanism. This contradicts the platform's stateless design (SecurityConfig sets SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS; CLAUDE.md states 'No HTTP sessions on the server') and the project's documented approach that the standalone frontend handles i18n client-side (translations.js). A SessionLocaleResolver writes the locale into an HttpSession, which (a) would cause sessions to be created despite the stateless intent, and (b) the LocaleChangeInterceptor bean is not registered with the InterceptorRegistry in WebMvcConfig (addInterceptors is not overridden), so it is effectively dead config. Also note WebMvcConfig.addViewControllers redirects '/' to '/dashboard' and addResourceHandlers references classpath:/static/... and comments mention Thymeleaf @{} URLs — all leftovers from a server-rendered design that does not match this REST-only backend. These are correctness/cleanliness issues with a minor security angle (unexpected session creation = small session-fixation surface; dead config obscures the true security posture).
rootCause: Carried-over server-side-MVC configuration (session locale + Thymeleaf-era resource handlers/view controllers) that was never removed when the project became a stateless REST API with a separate static frontend.
impact: Minimal direct attacker impact. Risk is unintended HttpSession creation (contradicting STATELESS, a minor session-fixation footprint) and misleading dead configuration that complicates security review. The interceptor not being wired means ?lang switching does not even function server-side.
reproduction: 1. Review LocaleConfig vs SecurityConfig — SessionLocaleResolver vs STATELESS. 2. Note LocaleChangeInterceptor bean is never added in WebMvcConfig.addInterceptors (method absent) -> not active. 3. Confirm REST controllers do not rely on server locale (frontend i18n via translations.js per CLAUDE.md).
resolution: Remove the server-side locale machinery (or replace SessionLocaleResolver with AcceptHeaderLocaleResolver if server-side message localization is genuinely needed for validation messages). Prune the Thymeleaf-era view controller and static resource handlers in WebMvcConfig that no longer apply to a REST-only backend. This reduces attack surface and clarifies the stateless posture.
references: CWE-1059: Insufficient Technical Documentation / stale configuration

title: Knowledge-base read endpoints guarded only by isAuthenticated() (defence-in-depth)
cvss: Risk rationale: any authenticated user can read INTERNAL-visibility KB articles in their tenant; content sensitivity is generally low and org-scoped
description: `GET /api/kb/articles` and `GET /api/kb/articles/{slug}` are gated only by `isAuthenticated()`. The service is tenant-scoped and only returns PUBLISHED articles, and the entity carries a `visibility` field (default INTERNAL) — but the read endpoints do not enforce that visibility, so any authenticated user can read every PUBLISHED article in their org regardless of intended audience. Write/transition/delete are correctly role-gated. Listed as Info because KB content is generally low-sensitivity and properly tenant-isolated; flagged for consistency with the module-guard convention and because the `visibility` column implies an access distinction that is not enforced at read time.
rootCause: Read endpoints use bare authentication and do not consult the article's `visibility` attribute, so the modelled audience restriction is not enforced.
impact: Minor over-exposure within a tenant: articles intended for a narrower audience (per the unused `visibility` field) are readable by any logged-in user. No cross-tenant exposure.
reproduction:
1. Authenticate as any user.
2. `curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" http://localhost:8084/api/kb/articles` — returns all PUBLISHED articles for the tenant irrespective of their visibility setting.
resolution: If the `visibility` field is meant to restrict access, filter list/read results by the caller's authorities/role; otherwise document that all authenticated tenant users may read published KB content. Consider a KB:READ permission for consistency with other modules.
references: CWE-639: Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key

title: Legacy static dev server sends Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * and no security headers (no CSP / X-Frame-Options)
cvss: CVSS 2.0 — dev-only static server; clickjacking + missing defence-in-depth headers
description: The legacy frontend's Python static server (server.py) emits `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` (line 18) and no Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options, or X-Content-Type-Options headers. The v2 index.html likewise ships no CSP meta tag. Consequently the UI relies entirely on the application server / reverse proxy for clickjacking protection (X-Frame-Options/frame-ancestors) and has no Content-Security-Policy to act as a second line of defence against the XSS in SEC-FE-001 (e.g. a `default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'` policy would block inline-event-handler payloads and exfiltration to attacker hosts). This is rated Info because server.py is described in CLAUDE.md as a dev launcher, not the production server; the real risk lives in whatever serves the UI in staging/prod. It is called out so the production deployment is verified to set CSP + X-Frame-Options.
rootCause: Static file servers configured for developer convenience (open CORS, no headers); no CSP defined at the document level either.
evidence: server.py:18 `self.send_header('Access-Control-Allow-Origin', '*')`. No `Content-Security-Policy` / `X-Frame-Options` anywhere in server.py or tss-grc-ui-v2/index.html.
impact: Without a CSP, an XSS payload (SEC-FE-001) executes unhindered and can freely exfiltrate the sessionStorage token to any host. Without X-Frame-Options/frame-ancestors the app can be framed for clickjacking. `ACAO: *` on the static server is low-impact (it serves no credentialed JSON) but is poor hygiene.
reproduction: Load any UI page and inspect response headers (curl -I) — no CSP/X-Frame-Options present; ACAO: * present on the legacy static server.
resolution: In production, serve the UI behind a server/proxy that sets `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; object-src 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'`, `X-Frame-Options: DENY`, and `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`. Scope CORS to known origins rather than `*`. Optionally add a CSP `<meta http-equiv>` to index.html as a baseline.
patchBefore:
self.send_header('Access-Control-Allow-Origin', '*')
# (no CSP / X-Frame-Options / X-Content-Type-Options)
patchAfter:
self.send_header('Access-Control-Allow-Origin', 'http://localhost:5173')  # scope it
self.send_header('Content-Security-Policy', "default-src 'self'; object-src 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'")
self.send_header('X-Frame-Options', 'DENY')
self.send_header('X-Content-Type-Options', 'nosniff')
references: CWE-1021: Improper Restriction of Rendered UI Layers (Clickjacking)
OWASP Content Security Policy Cheat Sheet

title: Authentication user lookup is not tenant-scoped (findByUsername) — username uniqueness assumed across all tenants
cvss: Risk rationale: design assumption to verify — username collisions across tenants would let one tenant's login resolve another tenant's account
description: CustomUserDetailsService.loadUserByUsername() resolves the login principal with UserRepository.findByUsername(username), which is NOT scoped by organisationId (a findByUsernameAndOrganisationId variant exists and is used elsewhere). UserService.create() only enforces uniqueness per-org (existsByUsernameAndOrganisationId), so two tenants CAN hold the same username. If that happens, findByUsername returns whichever single row JPA picks (or throws on multiple), making login resolution ambiguous/non-deterministic across tenants. This is the authentication path (outside the assigned controller set) so it is reported as Info for the auth-module owners to confirm: either usernames are globally unique by DB constraint (then this is safe) or the login flow must disambiguate by tenant.
rootCause: Per-tenant uniqueness on create vs. global lookup on authenticate — the two are only consistent if a global unique constraint on username also exists.
evidence: UserRepository: Optional<User> findByUsername(String username);  // used by loadUserByUsername. Creation guard is existsByUsernameAndOrganisationId(req.username(), orgId) — per-org only.
impact: If a global unique constraint on username is absent, a duplicate username across tenants causes ambiguous authentication: a user could authenticate against another tenant's account (cross-tenant account confusion) or logins could fail nondeterministically. No exploit confirmed without DB schema review — hence Info.
reproduction: Schema/behaviour check: 1. Create user 'admin' in org 1 and org 2 (allowed by per-org guard). 2. Attempt login as 'admin' and observe which org's account/authorities are loaded. Confirm whether a unique index on iam.users(username) prevents step 1.
resolution: Either enforce a global unique index on username (documenting that usernames are tenant-global), or make the login flow tenant-aware (resolve via username+tenant) so authentication cannot bind to the wrong tenant's account.
patchBefore:
User user = userRepository.findByUsername(username)
    .orElseThrow(() -> new UsernameNotFoundException("User not found: " + username));
references: CWE-639: Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key
OWASP A07:2021 Identification and Authentication Failures

title: Splunk verifySsl flag is documented but never wired into the RestClient
cvss: N/A — fails safe (TLS always verified); correctness/expectation gap, not an exploitable weakness
description: SplunkProperties exposes verifySsl (default true) and the bean Javadoc says 'SSL verification is controlled via verifySsl'. In practice splunkRestClient() builds a SimpleClientHttpRequestFactory and never reads props.isVerifySsl(); the default JDK trust store is always used. The good news is the flag is effectively dead in the secure direction — setting verifySsl=false does NOT actually disable TLS verification (so there is no accidental cert-bypass). The risk is the inverse expectation gap: an operator may believe they can toggle verification and the /config endpoint reports verifySsl=true, masking that the setting has no effect. If a future change wires the flag through, the disable path must be guarded to non-dev profiles. Flagged as Info because nothing is currently exploitable.
rootCause: Configuration property declared and surfaced in /config but not consumed by the HTTP client factory.
impact: No direct security impact today (TLS stays verified). Operational confusion only: the toggle and its /config readout are misleading. Documented here so a later 'make verifySsl work' change does not introduce an insecure default.
reproduction:
1. Set grc.integrations.splunk.verify-ssl=false and mode=LIVE.
2. Observe outbound HEC calls still validate the server certificate (handshake fails against a self-signed host), proving the flag is inert; GET /config still reports verifySsl=false while behaviour is verified=true.
resolution: Either remove the unused property (and its /config field) to avoid confusion, or wire it through a custom request factory while restricting the insecure value to dev-only profiles with a loud startup warning.
patchBefore: // verifySsl declared in SplunkProperties, never consumed by splunkRestClient()
patchAfter:
// Option A: delete the verifySsl property + /config field.
// Option B (if needed): build a request factory honouring verifySsl, and on prod profiles refuse verifySsl=false.
references: CWE-1059: Incomplete Documentation of Program Execution

title: Gitleaks: placeholder tokens in integration docs (Splunk HEC / Tenable) are illustrative, not real
cvss: No exploitable risk — documentation placeholders, not live credentials
description: Gitleaks raised two 'generic-api-key' hits inside integration setup documentation. SPLUNK.md line 46 shows `export SPLUNK_HEC_TOKEN="00112233-4455-6677-8899-aabbccddeeff"` — a sequential dummy UUID inside a '## Switching from STUB to LIVE' how-to. TENABLE.md line 128 shows `export TENABLE_ACCESS_KEY="abc123def456..."` — an obvious truncated placeholder, immediately followed by `export TENABLE_SECRET_KEY="..."   # never commit` (line 129). Both are example env-var assignments instructing operators where to paste THEIR own credentials at deploy time. Neither is a working secret. The Splunk doc even instructs generating the companion webhook secret with `openssl rand -hex 32` (line 48), reinforcing that nothing real is committed.
rootCause: Generic-API-key entropy/regex rules in gitleaks match any quoted token-shaped string, including documentation placeholders, producing false positives.
evidence:
SPLUNK.md:46  `export SPLUNK_HEC_TOKEN="00112233-4455-6677-8899-aabbccddeeff"`
TENABLE.md:128-129  `export TENABLE_ACCESS_KEY="abc123def456..."
export TENABLE_SECRET_KEY="..."   # never commit`
impact: None. The strings are non-functional examples; using them against a real Splunk HEC or Tenable.sc endpoint would fail authentication. No secret is exposed.
reproduction: N/A — verified by reading the surrounding documentation context confirming these are placeholder values in a setup guide.
resolution: No remediation required. Optionally add these fingerprints to a gitleaks allowlist (.gitleaks.toml) to suppress recurring noise, or change the doc placeholders to an unmistakable form such as `<your-hec-token>` to avoid future scanner hits.
patchBefore:
export SPLUNK_HEC_TOKEN="00112233-4455-6677-8899-aabbccddeeff"
export TENABLE_ACCESS_KEY="abc123def456..."
patchAfter:
export SPLUNK_HEC_TOKEN="<your-splunk-hec-token>"
export TENABLE_ACCESS_KEY="<your-tenable-access-key>"

title: Gitleaks: 'grc.*.v1' strings are localStorage persistence keys, not secrets (false positive, 16 hits)
cvss: No risk — application namespace identifiers, not credentials
description: Sixteen of the twenty-one gitleaks hits are dotted, versioned string constants of the form `grc.<module>.<thing>.v1` (e.g. `grc.mfa.enrolment.v1`, `grc.risk.treatment.v1`, `grc.cyber.filing.v1`, `grc.whitelabel.v1`, `c5BreachNotification`). The entropy-based generic-api-key rule matched them. On inspection every one is a browser localStorage key name used by the frontend persistence layer. persistence.ts defines a `PERSISTENCE_REGISTRY` (lines 204+) listing these keys with human labels and a `backendReady` flag; mfa.ts line 8 (`const KEY = 'grc.mfa.enrolment.v1'`) and the lifecycle modules use them as storage keys for client-side state. They are public, non-secret application identifiers — they grant no access and protect nothing.
rootCause: Versioned dotted identifiers have enough character variety to trip the generic-API-key entropy heuristic, even though they are namespace strings rather than credentials.
evidence:
mfa.ts:8  `const KEY = 'grc.mfa.enrolment.v1';`
persistence.ts:206  `key: 'grc.chains.fires.v1',` (inside PERSISTENCE_REGISTRY, with labelEn 'Cross-module chain fires')
platformPersistence.ts:194  `localKey: 'grc.risk.treatment.v1',`
impact: None. These keys are inherently visible in any browser's devtools (Application > Local Storage); they convey no authorization and reveal no sensitive data.
reproduction: N/A — verified by opening each cited file; every match is a localStorage key constant / registry entry.
resolution: No remediation required. Suppress via a gitleaks allowlist regex such as `grc\.[a-z.]+\.v\d+` (and the `c5*/c7*` assessment-criterion keys) in .gitleaks.toml to remove this recurring false-positive class.
patchBefore: # .gitleaks.toml — no allowlist for app namespace keys (current state)
patchAfter:
# .gitleaks.toml
[allowlist]
regexes = [
  '''grc\.[a-z0-9.]+\.v\d+''',   # frontend localStorage key namespace
]
references: CWE-798: Use of Hard-coded Credentials (false positive)

title: Gitleaks: open-banking FAPI 'client' values are OAuth client identifiers in demo seed, not secrets
cvss: No risk — public OAuth client_id in non-production seed data; no paired client_secret committed
description: Gitleaks flagged `fapi_client="lean-prod-aspsp1-2024"` (line 185) as a generic API key. Tracing the parameter: `insert_tpp(...)` (signature line 35) writes `fapi_client` into the `fapi_client_id` column (INSERT column list, line 46). It is therefore an OAuth/FAPI client_id — a public identifier for a Third-Party Provider, not a credential. The value lives in `setup_openbanking_seed.py`, an idempotent demo-data seeding script that populates illustrative TPPs (Lean, Tarabut, Drahim, etc.) for the three demo tenants. There is no `client_secret`/private-key column in the insert and none is committed anywhere in the file (grep for client_secret/fapi_secret returns nothing). A FAPI client_id without its private key or mTLS cert grants no access.
rootCause: An OAuth client identifier in seed data matched the entropy-based generic-api-key rule; the rule cannot distinguish a public client_id from a secret.
evidence:
setup_openbanking_seed.py:46  `" sama_licence_ref, fapi_client_id, roles, country, status, "`
setup_openbanking_seed.py:185  `sama_licence="SAMA-OB-AISP-2022-001", fapi_client="lean-prod-aspsp1-2024",`  (passed to insert_tpp -> fapi_client_id column)
impact: None. Client identifiers are non-secret by OAuth design and these are fabricated demo TPP records for non-production tenants. No authentication material (client secret, signing key, mTLS cert) is exposed.
reproduction: N/A — verified by reading the insert_tpp definition and confirming the value maps to fapi_client_id and that no secret column exists in the script.
resolution: No remediation required. The value is correctly an identifier, not a secret. Optionally allowlist this fingerprint in .gitleaks.toml. Ensure that when LIVE open-banking integration is configured, the real FAPI client secrets / private keys are externalised (env / secret manager) and never committed — consistent with the prod-profile externalised-secrets posture.
patchBefore:
lean = insert_tpp(
    org, "TPP-LEAN-001", "Lean Technologies KSA", ...,
    sama_licence="SAMA-OB-AISP-2022-001", fapi_client="lean-prod-aspsp1-2024", ...)
patchAfter:
# unchanged — fapi_client is a public OAuth client_id (demo seed).
# Real client secrets are never seeded; they are env-sourced in LIVE mode.
references: CWE-798: Use of Hard-coded Credentials (false positive)
RFC 6749 Section 2.2: client identifiers are not confidential

title: Ethics case cross-entity link lookup queries CaseLink without org scoping (post-filter mitigates leak)
cvss: No direct exposure — cross-tenant rows are post-filtered out before response; defence-in-depth gap only
description: EthicsCaseService.linksForEntity calls linkRepo.findByEntityTypeAndEntityId(entityType, entityId) which is NOT organisation-scoped at the repository level (CaseLinkRepository has no org parameter). The result set therefore spans all tenants. The service then re-fetches each link's parent case and filters out those whose case.getOrganisationId() does not match the current tenant, so cross-tenant data is not returned to the caller. The exposure is closed by the post-filter, but the query itself reads other tenants' link rows and relies on a correct downstream filter — a fragile pattern that would leak if the filter were ever weakened. Note the controller endpoint is correctly gated by hasPermission('COMPLIANCE','READ').
rootCause: The inverse-lookup finder was derived from (entityType, entityId) only; the tenant scope is enforced indirectly via the parent EthicsCase rather than in the query.
evidence: CaseLinkRepository.java:10  List<CaseLink> findByEntityTypeAndEntityId(String entityType, Long entityId);  used at EthicsCaseService.java:190 then filtered c.getOrganisationId().equals(org) at line 192.
impact: No confidentiality breach today because the parent-case org filter discards out-of-tenant rows. The risk is defence-in-depth: a future refactor that trusts the link list directly would expose cross-tenant case metadata. Rated Info.
reproduction: Code-review only: the repository finder lacks an organisationId parameter; correctness depends entirely on the service-layer post-filter at EthicsCaseService.java:192.
resolution: Add organisationId to the finder (findByOrganisationIdAndEntityTypeAndEntityId) so tenant scoping is enforced in SQL, keeping the parent-case check as belt-and-braces.
patchBefore:
List<CaseLink> findByEntityTypeAndEntityId(String entityType, Long entityId);
// service: linkRepo.findByEntityTypeAndEntityId(entityType, entityId)
patchAfter:
List<CaseLink> findByOrganisationIdAndEntityTypeAndEntityId(Long organisationId, String entityType, Long entityId);
// service: linkRepo.findByOrganisationIdAndEntityTypeAndEntityId(org, entityType, entityId)

title: Bidirectional Unicode control characters in source (B613 x2) and assert in dev script (B101 x1)
cvss: Risk rationale: both are benign in context. The U+200F (RIGHT-TO-LEFT MARK) characters appear inside legitimate Arabic string literals for correct RTL rendering, not as a Trojan-Source code-reordering attack. The single assert is a sanity check in a dev helper. No security impact.
description: Bandit raised 2 B613 ('source file contains bidirectional control characters U+200F', CWE-838) hits and 1 B101 ('use of assert'). Verified setup_regreporting_seed.py:581 — the U+200F (RLM) sits inside an Arabic data string ('...USSD \u200f*900# وSS7/SIGTRAN...') to keep the RTL/LTR boundary around the *900# token rendering correctly; it is data, not control flow. .tmp/reset_pw.py:15 is 'assert "'" not in h' guarding that a generated bcrypt hash contains no single quote before string-building SQL.
rootCause: B613: legitimate use of RLM in mixed Arabic/Latin/number strings (the platform is Arabic-primary). B101: a dev-time invariant check written with assert (stripped under python -O).
evidence:
setup_regreporting_seed.py:580-581
        'الملخّص الشهري للحوادث السيبرانية، نسبة الالتزام بالتحديثات، الشذوذ المرصود '
        'على USSD \u200f*900# وSS7/SIGTRAN، وسجل تدوير مفاتيح HSM.',

.tmp/reset_pw.py:15
        assert "'" not in h
impact: None. The bidi marks affect only how Arabic strings render; they are not positioned to reorder code in a way that misleads a reviewer (Trojan-Source). The assert is dev-only; if these scripts were ever run under -O the guard would vanish, but the input (a bcrypt hash) cannot contain a quote, so the check is defensive only.
reproduction:
1. bandit -r . | grep -E 'B613|B101' -> 3 hits.
2. Open setup_regreporting_seed.py:581 -> RLM is inside an Arabic string literal.
3. Open .tmp/reset_pw.py:15 -> assert guarding hash content.
resolution: B613: no action needed; optionally normalise by using explicit \u200f escapes (already the case) so the marker is visible in diffs, and confirm no bidi overrides (U+202E) exist. B101: replace the assert with an explicit check that raises ValueError so it survives optimisation, if reset_pw.py is ever promoted beyond throwaway use.
patchBefore: assert "'" not in h
patchAfter:
if "'" in h:
    raise ValueError("unexpected single quote in bcrypt hash")
references: CWE-838: Inappropriate Encoding for Output Context

title: KRI sourceQuery stores arbitrary SQL/source text — latent injection surface when auto-fetchers are bound
cvss: Not currently exploitable — no code path executes sourceQuery today; flagged to prevent a future injection regression
description: KriDefinition persists a client-supplied sourceQueryType (allows the value 'SQL') and a free-form sourceQuery string (set via applyFields from KriDefinitionRequest.sourceQuery). The scheduler entry point KriMeasurementService.evaluateAll explicitly does NOT execute these queries today — it logs KRI_EVALUATION_SKIPPED with the comment 'Auto-fetcher not yet bound', so there is currently no SQL/OS execution and thus no live injection. However the stored intent is to later run that operator-authored SQL against the database. If a future slice wires a SQL runner that concatenates or directly executes sourceQuery, it becomes a stored second-order SQL injection (and the SQL would run with the application's DB credentials, which can read across tenants).
rootCause: Free-form, client-supplied query text (sourceQuery) is stored with the declared intent of later execution; no design-level constraint (parameterisation, query allow-list, or read-only/least-privilege execution account) is recorded against it.
impact: No impact in the current build (no execution path). If the SQL auto-fetcher is implemented naively, an operator (or an attacker who reaches the KRI write role) could store arbitrary SQL that the scheduler later executes with the app DB account, enabling cross-tenant data read/exfiltration or worse.
reproduction: Not exploitable today. Future: create a KRI with sourceQueryType=SQL and a malicious sourceQuery; if a SQL runner is later bound that executes it verbatim, the payload runs on the next scheduler tick.
resolution: When implementing the auto-fetcher, do not execute operator-supplied SQL directly: use a curated/parameterised metric catalogue, force every fetch through a read-only least-privilege DB role scoped to the tenant, and reject/escape any sourceQuery that is not a named, pre-approved metric. Add a test asserting evaluateAll cannot run free-form SQL.
patchBefore:
// Future risk: KriDefinition.sourceQuery (free-form, client-set) intended for later execution
    if (req.sourceQuery() != null) d.setSourceQuery(req.sourceQuery());
references: CWE-89 Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command

title: Well-known seeded application credentials documented and reset via committed scripts
cvss: Info — intentional demo/dev credentials; dangerous only if the same accounts/passwords survive into a production deployment
description: A fixed set of demo credentials following the `<Role>@12345` scheme (admin/Admin@12345, riskmanager/Risk@12345, auditor/Audit@12345, plus compliance/analyst/viewer in `.tmp/reset_pw.py`) is documented in CLAUDE.md and re-applied to `iam.users` by the committed `.tmp/reset_pw.py` script, which bcrypt-hashes each password and writes UPDATE statements. The hashing itself is sound (bcrypt, cost 10) and the script defends against quote injection in the hash (`assert "'" not in h`). This is a normal seeded-demo-account pattern and is Info-rated. The only real risk is the standard one: if these well-known accounts are not disabled/rotated before go-live, an attacker who has read the public docs can log in directly.
rootCause: Predictable, publicly-documented demo passwords are convenient for development and onboarding but become a backdoor if they persist into production.
evidence: .tmp/reset_pw.py:4-10 — creds dict with "auditor": "Audit@12345", "rmanager": "Risk@12345", ... ; line 14 — "bcrypt.hashpw(pw.encode('utf-8'), bcrypt.gensalt(rounds=10))"
impact: If demo accounts reach production unchanged, full admin takeover is trivial (admin/Admin@12345 is in the committed docs). No impact in a properly bootstrapped, separately-seeded production environment.
reproduction: 1. Read CLAUDE.md credential table. 2. POST {username:'admin',password:'Admin@12345'} to /api/v1/auth/login on any environment still carrying the seed accounts -> authenticated as PLATFORM_ADMIN.
resolution: Ensure the production bootstrap does NOT run the demo seed; enforce must-change-password on first login for any seeded account; add a startup guard that refuses to start in prod if a user with a known default password hash/flag exists. Keep `reset_pw.py` out of any production tooling path.
patchAfter:
# Dev/demo only. In prod, seed no default users, or force must_change_password=1
# and randomise the initial password per account (do not commit it).
creds = {u: secrets.token_urlsafe(16) for u in ("auditor","rmanager",...)}
print("Generated one-time passwords:", creds)  # show once, never commit
references: OWASP A07:2021 Identification and Authentication Failures

title: CI workflow embeds static test secrets in plaintext (env block)
category: Insertion of Sensitive Information into Source Code (CWE-540)
cvss: Info — values are explicitly throwaway CI-only test secrets, never used against real infrastructure
description: The CI workflow defines `JWT_SECRET`, `DB_USERNAME=sa`, and `DB_PASSWORD=ci-test-Sql123!` directly in the workflow `env:` block rather than as GitHub Actions secrets. The comment correctly states these are 'Test secrets — only used inside the CI runners,' and they satisfy `JwtTokenProvider.validateSecret` (32+ chars, not a placeholder) so `mvn verify` can boot the context. Because these are deliberately disposable CI-only values with no connection to production systems, the finding is Info. The note is hygiene: putting even test secrets in workflow env (vs. repository/Org secrets) trains contributors that committing credentials is acceptable and risks a future copy-paste of a real value.
rootCause: Test fixtures were inlined into the workflow for convenience; there is no policy distinguishing disposable CI values from real secrets.
evidence:
.github/workflows/ci.yml:18-21 — "# Test secrets — only used inside the CI runners.
  JWT_SECRET: ci-test-secret-32-or-more-chars-not-a-placeholder-12345
  DB_USERNAME: sa
  DB_PASSWORD: ci-test-Sql123!"
impact: No direct impact — the values are CI-scoped and not reused elsewhere. The residual risk is cultural/process: normalising plaintext secrets in workflow files.
reproduction: 1. Open .github/workflows/ci.yml. 2. Observe JWT_SECRET/DB_PASSWORD literals in the top-level env block.
resolution: Acceptable as-is given the values are throwaway. If tightening: move them to GitHub Actions repository secrets (`${{ secrets.CI_JWT_SECRET }}`) and reference there, keeping the workflow file free of literal credentials and reinforcing the no-plaintext-secrets norm.

title: 188 of 368 JPA entities re-declare the full audit/soft-delete/versioning column block instead of extending the existing BaseEntity mapped superclass
cvss: Not a security CVE. Maintainability risk rated High: ~4,500 LOC of copy-pasted persistence boilerplate spread across 188 files. A change to the audit model (e.g. adding a tenant column to the audit listener, renaming row_version, fixing the soft-delete contract) must be hand-applied 188 times, and the inline copies bypass the @CreatedDate/@LastModifiedBy/@EntityListeners(AuditingEntityListener) wiring that BaseEntity provides, so the duplicated entities silently lose automatic audit population.
description: jscpd reports 404 java-entity <-> java-entity clone instances totalling 5,940 duplicated lines — the single largest Java duplication cluster. The root of the cluster is an audit/soft-delete/versioning field group that is copy-pasted verbatim into entity after entity: createdByUserId, createdAt, updatedAt, createdBy, updatedBy, isDeleted, deletedAt, deletedBy, and a @Version row_version byte[]. A static scan of all @Entity classes shows 188 of 368 entities (51%) declare this inline `@Column(name = "is_deleted", nullable = false)` block, while 137 entities correctly extend the project's own `BaseEntity` mapped superclass which already defines the exact same nine columns plus id and a softDelete() helper. None of the 188 both extend BaseEntity and inline the block, so this is pure copy-paste, not field shadowing. The two largest individual entity clones jscpd found (ObligationAttestationCampaign:102-143 vs VendorBcpCampaign:107-148, 42 lines; EmergingRisk:118-157 vs ContractClause:57-76, 40 lines) are both instances of this block.
rootCause: A canonical BaseEntity (@MappedSuperclass, @EntityListeners(AuditingEntityListener.class), with @CreatedDate/@LastModifiedDate/@CreatedBy/@LastModifiedBy and @Version) already exists at common/model/BaseEntity.java and is used by 137 entities. New modules (aml, ndi, tprm/*, bcm/*, sust/*, audit_lc, etc.) were scaffolded by copying an existing entity file wholesale rather than extending BaseEntity, so each new entity re-typed the same audit columns. There is no architectural guardrail (e.g. an ArchUnit test) requiring entities to extend BaseEntity.
evidence: Static counts on tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module: `@Column(name = "is_deleted", nullable = false)` appears in 187 files; `@Column(name = "row_version", insertable = false, updatable = false)` in 33 files; cross-reference script result: 368 @Entity classes total, 188 with inline is_deleted block and NOT extending BaseEntity, 0 that both inline and extend, 137 clean (extends + no inline). jscpd statistics.formats.java = 1008 clones / 7.87% / 12,532 dup lines; entity<->entity sub-cluster = 404 clones / 5,940 dup lines. Example block in ObligationAttestationCampaign.java lines 116-142 is identical column-for-column to BaseEntity.java lines 22-49.
impact: Every change to the audit/soft-delete contract is an O(188) hand edit with high risk of one file being missed (drift). Entities that inline the columns instead of inheriting BaseEntity's @EntityListeners do not get JPA auditing auto-population, so createdBy/updatedBy may be silently null unless each service sets them manually — a correctness and traceability gap in a GRC product where audit trails are a compliance requirement (PDPL/SAMA). The ~4,500 duplicated lines also inflate review surface and bury the entity-specific fields that actually matter.
reproduction: 1) Open tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/common/model/BaseEntity.java — note id + 8 audit columns + softDelete(). 2) Open ObligationAttestationCampaign.java — note it does NOT extend BaseEntity yet redeclares id (36-38) and the audit block (116-142). 3) Run: grep -rl '@Column(name = "is_deleted", nullable = false)' tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module --include=*.java | wc -l  → 187. 4) Run the cross-reference confirming 188 such files do not extend BaseEntity.
resolution: Migrate the 188 standalone entities to `extends BaseEntity`: delete the inline id and the nine audit columns from each entity, add the extends clause, and drop the now-redundant @Id/@GeneratedValue. Where an entity used `createdByUserId` distinctly from BaseEntity's `createdBy`, reconcile to a single field. Do this module-by-module behind tests. Add an ArchUnit (or simple reflection) test asserting that every class annotated @Entity (excluding pure join/lookup tables) is assignable from BaseEntity, to prevent regression. Because @Where(clause = "is_deleted = 0") is still declared per-entity, keep that annotation; only the columns move to the superclass.

_verification.rationale: Confirmed. ObligationAttestationCampaign (declared 'public class ... {' with no extends) manually re-declares the full audit/soft-delete/versioning block at lines 116-142 (createdAt, updatedAt, createdBy, updatedBy, isDeleted, deletedAt, deletedBy, @Version rowVersion) plus id at 36-38 — every one of which already exists in com.tss.grc.common.model.BaseEntity (verified: same column names and @Version byte[] rowVersion). So this is genuine duplication of a mapped superclass. Magnitude verified: 369 @Entity classes total (claim 368) and 189 declare the is_deleted column inline (claim 188) — i.e. roughly half the domain model bypasses BaseEntity. High is on the aggressive side for a pure maintainability/DRY issue but defensible given the scale; severity retained.

title: TSX pages duplicate whole presentational components and helpers (ProgressBar, card components, bilingual pickers) across modules — 609 clones / 8,602 lines
cvss: Not a security issue. Maintainability rated High: 8,602 duplicated lines across 439 TSX sources (5.44% of frontend). UI fixes (accessibility, RTL direction, theming token changes) must be applied in many copies; the copies drift, producing inconsistent UX across modules in a product whose key selling point is a uniform bilingual UI.
description: tsx <-> tsx is the largest single duplication cluster overall: 609 clone instances / 8,602 duplicated lines. The duplication is concentrated in (a) per-page copies of small presentational helpers and (b) whole card/sub-components copied between sibling pages. Confirmed examples opened on disk: the `ProgressBar({percent,label})` component is byte-for-byte duplicated in ObligationCampaignsPage.tsx:344-365 and at least one other campaigns page; the `ActiveInjectCard`/`ResponseCard` components are copied between FacilitatorConsolePage.tsx (683-761) and ObserverDashboardPage.tsx (568-646) — a 45-line + 35-line back-to-back clone, the two largest TSX clones in the report; and the consent panel is duplicated between components/privacy/ConsentTab.tsx:16-57 and pages/detail/ConsentDetailPage.tsx:38-71. The single most-cloned file is pages/ndi/NdiPage.tsx with 69 clone instances / 1,001 dup lines, including an intra-file 40-line clone (NdiPage.tsx:747-786 vs 828-867).
rootCause: No shared component library for the recurring building blocks (progress bars, stat/metric cards, status pills, campaign tables, bilingual label pickers). New pages were created by copying a nearby page. The bilingual `isAr && xAr ? xAr : xEn` selection idiom appears in 160 TSX files inline rather than via one helper, and a `tlabel(...)`-style label picker is reimplemented in ~30 files.
evidence: jscpd statistics.formats.tsx = 609 clones / 5.44% / 7,993 dup lines (8,602 by per-clone line sum). Top TSX files by clone instances: NdiPage.tsx (69), EsgPage.tsx (49), AiLifecycleRecertificationsPage.tsx (43), BcmExerciseWizard.tsx (28), CptyCounterpartiesPage.tsx (25). Largest single TSX clone = FacilitatorConsolePage.tsx:683-727 vs ObserverDashboardPage.tsx:568-612 (45 lines). grep: `function ProgressBar` in 2 files (identical bodies), inline bilingual `isAr ?`/`isAr &&` picker pattern in 160 tsx files.
impact: Inconsistent and drift-prone UI: a fix to ProgressBar color thresholds, an RTL `dir` correction, or a design-token rename only lands in the page the developer happened to edit, leaving others stale. Doubles the review burden for every page and obscures genuinely page-specific logic. Increases bundle size with repeated component definitions.
reproduction: 1) Open tss-grc-ui-v2/src/pages/compliance/ObligationCampaignsPage.tsx:344-365 and compare ProgressBar to the same function in another campaigns page. 2) Diff FacilitatorConsolePage.tsx:683-761 against ObserverDashboardPage.tsx:568-646 — ActiveInjectCard/ResponseCard are identical. 3) grep -rl 'function ProgressBar' tss-grc-ui-v2/src --include=*.tsx → 2 files with identical bodies.
resolution: Extract the recurring presentational components into a shared module (e.g. src/components/ui/ProgressBar.tsx, StatCard.tsx, StatusPill.tsx, CampaignTable.tsx) and the bilingual selection into a single helper (e.g. src/lib/i18n.ts exporting `pick(isAr, ar, en)` and `tlabel(map, key, isAr)`), then replace the inline copies with imports. Co-locate the BCM crisis-exercise cards (ActiveInjectCard/ResponseCard) in one shared file imported by both the facilitator and observer pages. Prioritize the highest-clone files (NdiPage, EsgPage, the campaigns pages) first.

_verification.rationale: Confirmed with a magnitude caveat.
