The cited example is real: ObligationCampaignsPage.tsx defines a local ProgressBar component at lines 344-365 rather than importing a shared one (a components/ui dir exists). The named function 'ProgressBar' literally recurs in only 2 page files, so the headline reads stronger than a name-grep shows; however clone detectors measure token-level duplicate blocks, and the broader pattern is substantiated: 70 page files contain the same inline progress-bar style block (height:8 + borderRadius) and 153 page files contain inline bilingual ternaries (lang === 'ar' ? ...), across 313 pages / ~128k LOC. The exact '609 clones / 8,602 lines' figure is tool-derived and not independently reproduced here, but the duplication is genuine and widespread. High retained as a maintainability finding.

title: God class: DataOfficerService implements 10 sub-modules in 1054 LOC with 14 injected repositories
cvss: Maintainability risk: a 1054-LOC class with 14 collaborators and 10 distinct domains is the single highest-churn merge-conflict hotspot in the module; every DSR/Consent/DPIA/Breach/Notice/Retention/NDR/Catalog/Quality/Ethics change touches it.
description: DataOfficerService is a single @Service that owns the full lifecycle of ten unrelated PDPL/NDMO sub-modules (DSR, Consent, DPIA, Breach, Privacy Notice, Retention/Disposal, NDR, Catalog/Lineage, Quality, Ethics). It declares 7 state-machine maps, injects 14 repositories + 1 event publisher (lines 120-134), and contains ~30 public methods and ~13 static mapper methods. This is a textbook Single-Responsibility violation: the class has ten reasons to change.
rootCause: All ten sub-modules were placed in one class to 'share a single tenant-scoped event timeline and a consistent state-machine validator' (class Javadoc, lines 24-44). The shared infrastructure (timeline/emit/validate) does not require co-location of the ten domains.
evidence: 1054 LOC (wc -l). 14 `private final ...Repository` fields (lines 120-133) plus ApplicationEventPublisher (134). 7 static transition maps DSR_ALLOWED..ETHICS_ALLOWED (lines 52-118). Sub-modules numbered 1..10 in section banners.
impact: High coupling and low cohesion: any change to one regulatory surface forces recompilation/retesting of the whole class and maximises merge conflicts across teams. Unit testing requires mocking all 14 repositories even to exercise one path.
reproduction: Open the file; observe section banners '1. DSR' (136) through '10. Ethics' (697) and the 14-field constructor block (120-134).
resolution: Extract one @Service per sub-module (DsrService, ConsentService, DpiaService, ...), each injecting only its own repository. Hoist the shared timeline/emit/validate/org/currentUserId helpers into a single injectable collaborator (e.g. DataOfficerTimeline / a common base), and keep the dashboard aggregation in a thin DashboardService that fans out to the sub-services.
references: Robert C. Martin, Clean Code, ch.10 (Classes)

_verification.rationale: Confirmed. DataOfficerService is exactly 1054 LOC (verified) and injects exactly 14 *Repository fields (verified). Its own class javadoc states it 'Implements 10 PDPL/NDMO/SDAIA-mandated sub-modules in one service', and the file embeds eight distinct state-machine maps (DSR, DPIA, Breach, Notice, Disposal, NDR, Ethics, plus Consent/Retention described) — a textbook god class / SRP violation aggregating many bounded contexts behind one @Service. All quantitative claims match. High is appropriate for a Quality-phase maintainability finding of this size.

title: EvidenceMatrixService.matrix() is a triple-nested N+1 query loop (86 LOC, queries scale with the whole framework catalog)
cvss: High operational risk: a single GET /api/v1/evidence/matrix fires O(frameworks + controls + sub-controls) DB round-trips. For a full NCA ECC / ISO 27001 catalog (hundreds of sub-controls per tenant) this is hundreds of queries per page load, causing slow dashboards and DB connection-pool pressure under concurrent users. Not a security CVSS, but a clear scalability defect.
description: matrix() loops over every active framework (frameworkRepo.findAll(), line 64), then for each framework queries controls (controlRepo.findByFrameworkIdAndIsActiveTrue, line 71), then for each control queries sub-controls (subControlRepo.findByControlIdAndIsActiveTrue, line 77), then inside the innermost loop runs itemRepo.findBySubControl(org, s.getId()) once per sub-control (line 85) plus an in-memory method-mix tally. The number of SQL statements grows linearly with the size of the entire control catalog, not with the data actually requested. The method is also a single 86-LOC block with three levels of nested loops and several inline aggregations (freshest-expiry, method mix, freshness band), giving it high cyclomatic complexity.
rootCause: Per-row repository lookups inside nested loops instead of set-based / batch queries. The matrix is materialized by walking the object graph one entity at a time rather than fetching counts/aggregates in bulk.
evidence: Innermost call at line 85: `List<EvidenceItem> items = itemRepo.findBySubControl(org, s.getId());` executed once per sub-control, nested inside `for (EvidenceControl c : controls)` (line 74) which is nested inside `for (EvidenceFramework fw : frameworks)` (line 68). The sibling GrcExpertService.listExpertCatalog() solves the identical framework→control→sub-control rollup with batch finders (findByControlIdInAndIsActiveTrue) and three aggregate queries (aggregateStatusBySubControl / aggregateExpiryBySubControl / aggregateFreshApprovedBySubControl) — proving the batch pattern already exists in the same package.
impact: Dashboard latency grows with catalog size; DB load multiplies under concurrent tenants; the read-only transaction holds a connection for the full duration of the loop.
reproduction: Seed a tenant with a full ECC framework (~100+ sub-controls), enable Hibernate SQL logging (show_sql), call GET /api/v1/evidence/matrix, and count the emitted SELECT statements — it equals 1 (frameworks) + N(controls-per-fw) + M(subs-per-ctrl) + K(findBySubControl per sub-control).
resolution: Replace the per-sub-control itemRepo.findBySubControl call with batch aggregation queries keyed by sub-control id (mirroring GrcExpertService.aggregate*BySubControl), fetch all controls/sub-controls for the active frameworks with findBy...In finders, then assemble the matrix in memory from the pre-fetched maps. Extract the sub-control block builder into a private helper to reduce the method below ~30 LOC.
references: Compare GrcExpertService.listExpertCatalog (same module) which uses aggregate queries

_verification.rationale: Verified in EvidenceMatrixService.java:57-143. matrix() loops frameworkRepo.findAll() (64) -> controlRepo.findByFrameworkIdAndIsActiveTrue (71) -> subControlRepo.findByControlIdAndIsActiveTrue (77) -> itemRepo.findBySubControl(org, s.getId()) per sub-control (85), with inline aggregations in one ~86-LOC method. Genuine triple/quad-nested N+1 plus high cyclomatic complexity. The batch pattern that fixes it already exists in the same package — GrcExpertService uses findByFrameworkIdInAndIsActiveTrue / findByControlIdInAndIsActiveTrue + aggregateStatusBySubControl/aggregateExpiryBySubControl/aggregateFreshApprovedBySubControl. Real quality defect; High is right.

title: EvidenceItemService.toResponse() issues up to 4 lookup queries per item, causing N+1 on every list/page endpoint
cvss: High operational risk: every list(), listExpired(), listBySubControl() and page response maps each EvidenceItem through toResponse(), which performs up to four extra single-row DB reads (sub-control, control, framework, owner). A 20-row page therefore costs up to 80 extra queries.
description: toResponse(EvidenceItem) resolves the sub-control code/name (subControlRepository.findById, line 390), then the parent control (controlRepository.findById, line 394), then the framework (frameworkRepository.findById, line 397), then the owner's name (userRepository.findById, line 405). Because list()/page().map(this::toResponse) (lines 110-117) and the other read methods all funnel through this mapper, the per-item cost is multiplied across every result row — a classic N+1.
rootCause: Enrichment by per-row findById inside a response mapper that is invoked once per row in a collection/page, instead of batching the joins or projecting them in the query.
evidence: Lines 389-407 chain four findById calls per item; list() at line 116 does `return page.map(this::toResponse);` so the mapper runs once per page row.
impact: Slow list endpoints and dashboard widgets, multiplied DB load. Latency scales with page size.
reproduction: Enable show_sql, GET /api/v1/evidence/items?size=20 and count SELECTs — base query plus up to 4 lookups per returned item.
resolution: Either (a) project the joined sub-control/control/framework codes and owner name directly in the EvidenceItemRepository query (DTO projection / JOIN FETCH), or (b) pre-fetch the referenced sub-controls/controls/frameworks/owners in bulk for the page and pass lookup maps into toResponse.

_verification.rationale: Verified in EvidenceItemService.java. toResponse() (lines 386-422) chains up to 4 findById lookups per item: subControlRepository.findById -> controlRepository.findById -> frameworkRepository.findById, plus userRepository.findById for the owner. It is invoked per-row on list/page endpoints: list() at line 116 does page.map(this::toResponse), and listExpired() (132) and listBySubControl() (139) do .stream().map(this::toResponse).toList(). This is a textbook N+1 with no batch fetch or JOIN mitigation. Severity High is appropriate for a per-row query-amplification defect on collection endpoints.

title: Two unrelated PolicyService classes with conflicting state machines split policy logic across modules
cvss: Maintainability risk: two same-named services with divergent lifecycles cause developer confusion and require a Spring bean qualifier hack; a change to 'policy lifecycle' can silently target the wrong code path.
description: There are two distinct classes named PolicyService. module/policy/service/PolicyService (V79, bean 'policyManagementService', 517 LOC) operates on PolicyDocument/PolicyException/PolicyAttestation with a DRAFT->REVIEW->APPROVED->PUBLISHED->EXPIRED|ARCHIVED state machine. module/compliance/service/PolicyService (176 LOC) operates on a separate Policy entity with a completely different DRAFT->LEGAL_REVIEW->EXEC_APPROVAL->PUBLISHED->REVIEW_DUE->RETIRED|REJECTED state machine. Two policy entities (PolicyDocument vs Policy), two services, two controllers (PolicyController vs RegChangePolicyController), and two state machines model the same business concept ('an organisational policy and its lifecycle'). The compliance PolicyService had to be left default-named and the policy module's one explicitly qualified ('@Service("policyManagementService")') with the comment 'because module.compliance ships another PolicyService' to avoid a bean-name collision.
rootCause: Two parallel implementations of policy management were built in separate sprints (compliance §5.3 rec #2 vs V79 policy module) without consolidating onto a single entity/service. No domain owner reconciled them.
evidence: policy/PolicyService.java:38 `@Service("policyManagementService")` with line-37 comment 'Bean qualified ... because module.compliance ships another PolicyService.' compliance/PolicyService.java:26 `public class PolicyService` (default bean name). Conflicting transition guards: policy/PolicyService.java:223-230 (DRAFT->REVIEW->APPROVED->PUBLISHED) vs compliance/PolicyService.java:88-155 (DRAFT->LEGAL_REVIEW->EXEC_APPROVAL->PUBLISHED).
impact: Developers and AI assistants editing 'policy lifecycle' frequently land in the wrong class. Status vocabularies diverge (REVIEW vs LEGAL_REVIEW; APPROVED vs EXEC_APPROVAL), so reporting/automation rules keyed on policy status must special-case both. Bug fixes applied to one are not reflected in the other.
reproduction: Search the codebase for `class PolicyService` — two hits in different packages. Inspect their `transition`/lifecycle methods to confirm divergent status enums.
resolution: Pick one canonical policy entity + service. Migrate the compliance Policy lifecycle onto the policy module's PolicyDocument (or vice-versa), deprecate the redundant class, and remove the bean-name qualifier hack. If both must coexist short-term, rename them to disambiguate (e.g. PolicyDocumentService vs LegacyCompliancePolicyService).

_verification.rationale: Two distinct PolicyService classes exist and were both read in full. module.compliance.service.PolicyService (cited lines 37-176) implements DRAFT -> LEGAL_REVIEW -> EXEC_APPROVAL -> PUBLISHED -> REVIEW_DUE -> RETIRED -> REJECTED. module.policy.service.PolicyService implements DRAFT -> REVIEW -> APPROVED -> PUBLISHED -> EXPIRED -> ARCHIVED (and is explicitly bean-qualified 'policyManagementService' because, per its own Javadoc, 'module.compliance ships another PolicyService'). These are two unrelated services with genuinely conflicting state machines and different Policy entities, splitting policy lifecycle logic across modules. Confirmed.

title: FrameworkAnchorController is a fat controller: 8 injected repositories across 4 modules, business logic in the web layer
cvss: Layering violation: a @RestController performs cross-module data aggregation, satisfaction tallying, and maturity averaging that belong in a service. Tightly couples the web layer to privacy/risk/compliance internals and is untestable without the full repository graph.
description: The controller injects 8 repositories directly — FrameworkRepository, PolicyRepository, PolicyFrameworkMappingRepository, AuditFindingRepository, ControlRepository, plus DpiaRepository (privacy module), KriDefinitionRepository and RiskRepository (risk module). It has no service layer at all: every endpoint builds raw HashMap rows by hand and the coverage() endpoint (lines 153-211, ~58 LOC) loops over frameworks computing satisfaction tallies (FULL/PARTIAL/OUT_OF_SCOPE/NA), open/closed finding counts, implemented-control counts, average maturity, and DPIA/KRI/risk counts. This is business logic in a controller and a controller reaching into other modules' repositories — both violate the documented layering (controller -> service -> repository) in CLAUDE.md.
rootCause: No FrameworkAnchorService was created; the aggregation logic was written inline in the controller and pulls peer modules' repositories rather than calling their services.
evidence: Fields at lines 54-61 inject 8 repositories including `private final DpiaRepository dpiaRepo;` (privacy), `private final KriDefinitionRepository kriRepo;` and `private final RiskRepository riskRepo;` (risk). coverage() lines 163-205 perform per-framework switch tallies and `Math.round((maturitySum * 10.0) / ctrls.size()) / 10.0`. jscpd flags the import/field block as duplicated with bcm/DependencyGraphController (FrameworkAnchorController.java:20-33 <=> DependencyGraphController.java:7-20).
impact: Cannot unit-test aggregation without standing up 8 repositories; changes to privacy/risk repository signatures break a compliance controller; the controller class is 347 LOC of mixed concerns and grows with every new anchorable entity type.
reproduction: Open FrameworkAnchorController; count `private final ...Repository` fields (8) and note coverage()/risksForFramework() build domain aggregates inline.
resolution: Extract a FrameworkAnchorService that owns coverage()/policiesForFramework()/etc. Have it call the owning modules' read services (or expose dedicated repository methods) rather than wiring foreign repositories into the web layer. Return typed DTOs instead of List<Map<String,Object>>.

_verification.rationale: FrameworkAnchorController (lines 52-339) injects exactly 8 repositories spanning 4 modules: FrameworkRepository, PolicyRepository, PolicyFrameworkMappingRepository, AuditFindingRepository, ControlRepository (compliance), DpiaRepository (privacy), KriDefinitionRepository and RiskRepository (risk). It runs non-trivial business logic in the web layer (coverage() aggregates satisfaction tallies, implemented-control counts, average-maturity math, union-by-id of risks across two framework dimensions). Fat controller / layering violation confirmed at the cited range.

title: Two parallel SAMA-outsourcing implementations (module/outsourcing vs module/tprm/outsourcing) duplicate the same regulatory bounded context
cvss: Maintainability risk: two complete, independently-evolving codebases implement the same SAMA Rules Governing Outsourcing domain. A regulatory change (e.g. SAMA notification window) must be applied in two places or one silently drifts. Not exploitable, but high long-term defect/divergence cost.
description: The codebase contains two independent SAMA-outsourcing modules. `module/outsourcing` (Sprint 30) defines entity `OutsourcingArrangement` mapped to schema `outsourcing.outsourcing_arrangement` with state machine PROPOSED->RISK_ASSESSED->BOARD_APPROVED->SAMA_NOTIFIED->LIVE->.... `module/tprm/outsourcing` (Sprint 13) defines a DIFFERENT `OutsourcingArrangement` mapped to schema `tprm.outsourcing_arrangement` with a different state machine PLANNED->DUE_DILIGENCE->AWAITING_SAMA->APPROVED->ACTIVE->.... Both ship their own `OutsourcingController`, `OutsourcingDtos`, repositories and services. They coexist only because they use different bean names (`outsourcingCloudController`) and base paths (`/api/v1/outsourcing` vs `/api/v1/tprm/outsourcing`).
rootCause: Two sprints (13 and 30) each built a SAMA-outsourcing register without consolidating onto a shared module. The bounded context (SAMA outsourcing governance) is the same; only the surrounding sprint scope differed.
evidence:
module/outsourcing/entity/OutsourcingArrangement.java:25-28  -> @Entity(name = "OutsourcingCloudArrangement") @Table(schema = "outsourcing", name = "outsourcing_arrangement"); state machine PROPOSED->...->SAMA_NOTIFIED->LIVE.
module/tprm/outsourcing/entity/OutsourcingArrangement.java:37-39 -> @Table(schema = "tprm", name = "outsourcing_arrangement"); state machine PLANNED->DUE_DILIGENCE->AWAITING_SAMA->APPROVED->ACTIVE.
Controllers: /api/v1/outsourcing (OutsourcingController.java:15) vs /api/v1/tprm/outsourcing (OutsourcingController.java:78). Two services totalling 612 + 473 LOC implementing the same regulation.
impact: Regulatory logic (materiality, SAMA non-objection, exit plans, 60-day notification) must be maintained twice. Auditors and operators see two outsourcing registers with conflicting lifecycles. High risk of one path being patched while the other rots.
reproduction: Open both OutsourcingArrangement entities and both OutsourcingControllers. Note identical domain (SAMA outsourcing) with divergent schemas, lifecycles and endpoints, both wired into the running app.
resolution: Pick one canonical module for SAMA outsourcing. Migrate the second module's data/endpoints onto it (or formally split responsibilities: e.g. `module/outsourcing` = cloud-service governance, `module/tprm/outsourcing` = vendor-arrangement governance) and document the boundary. At minimum, extract the shared lifecycle/materiality rules into one place so they cannot diverge.
references: Domain-Driven Design: one bounded context, one model

_verification.rationale: Two parallel SAMA-outsourcing bounded contexts confirmed by directory listing and source. module/outsourcing/* has OutsourcingArrangement entity+repository+controller+DTOs and OutsourcingService.java (verified exactly 612 lines, matching cited 1-612) with state machine PROPOSED->RISK_ASSESSED->BOARD_APPROVED->SAMA_NOTIFIED->LIVE... module/tprm/outsourcing/* independently re-implements the same regulatory context with its own OutsourcingArrangement entity+repository+controller+DTOs and OutsourcingArrangementService (plus DueDiligence/Monitoring/ExitPlan services), state machine PLANNED->DUE_DILIGENCE->AWAITING_SAMA->APPROVED->ACTIVE... Both cite SAMA Rules Governing Outsourcing. Genuine duplicated bounded context with divergent state vocabularies.

title: Integration LIVE clients duplicate the retry / exponential-backoff / sleep / url harness across CrowdStrike, Tenable and Splunk
cvss: Maintainability + correctness drift: the retry/backoff/401-refresh harness is the most safety-critical code in the adapters (it gates how the SOC integration behaves under partial outage). Three independent copies guarantee they will diverge; a fix to one (e.g. honour Retry-After) will not propagate.
description: Each LIVE integration client re-implements the same retry harness: a `BACKOFF_CAP_MS` constant, a `for (attempt=1..maxAttempts)` loop that catches `HttpServerErrorException | ResourceAccessException`, sleeps `delayMs`, multiplies by `backoffMultiplier` capped at `BACKOFF_CAP_MS`, a `doWithRetryOn5xx(Supplier)` wrapper, a private `sleep(long)` that re-throws on interrupt, and a `url(String path)` base-URL composer that strips a trailing slash. LiveTenableClient further contains THREE near-identical retry loops internally (the per-action POST loop, `runOutboundDelete` at 270-303, and `doWithRetryOn5xx` at 306-326).
rootCause: Per-vendor adapter packages were built by copying a reference client. No shared `AbstractRetryingRestClient` / retry utility was extracted.
evidence: grep counts: `BACKOFF_CAP_MS` in 3 files (crowdstrike, splunk, tenable LiveClient); `private static void sleep(long ms)` in 3 files; `doWithRetryOn5xx` in 2 files. Within LiveTenableClient the retry+backoff loop body (lines 255-262, 291-298, 311-321) is repeated 3x; jscpd also flags LiveTenableClient.java[290-301]<=>[313-324] as an intra-file duplicate.
impact: A resilience bug or required enhancement (jitter, Retry-After header, idempotency) must be fixed in 3+ places. Already shows drift: CrowdStrike retries with a one-shot 401 token refresh; Tenable's loop does not.
reproduction: Compare the retry loop in LiveCrowdStrikeClient.runDeviceAction (151-199) with LiveTenableClient (220-267) and LiveSplunkClient. Note identical structure and the duplicated `sleep`/`url`/`BACKOFF_CAP_MS`.
resolution: Extract a shared retry utility (e.g. `RestRetrySupport.withRetry(RetryConfig, Supplier<T>)`) or a Spring Retry / Resilience4j policy bean, and a shared `baseUrl(path)` helper. Each client supplies only the call and the vendor-specific 401 handling.

_verification.rationale: Verified the retry/backoff harness is copy-pasted across all three LIVE clients. LiveCrowdStrikeClient (lines 151-230) has the per-attempt loop and a doWithRetryOn5xx supplier using props.getRetry().getMaxAttempts()/getInitialDelayMs()/getBackoffMultiplier(), BACKOFF_CAP_MS=30_000L, sleep(delayMs), and catch(HttpServerErrorException | ResourceAccessException). LiveTenableClient repeats the identical pattern (BACKOFF_CAP_MS=30_000L line 76, doWithRetryOn5xx line 306, same delayMs = Math.min(BACKOFF_CAP_MS, Math.max(delayMs+1L, delayMs*mult)) line 320). LiveSplunkClient repeats it again (BACKOFF_CAP_MS=30_000L line 49, same loop lines 69-100). Three independent copies of the resilience logic. Confirmed.

title: Systemic dead-code: no-op _touch() methods and KEEP_* dummy fields used to suppress unused-import warnings across 11 classes
cvss: No runtime risk, but a pervasive maintainability smell: 11 classes carry deliberately useless members that confuse readers, defeat the compiler/IDE's unused-detection, and signal that genuinely unused imports/fields/loggers were papered over rather than removed.
description: A repeated anti-pattern appears across the assigned modules: a private no-op method `_touch()` (variously `{ log.trace("bound"); }` or `{ Objects.requireNonNull(this); }`) annotated `@SuppressWarnings("unused")`, plus dummy `private static final Class<?> KEEP = SomeType.class;` fields whose only purpose is to keep an otherwise-unused import 'referenced'. ExportService even comments `// Suppress unused warning for CellRangeAddress import (kept for future merging)`. CalendarService adds an unused `label()` method and `OBJECTS_KEEP_IMPORT = Objects.equals("a","a")`. These exist solely to silence the compiler/IDE rather than deleting the dead import, field, or logger they pretend to use.
rootCause: Imports / loggers / utility-class references became unused after refactors, but instead of deleting them the author added a fake consumer (`_touch`, `KEEP`) to suppress the warning. The pattern then got copy-pasted as new classes were created from old ones.
evidence: StrategyRoiService.java:536  `private Optional<StrategyRoiAnalysis> _touch() { log.trace("bound"); return Optional.empty(); }`  — keeps the otherwise-unused `Optional` import and `log` field alive. ExportService.java:494-495  `@SuppressWarnings("unused") private static final Class<?> KEEP = CellRangeAddress.class;`. BoardPackPptxService.java:403-406 has two such fields (KEEP_PICTURE_DATA, KEEP_TABLE_CELL). grep across the four modules: 10 distinct files match `_touch|KEEP|OBJECTS_KEEP_IMPORT` (11 member sites).
impact: Readers waste time deciphering why a service has a method that does nothing. The fake references mask which imports are truly needed, so the codebase can never be cleanly linted; future unused code hides behind the same noise. Each `_touch` is also a (tiny) reflectively-reachable method on a Spring bean.
reproduction: Run `rg -n "_touch|private static final Class<\?> KEEP|OBJECTS_KEEP_IMPORT" tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/{bcm,platform,dashboard,reporting}` — 10 files, ~11 member declarations.
resolution: Delete each `_touch()` method and each `KEEP*`/`OBJECTS_KEEP_IMPORT` field, then remove the now-genuinely-unused imports, loggers, and fields they were shielding. If a logger field (e.g. `log` in StrategyRoiService) has no real call site, drop the field and its slf4j imports. Configure the build (e.g. error-prone / checkstyle RedundantImport) to fail on unused imports so the workaround cannot reappear.

title: Duplicated runtime-projection helpers between ExerciseObserverService and ExerciseRuntimeService (summarise / toInjectView / toResponseView / nullSafe / truncate)
cvss: Two sibling services in the same sub-package carry byte-for-byte copies of the run-summary, inject-view and response-view projection logic. A change to the projection (or the inject-status set used to compute counts) must be made in two places or the two views silently diverge.
description: ExerciseObserverService reimplements `summarise(ExerciseRun)`, `toInjectView(...)`, `toResponseView(...)`, `nullSafe(...)` and `truncate(...)` identically to ExerciseRuntimeService. jscpd flags two clones between these files (27 lines / 195 tokens at ExerciseObserverService 589-615 ↔ ExerciseRuntimeService 615-641, and 16 lines / 171 tokens at 488-503 ↔ 749-764). Both `summarise` implementations issue five separate `countByOrganisationIdAndExerciseRunIdAndStatus` queries to derive total/dispatched/pending counts (see also QUAL-BCMP-006).
rootCause: ExerciseObserverService was created by copy-pasting projection helpers from ExerciseRuntimeService instead of extracting a shared mapper/projection component for the runtime entities.
evidence: ExerciseObserverService.java:593-602 `private InjectView toInjectView(Long orgId, ExerciseRunInject i) {...}` is identical to ExerciseRuntimeService.java:619-628. `toResponseView` (Observer 604-613) == Runtime 630-639. `nullSafe`/`truncate` duplicated (Observer 634-639, Runtime 646-653). jscpd-report.json lists both blocks as duplicates.
impact: Bug-fix and behaviour drift risk: e.g. if the inject-status taxonomy gains a new state, one `summarise` will count it and the other will not, producing inconsistent RunSummary totals depending on which service rendered them.
reproduction: Diff the two helper regions, or open audit/raw/jscpd/jscpd-report.json and filter for ExerciseObserverService vs ExerciseRuntimeService.
resolution: Extract a package-private `ExerciseRunProjections` (or a `@Component RuntimeViewMapper`) under `bcm/cycle/runtime` exposing `summarise`, `toInjectView`, `toResponseView`, plus the shared `nullSafe`/`truncate`. Inject it into both services. Consolidating also fixes the count-query fan-out in one place.

title: God service: BuyerGapService bundles 7 unrelated concerns and reaches into 6 other modules' repositories
cvss: A single 548-line service owns ERM risk-control linkage, appetite variance, evidence-freshness sweeps, evidence connectors, privacy cross-border listings, DSR SLA sweeps, and PDPL 72h crisis sweeps. It directly wires repositories from risk, evidence, privacy, privacy_lc, and bcm.cycle — a Single-Responsibility and module-boundary violation that concentrates cross-cutting blast radius in one class.
description: BuyerGapService is explicitly described in its own Javadoc as a grab-bag ("combined backend for the three module gaps the May-2026 buyer assessment flagged"). It injects 8 repositories spanning RiskControlRepository, RiskRepository, RiskAttestationRepository (risk module), EvidenceItemRepository, EvidenceConnectorRepository (evidence module), ProcessingActivityRepository (privacy module), DsrCaseRepository (privacy_lc module), and CrisisEventRepository (bcm.cycle module), and runs raw native/JPQL against risk.risks, risk.risk_appetite_statements, and EvidenceItem. It contains 7 distinct public operations plus 6 nested record DTOs. The class admits the design is convenience-driven: "Bundled into one service because each piece is a thin orchestrator ... Splitting into three services would spread the audit-trail wiring across near-empty classes."
rootCause: Organised by delivery milestone (a buyer-assessment checklist) rather than by domain. The platform module became a dumping ground for cross-module 'completion' logic that properly belongs in the risk, evidence, privacy, and bcm services.
evidence: Constructor-injected repos at lines 60-69 cross 5 module packages. appetiteVariance() (146-191) hand-writes a native join over risk.risks + risk.risk_appetite_statements. pdpl72hSweep() (480-521) mutates bcm CrisisEvent rows. evidenceFreshnessSweep() (219-270) mutates evidence EvidenceItem rows. Class length: 548 LOC.
impact: Any change to risk, evidence, privacy, or bcm schemas can force edits to this platform-layer class; the class cannot be reasoned about or tested in isolation; module ownership is blurred so two teams touch the same file. Cross-module repo reach circumvents the per-module service layer that owns audit/event wiring.
reproduction: Open the file; count distinct module packages in the import block (risk, evidence, privacy, privacy_lc, bcm.cycle) and the 7 public methods.
resolution: Split into domain-aligned services living in their owning modules: move risk-control linkage + appetite variance + attestation sweep into the risk module, the evidence freshness sweep + connector registry into the evidence module, and the DSR/PDPL sweeps into privacy/bcm respectively. If a thin orchestration facade is still wanted for the scheduler, have it delegate to those services rather than owning their repositories.

title: Long, high-complexity method: CrisisEventService.getActiveCrisisSummary() (114 LOC) embeds the entire multi-regulator deadline engine inline
cvss: A single 114-line method computes the shortest regulatory notification deadline across five Saudi regulators (SDAIA/PDPL, NCA, SAMA Cyber, SAMA BCF, NCEMA) with ~10 nested severity/flag conditionals, then derives escalation tier, an Arabic next-action label, builds a 16-field row, and sorts with a 6-branch comparator — all in one place. High branching makes the regulator-window rules hard to test and easy to break.
description: getActiveCrisisSummary() loops active crises and, per crisis, runs five branch blocks (lines 141-173) to find the earliest regulatory deadline, mixing severity thresholds (>=3, >=4), boolean flags (personalDataAffected, cyberRelated) and window constants. It then computes an escalation tier (3-way), a 6-case Arabic label switch, constructs a 16-arg row, and finally sorts via a comparator with six null-handling branches. The deadline computation is reusable domain logic (the same windows appear in RegulatorCountdownService and BuyerGapService.pdpl72hSweep) but is locked inside this view method.
rootCause: The mobile-summary view was built end-to-end in one method; the regulatory-deadline rules were never extracted into a dedicated, unit-testable component.
evidence: Method spans lines 125-238 (114 LOC, the largest in the 650-LOC file per a brace-depth scan). Branch count in the deadline block alone: 5 outer `if` + nested severity/comparison conditions ≈ cyclomatic complexity well above 15 for the method.
impact: The regulator-deadline logic is hard to test in isolation, easy to get wrong (a misplaced `isBefore` silently picks the wrong regulator/deadline), and is duplicated conceptually elsewhere. Long method hampers review and future regulator additions.
reproduction: Open lines 125-238; count the conditional branches in 141-173 and the comparator 221-236.
resolution: Extract a `RegulatoryDeadlineCalculator` returning `record Deadline(String regulator, LocalDateTime at)` from a `CrisisEvent`, with one unit test per regulator window. Extract `escalationTier(sev)` and `nextActionLabel(status)` helpers. Reduce getActiveCrisisSummary() to: load -> map(row) -> sort, delegating to the calculator and a named `Comparator`.

title: DashboardStats 'open critical' / 'open high' tiles are fed total counts, and pendingTasks is hardcoded 0L
cvss: The 15-arg DashboardStats record is constructed with positional args; positions 10/11 (openCriticalRisks/openHighRisks) are passed the SAME variables as positions 2/3 (criticalRisks/highRisks), so the 'open critical' and 'open high' dashboard tiles actually display the total critical/high counts, not the open subset. pendingTasks is hardcoded 0L. Misleading executive KPIs masquerading as real data.
description: In getStats(), the DashboardStats constructor call is `new DashboardStats(total, critical, high, medium, low, open, closed, totalUsers, activeUsers, critical, high, openIncidents, complianceScore, 0L, overdueItems)`. The record fields at those positions are `openCriticalRisks` and `openHighRisks` (DashboardStats.java:14) — explicitly documented as 'Aliases used by the dashboard UI'. They are populated with the unfiltered `critical`/`high` totals, so 'open critical risks' equals 'critical risks'. `pendingTasks` (position 14) is the literal `0L`, a placeholder the DTO comment confirms ('0 until those modules are implemented'). Passing 15 positional longs with no field names is itself error-prone and is what allowed this aliasing to go unnoticed.
rootCause: A wide positional record + duplicated UI 'alias' fields encouraged copy-pasting the total values rather than querying the open subset (e.g. countByOrganisationIdAndRiskLevelAndStatus). No compiler help because every parameter is `long`.
evidence: DashboardService.java:74-75 passes `critical`/`high` twice and `0L` once. DashboardStats.java:14-19 declares openCriticalRisks, openHighRisks, openIncidents, complianceScore, pendingTasks.
impact: The dashboard reports inflated 'open critical/high' figures (closed criticals are counted as open) and a permanently-zero 'pending tasks' tile, undermining the credibility of the executive dashboard — a core selling feature.
reproduction: Seed a CRITICAL risk in CLOSED status; call getStats(); observe openCriticalRisks == criticalRisks (closed ones included). pendingTasks is always 0.
resolution: Either compute the real open-by-level counts (add countByOrganisationIdAndRiskLevelAndStatus finders and pass them) or remove the redundant alias fields and have the UI derive them. Replace the wide positional constructor with a builder or named-component construction so position-mismatch bugs are impossible. If pendingTasks is genuinely not yet implemented, document it as such or drop the field.
patchBefore:
return new DashboardStats(total, critical, high, medium, low, open, closed,
        totalUsers, activeUsers, critical, high, openIncidents, complianceScore, 0L, overdueItems);

title: N+1 query pattern in KRI rendering (BoardPackService, ExportService) and 5-query fan-out in run summarise()
cvss: KRI report sections call findFirstByKriIdOrderByReadingAtDesc once per KRI to compute band counts, then again per KRI to fill the table — 2 queries per KRI on top of the list query. The board pack's executive summary also re-runs the same risk page query twice. Run summaries issue five count queries each. These multiply DB round-trips on read-heavy reporting endpoints.
description: BoardPackService.renderKris() loops KRIs computing band counts via readingRepo.findFirstByKriIdOrderByReadingAtDesc(k.getId()) (line 298), then loops the same KRIs again calling the identical finder per row (line 320) — 2N queries. ExportService.kriDashboardPdf() does the same (lines 191 and 219). BoardPackService.renderExecutiveSummary() calls riskRepo.findByOrganisationId(org, PageRequest.of(0,1000)) at line 170 (for getTotalElements) and again at line 176 — two full page loads to read two scalars. ExerciseRuntimeService.summarise()/ExerciseObserverService.summarise() each fire 5 separate countByOrganisationIdAndExerciseRunIdAndStatus queries per run (Runtime 600-610).
rootCause: Latest-reading lookups are done row-by-row instead of with a single grouped query; scalar counts are derived from full entity-page loads; status breakdowns use one COUNT per status instead of a GROUP BY.
evidence: BoardPackService.java:298 and :320 call the same per-KRI finder in two separate loops over the same list. ExportService.java:191 and :219 identical. BoardPackService.java:170 and :176 both call findByOrganisationId(org, PageRequest.of(0,1000)). ExerciseRuntimeService.java:602-610 issues 5 (then 3 more) count queries.
impact: Reporting endpoints scale O(2N) DB round-trips with KRI count; board-pack generation pays a double full-page risk load; run summaries issue 5+ count queries each. On large tenants these endpoints become slow and DB-chatty for no functional reason.
reproduction: Enable Hibernate SQL logging and hit /api/v1/reports board pack or KRI dashboard with N KRIs — observe ~2N+ latest-reading selects. For summarise, observe 5 count statements per run summary.
resolution: Add a repository query that returns each KRI's latest band in one shot (e.g. a JPQL projection grouped by kriId, or a window-function native query) and build a Map<Long,band> once. Replace the double findByOrganisationId with countByOrganisationId + countByOrganisationIdAndStatus. Replace the 5 per-status counts in summarise with a single GROUP BY status query mapped into a Map.
patchBefore:
for (KriDefinition k : kris) { ... findFirstByKriIdOrderByReadingAtDesc(k.getId()) ... } // count loop
for (KriDefinition k : kris) { ... findFirstByKriIdOrderByReadingAtDesc(k.getId()) ... } // table loop
patchAfter:
Map<Long,String> latestBand = readingRepo.latestBandByKri(org); // one grouped query
for (KriDefinition k : kris) { String band = latestBand.get(k.getId()); ... }

title: CyberService is a God class: 613 LOC, 10 repositories, 8 unrelated entity domains in one service
cvss: Maintainability risk: a single class owning frameworks, controls, sub-controls, assessments, vulnerabilities, exceptions, incidents, assets, evidence and action plans concentrates change risk and merge conflicts; no runtime exploit but high regression surface.
description: CyberService is a single @Service spanning 613 lines that injects 10 repositories (frameworkRepo, assetRepo, controlRepo, subControlRepo, assessmentRepo, vulnerabilityRepo, exceptionRepo, incidentRepo, evidenceRepo, actionPlanRepo — lines 25-34) and provides full CRUD plus workflow methods for EIGHT distinct domain concepts (frameworks, controls, sub-controls, assessments, vulnerabilities, exceptions, incidents, assets, evidence, action plans). Each domain has its own get/getAll/save/update/delete/workflow methods. This violates the Single Responsibility Principle: there is no cohesive reason these aggregates share a class beyond living under the same module. Compare with the vuln_sla and asm sub-packages, which split each concern into its own dedicated service (AttackSurfaceAssetService, AttackSurfaceFindingService, ShadowItService).
rootCause: Module was built as one flat service before sub-package extraction (asm/, vuln_sla/, threatintel/) became the pattern. The core cyber service was never decomposed to match.
evidence: 10 @final repository fields (lines 25-34); 8 domain regions each delimited by a banner comment (// Frameworks, // Controls, // Sub-Controls, // Assessments, // Vulnerabilities, // Exceptions, // Incidents, // Assets, // Evidence, // Action Plans); total 613 LOC measured with wc -l.
impact: Every cyber feature change touches one file; high merge-conflict probability across teams; harder to unit-test a single domain in isolation; the class is the largest in all 5 audited packages.
reproduction: wc -l tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/cyber/service/CyberService.java -> 613. Count @final repository fields -> 10. Count region banners -> 8 domains.
resolution: Split CyberService into per-aggregate services (CyberControlService, CyberVulnerabilityService, CyberIncidentService, CyberAssetService, CyberEvidenceService, CyberActionPlanService, CyberAssessmentService) mirroring the asm/ and vuln_sla/ sub-package convention. Keep a thin CyberDashboardService for the cross-cutting getDashboard aggregation. The controller can fan out to the new services without API changes.

title: PrivacyService swallows audit and event-bus exceptions with empty catch(Exception ignored) — no logging at all
cvss: Operational visibility risk: a failing audit-log write or failing F8 event publish on the regulator-discharge path (SDAIA breach notification) is silently dropped with zero log output, so an audit-trail gap or broken automation goes completely undetected.
description: recordSdaiaSubmission() wraps the F7 audit write and the F8 event publish in two try blocks each ending in `} catch (Exception ignored) { // ... }`. The catch bodies contain only a comment ('Audit failures must not block the regulator-discharge path.') and discard the exception entirely — no log.warn, no log.error, no stack trace, no cause. PrivacyService does not even declare a logger (no @Slf4j on the class). The intent (do not block the discharge path) is reasonable, but silently eating the exception means a persistent audit-sink outage or a serialization failure in the event payload is invisible in production logs. This is the textbook swallowed-exception anti-pattern on a compliance-critical PDPL Article 31 code path.
rootCause: Best-effort side-effects (audit + event) were made non-fatal by catching broadly, but the author omitted any logging and the class lacks a logger.
impact: A broken audit trail or non-firing BREACH_REPORTED_TO_SDAIA automation cannot be diagnosed from logs; for a regulator-facing 72-hour notification flow this defeats forensic accountability.
reproduction: Stop the audit-log datastore and call recordSdaiaSubmission(); the breach still saves and returns 200 with no log line indicating the audit write failed.
resolution: Add @Slf4j to the class and log at WARN with the exception inside both catch blocks: `log.warn("SDAIA audit write failed for breach {} — continuing", id, ex);`. Catch a narrower type if feasible. Keep the non-fatal behaviour but make the failure observable.
references: CWE-390 Detection of Error Condition Without Action

title: VulnerabilitySlaController does business logic, injects a repository, and reads the user id by reflection with a swallowed exception
cvss: Maintainability + correctness risk: the controller bypasses the service layer to query the repository and dereferences the security principal reflectively, so an API/refactor mismatch fails silently (returns null user id) and the dashboard aggregation logic lives in the wrong layer.
description: Three distinct layering smells in one controller: (1) it injects VulnerabilitySlaFindingRepository directly (line 52) and the dashboard() endpoint runs seven count queries plus list calls and assembles the DashboardSnapshot itself (lines 160-176) — data-access and aggregation that belong in a service. (2) currentUserId() (lines 180-193) resolves the authenticated user's id via reflection: principal.getClass().getMethod("getId").invoke(principal), to 'avoid an extra dependency from this leaf module to the security package'. (3) that reflective call is wrapped in `catch (Exception ignored) { return null; }`, so any rename of GrcUserDetails.getId(), or a different principal type, silently yields a null actor id with no log — the remediation audit row then records by=null.
rootCause: The module avoided a compile-time dependency on the security package by reflecting on the principal, and skipped the service layer for the read-heavy dashboard endpoint.
evidence: Line 52: `private final VulnerabilitySlaFindingRepository findingRepo;` in a @RestController. Lines 161-167: seven `findingRepo.countByOrganisationIdAndStatusAndIsDeletedFalse(...)` calls in the controller. Lines 186-192: `try { var m = principal.getClass().getMethod("getId"); ... } catch (Exception ignored) { return null; }`.
impact: Renaming/refactoring the principal accessor breaks user attribution with no error; dashboard query logic cannot be unit-tested without the web layer; controller and service responsibilities are blurred.
reproduction: grep for `findingRepo` in the controller (line 52, 161-167) and `getClass().getMethod("getId")` (line 187). Change GrcUserDetails.getId() to getUserId() and observe currentUserId() returns null silently.
resolution: Move the dashboard aggregation into VulnerabilitySlaComputeService (or a dedicated VulnSlaDashboardService) and drop the repository from the controller. Replace the reflective principal access with a typed cast to the security module's user-details type (add the dependency — it is the platform's own security package, not an external one) or inject an existing helper; on failure log at WARN instead of silently returning null.
references: Layered architecture — controllers must not access repositories
CWE-390 Detection of Error Condition Without Action

title: SocOpsScheduledSweep: 10 near-identical sweep methods and a broad catch that logs only getMessage(), losing the stack trace
cvss: Maintainability + diagnosability risk: the per-org sweep failure path catches Exception and logs only ex.getMessage() (no stack trace/cause), and the 10 sweep methods repeat the same loop/dedup/publish/markFired skeleton, so a NPE inside a sweep is hard to localize.
description: Two related issues. (1) ERROR HANDLING: tick() wraps each tenant's full sweep in `catch (Exception ex) { log.warn("[socops sweep] org={} scan failed: {}", orgId, ex.getMessage()); }` (lines 130-131). Logging only ex.getMessage() at WARN discards the stack trace and cause, so a NullPointerException (message=null) prints '... scan failed: null' with no class, line, or origin sweep. The sibling scheduler VulnerabilitySlaScheduler does this correctly — `log.error("...", ex)` (line 69). (2) DUPLICATION: the ten private sweepX methods (sweepSecurityEventSla, sweepRegulatorResponseDue, sweepCyberInsuranceRenewals, sweepIamPrivilegedReviewsDue, sweepCryptoCertExpiry, sweepPentestRetestDue, sweepSeasonalOverlayActivated, sweepForensicsHoldDisposalDue, sweepAppsecSlaBreached, sweepDlpCriticalUnreviewed) all repeat the identical body: fetch rows, loop, `if (alreadyFired(...)) continue;`, publishEvent(DomainEvent.of(...)), markFired(...), fired++. ~12 call sites of alreadyFired confirm the repeated skeleton.
rootCause: Each trigger was added by copy-paste of the previous sweep; the common loop was never abstracted. The catch was written for brevity without considering loss of the stack trace.
evidence: Line 131: `log.warn("[socops sweep] org={} scan failed: {}", orgId, ex.getMessage());` — message only. 12 `alreadyFired(...)` call sites (lines 164,183,203,213,232,252,262,284,307,330,353,377) each in an otherwise-identical for-loop body across the 10 sweep methods.
impact: A bug in any single sweep surfaces only as 'scan failed: <message-or-null>' with no stack trace, forcing a code read to find which of 10 sweeps failed; adding/changing the dedup+publish contract requires editing 10 methods.
reproduction: Inspect tick() lines 130-131 vs VulnerabilitySlaScheduler line 69; diff any two sweepX method bodies — only the repository call, entity type string, and payload map differ.
resolution: (1) Change the catch to log.error with the exception object: `log.error("[socops sweep] org={} scan failed", orgId, ex);`. (2) Extract a generic helper, e.g. `<E> int sweep(String entityType, List<E> rows, Function<E,Long> idOf, Function<E,String> triggerOf, Function<E,Map<String,Object>> payloadOf)` that owns the loop/alreadyFired/publish/markFired, so each sweepX becomes one call.

title: Service classes copy-paste the org()/currentUserId()/emit() tenant-and-actor helper trio instead of sharing a base service or utility
cvss: Not a security CVE, but adjacent to a security-relevant concern: the duplicated currentUserId()/org() helpers are how tenant id and actor id are resolved for writes. 259 service<->service clones / 3,219 dup lines. If one copy diverges (e.g. fails to null-check the principal, or reads the wrong tenant source), it produces a per-module tenant/actor-resolution bug that the other modules will not exhibit — exactly the kind of subtle multi-tenant isolation defect that is hard to spot. Rated Medium for maintainability + latent isolation risk.
description: java-service <-> java-service is the third-largest Java cluster: 259 clones / 3,219 dup lines. The recurring fragment is a trio of private helpers used by virtually every write path: `private static Long org() { return TenantContext.requireOrganisationId(); }`, `private static Long currentUserId()` (reads SecurityContextHolder, null-guards, casts to GrcUserDetails, returns userId), and a `private void emit(...)`/event-recording method. The top service clone the report found (ObService.java:625-656 vs ShariaService.java:672-703, 32 lines) is exactly this helper block plus the surrounding event-emit method. Static grep shows `private static Long currentUserId()` duplicated in 18 service/controller files and `TenantContext.requireOrganisationId()` referenced in 69 files.
rootCause: There is no abstract base service or shared SecurityUtils/TenantUtils class exposing currentUserId()/org(). Each module's service was bootstrapped by copying a prior module's service, carrying the private helpers along. The helpers are declared `private static`, so they cannot be reused even by sibling services in the same module.
evidence: jscpd: service<->service = 259 clones / 3,219 dup lines. grep on tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module: `private static Long currentUserId()` in 18 files; `TenantContext.requireOrganisationId()` in 69 files. Confirmed body in ObService.java:637-644 (Authentication auth = SecurityContextHolder...; instanceof GrcUserDetails u; return u.getUserId();) is identical to the ShariaService copy.
impact: Tenant- and actor-resolution logic is the security-critical seam of a multi-tenant GRC platform, yet it lives in ~18-69 hand-copied fragments. A divergence in any one copy (missing null check, wrong tenant accessor) is a per-module isolation or audit-attribution bug. Maintenance of the event-emit plumbing is likewise multiplied across every service.
reproduction: 1) Open ObService.java:635-644 and ShariaService.java around 672-703 — identical currentUserId()/org(). 2) grep -rl 'private static Long currentUserId()' tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module --include=*.java | wc -l → 18. 3) grep -rl 'TenantContext.requireOrganisationId()' ... | wc -l → 69.
resolution: Introduce a shared, package-visible utility (e.g. common/security/CurrentActor.java with `static Long userId()` and `static Long organisationId()`), or an `AbstractTenantService` base class exposing protected `org()`/`currentUserId()`/`emit(...)`. Replace the per-service private statics with calls to the shared helper. Centralising currentUserId() also gives one place to fix any future principal-type or null-handling change. Keep TenantContext as the source of truth; the utility just wraps it.

title: Copy-pasted tenant/event helpers (currentUserId, emit, validate, org) duplicated verbatim across services
cvss: Maintainability: identical helper blocks in 3+ target-module services (18 codebase-wide for currentUserId) mean a security/semantic fix to the principal-extraction or event-emit logic must be applied in every copy or it silently diverges.
description: The helper quartet validate(Map,from,to,label), emit(trigger,entityType,entityId,payload), org(), and currentUserId() is duplicated byte-for-byte across DataOfficerService, DataclassService and AiLifecycleService (and the per-entity timeline() differs only in which event entity it builds). jscpd flags AiLifecycleService:335-363 as a clone of DataclassService:383-408 and DataOfficerService:886-910, and the same block recurs in OutsourcingService, RegInspectService, OpResService, FraudService.
rootCause: No shared base class or injectable helper for the common multi-tenant + domain-event plumbing; each sprint copied the pattern into a new service.
evidence: grep for the exact line `auth.getPrincipal() instanceof GrcUserDetails u)) return null` matches 3 target-module services; `private static Long currentUserId() {` appears in 18 files codebase-wide. The `emit(...)` DomainEvent builder appears in 4 files. jscpd top hit: 29-line clone AiLifecycleService.java:335-363 <-> DataclassService.java:383-408.
impact: A change to principal resolution (e.g. handling a new GrcUserDetails subtype) or to the DomainEvent constructor signature must be made in every copy; missing one produces silent behavioural drift across modules.
reproduction: Diff DataclassService lines 392-406 against DataOfficerService lines 896-912 — identical apart from whitespace.
resolution: Introduce a shared component (e.g. TenantActor / DomainEventEmitter) exposing org(), currentUserId(), emit(...) and validate(...); inject it into each service. Keep only the entity-specific timeline() row construction local.

title: Swallowed exceptions: NdiAuditPublisher catches Exception and discards it with no logging
cvss: Operational risk: three write paths and currentUsername() swallow every exception with `catch (Exception ignored)` and no log statement, so audit-ledger write failures vanish silently — directly undermining the compliance value of the audit trail this class exists to populate.
description: publishTransition (40), publish (49) and publish-with-severity (60) each wrap the repo.save in `catch (Exception ignored) { /* swallow */ }`, and currentUsername() (82) does the same. The class Javadoc claims errors are 'intentionally swallowed at warn level' (lines 19-22) but there is NO Logger field and NO warn/error call anywhere in the file — the comment is false and the failures are completely invisible.
rootCause: Deliberate decision to never let an audit failure roll back the parent op (REQUIRES_NEW propagation), but implemented as a blind swallow rather than a logged swallow; the documenting comment was never reconciled with the code.
evidence: Lines 40, 49, 60, 82 all contain `catch (Exception ignored)`. No `Logger`/`LoggerFactory` import in the file. Javadoc lines 19-22 promise 'warn level' logging that does not exist.
impact: If the audit table is unavailable, schema-drifted, or a summary exceeds a constraint, NDI compliance/maturity/submission transitions still succeed but their audit rows silently disappear — an undetectable gap in the regulatory ledger and no signal to operators.
reproduction: Force NdiAuditEventRepository.save to throw (e.g. drop the table in a test); call any NDI transition — the operation succeeds and nothing is logged.
resolution: Add a SLF4J Logger and log at WARN with the full exception (cause) in each catch, matching the Javadoc's stated contract; keep the swallow so the parent op is unaffected.
patchBefore: } catch (Exception ignored) { /* audit failure never rolls back the parent op */ }
references: CWE-390: Detection of Error Condition Without Action

title: Hand-rolled JSON serializer and Markdown→HTML converter in ReportComposerService reinvent Jackson
cvss: Correctness + maintainability: a bespoke recursive toJson() (lines 461-487) silently mishandles types Jackson handles (no LocalDate/BigDecimal-as-number coercion, no Map-key escaping, dates only stringified upstream) and markdownToHtml() does O(n) `out.toString()` scans per cell, while Jackson is already a project dependency injected into peer services.
description: toJson(Object) (461-487) is a hand-written recursive JSON encoder; the comment at 459-460 explicitly says 'pulling Jackson isn't necessary'. Meanwhile NdiSubmissionPackageService and NdiReportService inject a Spring-managed ObjectMapper for exactly this. The encoder does not escape Map keys, only escapes a subset of control characters in strings, and renders any non-Map/Iterable/Number/Boolean (e.g. LocalDate, enum) via toString() with only quote-escaping. markdownToHtml (409-450) determines table-header vs cell by calling `out.toString().endsWith(...)` inside the per-cell loop (lines 424) — re-materialising the entire growing buffer on every cell.
rootCause: Author chose a local mini-implementation over the existing Jackson bean to avoid a perceived dependency, and a string-scan heuristic over tracking parser state in a variable.
evidence: Line 459-460 comment: 'Quick JSON serializer — service is small enough that pulling Jackson isn't necessary'. Line 424: `boolean isHeader = !out.toString().endsWith("</tr>") && out.toString().endsWith("<table><tr>");` — two full-buffer scans per cell. 14 injected fields (grep -c 'private final' = 14) but no ObjectMapper.
impact: Risk of malformed JSON in exported BOARD_ESG/CMA/GHG report bundles when a value is a date/enum/Map-with-special-key; quadratic-ish HTML rendering for large GHG/evidence tables; divergence from how every other report service serialises.
reproduction: Pass a Map whose value is a LocalDate into the JSON path (e.g. via dashboard 'overall') — it is emitted as a quoted toString, not the canonical Jackson form; build a GHG report with 1000 records and profile markdownToHtml.
resolution: Inject the existing ObjectMapper bean and call writeValueAsString for the JSON branch; for markdownToHtml track header-state in a local boolean (firstRowOfTable) instead of scanning out.toString(). Optionally replace with a maintained Markdown library.
references: Effective Java, Item 59: Know and use the libraries

title: Long high-branching method: suggestWorkflowSubmissionReview spans 120 LOC with a 7-way if/else ladder
cvss: Maintainability: a single method building seven near-identical bilingual checklist blocks via a long if/else-if chain on substring matches is hard to extend (each new wizard adds another branch) and hard to test in isolation.
description: suggestWorkflowSubmissionReview is 120 LOC. The body is a 7-branch if/else-if ladder (workflowId.contains('pdpl-breach') ... else generic, lines 307-392), each branch pushing 4 English + 4 Arabic strings into two lists and setting headline/decision/conf, followed by a second status-dependent if/else (395-397). Cyclomatic complexity is roughly 12+ from the chained predicates.
rootCause: Per-wizard checklist content is hard-coded inline as procedural branches rather than data-driven (a lookup table keyed by workflowId/module).
evidence: Method line span 291-411 = 120 lines. Branch conditions at 307, 320, 333, 345, 357, 369, 379 (else), plus status branches at 395-397.
impact: Every new wizard type requires editing this method and re-testing the whole ladder; the bilingual string pairs are easy to desynchronise (EN added without AR). The method mixes content definition with persistence (calls persist() at the end).
reproduction: Open the method; count the else-if branches from line 307 to 392.
resolution: Move the per-wizard content into a static Map<String, ReviewTemplate> (or a small enum/record table) keyed by workflowId-prefix/module; the method then becomes a lookup + a default, dropping branch complexity to ~2.
references: Replace Conditional with Polymorphism / table-driven design

title: Tenant/actor/event boilerplate triad (org(), currentUserId(), emit()) copy-pasted across financial-crime & audit services
cvss: Maintainability risk: a change to event/tenant/actor resolution (e.g. a new DomainEvent field, a fix to the SecurityContext principal cast) must be hand-applied in 13+ services; drift between copies is near-certain and already visible (ShariaService/RrpService/FraudService/OpResService carry byte-identical helpers while ScmService diverged into a different org() that defaults to 1L).
description: The same three private helpers — `static Long org() { return TenantContext.requireOrganisationId(); }`, `static Long currentUserId() { ... instanceof GrcUserDetails ... }`, and `void emit(String trigger, String entityType, Long entityId, String correlationId, Map payload) { publisher.publishEvent(new DomainEvent(...)); }` — are duplicated verbatim across ShariaService, RrpService, FraudService and OpResService (and at least 9 other modules platform-wide per the grep for `private static Long org() { return TenantContext.requireOrganisationId(); }`, which hits 13 files, and the `if (auth == null || !auth.isAuthenticated()` cast which hits 17 files). jscpd independently flags the `emit/currentUserId` block as a clone, e.g. FraudService:381 <-> OpResService:292 <-> AiLifecycleService:349 (19 lines) and ShariaService:672 <-> ObService:625 (32 lines).
rootCause: No shared base class or helper component for the cross-cutting concerns every event-emitting service needs (tenant id, acting user, DomainEvent publish). Each module's author copied the previous module's service.
evidence: grep `private static Long org() { return TenantContext.requireOrganisationId(); }` => 13 files. grep `if (auth == null || !auth.isAuthenticated()` => 17 files. jscpd clones: fraud/service/FraudService.java:381 <-> opres/service/OpResService.java:292 (19 lines); sharia/service/ShariaService.java:672 <-> openbanking/service/ObService.java:625 (32 lines); cpty/service/CptyService.java:528 <-> rrp/service/RrpService.java:592 (30 lines).
impact: High change-amplification cost; correctness divergence already present (ScmService.orgId() silently substitutes tenant 1L while the others throw — see QUAL-FA-007). A single security-relevant fix to currentUserId() would need 13 edits.
reproduction: Open ShariaService.java (682-699), RrpService.java (600-617), FraudService.java (384-400), OpResService.java (295-311) side by side; the org()/currentUserId()/emit() bodies are character-identical.
resolution: Extract a `protected abstract` base class (e.g. `EventEmittingService`) or a `@Component DomainEventPublisher` plus a `SecurityHelper.currentUserId()` and `TenantContext.requireOrganisationId()` wrapper, and have these services delegate. Removes ~17 LOC * 13 services of duplication and forces a single definition of actor resolution.

title: RiskControlFindingPivotService swallows all RuntimeExceptions silently via safeList/safeOpt across 8 foreign-module repositories
cvss: Reliability/observability risk: every cross-module repository call is wrapped in a catch-all that returns an empty list/Optional with no log, so a genuine DB/mapping failure in any of the 8 source modules degrades the pivot to 'no linked controls/findings/CAPA' indistinguishably from a legitimately empty graph — silently producing wrong analytics with no trace.
description: `safeList(Supplier<List>)` and `safeOpt(Supplier<Optional>)` catch `RuntimeException` and return `List.of()` / `Optional.empty()` with no logging. They wrap ~15 call sites spanning RiskRepository, ControlRepository, RiskControlLinkRepository, ControlAssessmentRepository, FindingRepository, two CapaTaskRepositories, ControlTestDefinitionRepository and ControlTestRunRepository. Any exception (lazy-init, mapping error, constraint, NPE) is absorbed and the pivot reports an empty section. The `dataCompletenessPct` metric then reads as a data-quality gap rather than an error.
rootCause: Defensive 'graceful missing-link handling' (documented in the class Javadoc) was implemented as a blanket catch-all rather than as null/empty handling on the actual finder return values.
evidence: Lines 656-663: `catch (RuntimeException ex) { return Collections.emptyList(); }` — no log. Lines 665-668: `catch (RuntimeException ex) { return Optional.empty(); }` — no log. The only logged catch in the class is emitPivotEvent (516-518). parseControlCodes (425-430) likewise catches Exception and silently falls back.
impact: A real failure in any source module is invisible: the pivot returns a misleadingly-empty graph, undermining the analytics the module exists to provide, and leaving no log breadcrumb for triage.
reproduction: Inject a repository that throws (e.g. simulate a mapping error in ccmRunRepo.findRecentForTest): ccmCoverageForControls returns zero-coverage stats with no warning logged; the pivot looks healthy.
resolution: At minimum log at WARN with the supplier context inside safeList/safeOpt (the class already has an Slf4j logger). Better: catch only the specific 'not visible to tenant' case and let infrastructure exceptions propagate to the controller's 500 handler.
references: Effective Java Item 77: Don't ignore exceptions

title: Governance pivot/3LoD services reach directly into 8+ other modules' repositories (cross-module layering violation)
cvss: Coupling/architecture risk: the governance module's services depend at compile time on the internal repositories and entities of risk, controls, audit_lc, capa, ccm, iam, policy, privacy_lc — so any schema/finder change in those modules can break governance, and the modular-monolith boundary the project documents (one repository layer per module) is bypassed.
description: RiskControlFindingPivotService injects RiskRepository, ControlRepository, RiskControlLinkRepository, ControlAssessmentRepository, FindingRepository, two CapaTaskRepository beans (capa + audit_lc), ControlTestDefinitionRepository and ControlTestRunRepository — 9 repositories owned by 6 other modules — and queries their entities directly. ThreeLinesService similarly injects RiskRepository, FindingRepository, CapaTaskRepository, PolicyDocumentRepository, DsrCaseRepository and UserRepository. Both also import foreign entities (Risk, Control, Finding, CapaTask, PolicyDocument, User...). This is heavier coupling than the documented per-module repository pattern.
rootCause: The aggregation/dashboard services need cross-module data and the codebase exposes no module-level read API (query service / facade), so they bind directly to foreign repositories. The pivot class Javadoc even acknowledges 'owns no tables' and reaches into source repos.
evidence: RiskControlFindingPivotService constructor (106-130) takes 9 repositories from risk/platform.controls/audit_lc/capa/ccm. ThreeLinesService fields (97-105) take 6 repositories from risk/audit_lc/capa/policy/privacy_lc/iam. jscpd also flags governance/pivot importing across modules indirectly. The CCM coverage method even pages 100 runs per definition in a loop (351-379) — N+1 over a foreign repo.
impact: Tight compile-time coupling: a finder rename in any of 6 modules forces a governance edit; the modular boundary is not enforceable; foreign N+1 query patterns (ccmRunRepo in a per-definition loop) live outside the owning module's control.
reproduction: Inspect imports of both services: each imports entity + repository types from 6+ sibling modules under com.tss.grc.module.*.
resolution: Introduce read-only query facades per source module (e.g. RiskQueryService.openRisksForOrg(orgId), CcmQueryService.coverageForControls(...)) and have governance depend on those interfaces instead of foreign repositories. This restores the one-repository-layer-per-module boundary and lets each module own its query/N+1 strategy.
references: CLAUDE.md: 'repository/ Spring Data JPA — org-scoped' per module

title: ScmService.orgId() silently defaults to tenant 1L on null context, diverging from the require-or-throw convention used everywhere else
cvss: Tenant-safety/consistency smell: when TenantContext is empty (e.g. a misconfigured filter, scheduler, or test) ScmService quietly behaves as if the caller were org 1 instead of failing fast — masking bugs and risking cross-tenant reads/writes, while all sibling services in scope throw via TenantContext.requireOrganisationId().
description: `private Long orgId() { Long id = TenantContext.getCurrentTenant(); return id != null ? id : 1L; }`. Every other service in the assigned set (ShariaService, RrpService, FraudService, OpResService, IaEngagementService, SanctionsScreeningService, SanctionsHitService) uses `TenantContext.requireOrganisationId()` which throws when the tenant is absent. ScmService instead silently falls back to organisation 1.
rootCause: An early dev convenience (so the SCM UI worked before auth wiring was complete) was never removed; it predates the requireOrganisationId convention adopted by later modules.
evidence: ScmService.java:39-42 returns 1L; contrast ShariaService.java:682 `static Long org() { return TenantContext.requireOrganisationId(); }` and OpResService.java:295 identical. ScmService is also the only in-scope module that performs NO audit.log/DomainEvent emission on any mutation — inconsistent with the F7/F8 convention every sibling follows.
impact: If the tenant filter ever fails to populate context, SCM operations execute against tenant 1's vendors/contracts silently — a latent cross-tenant data-exposure path and a debugging trap, since reads succeed instead of 401/500.
reproduction: Clear TenantContext and call ScmService.listVendors(): it returns org-1 vendors instead of throwing, unlike ShariaService.listScholars() which throws.
resolution: Replace the 1L fallback with TenantContext.requireOrganisationId() to fail fast and match the platform convention. Separately, add the missing F7/F8 audit/event emission for SCM mutations for consistency (track as its own item).
references: CLAUDE.md: 'Every repository query must filter by organisation_id'

title: EvidenceStorageService and AttachmentStorageService are ~90% duplicated (allow-list, size cap, store(), extensionOf, sha256Hex)
cvss: Medium maintainability risk: two near-identical file-storage implementations means security-relevant logic (extension allow-list, path-traversal guard, size cap) must be patched in two places. jscpd flags four overlapping duplicate blocks (20 + 17 + 13 + 10 lines) between these two files.
description: AttachmentStorageService and EvidenceStorageService have identical ALLOWED_EXTENSIONS sets (byte-for-byte the same 26 extensions), identical maxBytes/root constructor wiring, identical empty/size/extension validation, identical path-traversal guard, and identical extensionOf() and sha256Hex() helpers. The AttachmentStorageService javadoc even says it 'Mirrors the proven evidence storage'. sha256Hex() is in fact triplicated — EvidenceChainService has a third copy (lines 223-233).
rootCause: Copy-paste of a working storage service for a second entity type rather than extracting a shared base class / utility for validation + hashing + path-traversal.
evidence: jscpd-report.json reports four AttachmentStorageService <-> EvidenceStorageService duplicate blocks (20L, 17L, 13L, 10L). sha256Hex appears verbatim in AttachmentStorageService:103-112, EvidenceStorageService:112-122, and EvidenceChainService:223-233.
impact: Divergent fixes: e.g. tightening the extension allow-list or the traversal guard in one service silently leaves the other vulnerable. Higher maintenance cost.
reproduction: Diff the two files; or run jscpd over module/attachment and module/evidence.
resolution: Extract an abstract LocalFileStorage base (or a FileStorageSupport utility) holding ALLOWED_EXTENSIONS, the size cap, validate(), extensionOf(), the path-traversal guard, and sha256Hex(); have both services subclass/delegate. Move sha256Hex to a shared HashUtil so EvidenceChainService reuses it too.

title: ApprovalChainInstanceService.recordAction() is a 104-LOC method with the entire state machine inlined
cvss: Medium maintainability risk: the core approval-chain state-machine transition lives in one 104-line method with many branches (terminal-status guard, step-order match, parallel-rung resolution, delegation gating, REJECTED short-circuit, APPROVED rung-satisfied advance/finalise, fall-through statuses). High branch count concentrated in a single security-relevant method makes it hard to test and easy to regress.
description: recordAction() does, in one method: terminal-status validation (207), step-order match check (210), step rows lookup (219), actor->step resolution (230), two delegation guards (232-238), action-row persistence + audit + delegated-event (240-262), then the branching state machine for REJECTED (267-274), APPROVED-with-rung-satisfied advance-or-finalise (277-301), and the else fall-through (302-306). Each of the i.setUpdatedAt/instanceRepo.save pairs is repeated five times across the branches.
rootCause: All transition concerns (validation, persistence, audit, eventing, advancement) handled inline instead of being decomposed into helpers (validateActionable, persistAction, applyDecision).
evidence: Method spans lines 203-308 (104 LOC). instanceRepo.save(i) with a preceding i.setUpdatedAt(LocalDateTime.now()) appears at lines 271, 290, 295, 300, 305 — five duplicated save blocks within the one method.
impact: Hard to unit-test individual transitions; the repeated setUpdatedAt+save pattern invites a missed update on a new branch.
reproduction: Open the file and count branches/LOC of recordAction; note the five repeated save sites.
resolution: Extract: (1) a guard method validating terminal status + step order + delegation, (2) a recordActionRow(...) for persistence+audit, (3) an applyApproval(...) for the advance/finalise logic. Collapse the repeated setUpdatedAt+save into a single touch-and-save call at the end.

title: AuthController.refresh()/login() swallow the cause in broad catch(Exception) — no log, 500 with cause lost
cvss: Medium operability risk: when the server-side refresh-token store fails to persist/rotate, the controller returns a generic 500 but never logs the underlying exception (no logger is even present in AuthController). A real DB/store fault on the security-critical login/refresh path becomes invisible to operators, making incidents hard to diagnose.
description: In login() the issuance block catches `Exception ex` (line 94) and returns a 500 body but discards `ex` entirely — it is never logged. The refresh() rotation block does the same (lines 173-176). AuthController has no Logger field at all, so these failures leave no server-side trace. 'Fail closed' (returning 500) is the correct security behaviour, but losing the cause is an error-handling defect.
rootCause: Broad catch(Exception) used to fail-closed, but without log.error("...", ex) the stack trace and cause are dropped on the floor.
evidence: Lines 94-100: `} catch (Exception ex) { ... return ResponseEntity.status(500).body(Map.of("message", "Unable to record refresh token — please retry.")); }` — `ex` is captured but never used/logged. Same pattern at 173-176. No `private static final Logger` exists in the class.
impact: Refresh-store outages or persistence errors on login/refresh are undiagnosable from logs; on-call engineers see only client-side 500s.
reproduction: Force store.recordIssuance to throw (e.g. DB down), call POST /api/auth/login — client gets a 500 but no server log line records why.
resolution: Add a class Logger and `log.error("refresh-token issuance/rotation failed for user {}", userId, ex);` inside both catch blocks before returning the 500. Keep the fail-closed 500 behaviour.
references: Logging the cause when catching broadly

title: ComplianceService.getStats counts findings by status="CRITICAL" but CRITICAL is a severity — count is always 0
cvss: Correctness bug surfaced as dead logic: the compliance dashboard 'critical findings' tile silently always reports zero, masking real critical findings from board reporting.
description: getStats() computes `criticalFindings = findingRepo.countByOrganisationIdAndStatus(orgId, "CRITICAL")`. On AuditFinding, `status` defaults to "OPEN" and only ever holds workflow states (OPEN/CLOSED), while CRITICAL is a value of the separate `severity` column. No finding is ever persisted with status == "CRITICAL", so this count is unconditionally 0 and is fed straight into the ComplianceStats DTO that drives the dashboard.
rootCause: Field confusion between `severity` (LOW/MEDIUM/HIGH/CRITICAL) and `status` (OPEN/CLOSED). The repository finder name `countByOrganisationIdAndStatus` did not catch the mistake because the literal compiles.
evidence: ComplianceService.java:233 `long criticalFindings = findingRepo.countByOrganisationIdAndStatus(orgId, "CRITICAL");`. AuditFinding.java:26-27 `@Column(name = "severity", nullable = false) private String severity;`; AuditFinding.java:38-39 `@Column(name = "status") private String status = "OPEN";`. There is no countByOrganisationIdAndSeverity finder being used for this.
impact: The criticalFindings KPI returned by GET compliance stats is permanently 0, hiding genuinely critical findings from operators and board packs that consume the stat.
reproduction: Seed a finding with severity=CRITICAL, status=OPEN. Call the stats endpoint; criticalFindings returns 0 instead of 1.
resolution: Query by severity, not status: add/use `countByOrganisationIdAndSeverity` and pass "CRITICAL". Keep openFindings on status.
patchBefore:
long openFindings     = findingRepo.countByOrganisationIdAndStatus(orgId, "OPEN");
long criticalFindings = findingRepo.countByOrganisationIdAndStatus(orgId, "CRITICAL");
patchAfter:
long openFindings     = findingRepo.countByOrganisationIdAndStatus(orgId, "OPEN");
long criticalFindings = findingRepo.countByOrganisationIdAndSeverity(orgId, "CRITICAL");

title: Copy-pasted tenant/actor/event helper block (org(), currentUserId(), emit(), timeline()) duplicated across services
cvss: Maintainability risk: the same ~30-line helper cluster is duplicated verbatim across reginspect, regreporting and openbanking services; a fix to event emission or actor resolution must be applied in every copy.
description: RegReportingService and RegInspectService contain byte-identical private helpers: `org()` (TenantContext.requireOrganisationId), `currentUserId()` (resolve GrcUserDetails from SecurityContext), `emit(trigger,type,id,corrId,payload)` (publish DomainEvent), and a near-identical `timeline(...)` writer that constructs a *Event/*Update entity. jscpd confirms a 30-line clone between ObService.java:625-654 and RegReportingService.java:633-662, and a 19-line clone between AiLifecycleService.java:349-367 and RegInspectService.java:384-408. The currentUserId() and emit() implementations are identical character-for-character across all three services.
rootCause: No shared base class or helper component for tenant-scoped, audited, event-emitting services. Each workspace service (regreporting, reginspect, openbanking) was scaffolded by copy from the previous one.
