evidence: RegReportingService.java:643 `private static Long org() { return TenantContext.requireOrganisationId(); }`; lines 645-652 currentUserId(); lines 654-660 emit(). RegInspectService.java:387 / 389-396 / 398-404 — identical bodies. jscpd: 30 lines openbanking/ObService:625-654 <=> regreporting/RegReportingService:633-662.
impact: A change to actor resolution (e.g. handling service accounts) or DomainEvent construction must be edited in N places; drift between copies introduces subtle behavioural differences between modules.
reproduction: Diff the org()/currentUserId()/emit() methods of RegReportingService and RegInspectService — identical. See audit/raw/jscpd/jscpd-report.json clone entry for the 30-line block.
resolution: Introduce a shared collaborator (e.g. DomainEventPublisher component wrapping emit() + currentUserId(), and reuse TenantContext.requireOrganisationId() directly) or an abstract TenantAuditedService base. Inject it instead of re-declaring the helpers per service.

title: Campaign attestation services near-duplicated between ObligationCampaignService and VendorBcpCampaignService
cvss: Maintainability risk: the obligation attestation-campaign service (state machine, rollups, period math, reminders/escalation) is structurally cloned in the TPRM BCP campaign service; bug fixes and lifecycle changes must be mirrored.
description: ObligationCampaignService (454 LOC) implements a DRAFT/OPEN/IN_PROGRESS/ESCALATED/CLOSED/CANCELLED campaign with materialise-targets, sendReminders, escalateOverdue, recomputeRollups, guardTransition and an emit() payload builder. jscpd reports multiple clones against module/tprm/bcp_attestation: the entity rollup-counter block (ObligationAttestationCampaign.java:102-143 <=> VendorBcpCampaign.java:107-148, 42 lines), the service header (ObligationAttestationCampaign:20-43 <=> VendorBcpCampaignService:46-56), the import block (ObligationCampaignService:25-38 <=> VendorBcpCampaignService:26-39), and the repository finder set (14 lines). The two campaign engines are the same pattern over different attestation subjects (regulatory obligations vs vendor BCPs).
rootCause: The vendor BCP campaign was modelled by cloning the obligation campaign rather than abstracting a generic attestation-campaign engine parameterised by subject type.
evidence: jscpd entries: ObligationAttestationCampaign.java:102-143 <=> tprm/bcp_attestation/entity/VendorBcpCampaign.java:107-148 (42 lines); ObligationCampaignService.java:25-38 <=> VendorBcpCampaignService.java:26-39 (14 lines); ObligationAttestationCampaignRepository.java:11-24 <=> VendorBcpAttestationRepository.java:12-15 (14 lines).
impact: Two parallel campaign lifecycle engines must be kept in sync; a fix to reminder/overdue logic or rollup math applied to one is easily forgotten in the other, producing divergent regulator-facing behaviour.
reproduction: Compare ObligationCampaignService and VendorBcpCampaignService method-for-method; cross-check the jscpd clone entries referencing tprm/bcp_attestation.
resolution: Extract a generic AttestationCampaignEngine<TSubject> (state machine + rollups + reminder/escalate) and have both obligation and BCP campaigns supply a target-resolver + rollup-mapper strategy. Share the rollup-counter columns via a @MappedSuperclass on the campaign entities.

title: Inefficient findByOrganisationId(PageRequest.of(0,1000)) + in-memory framework filter copy-pasted 4×
cvss: Performance + duplication risk: the same fetch-1000-rows-then-filter-in-memory pattern for framework/finding aggregation is repeated across two controllers; it silently truncates at 1000 rows and loads the whole finding table per request.
description: Four code sites load up to 1000 findings via `findingRepo.findByOrganisationId(org, PageRequest.of(0, 1000))` and then filter/aggregate them in Java by framework or status: FrameworkAnchorController.coverage() (line 159), FrameworkAnchorController.findingsForFramework() (line 322), RegChangePolicyController.findingsAging() (line 204) and findingsAgingStats() (line 236). The magic 1000 page size silently truncates results for large tenants, and the per-framework filter (`if (fnd.getFrameworkId() == null || !fnd.getFrameworkId().equals(f.getId())) continue;`) runs the whole finding set through the loop for every framework in coverage().
rootCause: Missing repository finders (countByOrganisationIdAndFrameworkIdAndStatus, findByOrganisationIdAndFrameworkId) led developers to pull a wide page and filter in code, then copy that approach to each new endpoint.
evidence: Four occurrences of `findByOrganisationId(org, PageRequest.of(0, 1000))` (grep). coverage() lines 174-178 loop `tenantFindings` inside the per-framework loop; findingsForFramework() lines 322-325 filter in-memory; comment at line 321 even notes 'Pull a wide page; tenant filter applied in-memory below'.
impact: On tenants with >1000 findings, dashboard/coverage numbers are silently wrong (truncated). Each call materialises the full finding set into memory; coverage() is O(frameworks × findings). The duplicated pattern means a single fix (push filtering to SQL) must be applied in four places.
reproduction: grep for `PageRequest.of(0, 1000)` in module/compliance — 4 hits. Seed 1001 findings and observe coverage()/aging stats undercount.
resolution: Add derived repository finders that filter/count by framework_id and status in SQL (e.g. countByOrganisationIdAndFrameworkIdAndStatus, findByOrganisationIdAndFrameworkId). Replace the four fetch-1000 sites; eliminate the magic page size.
patchAfter:
List<AuditFinding> findings = findingRepo.findByOrganisationIdAndFrameworkId(org, id);
for (AuditFinding f : findings) { ... }   // filtered in SQL, no 1000-row cap

title: RegReportingService.dashboard() is a 75-LOC high-branching method mixing 6 query strategies and 3 in-method caches
cvss: Maintainability risk: a single 75-line method computes six dashboard metrics with five repository call patterns, ad-hoc quarter math, an inline obligation cache and two stream pipelines — hard to test and to change safely.
description: dashboard() (lines 457-532, ~75 LOC) computes active obligations, in-flight filings, due-within-7, overdue, submitted-this-quarter, in-flight breakdowns by regulator and status, an upcoming list and an overdue-recent list. It mixes count queries, list queries, two stream-filter pipelines, manual quarter-start arithmetic (`today.withMonth(((today.getMonthValue()-1)/3)*3+1)` at line 476-478), and an inline HashMap obligation cache built with computeIfAbsent — including a second computeIfAbsent inside the upcoming stream (line 508-509). This is well over the ~40 LOC threshold with many independent branches and is the most complex method in the file (756 LOC total).
rootCause: All dashboard aggregation accreted into one method instead of being decomposed into named private helpers (one per metric) or pushed into repository projections.
evidence: Method spans lines 457-532. Distinct concerns: countByOrganisationIdAndActive (459), countByOrganisationIdAndStatusIn (460), due-within-7 stream (464-469), countByOrganisationIdAndStatusNotInAndDueDateBefore (471-474), quarter-start magic (476-478), submittedThisQuarter stream (479-484), obligCache build (490-494), byRegulator/byStatus loop (495-502), upcoming stream with nested cache lookup (504-510), overdueRecent stream (512-519).
impact: Changing one metric risks the others; the nested computeIfAbsent obligation cache is easy to get wrong (one path uses obligCache.get, another computeIfAbsent); the method cannot be unit-tested per metric.
reproduction: Open RegReportingService.dashboard(); count statements/branches.
resolution: Decompose into private helpers (e.g. long countOverdue(), Map<String,Long> inflightByRegulator(List), List<FilingResponse> upcoming(...)) and extract the quarter-start math to a named helper (quarterStart(LocalDate)). Consider repository-level count projections for the scalar tiles.

title: DomainEvent emit() + org() + currentUserId() tenant/event plumbing copy-pasted across services (4 in scope, 13 codebase-wide)
cvss: Maintainability: the event-publishing and tenant/principal-resolution helpers are infrastructure concerns duplicated verbatim into every business service. A change to DomainEvent construction or principal extraction touches 13 files.
description: The identical trio `private void emit(String trigger, String entityType, Long entityId, String correlationId, Map payload)` (publishes a DomainEvent), `private static Long org()` (TenantContext.requireOrganisationId), and `private static Long currentUserId()` (extracts GrcUserDetails from SecurityContext) appears verbatim in ObService, CptyService and OutsourcingService, and across 13 services codebase-wide.
rootCause: No shared base class or `@Component` helper for tenant-scoped event emission; each service was authored by copying the helper block.
evidence: ObService.java:646-652 and CptyService.java:547-553 are byte-identical `emit(...)`. jscpd flags ObService.java[625-654]<=>RegReportingService[633-662] (30 lines) and ObService[625-656]<=>ShariaService[672-703] (32 lines). `grep 'private void emit(String trigger, String entityType, Long entityId,'` returns 13 files (openbanking, outsourcing, cpty, sharia, rrp, reginspect, regreporting, opres, fraud, data_officer, dataclass, ethics/coi, ai/lifecycle).
impact: 13 copies of identical plumbing. Any change (e.g. adding a correlation id, redacting payload keys, switching to a typed event) must be made 13x with no compiler enforcement of consistency.
reproduction: Diff ObService.java:635-652 against CptyService.java:536-553 — identical modulo whitespace.
resolution: Introduce a shared `DomainEventPublisher` (@Component) exposing `emit(...)`, and a `SecurityHelpers.currentUserId()` / reuse `TenantContext.requireOrganisationId()` directly. Inject the publisher into services instead of re-declaring the helper.

title: CCM runners copy-paste JSON helper cluster (parseJson/strOr/intOr/millisSince) despite an existing shared StubRunnerSupport
cvss: Maintainability: the same parsing/timing helpers are redeclared in each runner even though a shared helper class already exists in the package, so the duplication is gratuitous.
description: `CustomSqlRunner`, `SslCertExpiryRunner` and `LdapGroupMembershipRunner` each declare their own `static Map<String,Object> parseJson(String)`, `static String strOr(...)`, `static int intOr(...)` and `static int millisSince(long)` with identical bodies. Meanwhile `StubRunnerSupport` (a package-private final helper holder) already exists and even already declares its own `millisSince` (line 63), so there are 4 copies of `millisSince` in one package.
evidence: grep 'static int millisSince(long startNanos)' in module/ccm -> 4 files (CustomSqlRunner, SslCertExpiryRunner, LdapGroupMembershipRunner, StubRunnerSupport). grep 'static Map<String, Object> parseJson(String json)' -> 3 files. jscpd: CustomSqlRunner.java[155-182]<=>SslCertExpiryRunner.java[116-143] (28 lines), CustomSqlRunner.java[156-184]<=>LdapGroupMembershipRunner.java[121-149] (29 lines).
rootCause: Runners were each scaffolded from a template that inlined the helpers instead of calling a shared support class.
impact: Three+ copies of the JSON-coercion logic; a fix (e.g. trimming, locale-safe number parsing) must be repeated, and the existing StubRunnerSupport.millisSince is shadowed/ignored.
reproduction: Open the `Helpers` regions of CustomSqlRunner (158-184), SslCertExpiryRunner (119-147) and LdapGroupMembershipRunner (120-149) — identical method bodies.
resolution: Move parseJson/strOr/intOr/millisSince into StubRunnerSupport (or a `RunnerSupport` util) and have every runner call the shared versions; delete the per-runner copies.

title: Dead scaffolding methods kept only to silence unused-import warnings (__keepIfNeeded, _silenceUnused) and a no-op currentUserIdOrNull()
cvss: Code-health: methods that exist solely to reference an otherwise-unused import, plus a helper that always returns null while pretending to resolve a user id, mislead readers and hide the fact that audit user-attribution is not wired.
description: `OutsourcingController.currentUserIdOrNull()` (255-265) ALWAYS returns null — its body sets up `auth`, comments that it does not depend on `getId()`, then `return null` inside a try whose only purpose is an empty `catch (Exception ignore) { return null; }`. It is actually called at line 139 (`Long userId = currentUserIdOrNull();`), so `userId` is unconditionally null. `_silenceUnused()` (267-272) is `@SuppressWarnings("unused")` and exists purely to 'keep the import live'. Identically, `CptyService.__keepIfNeeded()` (557-558) is `@SuppressWarnings("unused") private static Set<String> __keepIfNeeded() { return Set.of(); }` — present only so the `java.util.Set` import is not flagged unused.
rootCause: Refactors removed the real usages of an import/helper but left placeholder methods rather than deleting the import.
evidence: OutsourcingController.java:255-265 returns null on every path; called at :139. :267-272 `_silenceUnused()` touches TenantContext only to keep its import. CptyService.java:558 `private static Set<String> __keepIfNeeded() { return Set.of(); }`.
impact: Misleading: a reader assumes user attribution is resolved for the audit trail when it is hard-coded null. The two `keep import alive` methods are pure noise and defeat the unused-import linter.
reproduction: Read the three methods; trace currentUserIdOrNull -> always null -> userId at line 139 always null.
resolution: Delete `_silenceUnused` and `__keepIfNeeded` and remove the now-unused imports. Either wire `currentUserIdOrNull()` to the real principal (GrcUserDetails.getUserId(), as ObService/CptyService do) or remove it and the line-139 call if user attribution is genuinely not needed here.

title: QuestionnaireService hand-parses SELECT-option points from JSON with indexOf/substring instead of Jackson, swallowing parse errors
cvss: Correctness + maintainability: vendor questionnaire scoring (which feeds the vendor risk rating) is derived by string-scanning options_json with raw indexOf/substring and a catch-all that returns null on any failure, so malformed or differently-formatted option JSON silently scores zero/null with no signal.
description: In `computeScoredPoints`, the SELECT case parses option points by searching for the quoted value in `options_json`, finding the next ':' and then walking characters that are digits/'.' to extract a number: `int colon = q.getOptionsJson().indexOf(':', i); int end = colon+1; while (end < ... && "0123456789.".indexOf(charAt(end))>=0) end++; try { return new BigDecimal(substring(colon+1,end).trim())...; } catch (Exception ex) { return null; }`. The comment even says 'Without a real JSON library reference here' — but the project uses Jackson throughout (ObjectMapper is used in the CCM runners and elsewhere).
rootCause: An ad-hoc parser was written under a false assumption that no JSON library was available, with a broad catch that masks any failure as a null score.
evidence: QuestionnaireService.java:360-370 — manual `"\"" + v + "\""` lookup, char-walk number extraction, terminating `catch (Exception ex) { return null; }`. Comment line 360-361 'Without a real JSON library reference here'.
impact: Brittle to formatting (whitespace, nested objects, the value appearing as a substring of another key). On any parse hiccup the question silently contributes a null score, skewing the vendor risk rating with no log/exception. Scoring is security/compliance-relevant.
reproduction: Provide an options_json where the option value is a substring of another option key, or with spaces around the colon — the manual parser mis-reads or returns null while a JSON parse would be correct.
resolution: Deserialize options_json with Jackson into Map<String,Number> (or a small DTO) once, look up the option value, and surface a clear validation error (as the SCALE_1_5/BOOLEAN branches already do) instead of returning null on parse failure.

title: Integration adapters duplicate config/properties (Retry, enabled/mode/baseUrl/timeout) and the StubInvocation/StatusDto DTOs across 4 vendors
cvss: Maintainability: per-vendor *Properties classes, IntegrationConfig classes, and small DTOs are near-identical, so cross-cutting config changes (new retry knob, common kill-switch semantics) must be applied 4x.
description: Each vendor adapter has its own *Properties with the same enabled/mode/baseUrl/timeoutMs fields and an identical nested `Retry { maxAttempts=3; initialDelayMs=500; backoffMultiplier=2.0 }` class plus identical getters/setters; the *IntegrationConfig classes share the same RestClient-builder shape; and `StubInvocation` (a record of at/method/targetId/payload) is copied into all 4 vendor dto packages while `StatusDto` is copied into 2.
rootCause: Adapters were templated per vendor with no shared `integrations.common` package for cross-vendor config and DTOs.
evidence: find StubInvocation.java -> 4 copies (crowdstrike, servicenow, splunk, tenable). find StatusDto.java -> 2 copies (crowdstrike, tenable). jscpd: CrowdStrikeProperties.java[110-126]<=>SplunkProperties.java[95-111] and <=>TenableProperties.java[127-143] (17 lines each, the Retry block); CrowdStrikeIntegrationConfig.java[1-15]<=> three other IntegrationConfig files.
impact: 4 copies of the Retry config and StubInvocation record; 2 of StatusDto. Adding a retry parameter or a stub field means editing every vendor package, and they can drift (Splunk's Properties already omits OAuth getters CrowdStrike has).
reproduction: Run `find tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/integrations -name StubInvocation.java` (4 hits) and compare the four records; diff CrowdStrikeProperties.Retry against TenableProperties.Retry / SplunkProperties.Retry — identical fields and defaults.
resolution: Create `integrations/common` holding a shared `RetryProperties` (composed via @NestedConfigurationProperty), a base config helper for the RestClient, and shared `StubInvocation` / `IntegrationStatus` records. Vendor properties extend/compose the shared pieces.

title: Dashboard read methods scan large paged result sets in memory with magic page sizes (ObService.dashboard, OutsourcingService.dashboard)
category: Long method / Magic numbers / Inefficient read pattern
cvss: Maintainability + scalability: dashboard aggregation is done by pulling fixed-size pages (500/200/10) into memory and filtering with streams, mixing query and aggregation concerns in one ~68-LOC method with unexplained constants.
description: `ObService.dashboard()` (511-579, ~68 LOC) computes 'revoked last 24h' by fetching `PageRequest.of(0, 500)` of consents and filtering in a stream (518-524), 'samaReportableOpen' from `PageRequest.of(0, 200)` of incidents (531-535), and consents-by-type from another 500-page (553-557). The page sizes 500, 200, 10 and the 30-day cert window are unexplained literals. A comment at 518 admits 'Approximate "revoked last 24h" by scanning paged set' — i.e. the figure is wrong once there are >500 consents.
rootCause: Aggregations were implemented with in-memory stream filtering over capped pages rather than COUNT/aggregate repository queries, and bounds were hard-coded inline.
evidence: ObService.java:519-524 stream over PageRequest.of(0,500); :531-535 over PageRequest.of(0,200); :543-546 certExpiring filter; comment :518 'Approximate ... by scanning paged set'. Method spans 68 LOC. OutsourcingService.dashboard (446-488) and CptyService.dashboard (425-470) follow the same shape.
impact: Results silently become inaccurate beyond the page cap (e.g. revokedConsents24h undercounts when >500 consents exist), and the method loads up to ~1200 rows per dashboard hit. Magic numbers obscure intent and are duplicated across dashboards.
reproduction: Seed >500 consents with >500 revoked in 24h; ObService.dashboard reports at most the 500-page subset's matches, not the true count.
resolution: Replace in-memory scans with repository COUNT/aggregate queries (e.g. countByOrganisationIdAndStatusAndRevokedAtAfter, group-by counts). Extract page sizes / windows into named constants. Consider splitting dashboard() into smaller private aggregators.
patchAfter: long revokedRecent = consentRepo.countByOrganisationIdAndStatusAndRevokedAtAfter(org(), "REVOKED", LocalDateTime.now().minusDays(1));
references: Avoid in-memory aggregation of capped pages
Replace magic numbers with named constants

title: Swallowed exception drops the cause when an exercise run completes (AAR draft failure logged without stacktrace)
cvss: On run completion, createAfterActionDraft is wrapped in `catch (RuntimeException ignored)` that logs only a generic warning with no exception object, discarding the stacktrace and cause. The transition is intentionally allowed to stand, but the failure becomes effectively undiagnosable in production.
description: When a run transitions to COMPLETED, the AAR draft is created in a try/catch where the catch parameter is named `ignored` and the log statement is `log.warn("AAR draft creation for run {} failed but transition stands", saved.getId());` — the caught exception is never passed to the logger, so the cause and stacktrace are lost. The intent (don't roll back the transition for a courtesy draft) is sound, but the diagnostic is gutted.
rootCause: Catch-and-continue written for resilience but logging the exception object was omitted; the `ignored` name signals the swallow.
evidence: Lines 283-285: `} catch (RuntimeException ignored) {\n    log.warn("AAR draft creation for run {} failed but transition stands", saved.getId());\n}` — no `ignored` reference in the warn call.
impact: If AAR draft creation starts failing (e.g. a NPE in buildObserverFindingsSection or a DB constraint), operators see only 'failed' with no reason, making the bug hard to triage. AAR drafts silently stop being produced.
reproduction: Force an exception inside createAfterActionDraft; complete a run; observe a warn line with no stacktrace/cause.
resolution: Log the exception object so the cause is preserved: `log.warn("AAR draft creation for run {} failed but transition stands", saved.getId(), ex);` and name the variable `ex` not `ignored`.

title: Over-broad catch(Exception) in XLSX export methods masks IOExceptions and unrelated runtime faults as 'Excel generation failed'
cvss: Three XLSX builders wrap their entire body in catch(Exception) and rethrow a generic ExportException, conflating genuine POI/IO failures with NPEs and other programming errors. The cause is preserved, but the blanket catch hides the failure category and makes data-shape bugs surface as 'Excel generation failed'.
description: riskRegisterXlsx(), findingsXlsx(), and kriDashboardXlsx() each end with `} catch (Exception e) { throw new ExportException("Excel", "Excel generation failed", e); }`. The only checked exception in scope is IOException from writeWorkbook(); catching Exception additionally swallows the category of every RuntimeException (e.g. a NullPointerException from a malformed reading) into the same generic message. The PDF path (buildReportPdf) correctly catches only the specific DocumentException.
rootCause: Defensive blanket catch added to guarantee a friendly error, at the cost of distinguishing IO failures from logic bugs.
evidence: ExportService.java:357, 401, 464 all `catch (Exception e)`; contrast buildReportPdf at line 280 which catches `DocumentException` specifically. writeWorkbook declares only `throws java.io.IOException`.
impact: A programming defect in row mapping is reported to callers as an Excel-generation infrastructure failure, sending triage in the wrong direction. RuntimeExceptions that should bubble to the global handler are reclassified.
reproduction: Introduce a NullPointerException in the row loop of riskRegisterXlsx(); call it; observe ExportException('Excel','Excel generation failed') instead of the NPE propagating.
resolution: Catch only IOException around writeWorkbook (the workbook try-with-resources already handles close), and let RuntimeExceptions propagate to the GlobalExceptionHandler. If a uniform export error is required, catch IOException specifically and wrap that.

title: Recommendation state machine encoded twice in StrategyRoiService (guardRecommendation vs allowedFrom) — guaranteed to drift
cvss: The same PENDING_REVIEW/APPROVED/REJECTED/DEFERRED transition table is written as two parallel switch expressions: one returning a boolean (validation), one returning the allowed-set (for the error message). Editing one without the other yields a guard that rejects/accepts a transition while reporting the wrong allowed set.
description: guardRecommendation(from,to) (401-412) and allowedFrom(from) (414-422) both hard-code the identical transition map by state. guardRecommendation checks `Set.of(...).contains(to)` per case; allowedFrom returns the same `Set.of(...)` per case. The two must be kept byte-aligned by hand.
rootCause: Need both a boolean check and the allowed-set for the IllegalTransitionException message; instead of deriving the boolean from the set, both were written out.
evidence: Both methods list `case "PENDING_REVIEW" -> Set.of("APPROVED","REJECTED","DEFERRED")` etc. The same data appears twice (also echoed a third time in the class Javadoc at lines 57-63 and 391-399).
impact: A future transition rule change applied to only one method produces inconsistent behaviour: guard allows a transition whose error message claims it isn't allowed, or vice-versa. Classic single-source-of-truth violation.
reproduction: Add a new allowed transition to guardRecommendation only; trigger an invalid transition; the thrown IllegalTransitionException's allowed-set (from allowedFrom) is now wrong.
resolution: Define one `Map<String,Set<String>> ALLOWED` (as ExerciseRuntimeService already does at its ALLOWED_TRANSITIONS) and derive both the boolean and the allowed-set from it.

title: null-safe string helpers (safe/nullSafe/truncate) re-implemented in 10+ classes across the four modules
cvss: The trivial `safe(String)` null-guard is hand-copied into 10 classes within the assigned modules (with two subtly different return values — empty-string vs em-dash), alongside duplicate `nullSafe` and `truncate` helpers. Harmless individually but a recurring copy-paste that should be one shared utility.
description: A `private static String safe(String)` helper is declared independently in at least 10 classes across reporting, platform, and bcm. Two distinct semantics coexist: reporting/PDF variants return em-dash ('—') for null while platform/calendar variants return empty string, so the helper name is overloaded with different meaning. Separately, `nullSafe(String)` and `truncate(String,int)` are duplicated between ExerciseRuntimeService and ExerciseObserverService (see QUAL-BCMP-002).
rootCause: No shared text/formatting utility; each exporter/service re-adds the tiny helper it needs.
evidence: grep `private static String safe(String` over the four modules: 10 matches with two return-value variants (`? "" :` vs `? "—" :`).
impact: Low functional risk, but the same-named helper meaning two different things (blank vs dash) is a trap for readers and code-search-driven edits; widens the surface that must be touched for any formatting policy change.
reproduction: Run `rg -n 'private static String safe\(String' tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/{bcm,platform,dashboard,reporting}`.
resolution: Introduce a single `common/util/Strings` (or `TextFormat`) with `orDash(String)` and `orEmpty(String)` plus `truncate(String,int)`, and replace the per-class copies. Picking distinct names removes the blank-vs-dash ambiguity.
patchBefore:
// repeated in 10 classes
private static String safe(String s) { return s == null ? "—" : s; }  // some return "" instead

title: Escalation-tier aging thresholds (30/60/90 days) and the day clamp (28) are magic numbers duplicated across reporting builders
cvss: The findings-aging escalation tier rule (>=90 EXEC, >=60 DIRECTOR, >=30 MANAGER) is hand-inlined in at least three places, and the month/quarter day clamp (28) is repeated. Changing escalation policy requires hunting down each literal; the three copies can silently diverge.
description: The aging-tier ternary `daysOpen >= 90 ? "EXEC" : daysOpen >= 60 ? "DIRECTOR" : daysOpen >= 30 ? "MANAGER" : "ON_TRACK"` is duplicated verbatim in ExportService.findingsAgingPdf (165) and ExportService.findingsXlsx (390); BoardPackService.renderFindings (257-260) re-implements the same 90/60/30 buckets inline. ReportSchedulerService clamps anchor day with `if (day < 1) day = 1; if (day > 28) day = 28;` twice (228, 237) — also two statements per line, hurting readability.
rootCause: Business thresholds embedded as bare integer literals at each use site rather than named constants or a shared classifier.
evidence: ExportService.java:165 and :390 identical tier ternary; BoardPackService.java:257-260 the same thresholds; ReportSchedulerService.java:228,237 duplicate `day>28` clamp.
impact: An escalation-policy change (e.g. tighten DIRECTOR to 45 days) must be applied in three files and risks the PDF and XLSX exports disagreeing; the 28-day clamp magic number is unexplained at the call site.
reproduction: grep for `>= 90` / `>= 60` / `>= 30` and `> 28` in the reporting package; observe the repeated literals.
resolution: Define named constants (AGING_EXEC_DAYS=90, AGING_DIRECTOR_DAYS=60, AGING_MANAGER_DAYS=30, MAX_ANCHOR_DAY=28) or a single `agingTier(long days)` helper, and reuse across the PDF, XLSX, and board-pack renderers.
patchBefore:
String tier = daysOpen >= 90 ? "EXEC" : daysOpen >= 60 ? "DIRECTOR" : daysOpen >= 30 ? "MANAGER" : "ON_TRACK"; // copied 3x
if (day < 1) day = 1; if (day > 28) day = 28;

title: Reflection-based principal probing with a blanket swallow in BcpBinderService.currentUserId()
cvss: currentUserId() uses reflection to call getUserId()/getId() on the security principal to avoid importing GrcUserDetails, wrapped in a catch(Exception ignored) that swallows everything. Reflection over the auth principal is fragile (breaks silently on principal-shape changes) and the swallow hides genuine failures.
description: currentUserId() obtains the Authentication, then reflectively probes method names {"getUserId","getId"} on the principal and returns the first Long result; the whole block is inside `catch (Exception ignored) { /* never bubble up */ }`. The codebase already has a concrete `GrcUserDetails` (referenced in CLAUDE.md security notes) exposing getUserId(); reflecting to avoid the import couples this service to method-name strings that the compiler cannot verify.
rootCause: An attempt to keep the binder service decoupled from the security package for test wiring, implemented via reflection + total exception suppression rather than a small shared accessor.
evidence: Lines 298-304 reflectively invoke getter names; lines 306-308 `catch (Exception ignored) { // never bubble up — current user id is informational only }`.
impact: If the principal type changes (or a getter is renamed), the user id silently becomes null with no log, degrading audit/attribution quietly. Reflection also bypasses compile-time safety and is slower than a direct call.
reproduction: Swap the principal to a type without getUserId/getId; call currentUserId(); it returns null with no diagnostic.
resolution: Replace with a shared `SecurityUtils.currentUserId()` that does an `instanceof GrcUserDetails` cast (the type already exists), or inject a small `CurrentUserProvider` bean. Keep the null-on-anonymous behaviour but drop the reflection and the blanket swallow; if a defensive catch is retained, log at debug with the exception.
patchAfter:
Object principal = a.getPrincipal();
return principal instanceof GrcUserDetails u ? u.getUserId() : null;

title: Legacy BcmController binds JPA entities directly as request bodies instead of validated DTOs
cvss: CRUD endpoints accept and return @Entity types (BcmPlan, CriticalProcess, BiaRecord, BcmExercise) directly over the wire with no request DTO or Jakarta validation, exposing persistence internals (e.g. organisationId, isDeleted, audit columns) to the client and allowing mass-assignment-style binding.
description: createPlan(@RequestBody BcmPlan req), createProcess(@RequestBody CriticalProcess req), createBia(@RequestBody BiaRecord req), createExercise(@RequestBody BcmExercise req) (and their update counterparts) accept the JPA entity directly. The controller is marked @Deprecated (legacy surface), and the module convention elsewhere uses dedicated request/response DTOs with `@Valid`. No `@Valid` appears on these bodies, so server-side validation messages (the messages*.properties machinery) are not exercised, and client-supplied entity fields like organisationId/isDeleted/createdAt can be bound.
rootCause: Legacy CRUD controller predates the DTO convention; entities double as the API contract.
evidence: BcmController.java:69 `public BcmPlan createPlan(@RequestBody BcmPlan req)`, :128 CriticalProcess, :156 BiaRecord, :190 BcmExercise — none annotated `@Valid`; methods return the entity directly too.
impact: Tenant-owned columns are part of the bind surface (defence relies entirely on the service overwriting organisationId); response leaks internal columns; no declarative validation; API contract is coupled to the DB schema so any entity change is a breaking API change.
reproduction: POST /api/v1/bcm/legacy-plans with a JSON body including organisationId and isDeleted; observe they bind onto the entity before the service runs.
resolution: Introduce request/response DTOs (BcmPlanRequest/Response, etc.) with Jakarta validation and `@Valid`, mapping in the service; never accept or return @Entity at the controller boundary. Since the controller is already @Deprecated, schedule this with the documented cycle-controller migration.
patchBefore:
@PostMapping("/legacy-plans")
public BcmPlan createPlan(@RequestBody BcmPlan req) { return bcmService.createPlan(req); }

title: Repetitive update/save/delete CRUD scaffolding duplicated across 8 entities in CyberService
cvss: Maintainability only: the same five-line 'copy id/orgId/externalId/createdAt, force isDeleted=false, save' block is repeated per entity; a bug fix in the merge logic must be applied 8 times.
description: The updateX(id, req) methods for CyberControl, CyberSubControl, ControlAssessment, Vulnerability, VulnException, CyberIncident, CyberAsset and CyberActionPlan are byte-for-byte identical except for the entity type: load existing, copy req.setId/setOrganisationId/setExternalId/setCreatedAt from existing, setIsDeleted(false), save. Likewise the deleteX(id) methods (8 copies of load + setIsDeleted(true) + save) and the saveX(entity, orgId) methods. This is the same 'reattach detached entity' merge pattern repeated ~24 times.
rootCause: No generic base service / mapper helper for the org-scoped soft-deletable CRUD pattern that every BaseEntity child shares.
evidence: updateControl (199-207), updateSubControl (240-249), updateAssessment (282-290), updateVulnerability (354-362), updateException (411-420), updateIncident (455-463), updateAsset (508-517), updateActionPlan (586-594) all repeat: req.setId(existing.getId()); req.setOrganisationId(existing.getOrganisationId()); req.setExternalId(existing.getExternalId()); req.setCreatedAt(existing.getCreatedAt()); req.setIsDeleted(false); return repo.save(req);
impact: Any change to the merge contract (e.g. also preserving a new audit column) must be hand-applied to 8 methods; easy to miss one and create an inconsistency or a mass-assignment hole.
reproduction: Diff updateControl against updateAsset / updateIncident in CyberService.java — only the type name and repository differ.
resolution: Introduce a small protected generic helper, e.g. protected <T extends BaseEntity> T merge(T req, T existing, JpaRepository<T,Long> repo) that copies id/orgId/externalId/createdAt and forces isDeleted=false, or use a MapStruct mapper with @MappingTarget. Each updateX collapses to load + merge.

title: SocOpsScheduledSweep.alreadyFired runs an unbounded per-entity audit scan inside every sweep loop
cvss: Performance risk that grows with audit-log size: dedup is implemented as a full fetch of an entity's audit rows followed by an in-memory linear scan, executed once per candidate row per sweep, per tenant, hourly.
description: alreadyFired() calls auditRepo.findByOrganisationIdAndEntityTypeAndEntityIdOrderByCreatedAtDesc(org, entityType, entityId) — fetching EVERY audit row ever written for that entity — and then linearly scans them in Java for a matching action_type marker. It is invoked for every candidate row in all 10 sweeps. As the audit ledger accumulates history for long-lived entities (a SecurityEvent or CyberInsurance policy may collect dozens of audit rows over time), this materializes and scans an ever-growing list to answer a boolean that the database could answer with a single exists query.
rootCause: Reused a generic audit finder instead of adding a targeted existsBy...AndActionType repository method.
evidence: Lines 393-398: `List<AuditLogEntry> rows = auditRepo.findByOrganisationIdAndEntityTypeAndEntityIdOrderByCreatedAtDesc(org, entityType, entityId); for (AuditLogEntry row : rows) { if (marker.equals(row.getActionType())) return true; } return false;` — loads all rows, scans in memory.
impact: Sweep cost scales with cumulative audit history rather than open-item count; on a large tenant the hourly sweep does N_candidates full-history fetches, increasing DB load and GC pressure over the system's lifetime.
reproduction: Read alreadyFired (391-399); note it fetches the full ordered list then iterates, called from 12 sites inside per-row loops.
resolution: Add a repository method `boolean existsByOrganisationIdAndEntityTypeAndEntityIdAndActionType(Long org, String type, Long id, String actionType)` and have alreadyFired delegate to it, pushing the predicate to SQL and avoiding the materialized scan.
patchAfter:
return auditRepo.existsByOrganisationIdAndEntityTypeAndEntityIdAndActionType(
    org, entityType, entityId, AUDIT_PREFIX + trigger);

title: ThreatIntelCorrelationService.correlate is a 115-line high-branching method with a copy-pasted hit-builder for IP and HOSTNAME
cvss: Maintainability only: the IOC-matching method is long and branches through a 4-way switch; the ASSET CorrelationHit construction is duplicated between the IP and HOSTNAME cases, so a field change must be made twice.
description: correlate() spans 115 lines (56-170) and does: empty-input guard, build CVE index, build IP index, then a per-IOC for-loop containing a 4-arm switch (CVE/IP/HOSTNAME/default), then sort + count. The IP arm (lines 112-127) and the HOSTNAME arm (lines 133-148) build a CorrelationHit for an asset with an identical 10-argument new CorrelationHit(...) call and the same CRITICAL/HIGH regulatorEscalation check — only the matching predicate differs (exact ipIndex lookup vs hostname substring). jscpd independently flags this self-duplication (113-128 <-> 134-149, 16 lines).
rootCause: The HOSTNAME case was added by copying the IP case; the shared asset-hit construction was never extracted to a helper.
evidence: jscpd-report.json: ThreatIntelCorrelationService.java:113-128 duplicates 134-149 (16 lines). Both arms call `hits.add(new CorrelationHit(ioc.type(), ioc.value(), ioc.severity(), "ASSET", a.getId(), a.getAssetName(), null, a.getCriticality(), blendedSeverity(ioc.severity(), a.getCriticality()), a.getAssetName(), ioc.sourceFeed() == null ? req.feedName() : ioc.sourceFeed()))` and the same escalation check.
impact: Adding a field to the asset-match hit (or changing the escalation rule) requires editing two places; the long method is harder to read and to test arm-by-arm.
reproduction: Compare lines 110-128 with 129-149 in ThreatIntelCorrelationService.java; the new CorrelationHit(...) and escalation block are identical.
resolution: Extract a private helper addAssetHit(List<CorrelationHit> hits, IndicatorOfCompromise ioc, CyberAsset a, CorrelationRequest req) that performs the escalation check and the hit construction, and call it from both the IP and HOSTNAME arms. Consider extracting the index-building blocks into separate methods to shorten correlate().
patchBefore:
case "IP" -> { for (CyberAsset a : matches) { if (CRITICAL||HIGH) escalate; hits.add(new CorrelationHit(...10 args...)); } }
case "HOSTNAME" -> { for (CyberAsset a : assetList) { ...same escalate; hits.add(new CorrelationHit(...same 10 args...)); } }

title: ComplaintService.generateQuarterlyReport is an 80-line method computing eight aggregates inline
cvss: Maintainability only: a single method computes received/resolved/escalated counts, average resolution, two SLA-breach percentages, top category, and total compensation, then upserts — many independent calculations in one transactional method.
description: generateQuarterlyReport(String) spans 80 lines and performs eight distinct aggregate computations over the complaint list (totalReceived, totalResolved, totalEscalated, avgResolution, ackBreaches+ackBreachPct, resBreaches+resBreachPct, byCategory top, totalCompensation) plus the report upsert and audit, all inline. The two SLA-breach calculations (lines 370-387) each contain a non-trivial nested ternary over null acknowledgedOn/resolvedOn. This is the highest-branching method in the consumer package and is harder to unit-test than the rest of the well-factored ComplaintService.
rootCause: The report aggregation was written as one procedural block rather than decomposed into per-metric helpers.
evidence: Method body lines 350-430 (80 LOC); eight separate stream/loop aggregations; nested ternaries at lines 372-374 and 378-380 for the breach predicates.
impact: Each metric cannot be tested in isolation; the breach-percentage logic (the part most likely to be wrong) is buried mid-method; future SAMA report fields lengthen the method further.
reproduction: Read ComplaintService.java:350-430; count the distinct aggregate computations (8) before the upsert at line 403.
resolution: Extract per-metric helpers, e.g. ackBreachCount(List<Complaint>), resolutionBreachCount(List<Complaint>), topCategory(List<Complaint>), and have generateQuarterlyReport orchestrate them. This shortens the method and makes the breach logic independently testable.

title: CyberService.getDashboard is a 73-line method performing 6 full-table loads and many stream passes inline
cvss: Maintainability + minor performance: a single dashboard method eagerly loads all controls, vulns, incidents, assets, action plans and evidence for the tenant and runs ~15 separate stream filter/count passes over them inline.
description: getDashboard(Long) is 73 lines. It calls findAllByOrganisationId on six repositories (controls, vulns, incidents, assets, action plans, evidence — lines 57,66,74,80,85,92) to pull entire tenant tables into memory, then runs roughly fifteen separate .stream().filter(...).count() passes plus four per-framework score computations (each scoreForFramework itself streams the controls twice — lines 134-145) and three additional paged recent-N queries. The counting could largely be pushed to repository count queries; at minimum the method should be decomposed per dashboard section.
rootCause: Dashboard was assembled by loading full lists and counting in Java for expedience, in one monolithic method.
evidence: Six findAllByOrganisationId calls (lines 57,66,74,80,85,92); ~15 stream counts (lines 59-104); scoreForFramework streams controls twice per framework x4 frameworks (lines 134-145, called 109-112).
impact: On large tenants the dashboard pulls every control/vuln/incident/asset/evidence/action-plan row into memory each call; method length makes the aggregation hard to follow and to test section-by-section.
reproduction: Read getDashboard (53-126); count repository findAll* calls (6) and stream count() passes (~15). scoreForFramework (132-147) streams the same list twice.
resolution: Extract per-section private methods (e.g. populateControlStats, populateVulnStats) and/or replace the in-memory counts with repository count-by-status queries (countByOrganisationIdAndImplementationStatus, etc.). Compute the four framework scores in a single pass over controls rather than two passes per framework.

title: REST controllers replicate identical import + class-annotation boilerplate header across 200+ controllers (CommitteeController is the canonical donor)
cvss: Not a security issue. Largely unavoidable Spring framework scaffolding; rated Low. 202 controller<->controller clones / 2,635 dup lines, but most is the import block + @RestController/@RequestMapping/@RequiredArgsConstructor/@Tag/@SecurityRequirement header that idiomatic Spring requires per class. Real but limited dedupe opportunity.
description: java-controller <-> java-controller = 202 clones / 2,635 dup lines. CommitteeController.java:5-39 is the most frequent clone donor in the whole report — it forms a 31-to-35-line clone with at least 30 distinct module controllers (openbanking, opres, reginspect, rrp, sharia, fraud, evidence, incident, intake, ...). The duplicated span is the import list plus the class-level annotation header: @RestController, @RequestMapping("/api/..."), @RequiredArgsConstructor, @Tag(...), @SecurityRequirement(name = "bearerAuth"), and the `private final XService service;` field. Beyond the header, many endpoint methods follow an identical CRUD shape (@GetMapping list with status/page/size params, @GetMapping/{id}, @PostMapping create returning 201, @PutMapping/{id}). There is no abstract base controller in the codebase (grep for BaseController/abstract *Controller → 0).
rootCause: Spring's annotation-driven style requires the same import set and class-level annotations on every @RestController, and the team standardized on a fixed header (RequiredArgsConstructor + Tag + SecurityRequirement). New controllers are created by copying the header from an existing one. No shared @PageableDefault/constant or meta-annotation consolidates the repeated @PreAuthorize/@SecurityRequirement.
evidence: jscpd: controller<->controller = 202 clones / 2,635 dup lines. CommitteeController.java:5-39 partners with 30 distinct controllers in the duplicates array (count of unique partner files). 233 files contain @RestController. Confirmed header identity by reading CommitteeController.java:20-27 and ObController.java:43-48 (same @RestController/@RequestMapping/@RequiredArgsConstructor/@Tag/@SecurityRequirement stack).
impact: Low functional risk — this is mostly idiomatic framework boilerplate. The realistic cost is that cross-cutting controller conventions (e.g. standardizing the default page size, adding a common @SecurityRequirement, a shared pagination param) can't be changed in one place. The repeated CRUD method bodies (list/get/create/update) are a secondary, more valuable dedupe target than the import header.
reproduction: 1) Open CommitteeController.java:5-39 and ObController.java:18-48 — identical annotation header. 2) In jscpd-report.json, filter duplicates where firstFile/secondFile contains CommitteeController.java → 30 distinct partner controllers. 3) grep -rl 'abstract class.*Controller' tss-grc-backend → 0 (no base controller).
resolution: Two targeted moves: (a) introduce a composed meta-annotation, e.g. `@GrcRestController` bundling @RestController + @RequiredArgsConstructor + @SecurityRequirement(name="bearerAuth") + @Tag, to collapse the annotation header; (b) for the genuinely repeated CRUD bodies, consider a thin generic `AbstractCrudController<TResp, TCreate, TUpdate>` or shared response helpers — but keep this optional, since over-abstracting controllers can hurt readability. The import-block portion of the clone is inherent to Java/Spring and is acceptable to leave; do not chase it. Prioritize this finding below DUP-001/002/003.

title: Repetitive synthesizer boilerplate: 12 near-identical row-mapping methods in NdiReportService
cvss: Maintainability: 12 private synthesizer methods (184-436) each repeat the same LinkedHashMap-build + stream-map-row + ReportResult-wrap shape, so a change to the result envelope or row convention must be replicated 12 times.
description: executiveSummary, maturityHeatmap, complianceStatus, opexDashboard, gapRegister, capaRegister, roadmap, evidenceInventory, domainRollup, cycleHistory, auditTrail, submissionExport all follow the same template: build a summary LinkedHashMap, map a row list with `Map<String,Object> row = new LinkedHashMap<>(); row.put(...); return row;`, and wrap in a ReportResult. The per-field row.put blocks (e.g. 215-222, 235-244, 257-267) are structurally identical and only differ in the entity getters.
rootCause: No generic row-projection helper; each report type was authored independently.
evidence: Pattern `Map<String, Object> row = new LinkedHashMap<>();` followed by N row.put(...) calls appears in 10 of the 12 synthesizers. dispatch switch at 165-179 routes to all of them.
impact: Adding a column convention (e.g. always include 'id') or changing ReportResult shape is a 12-site edit; high copy-paste surface invites inconsistency between report types.
reproduction: Compare maturityHeatmap (207-225) and complianceStatus (227-247) — same skeleton, different getters.
resolution: Extract a small generic helper `rows(List<T> src, Function<T, Map<String,Object>> projector)` and a `result(type, cycleId, summary, rows)` factory so each synthesizer reduces to a projector lambda; or drive projection from a column-definition map.
patchAfter:
return result("MATURITY_HEATMAP", cycleId, sum, project(rows, m -> Map.of(
    "id", m.getId(), "domain", m.getDomain(), "currentLevel", m.getCurrentLevel(), ...)));

title: Injected-but-unused ObjectMapper field flagged with @SuppressWarnings instead of removed
cvss: Minor: a constructor-injected dependency that is never used is dead weight that misleads readers about the class's collaborators and was deliberately masked with @SuppressWarnings rather than removed.
description: Field `@SuppressWarnings("unused") private final ObjectMapper json;` (line 58) is injected through the constructor (param at 71, assigned at 83) but never referenced anywhere in the class body. The @SuppressWarnings annotation acknowledges the dead dependency rather than removing it.
rootCause: Likely a leftover from an earlier design where the report service serialised JSON itself; the field was retained 'just in case' and silenced.
evidence: Line 58 declaration carries @SuppressWarnings("unused"); grep for `json.` in the file returns no usages (only the assignment `this.json = json;` at line 83).
impact: Misleading API surface and an unnecessary bean dependency; the suppression normalises leaving dead injected fields in place.
reproduction: Search the file for `json.` — there are no method calls on the field.
resolution: Remove the field, its constructor parameter, and the assignment. If JSON serialisation is planned, add it back when actually used.
patchBefore:
@SuppressWarnings("unused") private final ObjectMapper json;
... NdiReportService(..., ObjectMapper json) { ...; this.json = json; }
patchAfter: // field, constructor param, and assignment removed

title: Per-instance new ObjectMapper() in AiSuggestionService instead of injecting the shared bean
cvss: Minor: constructing a fresh ObjectMapper as a field initialiser ignores the Spring-managed, configured ObjectMapper used elsewhere (NdiReportService/NdiSubmissionPackageService inject it), so any project-wide Jackson config (modules, date handling) does not apply here.
description: Line 35: `private final ObjectMapper mapper = new ObjectMapper();` builds an un-configured mapper local to the service while the rest of the codebase autowires the Spring-configured ObjectMapper. The mapper is used in persist() (457-459) to serialise input/output payloads.
rootCause: Inconsistent dependency strategy — this service self-instantiates Jackson rather than injecting the application bean.
evidence: Line 35 `new ObjectMapper()`; compare NdiSubmissionPackageService line 60 / NdiReportService line 58 which take ObjectMapper via constructor injection.
impact: If the application customises Jackson (e.g. JavaTimeModule, fail-on-unknown), AiSuggestion input/output JSON is serialised with default settings, diverging from other modules; also two divergent ObjectMapper configs in one app are a known footgun.
reproduction: Add a global Jackson customiser and observe it is not reflected in AiSuggestion.outputJson.
resolution: Inject ObjectMapper via the constructor (Lombok @RequiredArgsConstructor already in use) and drop the `new ObjectMapper()` initialiser.
patchBefore: private final ObjectMapper mapper = new ObjectMapper();
patchAfter: private final ObjectMapper mapper; // injected; @RequiredArgsConstructor wires the Spring bean

title: Cross-tenant findAll() in NdiScheduler report loop and org-discovery shortcut
cvss: Correctness/scalability: reportScheduleSweep iterates reportDefs.findAll() across every tenant each minute and distinctOrgIds() derives the tenant universe from the report-definition table, a self-admitted demo shortcut that loads all orgs' rows into memory.
description: reportScheduleSweep (82) calls reportDefs.findAll() — a non-tenant-scoped query that pulls every organisation's report definitions every 60s. distinctOrgIds() (119-127) also calls findAll() and maps to distinct organisation ids to drive the evidence-expiry sweep. The class Javadoc (lines 34-41) explicitly notes this is a demo shortcut that 'in production a proper org-iteration service would replace'.
rootCause: No platform-level tenant registry; the scheduler improvises tenant discovery from a domain table and bypasses the org-scoped repository finders the rest of the module uses.
evidence: Line 84 `for (NdiReportDefinition def : reportDefs.findAll())`; lines 122-126 `reportDefs.findAll().stream().map(...).distinct().toList()`. Javadoc 34-41 documents the shortcut.
impact: Memory + query cost grows linearly with all tenants' report definitions on every minute tick; tenants with no report definitions are invisible to the evidence-expiry sweep, so their evidence never auto-expires. Repository usage bypasses the org-scoped finder convention.
reproduction: Add a tenant with NDI evidence but no report definitions; observe its evidence is never swept (distinctOrgIds omits it).
resolution: Introduce a platform tenant-registry service and iterate that; or add a dedicated paged/streamed query keyed by 'has schedule cron' to avoid full-table scans. Decouple expiry-sweep org discovery from the report-definition table.
patchAfter: for (Long orgId : tenantRegistry.activeOrgIds()) { ... reportDefs.findScheduledByOrg(orgId) ... }
references: CLAUDE.md: 'Every repository query must filter by organisation_id'

title: Per-entity DTO mappers and *_ALLOWED transition tables duplicated wholesale across sister services
cvss: Each new column on an entity requires touching both the entity, the request-apply block, AND the hand-written builder mapper; the builder-chain mappers are long, near-mechanical, and structurally identical between modules, so they are a steady source of 'forgot to map field X' defects.
description: Every service hand-rolls `private static XResponse toX(XEntity)` builder chains (RrpService has 5, ShariaService has 6, FraudService 3, OpResService 3) that mechanically copy 15-30 getters into a builder. The same pattern of static transition maps (`RESOLUTION_ALLOWED`, `FINDING_ALLOWED`, `NC_ALLOWED`, `PRODUCT_ALLOWED` in ShariaService; `ALLOWED` in Rrp/Fraud/OpRes/Finding/IaEngagement/SanctionsHit) plus an identical `guardTransition` body is repeated. jscpd flags the mapper region directly (RiskControlFindingPivotService:622 <-> :638; CptyService:528 <-> RrpService:592, 30 lines).
rootCause: Project convention is hand-written builder mappers (no MapStruct) and a private transition-map-per-service. Both are valid choices individually, but the verbatim repetition is unmanaged.
evidence: RrpService 5 mappers (lines 621-712, ~92 LOC of pure builder chains). ShariaService 6 mappers (701-819, ~119 LOC). ShariaService declares 4 separate `Map<String,Set<String>>` ALLOWED tables (78-105). The guardTransition body in FraudService:350-356 and OpResService:274-280 is identical apart from the message prefix.
impact: Field-mapping omissions are silent (a forgotten `.fieldX()` compiles fine and just returns null to the UI). High line-count with low information density inflates every service file.
reproduction: Compare RrpService.toOption (652-666) with the entity setters in addOption (220-241): both enumerate the same 14 fields; adding a 15th requires editing both.
resolution: Adopt MapStruct (or a shared reflective copy like the BeanUtils approach ScmService already uses) for response mapping, and factor the transition-guard into a tiny generic helper `StateMachine.guard(map, from, to, label)` reused by all services.

title: Dead dashboard query: FraudService counts status="TRIAGE" which the state machine never assigns
cvss: Functional-correctness smell rather than crash: the `triageCount` tile on the Fraud dashboard is hard-wired to always read 0 because no case is ever persisted with status TRIAGE, yet the field is presented to users as a live count.
description: `dashboard()` populates `.triageCount(caseRepo.countByOrganisationIdAndStatus(orgId, "TRIAGE"))`. The class-level comment (lines 71-76) and the ALLOWED_TRANSITIONS map (77-84) explicitly state TRIAGE is NOT a held state — `triage()` (151-183) sets `triagedAt` and immediately advances to INVESTIGATING or FALSE_POSITIVE. No code path ever calls `setStatus("TRIAGE")`. Therefore this count is permanently 0 and is dead/misleading.
rootCause: Dashboard was written against an earlier design where TRIAGE was a held state; when the team collapsed TRIAGE into a transient decision step (documented in the NOTE comment) the dashboard query was not removed.
evidence: grep '"TRIAGE"' in module/fraud => single hit at FraudService.java:333 (the dashboard). ALLOWED_TRANSITIONS has no TRIAGE key on either side; createCase sets status DETECTED, triage() sets INVESTIGATING/FALSE_POSITIVE.
impact: Users see a 'Triage' tile permanently stuck at 0, implying no cases are in triage when in fact cases pass through it instantly. Wastes a DB count round-trip every dashboard load.
reproduction: Create a fraud case, call triage(); query `dashboard().triageCount` — it returns 0 regardless of how many cases were triaged.
resolution: Either remove the triageCount tile, or repurpose it to count cases with `triagedAt != null && status == 'INVESTIGATING'` (i.e. currently-in-investigation-post-triage). Removing is cleaner given the documented design.
patchBefore:
.detectedCount(caseRepo.countByOrganisationIdAndStatus(orgId, "DETECTED"))
.triageCount(caseRepo.countByOrganisationIdAndStatus(orgId, "TRIAGE"))
.investigatingCount(caseRepo.countByOrganisationIdAndStatus(orgId, "INVESTIGATING"))

title: Unreachable guard branch in RrpService.transitionCycle for SUBMITTED
cvss: Logic-correctness smell: the defensive `if (Set.of("SUBMITTED").contains(to))` block can never be entered because the ALLOWED map upstream already rejects any transition whose target is SUBMITTED, so the bespoke 'use the /submit endpoint' message is dead and an actual SUBMITTED attempt yields the generic 'Illegal transition' message instead.
description: `transitionCycle` first computes `allowed = ALLOWED.getOrDefault(from, Set.of())` and throws if `!allowed.contains(to)` (144-148). The ALLOWED map (71-78) never lists SUBMITTED as a reachable target from any state. So by the time control reaches line 149 `if (Set.of("SUBMITTED").contains(to))`, `to` cannot be SUBMITTED — the branch is unreachable and its informative message ('Use the dedicated /submit endpoint to lodge with SAMA') is never shown.
rootCause: The author added a friendly redirect for SUBMITTED but placed it after the generic allow-list check that already short-circuits the same case.
evidence: ALLOWED map values: DRAFT->{IN_PREPARATION}, IN_PREPARATION->{BOARD_REVIEW}, BOARD_REVIEW->{APPROVED,IN_PREPARATION}, APPROVED->{IN_PREPARATION}, SUBMITTED->{ACKNOWLEDGED}, ACKNOWLEDGED->{CLOSED}, CLOSED->{}. No value set contains SUBMITTED.
impact: Misleading dead code; an operator who POSTs a SUBMITTED transition gets the generic error instead of the intended hint to use /submit. Minor, but the branch will confuse future maintainers reasoning about reachability.
reproduction: Call transitionCycle with toStatus=SUBMITTED on an APPROVED cycle: it throws 'Illegal transition APPROVED → SUBMITTED' from line 146, never reaching the friendlier message at 150.
resolution: Move the SUBMITTED hint ahead of the allow-list check, or delete it and document /submit in the controller. Preferred: hoist the special-case before the generic guard.

title: Long, high-branching methods in ShariaService and IncidentService exceed the 40-LOC guideline
cvss: Readability/testability risk: several single methods bundle querying, in-memory bucketing, builder assembly and side-effects, making them hard to unit-test in isolation and easy to break when a column is added.
description: Measured method spans over the ~40-LOC guideline: ShariaService.dashboard() = 73 LOC with ~20 repository calls plus three in-place LinkedHashMap bucketing loops (561-633); ShariaService.transitionProduct() = 56 LOC switch with 7 cases each mutating different fields (496-551); IncidentService.regulatoryTemplates() = 57 LOC building 5 near-identical template maps (282-338); ThreeLinesService.overview() = ~73 LOC mixing role resolution, 4 register pulls, in-memory bucketing and a hard-coded 8-arg band() builder (111-183). transitionResolution (235-282, 48 LOC) and transitionCycle in RrpService are similar.
rootCause: Dashboard/aggregation and transition-with-side-effect logic was kept inline rather than decomposed into per-section private helpers.
evidence: awk LOC counts: ShariaService.dashboard 561-633 => 73; transitionProduct 496-551 => 56; IncidentService.regulatoryTemplates 282-338 => 57. ThreeLinesService.overview 111-183 => ~73 with the 8-positional-arg band() calls (160-167) that are themselves error-prone (all those bare 0 literals).
impact: Each method is hard to read and test; the positional band(...) calls in ThreeLinesService (e.g. `band(LINE_1, roles, line1Risks, 0, line1Capa, 0, 0, line1Overdue, 0)`) are especially fragile — a transposed zero is a silent metric bug.
reproduction: Open the cited ranges; count branches/statements. dashboard() has 3 loops + ~20 sequential repo calls in one method body.
resolution: Extract per-section private helpers (e.g. resolutionStats(), findingStats(), productStats() for the dashboard; one renderTemplate-driven loop over a small template descriptor list for regulatoryTemplates) and replace the 8-positional-arg band() with a small builder/record to make the zeros self-documenting.

title: IllegalTransitionException constructed with an empty allowed-set, discarding the real allowed transitions from the error message
cvss: Diagnostics-quality smell: the transition exception is designed to carry the set of legal next states, but several call sites pass Set.of(), so the resulting 400 error tells the caller nothing about what would have been valid — degrading API ergonomics and support triage.
description: AuditLifecycleService validates transitions with an inline `switch` returning a boolean and, on failure, throws `new IllegalTransitionException(from, to, Set.of())` (lines 104, 178, 250). The exception's third argument is meant to be the legal target set (cf. FindingService.java:115 and IaEngagementService.java:234 which pass the real `allowed` set). Because the allowed set was computed implicitly inside the switch and never materialised, an empty set is passed and the helpful 'allowed: [...]' detail is lost.
rootCause: AuditLifecycleService uses a boolean-returning switch for transition validation instead of the Map<String,Set<String>> approach the other services use, so there is no allowed-set object to hand to the exception.
evidence: AuditLifecycleService.java:104 `if (!ok) throw new IllegalTransitionException(from, to, Set.of());` (repeated at 178, 250). Compare FindingService.java:113-115 which builds `allowed` then throws `new IllegalTransitionException(f.getStatus(), req.getStatus(), allowed)`.
impact: Clients/operators receive 'illegal transition X -> Y' with no hint of valid targets; inconsistent error payloads between audit_lc artefacts (AnnualPlan/WorkingPaper/CapaTask) and the rest of the platform.
reproduction: POST an invalid AnnualPlan transition (e.g. DRAFT -> CLOSED): the IllegalTransitionException is raised with an empty allowed set, so the message omits the legal {AC_REVIEW}.
resolution: Replace the boolean switches with the same `Map<String,Set<String>>` pattern (AP_ALLOWED/WP_ALLOWED/CAPA_ALLOWED) used elsewhere and pass the resolved set to the exception, restoring the informative message.
patchAfter:
Set<String> allowed = AP_ALLOWED.getOrDefault(from, Set.of());
if (!allowed.contains(to)) throw new IllegalTransitionException(from, to, allowed);

title: FraudService.closeCase reconstructs prior status from timestamps after overwriting it — fragile derivation with stale comment
cvss: Correctness-fragility smell: the F8 event's priorStatus is guessed from outcome timestamps because the real prior status was already overwritten, producing values ('RESOLVED','OPEN') that are not even members of the case status vocabulary and can mislead downstream rules.
description: closeCase() sets status to CLOSED at line 283, then at 295-301 emits FRAUD_CASE_CLOSED with `priorStatus` derived as `saved.getConfirmedLossSar() != null ? "CONFIRMED" : saved.getOutcomeSetAt() != null ? "RESOLVED" : "OPEN"`. The real prior status (CONFIRMED/CLEARED/FALSE_POSITIVE) was available before the overwrite but was not captured. The emitted strings 'RESOLVED' and 'OPEN' are not valid FraudCase statuses, so any rule matching on priorStatus equality will misfire.
rootCause: The prior status was not saved into a local before `c.setStatus("CLOSED")`, forcing a lossy timestamp-based reconstruction (the inline comment admits 'we already overwrote it').
evidence: Line 283 `c.setStatus("CLOSED")`; lines 297-300 reconstruct priorStatus from confirmedLossSar/outcomeSetAt yielding 'CONFIRMED'/'RESOLVED'/'OPEN'. ALLOWED_TRANSITIONS shows the only legal pre-CLOSED states are CONFIRMED, CLEARED, FALSE_POSITIVE — none of which is 'RESOLVED' or 'OPEN'.
impact: Automation rules conditioning on the FRAUD_CASE_CLOSED priorStatus receive fabricated/incorrect values (CLEARED and FALSE_POSITIVE both collapse to 'RESOLVED'); breaks the F8 contract subtly.
reproduction: Close a CLEARED case: the emitted priorStatus is 'RESOLVED', not 'CLEARED'.
resolution: Capture `String prior = c.getStatus();` before setting CLOSED and emit the real value, mirroring how transitionResolution/transitionProduct capture `from` first.

title: Unused Logger field and SLF4J imports in ApprovalChainInstanceService (dead code)
cvss: Low: cosmetic dead code. A declared-but-unused logger plus its two imports add noise and falsely suggest the service logs at debug/info level when it does not.
description: Line 79 declares `private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(ApprovalChainInstanceService.java)`, but a grep of the file shows `log` is never invoked (only `audit.log(...)` from the AuditLogService is used). The org.slf4j Logger/LoggerFactory imports at lines 24-25 exist solely for this dead field.
rootCause: Logger scaffolding added by convention but never wired to any log statement.
evidence: grep for `log` invocations returns only the declaration at line 79 and audit.log(...) calls; no `log.info/debug/warn/error` exists in the file.
impact: Negligible runtime impact; minor readability/IDE-warning noise.
reproduction: grep -n 'log\.' on the file — only audit.log matches, the slf4j field is never called.
resolution: Remove the unused Logger field (line 79) and the two slf4j imports (lines 24-25), or add the intended log statements (e.g. on escalate()).
patchAfter: // removed: unused Logger field and slf4j imports

title: LdapRoleMapper is annotated with both @Configuration and @Component
cvss: Low: redundant/confusing stereotype. Both @Configuration and @Component are class-level stereotypes that register the bean; pairing them on a plain ConfigurationProperties POJO is contradictory and can mislead readers into thinking the class is a @Bean factory.
description: The class carries @Slf4j (52), @Component (53) and @ConfigurationProperties (54) — and also imports @Configuration (line 6). The @Configuration import is present and the class is documented as a plain List<String>->Set<String> mapper bean. A bean should not be both @Component and @Configuration; @Configuration implies a CGLIB-proxied @Bean factory, which this class is not. (Note: the active annotations are @Component + @ConfigurationProperties, but the unused @Configuration import signals confused intent and at minimum is a dead import.)
rootCause: Annotation scaffolding left over from an earlier shape; the @Configuration import was never removed when @Component was chosen.
evidence: Line 6 `import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;` with no @Configuration usage on the class (the class uses @Component at line 53). Unused import + ambiguous stereotype intent.
impact: Reader confusion; lint warning for the unused import. No functional bug while only @Component is active.
reproduction: Open the file; the Configuration import (line 6) is unused given the class is annotated @Component.
resolution: Remove the unused @Configuration import. Keep exactly one stereotype — @Component (with @ConfigurationProperties) is correct for this binder POJO.

title: AttachmentService duplicates docType-validation logic across upload/replaceVersion/update; DOC_TYPES check copied 3x
cvss: Low maintainability risk: the same 'normalize to upper-case, validate against DOC_TYPES, throw IllegalArgumentException' block is hand-copied into three methods. A change to the validation rule must be applied in all three.
description: upload() (41-44), replaceVersion() (78-81) and update() (122-127) each repeat the pattern: derive `type` from docType (defaulting/upper-casing), then `if (!DOC_TYPES.contains(type)) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown docType ...")`. Three copies of the same string-literal error message and the same allow-list check.
rootCause: No shared resolveDocType(...) helper; the validation was inlined where needed.
evidence: Identical `if (!DOC_TYPES.contains(type)) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown docType '" + docType + "'. Valid: " + DOC_TYPES);` at lines 42-44, 79-81 and 124-126.
impact: Drift risk if the error wording or normalization changes; mild bloat.
reproduction: Read the three methods; compare the validation blocks.
resolution: Extract a private `String resolveDocType(String docType, String fallback)` helper that normalizes and validates once, and call it from all three methods.

title: Repeated nullSafe/nullSafeStr/payload helpers duplicated across approval & evidence services
cvss: Low maintainability risk: the same tiny null-coercion helpers and F8 payload-builder shape are re-implemented per service. jscpd flags many service-to-service blocks across approvals/evidence/committee. The behaviour is correct but the pattern is copy-pasted, not shared.
description: ApprovalRequestService defines `nullSafeStr` (returns "" for null, line 84) and `nullSafe` (returns "<not provided>", line 232) plus a HashMap payload-builder (66-81). EvidenceItemService defines the identical pair `nullSafeStr` (90) and `nullSafe` (93) plus its own payloadFor (74-87). The DomainEvent payload-building idiom (put each field via nullSafeStr) is repeated verbatim in shape across these and the committee services. jscpd reports numerous matching blocks among approvals/evidence/committee service files.
rootCause: Per-service copies of trivial helpers and the event-payload idiom instead of a shared utility (e.g. a Nulls util and a DomainEvent payload builder).
evidence: Identical method `private static String nullSafeStr(Object o) { return o == null ? "" : o.toString(); }` in ApprovalRequestService:84 and EvidenceItemService:90; identical `nullSafe` returning "<not provided>" in ApprovalRequestService:232 and EvidenceItemService:93. jscpd-report.json lists ApprovalRequestService duplicated against capa/cyber_lc/privacy_lc/regchange/risk_lc service files.
impact: Minor drift risk and bloat; harmless individually but adds up across the many services using the F7/F8 idiom.
reproduction: grep -rn 'nullSafeStr\|<not provided>' across module services; or inspect jscpd-report.json entries for ApprovalRequestService.
resolution: Move nullSafe/nullSafeStr into a shared com.tss.grc.common util and provide a small DomainEvent payload-builder (fluent put) so services stop re-declaring identical helpers.
patchBefore:
private static String nullSafeStr(Object o) { return o == null ? "" : o.toString(); }
private static String nullSafe(Object o) { return o == null ? "<not provided>" : o.toString(); }
patchAfter: // in common: Nulls.str(o) / Nulls.label(o); services call the shared util

title: Status state machines hard-coded as string literals scattered per service (magic strings, no shared enum/constant)
cvss: Low risk: lifecycle states ('PENDING', 'APPROVED', 'REJECTED', 'DELEGATED', 'EXPIRED', 'IN_PROGRESS', etc.) are bare string literals compared with .equals across multiple services. A typo in any branch silently fails to match, and there is no compile-time guarantee transition tables and branches use the same vocabulary.
description: Each lifecycle service re-expresses its states as raw strings: ApprovalRequestService compares req.getStatus() against "APPROVED"/"REJECTED"/"DELEGATED"/"PENDING"/"EXPIRED" (157-176); DigitalSignatureService against "REQUESTED"/"SIGNED"/"REJECTED"/"EXPIRED" (138, 147-153); ApprovalChainInstanceService against "APPROVED"/"REJECTED"/"DELEGATED" plus a TERMINAL_STATUSES set (81); EvidenceItemService keeps a transition Map keyed by string states (48-58). There is no shared enum or per-module constant class, so the same status vocabulary is duplicated as literals.
rootCause: Statuses modeled as free-form String columns and compared with literal .equals rather than enums or named constants.
evidence: ApprovalRequestService:157 `if ("APPROVED".equals(req.getStatus()) || "REJECTED".equals(req.getStatus()))`; DigitalSignatureService:138 `if (!"REQUESTED".equals(d.getStatus())) return d;`. The literals recur across at least four services in scope.
impact: Typos in a state literal fail silently (no match) rather than at compile time; harder to enumerate valid states for docs/UI.
reproduction: grep -rn '"APPROVED"\|"REJECTED"\|"PENDING"' across the in-scope services to see the literal spread.
resolution: Introduce per-domain status enums (or at minimum a constants class per module) and convert at the persistence boundary; replace literal comparisons with enum/constant references.
patchBefore: if ("APPROVED".equals(req.getStatus()) || "REJECTED".equals(req.getStatus())) { ... }
patchAfter: if (status == ApprovalStatus.APPROVED || status == ApprovalStatus.REJECTED) { ... }

title: noRollbackFor + missing-table swallowing pattern duplicated across committee services and lacks try/catch on get()
cvss: Low risk: the 'catch RuntimeException, sniff message for invalid object name, return empty page' workaround is repeated in CommitteeService and CommitteeActionItemService, and one method declares noRollbackFor without any try/catch, making the annotation misleading. Message-string sniffing for schema errors is brittle.
description: CommitteeService.listCommittees/listMeetings (72-86, 152-166) and CommitteeActionItemService.list/listByMeeting/listByCommittee/openActions* (43-106) all repeat: @Transactional(noRollbackFor=RuntimeException.class) + try { repo... } catch (RuntimeException e) { if (isMissingObjectError/CommitteeSqlGuards.isMissingObjectError) return empty; throw e; }. isMissingObjectError works by lower-casing the exception message and searching for 'invalid object name'/'does not exist'/'not found' — fragile message-sniffing. Worse, CommitteeActionItemService.get() (56-60) carries `noRollbackFor = RuntimeException.class` but has NO try/catch, so the annotation does nothing there and misleads readers.
rootCause: Dev-profile schema-not-bootstrapped tolerance bolted on per read method via copy-paste, with string-based error detection; the annotation was pasted onto get() without the matching handler.
evidence: CommitteeService.isMissingObjectError (51-64) checks `low.contains("invalid object name")`. CommitteeActionItemService.get (56) is annotated `@Transactional(readOnly = true, noRollbackFor = RuntimeException.class)` but its body (57-59) has no try/catch and just rethrows EntityNotFoundException.
impact: Message-sniffing breaks if the DB driver/locale changes the wording; the no-op noRollbackFor on get() is confusing; logic is duplicated across two services.
reproduction: Read CommitteeActionItemService.get (no try/catch despite noRollbackFor); compare isMissingObjectError in CommitteeService with CommitteeSqlGuards.
resolution: Centralize the missing-table tolerance in a single helper (CommitteeSqlGuards already exists — use it everywhere instead of CommitteeService's private copy) and prefer detecting SQLServerException error code over message text. Remove noRollbackFor from get() since it has no handler.
references: Detect SQL errors by error code, not message text

title: ApprovalRequestService.transition() has empty no-op if-block and is a 66-LOC method mixing status mutation with event dispatch
cvss: Low risk: transition() contains an `if ("PENDING".equals(...)) { /* comment only */ }` empty block that does nothing, and the method bundles status-field mutation, a second status switch for trigger/message, audit, emit, and broadcast into 66 lines. The empty branch is dead code that reads as if logic were intended but omitted.
description: Lines 171-173 are `if ("PENDING".equals(req.getStatus())) { // From DELEGATED back to PENDING — assignedTo is already updated... }` — an empty conditional whose only content is a comment. It compiles to a no-op branch. The method also evaluates the status twice: once as a chain of if-blocks (157-176) to set fields, then again as a switch (183-204) to choose the trigger/message. Combining these would shrink the method and remove the dead branch.
rootCause: A placeholder branch left in to document intent, plus duplicated status dispatch (if-chain then switch).
evidence: Lines 171-173 form an if statement with no executable body. The same req.getStatus() is branched on at 157, 163, 171, 174 (field mutation) and again at 183 (switch for trigger/message).
impact: Reader confusion (looks like missing logic); minor over-length method.
reproduction: Read lines 171-173; observe the empty if body.
resolution: Delete the empty if-block (the comment can move to the DELEGATED branch or be dropped). Optionally merge the field-mutation if-chain and the trigger/message switch into a single switch to remove the double dispatch.
patchAfter: // (removed empty no-op branch)

title: Identical-bodied nullSafe() and safe() helpers coexist in the same class (BowTieAnalysisService, RiskService)
