The i18n provider defaults the language to Arabic ('ar', RTL) unless localStorage explicitly holds 'en' (i18n.tsx: initial state returns 'ar' for first-time visitors), and only sets `document.documentElement.dir = dir` inside a useEffect that runs AFTER the first render/paint (i18n.tsx:27-31). So on the default first visit the page paints LTR, React mounts, then the effect flips the document to RTL — mirroring the whole layout and producing a large layout shift. CLS is measured at 0.344, well into the failing range. This is on top of any web-font / late-CSS shift; the dir flip alone is a structural full-page reflow.
rootCause: The static HTML's dir/lang attributes are hard-coded to en/ltr and do not match the app's runtime default (ar/rtl). The correct direction is only applied imperatively after mount, so the first paint is always in the wrong direction for the default-language user.
evidence: index.html:2 `<html lang="en" dir="ltr">`. i18n.tsx initial state: `const stored = localStorage.getItem(LANG_KEY); return stored === 'en' ? 'en' : 'ar';` (defaults to Arabic). i18n.tsx:27-31 effect: `document.documentElement.lang = lang; document.documentElement.dir = dir;` runs in useEffect (post-paint). Lighthouse cumulative-layout-shift numericValue = 0.34425702372849826, score 0.32.
impact: Every default (Arabic) first load mirrors the entire UI after first paint — a jarring shift and a failing CLS contribution. Returning English users who toggled also pay a one-frame flip. Directly depresses the Lighthouse Performance and stability scores.
reproduction: 1) Clear localStorage, open the app — page paints LTR then snaps to RTL. 2) Lighthouse /login report: cumulative-layout-shift = 0.344 (failing). 3) Compare index.html dir="ltr" against i18n.tsx default 'ar'.
resolution: Set the document direction/lang before first paint so the first frame matches the resolved language. Cheapest fix: a tiny inline script in index.html <head> that reads localStorage('grc.lang') (defaulting to 'ar') and sets document.documentElement.lang/dir synchronously before the module bundle loads. Then change index.html's static default to dir="rtl" lang="ar" to match the app default. This eliminates the post-hydration flip entirely.
patchBefore:
<!-- index.html -->
<html lang="en" dir="ltr">
  <head>
    <!-- ... no direction bootstrap ... -->
patchAfter:
<!-- index.html -->
<html lang="ar" dir="rtl">
  <head>
    <script>
      (function () {
        var l = localStorage.getItem('grc.lang');
        var lang = l === 'en' ? 'en' : 'ar';
        document.documentElement.lang = lang;
        document.documentElement.dir = lang === 'ar' ? 'rtl' : 'ltr';
      })();
    </script>

title: In-thread Thread.sleep retry/backoff inside transactional integration calls extends DB-connection hold time to as much as ~75s-2min
cvss: Medium — the retry loops in the LIVE clients block the calling (request or scheduler) thread with Thread.sleep between attempts. Because the call originates inside an open transaction (PERF-IO-001/002), the backoff sleeps are added on top of the remote latency to the connection-hold time, multiplying the pool-exhaustion window. Bounded but large worst case; depends on a failing remote system.
description: Every LIVE client retries 5xx/connection failures with an in-thread exponential backoff that calls Thread.sleep on the calling thread. Splunk and CrowdStrike cap the per-attempt backoff at BACKOFF_CAP_MS = 30_000L (LiveSplunkClient.java:49, LiveCrowdStrikeClient.java:54) over up to 3 attempts. ServiceNow's withRetry (LiveServiceNowClient.java:194-216) sleeps starting at 250ms, doubling, capped at 5000ms, with max-retries=3 (so up to 4 attempts) and a read timeout of 30s per attempt (ServiceNowProperties timeout-seconds=30, application.yml:183). Because these clients are called from inside @Transactional service methods, the entire sleep+timeout budget is added to the DB-connection-hold time. ServiceNow worst case approaches 4 x 30s read timeout + backoffs ~= 2 minutes; Splunk/CrowdStrike approach 3 x 5s timeout + ~30s+ backoff ~= 45-75s.
rootCause: Retry/backoff is implemented synchronously on the calling thread (Thread.sleep) AND the call is made while a transaction (and therefore a pooled connection) is open. The two together convert transient remote failures into prolonged connection occupancy.
evidence: LiveSplunkClient.java:99 'sleep(delayMs);' line 100 'delayMs = (long) Math.min(BACKOFF_CAP_MS, ...)' with BACKOFF_CAP_MS=30_000 (line 49) and maxAttempts from props (default retry max-attempts=3). LiveCrowdStrikeClient.java:192 'sleep(delayMs);' line 193 cap 30_000 (line 54). LiveServiceNowClient.java:207 'Thread.sleep(backoffMs);' line 212 'backoffMs = Math.min(backoffMs * 2, 5000);' with attempts = maxRetries+1 (line 195) and read timeout 30s (ServiceNowIntegrationConfig.java:61 setReadTimeout(props.getTimeoutSeconds())). All invoked from @Transactional service methods (see PERF-IO-001).
impact: A degraded third party (intermittent 503s, slow responses) turns each push into a connection held for tens of seconds to ~2 minutes. With only 20 (base) / 10 (dev) connections, even a handful of concurrent retrying pushes meaningfully shrinks the pool's effective capacity, and the leak-detection-threshold of 60s (application.yml:26) will start emitting false 'connection leak' warnings on the longest ServiceNow retry chains — masking real leaks in operational logs.
reproduction: 1) Point ServiceNow LIVE at an endpoint returning HTTP 503 on every attempt. 2) Call POST /test-push. 3) Observe the request thread (and its borrowed connection) blocked for ~ (4 x 30s) + (0.25+0.5+1.0s) ~= 121s before failing. 4) Repeat 20x concurrently and watch GrcHikariPool exhaust and unrelated DB calls time out at 30s.
resolution: First and primarily, remove the remote call from the transaction (PERF-IO-001) so retry sleeps no longer occupy a connection. Additionally, prefer non-blocking retry (Resilience4j / Spring Retry with a separate scheduler, or async + outbox) over Thread.sleep, and lower the ServiceNow read timeout from 30s toward the 5s the other adapters use unless a specific SLA requires longer. Cap total retry budget (sum of timeouts + backoffs) well under the 60s leak-detection threshold and the 30s connection-timeout to avoid cascading symptoms.

title: OAuth token refresh performs a synchronized blocking HTTP fetch while a transaction holds a DB connection, serialising all callers
category: Synchronized blocking I/O on hot path inside transaction
cvss: Medium — token refresh (every ~1h, or on any 401) runs a blocking HTTP POST under a single object monitor (synchronized) and is reached from inside the @Transactional push path via the auth-header callback. During refresh, one thread blocks on the remote token endpoint while holding both its DB connection and the lock; every other caller needing a token blocks on that lock, so a slow token endpoint stalls multiple integration requests at once.
description: ServiceNowOAuthTokenManager.getAccessToken() (line 53) and refresh() (line 61) are both 'synchronized' on the manager instance. refresh() performs a blocking restClient.post() to the token URL (lines 76-81). getAccessToken() is invoked from LiveServiceNowClient.authHeader() (lines 137-147), which runs while building every outbound request — i.e. inside the @Transactional push()/update() flow. When the cached token is within the 60s expiry skew (line 33 EXPIRY_SKEW) or after a 401, the next caller triggers a blocking remote fetch while holding the monitor; all other threads calling getAccessToken() queue behind that lock. Combined with PERF-IO-001, the refreshing thread also holds its pooled DB connection for the duration of the token fetch.
rootCause: A coarse-grained 'synchronized' guards the entire refresh including the blocking network call, rather than only the cached-slot read/write, so the remote latency is held under the lock. The refresh is reached transitively from within an open transaction, compounding the connection-hold problem.
evidence: ServiceNowOAuthTokenManager.java:53 'public synchronized String getAccessToken()'; line 61 'public synchronized String refresh()'; lines 76-81 blocking 'restClient.post()....body(Map.class)' inside the synchronized method. Reached via LiveServiceNowClient.java:139-140 'case OAUTH2_CLIENT_CREDENTIALS -> h.setBearerAuth(tokenManager.getAccessToken());' inside authHeader(), called from createIncident()/getIncident()/updateIncident() which run under ServiceNowOutboundService @Transactional methods. CrowdStrike has the analogous CrowdStrikeOAuthTokenManager used by LiveCrowdStrikeClient.authHeader() (LiveCrowdStrikeClient.java:234-239).
impact: On token expiry (hourly) or a Falcon/ServiceNow secret rotation (401 path), the first integration push pays the full token-endpoint latency under the lock and under an open transaction; concurrent integration requests block on the lock and cannot proceed, amplifying connection-hold and tail latency precisely during credential refresh windows. A slow or flaky token endpoint can briefly serialise the whole integration subsystem.
reproduction: 1) ServiceNow LIVE with OAUTH2_CLIENT_CREDENTIALS; point token-url at an endpoint that delays the token response by 10s. 2) Let the cached token reach the 60s expiry skew. 3) Fire several concurrent /test-push calls. 4) Observe exactly one thread doing the token fetch (10s) while the others block on the monitor, all within their transactions/connections; measure the resulting 10s tail on every concurrent push.
resolution: Narrow the lock so the blocking HTTP fetch happens outside the monitor (double-checked refresh, or single-flight via AtomicReference + a separate guarded fetch), and ensure token acquisition does not occur inside an open DB transaction (fixed transitively by PERF-IO-001 moving the whole client call out of @Transactional). Optionally refresh tokens proactively on a background scheduler before expiry so the request path never pays refresh latency.

title: Early core-module migrations (compliance, incident, tprm) create tables with zero secondary indexes — inconsistent indexing discipline left foundational registers unindexed
cvss: High: these are the original, most-used GRC registers (controls, assessments, findings, vendors, incidents). They were created first, are referenced by the most screens, and received no indexes at all — neither for tenant scoping nor for their FK joins. The defect is structural (a whole file with 0 indexes), not a one-off omission.
description: Indexing discipline in the migration chain is inconsistent: later migrations (V8 evidence: 8 indexes, V11 intake: 5 indexes, and most post-V90 modules) add nonclustered indexes, but the earliest module migrations create their tables with none. V3__compliance_module.sql creates compliance.controls, compliance.assessments and compliance.findings (3 tables, all with organisation_id + status) and contains 0 CREATE INDEX statements. V4__incident_module.sql (1 table) and V7__tprm_module.sql (tprm.vendors + tprm.vendor_assessments) likewise contain 0 indexes. These are not obscure tables — they are the foundational Compliance, Incident and Third-Party registers that nearly every dashboard, report and cross-module link reads.
rootCause: No enforced 'every CREATE TABLE ships with its indexes' rule. The team added indexes ad hoc as performance problems surfaced in later sprints, but never went back to backfill the Sprint-1/Sprint-2 core tables. The dedicated index files under db/sqlserver/indexes/ (which DO contain IX_assessments_org_framework, IX_findings_assessment_status, etc.) were authored separately and never wired into the applied migration chain (see PERF-IX-006).
evidence: grep -c 'CREATE.*INDEX' per file: V3__compliance_module.sql=0 (3 tables), V4__incident_module.sql=0 (1 table), V7__tprm_module.sql=0 (2 tables) — versus V8__evidence_module.sql=8 (7 tables), V11__intake_records.sql=5 (2 tables). compliance.findings even declares an FK on assessment_id (V3 lines 103-104) with no backing index. tprm.vendors (V7 lines 18-43): organisation_id NOT NULL, status NVARCHAR(50) with CHECK, only PK_vendors clustered on id.
impact: The most heavily-trafficked registers in the product are the slowest to read at scale. Compliance assessment lists, audit-finding inboxes, and the third-party vendor register all scan. The unindexed FK on compliance.findings.assessment_id forces a scan whenever findings are loaded for an assessment (a per-assessment drill-down) and whenever the parent assessment row is updated/deleted (FK integrity check scans the child).
reproduction: 1) `grep -c -iE 'CREATE.*INDEX' V3__compliance_module.sql` returns 0. 2) Apply V3 to a SQL Server DB and run `SELECT name, type_desc FROM sys.indexes WHERE object_id = OBJECT_ID('compliance.findings');` — only the clustered PK is returned. 3) `SELECT * FROM compliance.findings WHERE assessment_id = 42;` produces a Clustered Index Scan in the actual plan.
resolution: Backfill index migrations for the V3/V4/V7 core tables (folding the already-authored definitions from db/sqlserver/indexes/02-module-indexes.sql) and institute a review rule that any migration adding a CREATE TABLE must also add (a) a leading-organisation_id index and (b) an index on every FK column.
patchBefore:
-- V3__compliance_module.sql (findings) — no index on the FK column
CREATE TABLE compliance.findings (
    id BIGINT IDENTITY(1,1) NOT NULL,
    organisation_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
    assessment_id BIGINT NULL,
    status NVARCHAR(50) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'OPEN',
    ...
    CONSTRAINT FK_findings_assessment FOREIGN KEY (assessment_id)
        REFERENCES compliance.assessments(id)
);
-- 0 CREATE INDEX in this file
patchAfter:
-- Add at the end of the migration (or a new backfill migration)
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_findings_org_status
    ON compliance.findings (organisation_id, status, severity)
    WHERE is_deleted = 0;
GO
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_findings_assessment
    ON compliance.findings (assessment_id)
    WHERE is_deleted = 0;
GO
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_controls_org_status
    ON compliance.controls (organisation_id, status) WHERE is_deleted = 0;
GO
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_vendors_org_status
    ON tprm.vendors (organisation_id, status) WHERE is_deleted = 0;
GO

_verification.rationale: Verified: V3__compliance_module.sql (3 tables), V4__incident_module.sql (1 table) and V7__tprm_module.sql (2 tables) contain 0 CREATE INDEX statements while V8__evidence_module.sql has 8; compliance.findings declares FK_findings_assessment on assessment_id (V3:103-104) with no backing index; no later migration backfills indexes onto these exact tables. The inconsistency is real. But these are low-cardinality GRC registers (controls/assessments/findings/vendors) with a clustered PK, where table scans remain acceptable at realistic data volumes, and dev uses Python-bootstrapped DBs. A genuine schema-discipline gap with modest real-world impact — Medium, not High.

title: status / workflow_status columns are queried as filters but lack supporting indexes on several cyber tables
cvss: Medium: status and workflow_status are common WHERE/ORDER predicates (findByOrganisationIdAndStatus appears 30x, findByOrganisationIdAndStatusOrderByCreatedAtDesc 25x). Where the underlying table also lacks an org index, status filtering compounds the scan. Bounded scope (cyber tables most affected) keeps this Medium.
description: Of the tables that carry a workflow_status column, several have no index on workflow_status or status: cyber.cyber_action_plans, cyber.cyber_incidents, cyber.vuln_exceptions, cyber.vulnerabilities. These tables are filtered by status in the service layer (workflow state machines) and via repository finders. The cyber.* tables are created by setup_cyber_db.py with only an IDENTITY clustered PK and no secondary indexes at all (the script contains 0 CREATE INDEX), so a query like 'open vulnerabilities for org N' scans the whole table and filters status as a residual predicate. Even the migration-defined cyber.incidents (V1 line 781) only adds IX_cyber_inc_nist on nist_phase, not on (organisation_id, status).
rootCause: Status/workflow_status filtering was implemented in the service layer and repositories but the corresponding columns were never indexed. The dev bootstrap scripts for cyber and bcm (setup_cyber_db.py, setup_bcm_db.py) create tables with no indexes (grep CREATE INDEX = 0 in both), so status-driven queries have no seek path.
evidence: Parser: 5 tables carry workflow_status; 4 have no index on workflow_status/status (cyber.cyber_action_plans, cyber.cyber_incidents, cyber.vuln_exceptions, cyber.vulnerabilities). setup_cyber_db.py creates 10 cyber tables each with `organisation_id BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 1` and `id INT IDENTITY(1,1) PRIMARY KEY`, with grep -c 'CREATE INDEX' = 0. Repository pattern counts: findByOrganisationIdAndStatus=30, findByOrganisationIdAndStatusOrderByCreatedAtDesc=25, findByOrganisationIdAndStatusOrderByIdDesc=9.
impact: Status-filtered dashboards and worklists on cyber tables (open vulnerabilities, in-progress incidents, pending action plans) scan the full table per tenant. Because these tables also lack an org index, the cost is the union of both problems; remediating with a composite (organisation_id, status) index resolves both at once.
reproduction: 1) Run setup_cyber_db.py and `SELECT name FROM sys.indexes WHERE object_id=OBJECT_ID('cyber.vulnerabilities');` — only the PK. 2) `SELECT * FROM cyber.vulnerabilities WHERE organisation_id=1 AND status='OPEN';` shows a scan. 3) Confirm 0 status indexes: `SELECT i.name FROM sys.indexes i JOIN sys.index_columns ic ON i.object_id=ic.object_id JOIN sys.columns c ON ic.object_id=c.object_id AND ic.column_id=c.column_id WHERE c.name IN ('status','workflow_status') AND i.object_id=OBJECT_ID('cyber.vulnerabilities');`
resolution: Add composite indexes leading with organisation_id and including status/workflow_status for the affected cyber tables, mirroring the design already present in db/sqlserver/indexes/02-module-indexes.sql (IX_vulnerabilities_org_status etc.). Apply via Flyway and update setup_cyber_db.py so the dev DB matches.
patchBefore:
-- setup_cyber_db.py
CREATE TABLE cyber.vulnerabilities (
    id              INT IDENTITY(1,1) PRIMARY KEY,
    organisation_id BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
    ...
    status          NVARCHAR(...) ,
    workflow_status NVARCHAR(...)
);
-- no CREATE INDEX in the whole script
patchAfter:
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_vulnerabilities_org_status
    ON cyber.vulnerabilities (organisation_id, status, severity)
    WHERE is_deleted = 0;
GO
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_cyber_incidents_org_wf
    ON cyber.cyber_incidents (organisation_id, workflow_status)
    WHERE is_deleted = 0;
GO
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_cyber_action_plans_org_status
    ON cyber.cyber_action_plans (organisation_id, status) WHERE is_deleted = 0;
GO

title: Foreign-key columns are not indexed — SQL Server does not auto-index FKs, so child-table joins and parent delete/update integrity checks scan
cvss: Medium: SQL Server creates no index for a FOREIGN KEY constraint. ~23 distinct FK column names across the schema are never used as a leading index key, so the standard 'children of parent X' drill-down and the FK integrity check on parent modify both scan the child table. Approximate (name-based) detection keeps this Medium.
description: Across the applied migrations there are 92 FOREIGN KEY declarations on 55 distinct FK column names. Of those, 23 FK column names are never used as the leading key of any index anywhere in the schema — including assessment_id, asset_id, engagement_id, playbook_id, subprocessor_id, parent_processor_id, parent_audit_id, step_id, snapshot_id, primary_vendor_id, reporting_year_id and others. Because SQL Server does not auto-create an index to back a FOREIGN KEY constraint, every join from parent to child on these columns (and every cascade/integrity check when the parent is modified) performs a scan of the child table. compliance.findings.assessment_id (FK_findings_assessment, V3 lines 103-105) and tprm.vendor_assessments.vendor_id (V7) are concrete examples.
rootCause: FK constraints were declared for referential integrity but the matching index on the FK column was not created. This is a well-known SQL Server gap: PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE auto-create indexes, but FOREIGN KEY does not.
evidence: Parser: 92 FK declarations, 55 distinct FK columns, 23 of those never appear as a leading index key. compliance.findings: `CONSTRAINT FK_findings_assessment FOREIGN KEY (assessment_id) REFERENCES compliance.assessments(id)` (V3:103-105) with no index on assessment_id. Note detection is name-based (a FK column may be indexed under a synonymous name), so treat the 23 as an upper bound and verify per table.
impact: Parent->child drill-downs (e.g. all findings for an assessment, all assessments for a vendor, all steps for a playbook) scan the child. Deleting or soft-deleting a parent row triggers a child scan per FK integrity check, slowing writes on busy registers.
reproduction: 1) `SELECT fk.name, c.name col FROM sys.foreign_key_columns fkc JOIN sys.foreign_keys fk ON fkc.constraint_object_id=fk.object_id JOIN sys.columns c ON fkc.parent_object_id=c.object_id AND fkc.parent_column_id=c.column_id;` to list FK columns. 2) For each, `SELECT 1 FROM sys.index_columns ic JOIN sys.columns c2 ON ic.object_id=c2.object_id AND ic.column_id=c2.column_id WHERE ic.key_ordinal=1 AND c2.name=@fkcol AND ic.object_id=@parent;` — empty means unindexed. 3) `SELECT * FROM compliance.findings WHERE assessment_id=1;` shows a scan.
resolution: Create a nonclustered index on each FK column (leading with organisation_id where the child is tenant-scoped, otherwise leading with the FK column). Add to the schema-standard checklist alongside the org-index rule from PERF-IX-001.
patchBefore:
CONSTRAINT FK_findings_assessment FOREIGN KEY (assessment_id)
    REFERENCES compliance.assessments(id)
-- no index on assessment_id

title: Curated index files (db/sqlserver/indexes/*.sql) are orphaned — never wired into the Flyway chain or the dev Python bootstrap, so ~40 designed indexes never get created
cvss: Medium: the project already CONTAINS well-designed organisation_id/status/FK indexes for iam.users, risk.risks, cyber.assets, compliance.assessments, etc. in db/sqlserver/indexes/01-shared-indexes.sql and 02-module-indexes.sql — but neither file is on the Flyway classpath nor invoked by any setup_*.py, so they are dead. This is the root cause behind several other findings and an easy, high-leverage fix.
description: The repository contains two hand-authored index files: 01-shared-indexes.sql (~25 indexes: organizations, business_units, iam.users, user_roles, controls, workflow_instances, attachments, notifications, audit_logs, licenses) and 02-module-indexes.sql (~15 indexes: risk.risks, risk_assessments, cyber.assets, vulnerabilities, incidents, bcm.*, privacy.*, compliance.*, reporting.*). These define exactly the organisation_id/status/FK composite indexes the other findings call for. However: (a) prod Flyway is configured with `locations: classpath:db/migration/sqlserver` (application-prod.yml:28) — i.e. only the V*.sql files under src/main/resources, NOT tss-grc-backend/db/sqlserver/indexes/; (b) the dev DB is bootstrapped by setup_*.py + seed_real_data.py, none of which reference these files; (c) the only mention of them anywhere in the repo is SESSION_SUMMARY.md. The migrations/README.md even describes a legacy layout (V1.0.13__create_shared_indexes.sql / V1.0.14__create_module_indexes.sql) that does not exist in the actual V1..V224 chain. Net effect: these ~40 designed indexes are never created in any environment.
rootCause: Index DDL was authored as standalone scripts under a parallel db/sqlserver/ tree that was superseded by the consolidated src/main/resources/db/migration/sqlserver/V*.sql chain. The migration toward the V* layout never folded the index files in, and the README documenting the intended wiring went stale.
evidence: application-prod.yml:28 `locations: classpath:db/migration/sqlserver` (resolves under src/main/resources only; the indexes/ files live under tss-grc-backend/db/sqlserver/ and are not on the classpath). `grep -ril '01-shared-indexes|02-module-indexes|sqlserver/indexes'` across *.py/*.md/*.bat/*.ps1/*.sql returns only SESSION_SUMMARY.md. application-dev.yml: flyway.enabled=false and ddl-auto=none, so neither Flyway nor Hibernate creates them in dev; application.yml base uses ddl-auto=validate (Hibernate creates nothing). The 01-shared-indexes.sql file itself contains the missing IX_users_org / IX_users_active_login (lines 40-55) and IX_controls_org_active (lines 86-90) referenced by PERF-IX-003 and PERF-IX-001.
impact: The team believes the platform is indexed (the files exist and look complete) while production runs with only the inline V* indexes, leaving the gaps quantified in PERF-IX-001..005. This false sense of coverage is itself a risk: a perf regression in prod has no quick lever because the prepared indexes are not deployable as-is.
reproduction: 1) Inspect application-prod.yml:28 — Flyway location does not include db/sqlserver/indexes/. 2) `grep -ril 'sqlserver/indexes'` over the repo returns only SESSION_SUMMARY.md. 3) After a clean Flyway migrate of V1..V224 into a fresh DB, `SELECT name FROM sys.indexes WHERE name LIKE 'IX_users_%';` returns nothing (IX_users_org was never applied).
resolution: Convert 01-shared-indexes.sql and 02-module-indexes.sql into a properly versioned Flyway migration under src/main/resources/db/migration/sqlserver/ (e.g. V225__shared_and_module_indexes.sql) so they apply in prod, and update the dev bootstrap to run them (or run the same SQL from a setup_indexes.py). Reconcile the index set against PERF-IX-001's gap list before applying. Delete or clearly deprecate the stale migrations/README.md layout.
patchBefore:
# application-prod.yml
flyway:
  locations: classpath:db/migration/sqlserver   # excludes db/sqlserver/indexes/*.sql

# db/sqlserver/indexes/01-shared-indexes.sql, 02-module-indexes.sql
#   -> referenced nowhere except SESSION_SUMMARY.md (orphaned)
patchAfter:
# Move/convert the curated index DDL into the applied chain:
#   src/main/resources/db/migration/sqlserver/V225__shared_and_module_indexes.sql
# containing the contents of 01-shared-indexes.sql + 02-module-indexes.sql
# (wrapped in IF NOT EXISTS guards), then for dev add a setup_indexes.py that
# executes the same SQL after the setup_*_db.py bootstrap.

title: ControlMapService resolves each mapping with 3 findById queries (sub-control + control + framework) per row
cvss: Medium: getMappings and getEvidenceReadiness both map every ControlLink through a resolver that fires three sequential findById queries (EvidenceSubControl, EvidenceControl, EvidenceFramework). For an entity mapped to N sub-controls this is 1 + 3N queries. N is typically modest (a single entity's control map), so impact is moderate, but the pattern runs on interactive mapping/readiness screens and the reference data involved is fully cacheable, making the cost gratuitous.
description: getMappings (49-53) maps each ControlLink via resolve(scId, satisfaction). resolve (166-181) calls subControlRepository.findById, then controlRepository.findById(sc.getControlId()), then frameworkRepository.findById(ctrl.getFrameworkId()) - three per-row lookups. getEvidenceReadiness (113-127) repeats the identical three-findById chain inside its per-link loop. The aggregate rollups in getEvidenceReadiness (95-109) are correctly written as GROUP BY queries, but the sub-control/control/framework metadata resolution is per-row.
rootCause: Per-row FK chasing for reference data (the framework/control/sub-control catalog is shared, static, and small) instead of batch-loading the distinct ids or caching the catalog. The sub-control -> control -> framework chain is fixed reference data ideal for a one-time load or Caffeine cache.
evidence:
ControlMapService.java:168 `EvidenceSubControl sc = subControlRepository.findById(scId).orElse(null);`
:173 `EvidenceControl ctrl = controlRepository.findById(sc.getControlId()).orElse(null);`
:176 `EvidenceFramework fw = frameworkRepository.findById(ctrl.getFrameworkId()).orElse(null);`
The same triple appears at lines 115/121/124 inside getEvidenceReadiness's per-link loop. Query count for N mapped sub-controls = 1 (links) + 3N.
impact: Moderate latency on the control-map and evidence-readiness panels; unnecessary DB chatter for data that never changes within a request and is identical across tenants. Scales linearly with the number of sub-controls mapped to an entity.
reproduction: 1. Map an entity to several sub-controls via setMappings. 2. Enable SQL logging. 3. Call getMappings(entityType, entityId) (and getEvidenceReadiness). 4. Observe three findById SELECTs per returned mapping row.
resolution: Batch-resolve: collect the distinct subControlIds from the links, load them with findAllById, collect their controlIds and load with findAllById, collect frameworkIds and load with findAllById, then resolve from in-memory maps. Alternatively, since framework/control/sub-control are a static shared catalog, cache the lookup maps with the existing Caffeine cache (@Cacheable) and resolve from cache.
references: CLAUDE.md — Caching: Caffeine L1 (suited to static reference catalogs)

title: TreatmentPlan @OneToMany actions is EAGER, causing per-plan child query on list views (and a count that loads all children)
cvss: Medium: TreatmentPlan.actions is an EAGER @OneToMany. listForOrg() / listForRisk() load the plans for a tenant and Hibernate eagerly issues a separate actions SELECT per plan (TreatmentPlanDto.from reads e.getActions()). For P plans that is 1 + P queries. Additionally generateExternalId() calls .size() on the full plan list purely to count, materialising every plan and its actions just to derive the next sequence number.
description: TreatmentPlan.actions is annotated @OneToMany(..., fetch = FetchType.EAGER) (TreatmentPlan.java:77). TreatmentPlanService.listForOrg() (94-99) and listForRisk() (101-106) load all plans for the tenant/risk and map each via TreatmentPlanDto.from, which dereferences e.getActions() (TreatmentPlanDto.java:43). Because the collection is EAGER and the finder returns a list (not a fetch-join), Hibernate issues one actions SELECT per plan. Separately, generateExternalId() (197-201) does repo.findByOrganisationIdOrderByCreatedAtDesc(orgId).size() - loading every plan (and, due to EAGER, every plan's actions) merely to compute count+1 for the next external id.
rootCause: EAGER child collection on a list-rendered entity, plus a count derived by materialising and sizing a full entity list instead of a COUNT query. EAGER ToMany cannot be batch-fetched for a list/page result, so it degrades to per-row child loads.
evidence:
TreatmentPlan.java:77 `@OneToMany(mappedBy = "plan", cascade = CascadeType.ALL, orphanRemoval = true, fetch = FetchType.EAGER)` -> `List<TreatmentAction> actions`.
TreatmentPlanDto.java:43 `.actions(e.getActions() == null ? List.of() : e.getActions().stream().map(TreatmentActionDto::from)...)` - touches the collection for every plan.
TreatmentPlanService.java:199 `long count = repo.findByOrganisationIdOrderByCreatedAtDesc(orgId).size();` - full materialisation to count.
impact: Treatment-plan list endpoints scale at 1 + P queries with EAGER children; the external-id generator loads the entire plan+action graph on every create. Moderate latency and DB load that grows with the number of treatment plans per tenant. The EAGER collection also blocks adopting projection-based list reads later.
reproduction: 1. Seed several treatment plans, each with multiple treatment actions. 2. Enable SQL logging. 3. Call listForOrg(): observe one treatment_actions SELECT per plan in addition to the plans query. 4. Call create(): observe generateExternalId loading all plans (and their actions) to compute .size().
resolution: Change actions to FetchType.LAZY. For list views that need actions, add a JOIN FETCH / @EntityGraph finder so the collection is fetched in one query; for list views that do not need actions, the DTO simply omits them. Replace generateExternalId's list().size() with a repository count query (e.g. countByOrganisationId) - the repository already exposes countByOrganisationIdAndStatus, so add countByOrganisationId.

title: TPRM /assessments loads ALL vendors via Pageable.unpaged() then runs an unbounded IN-clause over every vendor id
cvss: Medium: the endpoint is reachable by any TPRM:READ user and degrades super-linearly with vendor count (full vendor scan + a single IN-list with one parameter per vendor). Lower blast radius than PERF-PG-001 because vendor counts are typically smaller than asset/finding registers, but the explicit use of Pageable.unpaged() defeats the very pagination the module otherwise offers.
description: GET /api/v1/tprm/assessments (no vendorId param) calls TprmService.listAssessments(null). The implementation first fetches EVERY vendor for the tenant using vendorRepo.findByOrganisationId(orgId, Pageable.unpaged()) — explicitly disabling pagination — maps them to a List<Long> of ids, then calls assessmentRepo.findByVendorIdIn(vendorIds), which has no Pageable and emits a SQL IN (?, ?, ... ) with one bind parameter per vendor. The result List<VendorAssessment> contains every assessment for the org. So a single request does a full vendor table scan plus a full assessment fetch, with the IN-list growing with vendor count. SQL Server has a practical/parser ceiling on IN-list and parameter counts (and a 2100-parameter limit), so beyond a few thousand vendors this can also fail outright rather than merely being slow.
rootCause: The list endpoint returns the full register but the data model has no direct organisation_id on VendorAssessment, so the author worked around it by materialising all vendor ids client-side (in the service) and using findByVendorIdIn. Pageable.unpaged() was used to grab the whole vendor set, which is the anti-pattern.
impact: Two unbounded fetches per request plus a parameterised IN-clause that scales with vendor count. On large tenants this is both slow (two full result sets into the heap) and potentially failing (SQL Server parameter/IN-list ceiling), turning a routine register read into an error or a long-running query that holds a DB connection.
reproduction:
1. Seed many vendors and assessments for organisation_id = 1.
2. Call GET /api/v1/tprm/assessments (omit vendorId).
3. Enable Hibernate SQL logging and observe (a) SELECT of all vendors, (b) a single SELECT ... WHERE vendor_id IN (?, ?, ...) with one bind var per vendor, and the full assessment list returned with no page envelope. Scale vendors past a few thousand to hit the IN/parameter ceiling.
resolution: Add organisation_id (or a join) to VendorAssessment and a paged org-scoped finder: Page<VendorAssessment> findByOrganisationId(Long orgId, Pageable pageable). Change the controller to return Page<VendorAssessment> with @PageableDefault and the service to delegate directly to the paged finder, eliminating both the Pageable.unpaged() vendor scan and the IN-list. For the vendorId-scoped branch, accept a Pageable and return a Page instead of .getContent().
references: SQL Server limit of 2100 parameters per statement

title: No global maximum page size — paginated Page<> endpoints accept arbitrary ?size= and can be coerced to return all rows
category: Unbounded result set / missing page-size cap
cvss: Medium: turns the otherwise-correct Page<> endpoints (risk, incident, compliance, evidence, users, vendors, cyber, etc.) back into unbounded queries on demand. Any authenticated reader can request ?size=2147483647 and force a full-table fetch, so the pagination defence is bypassable.
description: The project relies on @PageableDefault(size = 20) for the DEFAULT page size, but there is no configured maximum. A scan for spring.data.web.pageable.max-page-size / PageableHandlerMethodArgumentResolver.setMaxPageSize / maxPageSize across src/main returned no matches, so Spring's resolver uses its built-in default behaviour where the client-supplied ?size= overrides the default with no server-side ceiling. Consequently every 'correctly paginated' endpoint — e.g. GET /api/v1/risk/risks?size=1000000, GET /api/v1/admin/users?size=1000000, GET /api/v1/incidents?size=1000000 — will attempt to fetch and serialise that many rows in one page, re-introducing exactly the unbounded-result-set problem the Page<> envelope was meant to prevent. AuditLogController even hand-rolls page/size as plain @RequestParam(defaultValue = "100") int size with no clamp, so the same applies there.
rootCause: Spring Data web pagination ships without a max page size unless one is configured; the platform never set spring.data.web.pageable.max-page-size (nor clamped hand-rolled size params), so the per-endpoint @PageableDefault only constrains the default, not the maximum a caller may request.
evidence:
grep -rniE 'max-page-size|maxPageSize|setMaxPageSize|PageableHandlerMethodArgumentResolver|spring.data.web' src/main  ->  (no matches)
RiskController.java:32  @PageableDefault(size = 20, sort = "createdAt") Pageable pageable   // default only; no max
AuditLogController.java:38-39  @RequestParam(defaultValue="0") int page, @RequestParam(defaultValue="100") int size  // unclamped
Result: ?size=<arbitrary> is honoured on all Page<> endpoints, defeating pagination.
impact: The pagination control protecting ~122 endpoints is bypassable by a query parameter. A single authenticated user can issue ?size=2_000_000_000 against the largest register and force a full-table fetch + serialisation, reproducing the heap pressure / latency / OOM risk of PERF-PG-001 even on the modules that were done correctly. It also undermines any fix for PERF-PG-001 unless the cap is added at the same time.
reproduction: 1. Authenticate as any READ user. 2. Call GET /api/v1/risk/risks?size=1000000 (or /api/v1/admin/users?size=1000000, /api/v1/audit-log?size=1000000). 3. Observe the server attempts to return up to that many rows in one page (no clamp); response size and DB fetch scale with the requested size rather than being capped.
resolution: Set a global maximum page size via configuration (spring.data.web.pageable.max-page-size: 100) so the resolver clamps any oversized ?size=. For hand-rolled size params (AuditLogController, CyberController pageOf, etc.), clamp explicitly with Math.min(size, MAX). Optionally also set spring.data.web.pageable.default-page-size to centralise the default. Combine with PERF-PG-001 so that both the missing pagination and the missing cap are closed together.
patchBefore:
# application.yml — no pagination limits configured
spring:
  jpa:
    open-in-view: false
# (no spring.data.web.pageable.* keys present anywhere)
patchAfter:
# application.yml
spring:
  data:
    web:
      pageable:
        default-page-size: 20
        max-page-size: 100   # resolver clamps any client-supplied ?size= to <=100
  jpa:
    open-in-view: false

// AuditLogController.java (hand-rolled size) — clamp explicitly
int safeSize = Math.min(Math.max(size, 1), 100);
return service.list(actionType, sourceModule, severity, page, safeSize);
references: OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023) API4:2023 Unrestricted Resource Consumption

title: Hikari pool sizing (base=20 / dev=10) is undersized for blocking-integration workloads and dev overrides drop leak-detection visibility
cvss: Low — sizing itself is reasonable for pure DB work against SQL Server Express, but given the blocking-I/O-under-transaction patterns (PERF-IO-001..004) the effective pool capacity is much lower than the nominal 20/10. The k6 breakpoint run did not reach an error threshold in the captured log (no failed iterations through ~67 VUs / ~325 iters/s on a read-only endpoint that does not touch the integration paths), so this is a forward-looking sizing/observability concern rather than an observed outage.
description: The base Hikari pool is maximum-pool-size=20 with minimum-idle=5, connection-timeout=30000, leak-detection-threshold=60000 (application.yml:21-26). The dev profile overrides ONLY minimum-idle (2) and maximum-pool-size (10) (application-dev.yml:27-29), inheriting the base connection-timeout and leak-detection-threshold. Two observations: (1) Sizing of 20 is fine for CPU-bound DB work on SQL Server Express (Express has no hard low connection cap; the real Express limits are ~1.4 GB buffer pool / 4 cores / 10 GB data), but it is small once connections are routinely tied up for seconds-to-minutes by the blocking integration paths — the formula connections = ((core_count x 2) + effective_spindle_count) assumes connections are released quickly, which the integration code violates. (2) The leak-detection-threshold=60000 is below the worst-case integration connection-hold computed in PERF-IO-003 (~121s for ServiceNow), so once those slow paths run they will emit spurious leak warnings, eroding trust in the leak detector. The k6 load.js exercises only GET /api/v1/risk/risks (load.js readRisks), which never touches the integration adapters, so the load test does not characterise the at-risk path.
rootCause: Pool size and connection-timeout were tuned for fast DB-only requests; the integration adapters' blocking-under-transaction behaviour was not accounted for, so nominal pool capacity overstates real capacity. The leak-detection threshold is not aligned with the (unintended) long connection holds the integration code can produce.
evidence: application.yml:22 'maximum-pool-size: 20'; :24 'connection-timeout: 30000'; :26 'leak-detection-threshold: 60000'. application-dev.yml:29 'maximum-pool-size: 10' (overrides only size + minimum-idle; inherits the rest). k6 load.js: readRisks() hits GET /api/v1/risk/risks only; k6.log shows the breakpoint scenario climbing to ~67 VUs / ~325.75 iters/s with '0 interrupted iterations' and no captured error spike (the log ends mid-breakpoint at ~93%; no final handleSummary block / k6-summary.json was produced).
impact: Under any real integration load the platform behaves as if it had far fewer than 20 connections, making pool exhaustion (PERF-IO-001/002) reachable at modest concurrency. The mismatch between leak-detection-threshold (60s) and integration connection-hold (up to ~121s) will generate misleading leak warnings. The current load test gives false confidence because it does not exercise the integration code paths.
reproduction: 1) Compare application.yml:19-26 vs application-dev.yml:27-29 — confirm dev inherits connection-timeout/leak-detection from base. 2) Note k6 load.js exercises only a read endpoint. 3) Combine with the PERF-IO-001 reproduction to show exhaustion at < 20 concurrent integration pushes despite a nominal pool of 20.
resolution: Primary fix is PERF-IO-001..004 (stop holding connections across remote I/O). Independently: (a) make the integration HTTP work run on a bounded, separate executor/outbox so it cannot consume the primary DB pool at all; (b) once remote calls are out of transactions, keep maximum-pool-size=20 for base but add a dedicated, smaller bounded thread pool for outbound integration work; (c) raise leak-detection-threshold above the realistic worst-case hold OR (preferably) reduce the worst-case hold below 60s so the existing threshold stays meaningful; (d) extend the k6 suite with a scenario that drives the integration endpoints (test-push / poll) to characterise the actually-at-risk path.
patchBefore:
# application.yml
hikari:
  maximum-pool-size: 20
  connection-timeout: 30000
  leak-detection-threshold: 60000
# application-dev.yml (overrides only size + idle)
hikari:
  minimum-idle: 2
  maximum-pool-size: 10
patchAfter:
# Keep DB pool for fast DB work; run integration HTTP off-pool (async/outbox).
# After PERF-IO-001..004, integration calls no longer borrow DB connections, so
# 20 (base) / 10 (dev) is adequate. Ensure leak-detection-threshold stays above the
# realistic max DB-only transaction time (now << 60s) so it flags only true leaks.
# Add a k6 scenario that exercises /api/v1/integrations/*/test-push to load-test the
# real at-risk path (current load.js hits only GET /api/v1/risk/risks).

title: BcmDependencyGraphService re-queries BIA per plan despite already holding all BIAs in memory
cvss: Low: build() loads all BIAs up front (paged at 1000), then in the BCP/DRP plan loop calls bias.findByIdAndOrganisationId per plan to perform RTO-mismatch detection. That is one extra query per plan for data already resident in memory. Bounded by plan count (paged at 1000) and only on the dependency-graph endpoint, so impact is limited, but it is a clear avoidable N+1.
description: build() first loads all BIAs for the tenant into biaRows (lines 71-73). It then loops over BCP/DRP plans (line 106) and, for each plan with a sourceBiaId and rtoHours, calls bias.findByIdAndOrganisationId(p.getSourceBiaId(), org) (line 127) to compare the plan's RTO against the source BIA's RTO. Since every BIA was already loaded at line 71, this is a redundant per-plan query - the BIA could be looked up from a Map<Long, BcmBiaAssessment> built from biaRows.
rootCause: The already-materialised BIA list is not indexed into a map for reuse; the RTO-mismatch check re-fetches the parent BIA from the repository inside the plan loop.
evidence:
Line 71-73 `List<BcmBiaAssessment> biaRows = bias.findByOrganisationIdOrderByIdDesc(org, PageRequest.of(0, 1000)).getContent();`
Line 127 `bias.findByIdAndOrganisationId(p.getSourceBiaId(), org).ifPresent(b -> { ... });` inside `for (BcpPlan p : plans...)`.
Query count adds one BIA SELECT per plan that has a sourceBiaId, all redundant because biaRows already contains them.
impact: One redundant DB round trip per BCP/DRP plan on the dependency-graph build. Minor latency and DB load; the feature is called out as a common first-demo screen, so the waste is visible under demo conditions but bounded.
reproduction: 1. Seed BIAs and BCP/DRP plans with sourceBiaId set and rtoHours populated. 2. Enable SQL logging. 3. Call BcmDependencyGraphService.build() (the /bcm-dependency graph endpoint). 4. Observe one BIA SELECT per plan in addition to the initial bulk BIA query.
resolution: Build a Map<Long, BcmBiaAssessment> from biaRows once, and resolve the source BIA from that map inside the plan loop instead of calling bias.findByIdAndOrganisationId. This removes the per-plan query entirely and reuses data already in the persistence context.

title: Cyber & SCM expose explicit '/all' register dumps (assets, controls, vendors) that bypass the module's own pagination
category: Unbounded result set / intentional full-dump endpoint without cap
cvss: Low: these endpoints are deliberately unpaged for UI dropdowns, but they carry no server-side row cap, so they grow unbounded with the asset/control/vendor inventory. Lower severity because they are typically backing select boxes (smaller cardinality and used less often than the main register), but they still allow a full-table fetch on demand.
description: Several modules pair a properly-paginated register endpoint with an explicit '/all' (or root) variant that returns the entire org-scoped set, for populating UI dropdowns. CyberController exposes GET /api/v1/cyber/controls (Page<CyberControl>) alongside GET /api/v1/cyber/controls/all (List<CyberControl>), and GET /api/v1/cyber/assets (Page) alongside GET /api/v1/cyber/assets/all (List), plus GET /api/v1/cyber/frameworks (List). Each '/all' calls cyberService.getAllControls/getAllAssets/getFrameworks which delegate to controlRepo/assetRepo/frameworkRepo.findAllByOrganisationId(orgId) — repository finders that return List with no Pageable. ScmController.allVendors() is documented '/vendors/all — List all vendors (no pagination — for dropdowns)'. The asset inventory in particular (regulator-grade asset register) can grow very large, so a dropdown that fetches every asset is unbounded.
rootCause: Intentional convenience endpoints for select-box population that were never given an upper bound. The repository exposes both findByOrganisationId(orgId, Pageable) and an unbounded findAllByOrganisationId(orgId); the '/all' endpoints deliberately call the unbounded one.
impact: On large tenants a dropdown population request pulls the entire asset/control/vendor inventory into memory and over the wire. For the cyber asset register (which the platform markets as regulator-grade and can hold thousands of assets) this is a meaningful per-request cost and another path to the PERF-PG-001 heap-pressure problem, even though the main register endpoint is paginated.
reproduction: 1. Seed many cyber assets for organisation_id = 1. 2. Call GET /api/v1/cyber/assets/all. 3. Observe the full asset set is returned with no page envelope and no size cap, regardless of how many rows exist (contrast GET /api/v1/cyber/assets which caps at 20).
resolution: Cap the '/all' endpoints server-side. Prefer returning a lightweight projection (id + label only) for dropdowns and hard-limit the row count (e.g. PageRequest.of(0, 500)); if a register legitimately exceeds the cap, the UI should switch to a server-side type-ahead search endpoint instead of a full dump. At minimum add an explicit limit so the query can never fetch the entire table.
references: OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023) API4:2023 Unrestricted Resource Consumption

title: Lighthouse /login (Performance 38) was captured against the Vite DEV server (unbundled, unminified) — FCP 37s / LCP 72s / unminified-JS 7.5 MB are dev-mode artefacts, not production metrics
cvss: Informational: this finding does not describe a code defect but warns that the headline numbers (Performance 38, FCP 37.4s, LCP 72.3s, unminified-javascript est. savings 7,521 KiB) come from a development build and overstate the production penalty. Acting on the raw dev numbers without a production-build re-measure would mis-prioritise the audit. The structural findings (PERF-FE-001..005) remain valid regardless.
description: The Lighthouse report's network-requests and total-byte-weight items are all served from http://localhost:5173 — the Vite dev server (vite.config.ts server.port 5173) — including raw unbundled modules like /src/App.tsx, /src/translations/ar.ts, /@vite/client, /@react-refresh and /node_modules/.vite/deps/*. In dev mode Vite serves unminified, unbundled ES modules with HMR injected, so: (a) unminified-javascript reports 'Est savings of 7,521 KiB' (essentially the whole app, because dev code is never minified) and (b) FCP 37.4s / LCP 72.3s reflect waterfall module fetching + on-the-fly transform, not a production bundle. These specific numbers will improve dramatically against `vite build` output. Notably, the dev-only metrics that do NOT depend on minification — total-blocking-time (40 ms), bootup-time (0.17s), main-thread work (1.2s) — already pass, and CLS (0.344) is a real code issue independent of build mode.
rootCause: Lighthouse was pointed at the dev server (npm run dev / port 5173) rather than a production preview (npm run build && npm run preview). Dev servers intentionally trade size/latency for fast HMR.
evidence: All Lighthouse resource URLs are localhost:5173 with dev-only paths: /@vite/client (137,996 B), /@react-refresh (117,841 B), /node_modules/.vite/deps/lucide-react.js?v=8de9a796 (1,157,309 B), /src/App.tsx (463,783 B raw TSX), /src/translations/ar.ts (1,076,314 B raw TS). unminified-javascript displayValue 'Est savings of 7,521 KiB' — characteristic of an unminified dev build. FCP/LCP numericValue 37,409 ms / 72,262 ms.
impact: Risk of mis-prioritisation: the catastrophic-looking FCP/LCP and 'unminified JS' savings are largely eliminated by a production build alone, whereas the genuine structural wins are PERF-FE-001 (eager heavy pages), PERF-FE-002 (dual dictionaries), PERF-FE-004 (no vendor chunking) and PERF-FE-005 (CLS). Those persist in production.
reproduction: Inspect audit/raw/lighthouse-login.report.json network-requests: every URL is localhost:5173 with /@vite, /@react-refresh, /node_modules/.vite/deps and raw /src/*.ts(x) paths — the signature of `vite` (dev), not `vite preview` (prod).
resolution: Re-run Lighthouse against a production preview: `npm run build && npm run preview` (or serve dist/ behind a static host with gzip/brotli), then capture /login again. Use that report as the audit baseline for FCP/LCP/byte-weight, and keep the dev report only as evidence for the structural findings. Then re-confirm PERF-FE-001/002/004 against the real bundle/chunk graph.
patchBefore:
# Measured against dev server:
npm run dev   # http://localhost:5173 — unbundled, unminified, HMR
patchAfter:
# Measure against production build:
npm run build && npm run preview   # serves dist/ minified + chunked
# then run Lighthouse on the preview URL /login

title: Frontend (tss-grc-ui-v2) ships with zero executable automated tests and no test runner wired into the build
cvss: High business risk (not a CVSS-scored vuln). The entire React/TypeScript SPA — auth flow, tenant-scoped data tables, RTL bilingual rendering, 200+ pages across 17 modules — has no executed regression net. Any refactor or dependency bump can silently break the only interface end users touch; defects reach production undetected because the sole automated check is type-checking, which proves nothing about runtime behaviour.
locations: tss-grc-ui-v2/package.json (devDependencies: no vitest, jest, @testing-library/* or playwright)
description: The active frontend (tss-grc-ui-v2) is the production UI, yet it has no test runner installed and no executable test suite. package.json defines only four scripts — dev, build, preview, typecheck — and the devDependencies list (@types/*, @vitejs/plugin-react, typescript, vite) contains no test framework (no vitest, jest, @testing-library/react, or playwright). Two files exist under src/__tests__ (threeLines.test.ts, mobileCrisis.test.ts) but they import from Node's built-in node:test/node:assert and, per their own header comments, were written because 'The tss-grc-ui-v2 project has no test framework installed yet'. They are never executed by any npm script and are only fed through tsc --noEmit. So while two test FILES are present, the count of tests actually RUN in CI/build is zero. The only automated frontend signal captured in the audit is `tsc --noEmit` (audit/raw/tsc.log) which reported 0 errors — type correctness, not behavioural correctness — and a 6-case Playwright smoke suite that lives OUTSIDE the repo in audit/artifacts/e2e (it covers login happy/sad path and screenshots only, not module CRUD, validation, tenant scoping, or workflow transitions).
rootCause: No testing dependency or `test` npm script was ever added to tss-grc-ui-v2; the v1 static UI (tss-grc-ui) likewise has none. Component, hook, and integration testing was deferred ('once a runner is added', per the test-file comments) and never picked up. CI therefore gates the frontend on type-checking alone.
evidence: audit/raw/tsc.log: `tss-grc-ui-v2@0.1.0 typecheck` / `tsc --noEmit` (clean, 0 errors). package.json scripts block contains no "test" entry; devDependencies = [@types/node, @types/react, @types/react-dom, @types/sockjs-client, @vitejs/plugin-react, typescript, vite] — no test framework. `find tss-grc-ui-v2/src -iname '*.test.*' -o -iname '*.spec.*'` => 2 files, both using node:test and unrunnable by the project toolchain. No vitest.config.* / jest.config.* present. Backend, by contrast, runs 1858 JUnit tests (audit/raw/mvn-test.log, 174 surefire reports, 0 failures/0 errors/0 skipped).
impact: Regressions in authentication, multi-tenant data display, bilingual/RTL layout, form validation, and workflow UI ship undetected. There is no guard against breaking changes during dependency upgrades (e.g. React/Vite/Bootstrap bumps) or refactors. Frontend defects are caught only by manual QA or in production. Given the platform is bilingual + multi-tenant, subtle locale/tenant bugs are exactly the class of error unit/component tests catch cheaply and humans miss.
reproduction: 1) `cd tss-grc-ui-v2 && cat package.json` — observe no `test` script and no test framework in devDependencies. 2) `npm test` — fails / no-op (no script). 3) `cat src/__tests__/threeLines.test.ts` — header states there is no test framework; it imports node:test. 4) Confirm the only CI signal is `npm run typecheck` (tsc --noEmit), which passed with 0 errors but executes 0 assertions.
resolution: Adopt Vitest + @testing-library/react + jsdom (Vite-native, minimal config). Add a `test` script and a `coverage` gate. Convert the two existing node:test files to Vitest. Prioritise: (1) auth/session helpers and the API client (token handling, 401 refresh), (2) the i18n/RTL switch, (3) per-module list/detail pages with mocked API responses, (4) form validation. Add Playwright as a committed e2e dependency (the audit's external 6-case suite proves the app is automatable) and expand beyond login to module CRUD and tenant-switch flows. Target an initial 40% line coverage gate, rising per sprint.

_verification.rationale: Verified: package.json scripts = dev/build/preview/typecheck only (no "test"), devDependencies carry no vitest/jest/@testing-library/playwright, and no vitest.config/jest.config exists. The only two test files (src/__tests__/threeLines.test.ts, mobileCrisis.test.ts) both import node:test and are unrunnable by the project toolchain — fed only through tsc --noEmit. The production UI ships zero executable automated tests wired into the build; CI gates the frontend on type-checking alone. High is correct for the active production UI.

title: Backend branch coverage is 26.0% and 762 of 1324 classes (57.6%) have 0% coverage — decision logic is largely unexercised
cvss: High quality risk. 1858 passing tests give false confidence: only 26% of branches and 22.3% of cyclomatic complexity are exercised, and over half of all classes are never touched at runtime by any test. Conditional logic — exactly where defects and security checks live — is the least-covered dimension. Untested error paths, validation branches, and authorization decisions can regress without any test turning red.
description: JaCoCo (computed from tss-grc-backend/target/site/jacoco/jacoco.csv over 1324 classes) reports: LINE 38.5% (17,324 covered / 27,728 missed), INSTRUCTION 37.1% (93,819 / 159,128), BRANCH 26.0% (5,308 / 15,079), METHOD 31.9% (2,656 / 5,667), and COMPLEXITY (cyclomatic) just 22.3% (4,203 / 14,636). Branch and complexity are the weakest, which is the worst dimension to be weak in: branches are the if/else, switch, ternary, and exception decisions where logic errors hide. Aggregating per-class, 762 of 1324 classes (57.6%) have ZERO instruction coverage — no test ever loads them. Notably, several classes carrying confirmed Critical/High findings sit at 0%: AuthController (SEC-AUTH-001), EvidenceMatrixService (Critical PERF-NQ-003 + High QUAL-IE-001), DataOfficerService (QUAL-ESG-001), OtAssetService (Critical SEC-CYB-002). The 1858-test count is real and all pass, but it is concentrated in service happy-paths; whole layers (controllers, integration glue, error handling) are dark.
rootCause: Tests are predominantly Mockito unit tests on service classes covering nominal flows. Controllers, exception handlers, validation branches, and many newer modules were never given tests. There is no enforced coverage gate (no JaCoCo `check` rule failing the build below a threshold), so coverage drifted down as modules were added faster than tests.
evidence: jacoco.csv aggregate: BRANCH covered=5308 missed=15079 => 26.0%; COMPLEXITY covered=4203 missed=14636 => 22.3%; INSTRUCTION 37.1%; LINE 38.5%; METHOD 31.9%. Per-class scan: 762/1324 classes at 0% instruction coverage. Vulnerable-class coverage sample — AuthController 0%/0%/0% (instr/branch/line), EvidenceMatrixService 0%/0%/0%, DataOfficerService 0%/0%/0%, OtAssetService 0%/0%/0%, BcmService 25%/43%/31%, CyberService 44%/55%/45%, EvidenceItemService 60%/36%/61%. Test totals from surefire: 1858 tests, 0 failures, 0 errors, 0 skipped across 174 classes (audit/raw/mvn-test.log).
impact: High-complexity, low-coverage classes are the most likely to harbour latent bugs and to regress silently. Because branch coverage is 26%, most conditional paths — including authorization checks, tenant-scope guards, status-transition guards, and error handling — are never asserted. A change that flips a condition (e.g. removes a tenant predicate, as in several confirmed IDOR findings) will not fail any test. Refactoring the 0%-covered god-services (DataOfficerService 1000+ lines, OutsourcingService) is effectively unguarded.
reproduction: 1) Open tss-grc-backend/target/site/jacoco/jacoco.csv and sum BRANCH_COVERED / (BRANCH_COVERED+BRANCH_MISSED) => 0.260. 2) Count rows where INSTRUCTION_COVERED=0 and INSTRUCTION_MISSED>0 => 762. 3) Filter those rows by CLASS ending 'Controller' => 201 fully-uncovered controllers. 4) Grep AuthController / EvidenceMatrixService rows => 0 across all metrics.
resolution: Introduce a JaCoCo coverage gate in pom.xml that fails the build below a floor and ratchets up over time (e.g. start at line 38% / branch 26% — current levels — then +2% per sprint). Prioritise the 0%-coverage classes that carry findings or high complexity: write branch-focused tests for AuthController (login success/lockout/refresh-rotation), EvidenceMatrixService (matrix build + N+1 path), and the god-services. Track branch coverage specifically, not just line, in CI reporting.
patchBefore:
<!-- tss-grc-backend/pom.xml — jacoco plugin used for report only, no gate -->
<plugin>
  <groupId>org.jacoco</groupId>
  <artifactId>jacoco-maven-plugin</artifactId>
  <executions>
    <execution><goals><goal>prepare-agent</goal></goals></execution>
    <execution><id>report</id><phase>test</phase><goals><goal>report</goal></goals></execution>
  </executions>
</plugin>
patchAfter:
<!-- tss-grc-backend/pom.xml — add a ratcheting coverage gate -->
<plugin>
  <groupId>org.jacoco</groupId>
  <artifactId>jacoco-maven-plugin</artifactId>
  <executions>
    <execution><goals><goal>prepare-agent</goal></goals></execution>
    <execution><id>report</id><phase>test</phase><goals><goal>report</goal></goals></execution>
    <execution>
      <id>coverage-gate</id><phase>verify</phase><goals><goal>check</goal></goals>
      <configuration><rules>
        <rule>
          <element>BUNDLE</element>
          <limits>
            <limit><counter>LINE</counter><value>COVEREDRATIO</value><minimum>0.38</minimum></limit>
            <limit><counter>BRANCH</counter><value>COVEREDRATIO</value><minimum>0.26</minimum></limit>
          </limits>
        </rule>
      </rules></configuration>
    </execution>
  </executions>
</plugin>

// Example: cover AuthController login branches (0% -> exercised). Uses MockMvc with security.
@SpringBootTest @AutoConfigureMockMvc
class AuthControllerIT {
  @Autowired MockMvc mvc;
  @Test void login_success_returns_token() throws Exception {
    mvc.perform(post("/api/auth/login").contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
        .content("{\"username\":\"admin\",\"password\":\"Admin@12345\"}"))
       .andExpect(status().isOk())
       .andExpect(jsonPath("$.accessToken").exists());
  }
  @Test void login_bad_credentials_returns_401() throws Exception {
    mvc.perform(post("/api/auth/login").contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
        .content("{\"username\":\"admin\",\"password\":\"wrong\"}"))
       .andExpect(status().isUnauthorized());
  }
}

_verification.rationale: Recomputed directly from jacoco.csv (1324 class rows): BRANCH 26.0% (5308 covered / 15079 missed), COMPLEXITY 22.3% (4203/14636), INSTRUCTION 37.1%, LINE 38.5%, METHOD 31.9% — every cited figure matches. 762/1324 classes (57.6%) have 0 instruction coverage. The named vulnerable classes are confirmed at 0%: AuthController, EvidenceMatrixService, DataOfficerService, OtAssetService. Decision logic is largely unexercised. High is correct.

title: Confirmed Critical/High security findings have no test asserting the vulnerable path — 5 of 6 Critical findings sit on classes at 0% coverage or with tests that miss the exploit
cvss: High. The test suite gives no protection against the platform's most serious confirmed defects. Of the 6 Critical security findings in audit/crit_high.json, 3 sit on classes with NO test file at all and the other 3 have a *Test.java that exercises only nominal paths, never the cross-tenant/SQLi/mass-assignment exploit. There is therefore no regression net: a future fix could be reverted and every test would still pass. This is the gap that lets IDOR/BFLA findings persist undetected.
locations: tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/ccm/runner/CustomSqlRunner.java (SEC-INT-001 Critical — test exists but only checks DML rejection, not cross-tenant SELECT)
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/cyber/service/CyberService.java (SEC-CYB-001 Critical — test exists, no cross-tenant assertion)
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/bcm/service/BcmService.java (SEC-BCM-001 High — test covers plan tenant-scope but NOT the vulnerable BIA path)
description: Cross-referencing every Critical/High Java finding in audit/crit_high.json against the 174 backend test classes shows the suite does not exercise the vulnerable code paths. Of 6 Critical findings: SEC-CYB-002 (OtAssetService mass-assignment), SEC-FIN-001 (IntakeController unauthenticated PII leak), and SEC-IAM-001 (ApprovalChainController approval forgery) have NO corresponding *Test.java and their classes are at 0% JaCoCo coverage. SEC-INT-001 (CustomSqlRunner cross-tenant SQL exfiltration) has CustomSqlRunnerTest, but reading it shows 8 tests that only verify INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/chained-statement REJECTION and threshold logic — none asserts that a legitimate SELECT (e.g. `SELECT * FROM iam.users`) is constrained to the caller's tenant; indeed the source has no organisation/tenant predicate at all. SEC-CYB-001 (CyberService IDOR) has CyberServiceTest (14 tests) that stub repos with the caller's own ORG_ID and never simulate an attacker requesting another org's id. The clearest example is SEC-BCM-001: BcmServiceTest DOES contain tenant-isolation tests (getPlan_other_tenant_throws_EntityNotFound, invokePlan_other_tenant_throws) for the BcmPlan path — proving the team knows the pattern — yet the High finding is on the BIA path (updateBia/deleteBia at BcmService.java:221-236 call biaRepo.findById(id)/deleteById(id) with NO tenant scope), and there is no test for createBia/updateBia/deleteBia or any cross-tenant BIA assertion. The defensive test pattern exists but was simply never applied to the vulnerable method.
rootCause: Security-negative test cases (attacker requests another tenant's id; SQLi payload; mass-assignment of a foreign id) were not written. Tests assert what the code does on the happy path, not what it must refuse. Controllers carrying authorization findings have no MockMvc/security-context tests, so missing @PreAuthorize annotations are invisible to the suite.
evidence: Automated cross-reference (audit/crit_high.json x src/test): Critical findings missing any *Test.java => OtAssetService, IntakeController, ApprovalChainController (all 0% JaCoCo). BcmService.java:221-232 updateBia / 235-237 deleteBia call `biaRepo.findById(id)` and `biaRepo.deleteById(id)` with no TenantContext predicate; BcmServiceTest method list contains getPlan_other_tenant_throws_EntityNotFound and invokePlan_other_tenant_throws_EntityNotFound but ZERO methods referencing bia/createBia/updateBia/deleteBia (grep 'bia' => only the @Mock field). CustomSqlRunnerTest (115 lines, 8 tests): insertIsRejected/updateIsRejected/deleteIsRejected/chainedSelectIsRejected/threshold tests only — no cross-tenant SELECT test; CustomSqlRunner.java has 0 matches for 'organisation|tenant|TenantContext'. CyberServiceTest: all repo stubs use ORG_ID (the caller's own org); no OTHER_ORG/forbidden/cross-tenant case.
impact: The most severe confirmed defects (cross-tenant data theft, unauthenticated PII exposure, approval forgery, SQL-driven exfiltration) are completely unguarded by automated tests. When these are remediated, nothing prevents a later change from re-introducing them. Conversely, until remediated, the green test suite actively masks their existence and gives auditors/management false assurance.
reproduction: 1) `python` cross-reference: for each finding in audit/crit_high.json, derive ClassNameTest.java and check existence in src/test => OtAssetService/IntakeController/ApprovalChainController have none. 2) Read BcmServiceTest.java — confirm tenant tests exist only for plan, none for BIA; read BcmService.java:221-237 — confirm biaRepo.findById/deleteById are unscoped. 3) Read CustomSqlRunnerTest.java — confirm only DML-rejection tests; read CustomSqlRunner.java — confirm no tenant predicate. 4) Read CyberServiceTest.java — confirm all stubs use the caller's ORG_ID with no foreign-org case.
resolution: Add a security-negative test for every Critical/High finding, co-located with the fix, asserting the exploit is now refused. Pattern: arrange a record owned by OTHER_ORG, set TenantContext to ORG_ID, assert EntityNotFound/AccessDenied. For controllers, use @SpringBootTest + MockMvc + @WithMockUser to assert 403 for unauthorized roles and isolation across tenants. Mirror the existing BcmServiceTest plan-tenant pattern onto the BIA path. For CustomSqlRunner, assert a SELECT against a foreign tenant's rows is blocked (after adding a tenant guard / read-only constrained datasource). Make these tests part of the regression gate so the findings cannot silently return.
references: OWASP ASVS v4 V4.1 (Access Control), V5.3 (SQLi), V1.14 (CI verification)
CWE-639 (IDOR), CWE-862 (Missing Authorization), CWE-915 (Mass Assignment), CWE-89 (SQLi)

_verification.rationale: Verified end-to-end. OtAssetService, IntakeController and ApprovalChainController have 0 *Test.java files (and 0% JaCoCo). CustomSqlRunner.java (module/ccm/runner) has 0 references to organisation/tenant/TenantContext, so no test could assert tenant-scoped SELECT. BcmService.java:221-232 updateBia and 235-237 deleteBia call biaRepo.findById(id)/deleteById(id) with no tenant predicate (unlike the tenant-scoped listExercises), while BcmServiceTest has getPlan_other_tenant_throws / invokePlan_other_tenant_throws but ZERO bia tests (only the @Mock field references 'bia'). The exploit-path test gap is real. Minor nit: the narrative says '6 Critical findings' but crit_high.json actually holds 8 Critical / 57 High; the count is slightly off but the substantive claim is fully supported. High.

title: Authorization is untested end-to-end: 201 of 231 controllers (87%) have 0% coverage and only 4 tests use MockMvc — BFLA findings are invisible to the suite
cvss: Medium-to-High. The eleven 'Broken Function Level Authorization' findings in audit/crit_high.json (controllers gated only by isAuthenticated() or missing @PreAuthorize entirely) cannot be caught by the current suite because controller tests instantiate the controller with @InjectMocks and call methods directly, bypassing Spring Security. Only 4 of 174 test classes wire MockMvc/SpringBootTest, and none target the vulnerable controllers. Authorization correctness is therefore asserted nowhere.
description: The platform exposes 2175 endpoints across 231 controllers, but only 28 controllers (12%) have a *ControllerTest, and JaCoCo shows 201 of those 231 controllers (87%) at 0% coverage. More importantly, the EXISTING controller tests do not test authorization: the representative pattern (e.g. ObligationControllerTest) uses `@Mock` for the service and `@InjectMocks` for the controller, then calls controller methods as plain Java — Spring Security, the @PreAuthorize layer, and the JWT/tenant filter are never in the loop. Only 4 of 174 test classes reference MockMvc/SpringBootTest/WebMvcTest/@AutoConfigureMockMvc (CoiControllerTest and the three integration-webhook controller tests), and 19 reference @WithMockUser. Crucially, NONE of those security-aware tests cover the eleven BFLA findings (PolicyController, ControlMapController, CloudServiceController, GhgEmissionRecordController, AttachmentController, ConsentRecordController, NdiAssessmentCycleController/NdiAuditController, LicensingController, AutomationRuleController, SupplierResilienceController). Because authorization is enforced by annotations resolved at the Spring proxy/filter layer — not in the method body — a missing or wrong @PreAuthorize is structurally invisible to @InjectMocks-style tests. The suite can be fully green while every BFLA hole is open.
rootCause: Controller tests were written as plain unit tests (service mocked, controller called directly) rather than as MockMvc slice/integration tests that route through Spring Security. No convention exists for asserting @PreAuthorize / role gates / tenant isolation at the HTTP boundary. The bulk of controllers have no test at all.
evidence: jacoco.csv: 231 classes ending 'Controller'; 201 at 0% instruction coverage. `find -name '*ControllerTest.java'` => 28. `grep -rlE 'WebMvcTest|MockMvc|SpringBootTest|@AutoConfigureMockMvc' src/test` => 4 files (CoiControllerTest, CrowdStrikeControllerTest, ServiceNowControllerTest, TenableControllerTest). `grep -rlE 'WithMockUser' src/test` => 19. ObligationControllerTest header: `@Mock private ObligationService service; @InjectMocks private ObligationController controller;` (no MockMvc, no security). Endpoint total 2175 across 231 controllers per audit facts.
impact: The platform's authorization model is unverified at runtime. Adding, removing, or mis-scoping a @PreAuthorize on any of 2175 endpoints produces no test failure. This is the direct cause of the BFLA findings going undetected in development. For a multi-tenant GRC product where tenant isolation and least-privilege are core selling points, having zero HTTP-level authorization tests is a material assurance gap.
reproduction: 1) `find tss-grc-backend/src/test -name '*ControllerTest.java' | wc -l` => 28; `find tss-grc-backend/src/main -name '*Controller.java' | wc -l` => 231. 2) `grep -rlE 'MockMvc|SpringBootTest|WebMvcTest' tss-grc-backend/src/test | wc -l` => 4. 3) Open ObligationControllerTest.java — confirm @InjectMocks direct-call style, no security. 4) jacoco.csv => 201/231 controllers at 0%.
resolution: Establish a MockMvc-based authorization test convention. For each controller, add a security slice test asserting: (a) anonymous => 401, (b) authenticated-but-wrong-role => 403, (c) correct role => 2xx, (d) cross-tenant id => 404/403. Start with the controllers carrying BFLA findings, then expand. Consider an automated guard test that scans all @RequestMapping handler methods and fails if any write/delete endpoint lacks a @PreAuthorize (reflection-based meta-test) to prevent regressions across all 2175 endpoints cheaply.
references: OWASP API Security Top 10 — API5:2023 Broken Function Level Authorization

title: End-to-end coverage is a 6-case external smoke suite (login + screenshots only); business workflows and module CRUD are untested e2e
cvss: Low-to-Medium. The only browser-level automation that exists is a 6-test Playwright smoke suite living outside the repo (audit/artifacts/e2e), covering login happy/sad path, a demo-skip bypass, session persistence, and a11y/responsive screenshots. It does not exercise any module's create/read/update/delete, workflow state transitions, tenant switching, or bilingual data entry. The integrated stack — frontend calling the 2175 backend endpoints under real auth — is essentially unverified by automation.
description: A Playwright run captured in audit/raw/playwright.log executed 6 tests, all passing (1.1m): E2E login success -> /risk, login failure -> error shown, demo-skip bypass navigates without auth, session persists across reload, plus an a11y+screenshots pass across key pages and a responsive mobile-screenshots pass. This suite lives in audit/artifacts/e2e (an audit-time scaffold), not in tss-grc-ui-v2, so it is not part of the project's committed build and would not run in the team's CI. Functionally it is a thin smoke test: it proves the app boots, login works, and pages render for screenshotting — it asserts nothing about creating a risk, advancing a workflow (e.g. the 9-step cyber incident state machine), submitting a BIA, switching tenants, or rendering Arabic/RTL data correctly. Combined with FUNC-001 (no committed frontend unit tests) and FUNC-004 (no HTTP authorization tests), there is no automated check that the integrated system behaves correctly for any real user task beyond logging in.
rootCause: E2E testing was set up only as an audit artifact, not adopted into the repo. No page-object structure, no per-module scenarios, and the suite is not wired to any npm script in tss-grc-ui-v2. The 'demo-skip bypass navigates without auth' case being a passing test also hints at an intentional auth-bypass affordance that itself warrants review.
evidence: audit/raw/playwright.log: 'Running 6 tests using 1 worker ... 6 passed (1.1m)'; test titles = login success->/risk, login failure, demo-skip bypass navigates without auth, session persists across reload, a11y + screenshots across key pages, responsive mobile screenshots. Suite location: audit/artifacts/e2e/tests/audit.spec.ts (single spec file) with its own package.json/playwright.config.ts under audit/artifacts/e2e — outside tss-grc-ui-v2. tss-grc-ui-v2 has no playwright dependency or e2e script.
impact: Integration regressions — broken API contracts between the SPA and the 2175 endpoints, workflow transition bugs, tenant-scope leaks visible only through the UI, RTL/locale data defects — are not caught automatically. Manual QA is the only safety net for full user journeys. The e2e harness exists but delivers near-zero functional assurance beyond authentication.
reproduction: 1) `cat audit/raw/playwright.log` — observe 6 tests, all smoke/login/screenshot. 2) `ls audit/artifacts/e2e/tests` => single audit.spec.ts; confirm it lives outside tss-grc-ui-v2. 3) `grep -i playwright tss-grc-ui-v2/package.json` => no match (not a committed dependency).
resolution: Promote the Playwright harness into tss-grc-ui-v2 (add @playwright/test devDependency and an `e2e` script). Build a small page-object layer and add critical-journey specs per module: create+list a risk, run an evidence review four-eyes flow, advance a cyber incident through its state machine, switch tenants and assert data isolation in the UI, and toggle EN/AR asserting RTL + Arabic field rendering. Run e2e against a seeded DB (seed_real_data.py) in CI nightly. Separately, security-review the 'demo-skip bypass' that navigates without auth — ensure it is dev-only and cannot reach production.

title: Access token (full JWT with roles) stored in JS-readable sessionStorage — confirmed by E2E artifact
category: Session Management / Token Storage (CWE-522, CWE-1004 analog)
cvss: CVSS ~5.4 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:L/A:N) — a single XSS or malicious dependency can read the bearer token and impersonate the user for the token lifetime
description: The login-success test reads the access token directly from sessionStorage via page.evaluate(sessionStorage.getItem('grc.accessToken') || sessionStorage.getItem('accessToken') || keys.join(',')) and writes it to session-keys.txt. The artifact contains a complete, decodable JWT. The header is {"alg":"HS384"}; the payload carries sub:1, usr:admin, org:1, a full roles array (incl. ROLE_PLATFORM_ADMIN, CYBER_WRITE/DELETE, SCM_WRITE/DELETE, EVIDENCE_WRITE/DELETE), enabled_modules, iat and exp.
