Because the token lives in sessionStorage it is readable by any JavaScript running in the page (XSS, malicious npm dependency, browser extension). This matches CLAUDE.md's documented design ('access token ... stored in sessionStorage') and is corroborated dynamically here. Refresh is in an HttpOnly cookie (good), but the access token itself is exposed.
rootCause: Architectural choice to keep the bearer access token in Web Storage (sessionStorage) so api.js can attach Authorization: Bearer headers. Web Storage has no HttpOnly equivalent, so any script in the origin can exfiltrate it.
evidence: session-keys.txt holds a raw JWT 'eyJhbGciOiJIUzM4NCJ9.<payload>.<sig>'. Decoded header: {"alg":"HS384"}. Decoded payload includes: roles=[CYBER_READ,SCM_READ,SCM_DELETE,EVIDENCE_WRITE,SCM_WRITE,EVIDENCE_DELETE,CYBER_DELETE,EVIDENCE_READ,ROLE_PLATFORM_ADMIN,CYBER_WRITE], org=1, exp=1781793757. The test wrote a token value (not just key names), proving getItem returned the JWT from sessionStorage.
impact: Any XSS, compromised third-party script, or malicious browser extension on the app origin can read the full bearer token and replay it against :8084 as the authenticated user (here, a platform admin) until exp. The token also leaks the role/module entitlement model to the client. Severity capped at Medium because exploitation still requires script execution in the origin (no independent XSS confirmed by this artifact).
reproduction: 1) Log in as admin on :5173. 2) Open DevTools console and run sessionStorage.getItem('grc.accessToken'). 3) Observe the full JWT is returned and base64url-decodes to the claims above. Equivalent to audit.spec.ts:41-42 / session-keys.txt.
resolution: Prefer keeping the access token in memory (a module-scoped variable, never persisted) and relying on the existing HttpOnly refresh cookie + silent refresh to survive reloads, instead of persisting the access token to sessionStorage. If Web Storage must be used, add a strict Content-Security-Policy to shrink the XSS surface, keep access-token TTL short (prod is already 15m), and bind tokens where feasible. Treat session-keys.txt as a secret artifact and exclude it from any shared/committed report bundle.

title: No E2E coverage for CRUD or multi-step workflow journeys (create -> approve -> archive)
category: Test Coverage Gap — Business Workflows / State Machines
cvss: N/A (coverage gap) — the documented module state machines have zero end-to-end verification despite being the platform's core value
description: The only interaction with the module pages (/risk, /compliance, /cyber, /privacy, /tprm, /bcm, etc.) is page.goto + screenshot + axe scan. There is NO journey that creates a record, transitions it through its documented workflow_status state machine (e.g. cyber incident DETECTION -> ... -> LESSONS_LEARNED, or a risk/compliance create -> submit -> approve -> archive), and verifies the resulting state and persistence. The workflows are the heart of a GRC product; state-transition guards live in the service layer (per CLAUDE.md) and are exactly the logic most likely to regress, yet nothing exercises them through the UI + API together.
rootCause: The E2E suite was built as a login + visual/a11y smoke harness. Authoring data-mutating, multi-step workflow journeys (and the fixtures/teardown they need) was out of scope for this pass.
evidence: audit.spec.ts iterates AUTH_PAGES (lines 10-20) only to goto+screenshot+axe (lines 86-97); the loop body contains no .fill on a record form, no submit of a create, and no assertion on workflow_status or row presence. playwright.log shows the AUTH_PAGES work folded into one test: 'a11y + screenshots across key pages (47.1s)'.
impact: A broken state transition (e.g. an incident that can be archived while skipping approval, or a risk that loses its workflow_status on save) would not be caught. For an auditable compliance platform, undetected workflow-integrity regressions are high-business-impact.
reproduction: Inspect the AUTH_PAGES loop in audit.spec.ts: it never mutates data. No create/approve/archive assertion exists anywhere in the spec.
resolution: Add at least one full lifecycle journey per high-value module (start with risk and cyber-incident). Drive the real UI: create a record, advance it through each allowed transition, and assert both the rendered state and the persisted state (via an API read). Use a dedicated throwaway tenant/fixture and clean up in afterEach.

title: No negative / permission-denied E2E (403 / hidden-action) journeys
cvss: N/A (coverage gap) — method-level @PreAuthorize and UI gating are unverified end-to-end; a privilege-escalation regression would ship silently
description: Every journey authenticates as admin (PLATFORM_ADMIN with a broad roles array — confirmed in the decoded JWT in session-keys.txt) and only exercises allowed actions. There is no test that logs in as a lower-privileged seeded role (riskmanager / Risk@12345, auditor / Audit@12345) and asserts that a forbidden action is blocked: that the API returns 403 for an action the role lacks (e.g. an AUDITOR attempting CYBER:WRITE) and that the corresponding UI control is hidden/disabled. The backend relies on @PreAuthorize(hasPermission('MODULE','ACTION')) via ModulePermissionEvaluator (per CLAUDE.md); none of that authorization surface is exercised end-to-end.
rootCause: doLogin() is hard-coded to the admin superuser (audit.spec.ts:24-30), so the suite can only ever observe the permit path. No per-role fixtures exist.
evidence: audit.spec.ts:24-30 doLogin always fills 'admin'/'Admin@12345'. session-keys.txt decodes to roles including ROLE_PLATFORM_ADMIN + CYBER_WRITE/DELETE + SCM_WRITE/DELETE + EVIDENCE_WRITE/DELETE — the most-privileged principal, so no denial is ever observable. No 'expect(...).toBe(403)' or 'toBeHidden' on a gated control appears in the spec.
impact: A broken-access-control regression (a missing @PreAuthorize, an over-broad role grant, or a UI control that should be hidden but is not) would pass CI undetected. Broken access control is OWASP A01 and directly relevant to a multi-tenant GRC tool.
reproduction: Review doLogin (audit.spec.ts:24-30) — only admin is used. No lower-privilege login or 403 assertion exists.
resolution: Add per-role login helpers and at least one negative journey per sensitive action: log in as auditor (read-only), assert a write control is absent/disabled in the UI, and assert the corresponding API call returns 403. Repeat for riskmanager attempting an admin-only action.

title: No cross-tenant isolation E2E (multi-tenant data-leak regressions unverified)
category: Test Coverage Gap — Multi-Tenancy / Tenant Isolation (CWE-639 analog)
cvss: N/A (coverage gap) — the per-query organisation_id filter (the core tenancy control) has no end-to-end verification
description: The decoded session JWT carries org:1, meaning every journey runs entirely inside tenant org_id=1 (TSS GRC). CLAUDE.md documents that there is NO global Hibernate tenant filter — every repository query must hand-filter by organisation_id, making this an error-prone, per-query control. The seed data sets up three tenants (org_id 1, 2, 3: TSS GRC, Aramco Trading, STC Bank). Nothing in the suite logs in under two different tenants and asserts that tenant A cannot read tenant B's records (neither via the UI nor by directly requesting another tenant's resource id from tenant A's session). Tenant isolation is therefore completely unverified end-to-end.
rootCause: Single-tenant test fixture (admin in org 1 only) and no second-tenant credential, so a cross-tenant read can never be attempted, let alone asserted to fail.
evidence: session-keys.txt JWT payload: 'org':'1'. CLAUDE.md: 'Every repository query must filter by organisation_id ... There is no global Hibernate filter for this; it is the developer's responsibility per query.' seed_real_data.py documents tenants org_id 1/2/3. The spec has no second-tenant login and no cross-tenant fetch assertion.
impact: A single repository method that forgets its findBy...OrganisationId filter would leak another tenant's GRC data (risks, incidents, evidence). For a multi-tenant compliance platform this is among the highest-impact failure modes, and it is invisible to the current suite.
reproduction: Inspect the suite — only org_id=1 (admin) is ever authenticated. No tenant-B principal or cross-tenant resource fetch exists.
resolution: Seed a user in a second tenant (org_id=2). Add an E2E that: as tenant A, creates/locates a record and notes its id; as tenant B, attempts to GET that id and asserts 403/404 (not 200 with the row); and asserts tenant B's list views never contain tenant A's records. This must be re-run whenever a repository finder changes.
patchBefore: // every test runs as admin in org_id=1 only; no second tenant is ever authenticated

title: No E2E coverage for logout / session termination
cvss: N/A (coverage gap) — the entire logout / session-invalidation path is unverified by any automated journey
description: The suite covers login success, login failure, route-guard bypass attempt, session-on-reload, a11y and responsive screenshots, but there is NO test that logs out and verifies the session is actually terminated: that the access token is cleared from sessionStorage, that the HttpOnly refresh cookie is invalidated server-side, and that subsequently navigating back to a protected route (or hitting Back) bounces to /login. Given that the access token is held in sessionStorage (see E2E-003) and refresh in an HttpOnly cookie, logout correctness is security-relevant and currently unverified end-to-end.
rootCause: Suite was scoped to login + a11y/screenshot smoke tests; the destructive/lifecycle half of the auth flow (logout, refresh-token revocation, back-button after logout) was never authored.
evidence: playwright.log lists exactly 6 tests (login success, login failure, demo-skip, reload, a11y, responsive) — none reference logout. Grep of audit.spec.ts shows no 'logout', 'signout', or refresh-revocation step; the spec ends at line 121.
impact: A regression that fails to clear the sessionStorage token, fails to revoke the refresh cookie, or lets the Back button restore an authenticated view after logout would ship undetected. For a multi-tenant GRC platform this is a real session-fixation / shared-device risk.
reproduction: Review audit.spec.ts — no logout test exists. Manually: log in, log out, press Back / re-navigate to /risk; today nothing asserts you are bounced to /login.
resolution: Add an E2E that logs in, triggers logout, then asserts: (a) sessionStorage no longer holds the access token, (b) the refresh cookie is cleared/rejected (a subsequent /api/auth/refresh returns 401), and (c) navigating to /risk lands on /login.
patchBefore: // no logout test exists in audit.spec.ts

title: Route guard enforces authentication: unauthenticated deep-link bounces to /login (verified)
cvss: N/A (positive finding) — confirms the SPA refuses to render a protected route without a session and preserves the intended destination via ?next=
description: The Playwright test named 'E2E: demo-skip bypass navigates without auth' clicks the first type=button (the ghost 'continue as demo / skip login' control) on the login form and records the resulting URL. The test name expects an auth bypass, but the captured artifact shows the route guard correctly intercepted the navigation: instead of landing on /risk, the browser ended up at /login with the intended destination preserved as a query parameter. The test still reports 'ok' because it only writes the URL to a file (no assertion), but the recorded URL is the real verified outcome and demonstrates the front-end route guard is working as designed.
rootCause: Client-side route guard redirects any navigation toward a protected path to /login?next=<encoded-path> when no valid session token is present, rather than rendering the protected view.
evidence: audit/artifacts/e2e/results/demo-bypass-url.txt contains exactly: 'http://localhost:5173/login?next=%2Frisk' — the ghost button did NOT reach /risk; it was bounced back to /login with next=%2Frisk. playwright.log: 'ok 3 ... E2E: demo-skip bypass navigates without auth (3.0s)'.
impact: Positive: confirms protected routes (e.g. /risk) cannot be reached by clicking the demo/skip control or by direct deep-linking without authentication. The ?next redirect also means UX intent is preserved post-login.
reproduction: 1) Run the live stack (frontend :5173, backend :8084). 2) Open /login. 3) Without entering credentials, click the ghost/skip button (form.login-form button[type=button]). 4) Observe the URL resolves to /login?next=%2Frisk, not /risk. Reproduced by audit.spec.ts:54-61, artifact demo-bypass-url.txt.
resolution: No code fix required for the guard itself. Recommend renaming the test and adding a real assertion (expect(page.url()).toMatch(/\/login/)) so the suite fails loudly if the guard ever regresses; the current test would pass even if the bypass succeeded because it makes no assertion.

title: Happy-path authentication journeys verified: login success, login failure, and session-on-reload
cvss: N/A (positive finding) — three core auth journeys exercised end-to-end against the live app and all pass
description: Three authentication journeys are exercised end-to-end against the running app: (1) valid admin login (admin/Admin@12345) submits the real login form and lands on /risk; (2) invalid login (admin/WrongPassword!1) surfaces a visible .login-error element and stays on /login; (3) after a successful login a full page reload re-renders the authenticated route (/risk) rather than bouncing to /login, proving the session token survives a reload. report.json records expected:6, unexpected:0, flaky:0.
rootCause: N/A — positive verification of intended behavior.
evidence: playwright.log: 'ok 1 ... login success -> lands on /risk (1.7s)', 'ok 2 ... login failure -> error shown, stays on /login (1.7s)', 'ok 4 ... session persists across reload (3.8s)'. reload-url.txt contains exactly 'http://localhost:5173/risk' (still authenticated after reload). report.json stats: expected 6, unexpected 0, flaky 0.
impact: Positive: the primary login success/failure paths and post-reload session persistence are confirmed working on the live stack. These are the journeys most likely to break a release, and they now have automated coverage.
reproduction: Run `npx playwright test` from audit/artifacts/e2e against frontend :5173 / backend :8084 with admin/Admin@12345 seeded. Tests at audit.spec.ts:38, 45, 63.
resolution: No fix needed. Keep these as smoke tests in CI. Consider asserting on the .login-error TEXT (not just visibility) so a future error-message regression is caught, and parameterizing credentials via env so the secret is not hard-coded in the spec.
patchBefore:
await expect(page.locator('.login-error')).toBeVisible({ timeout: 15000 });
expect(page.url()).toMatch(/\/login/);

title: Recommended Playwright suite structure to close the verified E2E coverage gaps
cvss: N/A (recommendation) — proposes the file/fixture layout that would land E2E-004 through E2E-007
description: The current single-file audit.spec.ts mixes auth smoke, a11y, and responsive screenshots and has no role/tenant fixtures, no API-level assertions, and no data cleanup. To close gaps E2E-004 (logout), E2E-005 (workflow lifecycle), E2E-006 (permission-denied) and E2E-007 (tenant isolation), split into per-concern specs backed by shared auth fixtures (one storageState per seeded role/tenant) so journeys are fast and isolated, and add API assertions alongside DOM assertions so persisted state — not just rendered state — is verified.
rootCause: Audit harness was intentionally minimal (one smoke file). Production-grade coverage needs fixtures, projects, and teardown that the current single spec lacks.
evidence: audit.spec.ts is a single 121-line file with all six tests; report.json shows one project, workers:1, no globalSetup/globalTeardown (config lines 13-14). No fixtures or storageState are used.
impact: Adopting the skeleton makes role- and tenant-scoped journeys cheap to add and keeps the security-relevant gaps (logout, authz, isolation, workflow integrity) under continuous verification.
reproduction: N/A — structural recommendation derived from the existing spec/config.
resolution: Introduce a fixtures module that produces authenticated contexts per role/tenant via storageState, a global setup that logs each principal in once, and per-domain spec files. Keep the existing a11y/responsive specs as-is.
patchBefore: // tests/audit.spec.ts  (single file: login smoke + a11y + responsive, admin-only, no fixtures)

title: Login form ships with pre-filled admin / Admin@12345 credentials and a plaintext credential hint
cvss: Not a CVSS-scored vuln, but security-adjacent UX: real, well-known credentials are pre-typed into the form and printed beneath it. On any deployment that reuses the seeded accounts this is a one-click foothold; even in demo it trains users to expect default creds and normalises credential exposure on the most security-sensitive screen in the product. Rated High for the UX+trust impact.
description: The username/password React state is initialised to the live seeded super-user: useState('admin') and useState('Admin@12345'). The fields render pre-populated, and below the form loginHint prints 'Demo · admin / Admin@12345 — riskmanager / Risk@12345' verbatim. A first-time user is presented with a fully-armed login form for the PLATFORM_ADMIN account and a printed cheat-sheet of two real accounts.
rootCause: Developer convenience defaults left in the production component. The credentials live in component state (not behind an import.meta.env.DEV guard) and the hint string is an always-rendered translation key, so they appear in every build and every locale.
evidence: Captured live login screenshot audit/artifacts/e2e/results/shots/login.png shows the username field reading 'admin', the password field pre-filled (masked dots), and the footer line 'admin / Admin@12345 — riskmanager / Risk@12345' rendered in full. Source confirms: LoginPage.tsx:25 const [username, setUsername] = useState('admin'); :26 const [password, setPassword] = useState('Admin@12345'); en.ts:116 loginHint: 'Demo · admin / Admin@12345 — riskmanager / Risk@12345'. The e2e doLogin() helper in audit/artifacts/e2e/tests/audit.spec.ts logs in with exactly these creds and the JWT in results/session-keys.txt decodes to sub=1, usr=admin, ROLE_PLATFORM_ADMIN — i.e. the pre-filled account is the real platform admin.
impact: Anyone who opens /login can sign in as platform admin with one click, with no need to know or guess anything. On a shared demo, staging, or any environment where the seed accounts were not rotated this is an immediate account takeover. From a pure UX standpoint it sets the wrong tone for a GRC/security product, and the hint clutters the cleanest screen in the app with operational secrets.
reproduction: 1. Run the v2 UI (npm run dev, http://localhost:5173). 2. Navigate to /login WITHOUT touching the form. 3. Observe username='admin', password pre-filled, and the credential hint beneath the form (see audit/artifacts/e2e/results/shots/login.png). 4. Click Sign In with no edits — you are authenticated as PLATFORM_ADMIN and land on /risk (e2e test 'login success → lands on /risk' passes).
resolution: Start both fields empty in any non-dev build. If a quick-fill is genuinely wanted for demos, gate it behind import.meta.env.DEV and surface it as an explicit, dismissible 'Fill demo credentials' affordance rather than a pre-typed password. Remove the live password from loginHint entirely; if a demo nudge is needed, point users to documented demo accounts without printing the password on screen.
references: NN/g: Password and login form usability

_verification.rationale:
Verified in LoginPage.tsx: line 25 useState('admin'), line 26 useState('Admin@12345') (live PLATFORM_ADMIN seed creds), rendered pre-filled. Line 114 renders
{t('loginHint')}
, and en.ts:116 loginHint = 'Demo · admin / Admin@12345 — riskmanager / Risk@12345'. Creds are plain component state with no import.meta.env.DEV guard and the hint is an always-rendered translation key, so both ship in every build/locale. Real security-adjacent UX defect; High.

title: Critical-path module pages eagerly imported in App.tsx defeat code-splitting on the public /login route
cvss: Not a CVE. Performance/UX impact: the public, unauthenticated login screen downloads and parses the JS for nine authenticated module landing pages (Risk, Cyber, BCM, Privacy, Compliance, TPRM, Incidents, Evidence, SCM) that a logged-out user can never reach. Lighthouse Performance category = 0.38 (38/100). High because it inflates Time-to-Interactive for every first-time visitor and every logged-out user, and the fix is squarely in app code (App.tsx import strategy).
description: App.tsx splits routes into a lazy()/Suspense set (the bulk of the file, ~hundreds of lazy chunks) but deliberately keeps the heavy module landing pages eager: LoginPage, DashboardPage, SettingsPage, RiskRegisterPage, CyberPage, BcmWorkspacePage, PrivacyPage, CompliancePage, TprmPage, IncidentsPage, EvidencePage (lines 8-18) and ScmPage (line 167). Because these are top-level static `import` statements, the bundler/dev-server folds them into the entry graph that loads on EVERY route — including /login. Lighthouse confirms it: on /login the byte-weight report lists src/App.tsx, src/pages/compliance/CompliancePage.tsx, src/pages/scm/ScmPage.tsx, src/pages/cyber/CyberPage.tsx and src/pages/tprm/TprmPage.tsx as downloaded resources, and unused-javascript attributes 108 KiB (Compliance), 95 KiB (TPRM), 93 KiB (SCM), 82 KiB (Cyber), 63 KiB (Evidence), 56 KiB (Risk) of wasted bytes to exactly these pages — proof their code shipped to the login page but went unexecuted. The /login navigation issued 196 network requests (182 to localhost:5173).
rootCause: The comment at App.tsx:7 ('Critical-path pages (sidebar landings + login + dashboard) stay eager') treats authenticated module landings as critical path for ALL routes. They are critical for the authenticated shell, but not for /login. Eager top-level imports cannot be tree-shaken away from the entry chunk that the login route also loads.
evidence: audit/raw/lighthouse-login.report.json: categories.performance.score=0.38; audits.total-byte-weight: 'Total size was 12,119 KiB', items include CompliancePage.tsx (337,307 B), ScmPage.tsx (289,426 B), CyberPage.tsx (286,941 B), TprmPage.tsx (258,133 B) all on /login. audits.unused-javascript displayValue 'Est savings of 1,742 KiB' with per-page waste: CompliancePage 108,588 B, TprmPage 95,159 B, ScmPage 93,529 B, CyberPage 82,234 B. audits.network-requests = 196 total / 182 to localhost:5173. App.tsx:8-18 static imports; App.tsx:167 `import { ScmPage } from './pages/scm/ScmPage';`.
impact: Every first-time and logged-out visitor downloads ~1.7 MiB of authenticated-only module code that is never executed on /login, inflating parse/compile time and contributing to the catastrophic FCP/LCP/TTI on this route. Highest-impact lever to move the Performance score off 38.
reproduction: 1. Serve the v2 UI (vite, port 5173). 2. Run Lighthouse mobile against http://localhost:5173/login. 3. Open the Treemap / byte-weight & unused-javascript audits and observe authenticated module pages (Compliance/SCM/Cyber/TPRM/Risk/Evidence) listed as resources loaded on the login page. Reproduced in audit/raw/lighthouse-login.report.json.
resolution: Move the authenticated module landing pages to lazy() like every other route. Only LoginPage (and any genuinely public pages) should be eager. Each lazy page becomes its own chunk fetched on first navigation after auth, so /login no longer pulls them. Optionally split the auth shell (eager) from the marketing/login shell so the entry chunk for unauthenticated routes is minimal.

_verification.rationale: Verified: App.tsx:8-18 statically (eagerly) imports LoginPage, DashboardPage, SettingsPage, RiskRegisterPage, CyberPage, BcmWorkspacePage, PrivacyPage, CompliancePage, TprmPage, IncidentsPage, EvidencePage, and line 167 imports ScmPage — all top-level, folded into the entry graph loaded on /login. lighthouse-login.report.json total-byte-weight items confirm CompliancePage.tsx (337,307 B), ScmPage.tsx (289,426 B), CyberPage.tsx (286,941 B), TprmPage.tsx (258,133 B) downloaded on /login; unused-javascript displays 'Est savings of 1,742 KiB'; 196 network requests. Real bundle/code-splitting defect; High.

title: Both full-language translation dictionaries (ar.ts ~1.05 MiB + en.ts ~0.84 MiB) statically imported and shipped to /login
cvss: Not a CVE. Performance impact: i18n.tsx statically imports both the Arabic and English translation files, so ~1.9 MiB (uncompressed, dev) of string data loads on every route including the public login page, where only one locale is needed. Two of the three largest resources on /login are these files. High because it is a large, ever-growing payload on the critical path with a clean lazy-loading fix.
description: i18n.tsx (lines 2-3) does `import { en } from '../translations/en'` and `import { ar } from '../translations/ar'` at module scope. Both dictionaries are bundled into the eager i18n provider, which the app shell mounts on every route. On /login, Lighthouse byte-weight lists src/translations/ar.ts (1,076,314 B) and src/translations/en.ts (860,108 B) as the #2 and #4 largest resources downloaded — together ~1.84 MiB. A login page that renders a single locale only needs one of them, and a freshly logged-out user needs only the strings on the login form.
rootCause: Static (eager) import of both locale bundles in the i18n provider. There is no dynamic-import-per-locale or split between login-shell strings and the full module-string corpus, so the entire translation corpus for both languages is on the initial critical path.
evidence: audit/raw/lighthouse-login.report.json audits.total-byte-weight.items: {url: '.../src/translations/ar.ts', totalBytes: 1076314} and {url: '.../src/translations/en.ts', totalBytes: 860108}. On disk: ar.ts = 417,903 bytes source, en.ts = 325,194 bytes source (dev-served + sourcemap inflates the transferred size). i18n.tsx:2-3 static imports confirm both are eager.
impact: ~1.9 MiB of translation strings (dev) load on the public login page regardless of active locale; the figure grows with every new module's strings. Even after minification/gzip in prod this is a large, monotonically growing payload that blocks an already-slow login render.
reproduction: 1. Open the byte-weight / treemap audit in audit/raw/lighthouse-login.report.json. 2. Observe ar.ts and en.ts as the 2nd and 4th largest resources on /login. 3. Confirm i18n.tsx imports both statically at lines 2-3.
resolution: Load only the active locale, lazily. Replace the two static imports with dynamic imports keyed on the current locale and await them in the provider (with a small synchronous fallback set for the very first paint). Longer term, split each locale dictionary by module/namespace so a route only fetches the strings it renders, and ship login-form strings in a tiny always-loaded base namespace.

_verification.rationale: Verified: i18n.tsx lines 2-3 statically import { en } and { ar } at module scope into the eager I18nProvider mounted on every route. lighthouse-login.report.json total-byte-weight lists src/translations/ar.ts at 1,076,314 B and src/translations/en.ts at 860,108 B (~1.84 MiB) downloaded on /login, the #1 and #2 largest resources. A single-locale login page needs neither full dictionary. Real critical-path bloat; High.

title: "Continue without backend (demo mode)" CTA silently bounces the user back to /login
cvss: No security impact. UX-only: a primary-looking secondary CTA promises an offline demo experience but lands the user back on the page they started from, with no message. Rated Medium because it is a visible, reproducible broken promise on the entry screen that erodes first-run trust.
description: The ghost button labelled 'Continue without backend (demo mode)' calls continueDemo(), which just navigate(landing) (default '/risk') with no token. Because the destination pages immediately call the API and there is no offline/demo data layer, the first 401 triggers redirectToLogin() in api.ts, which does window.location.replace('/login?next=/risk'). The net effect: clicking the demo CTA round-trips straight back to /login. The CTA's promise ('continue without backend') is the one thing the app cannot actually do.
rootCause: The label advertises an offline 'demo mode' that was never implemented — there is no client-side mock/data layer. continueDemo() only changes the route; the global 401 handler in api.ts (lines 71-73) then bounces any tokenless page back to /login, so the CTA is a no-op that looks like a dead end.
evidence: Live e2e artifact audit/artifacts/e2e/results/demo-bypass-url.txt contains exactly 'http://localhost:5173/login?next=%2Frisk' — i.e. after clicking the demo button the browser ended up back on /login (with ?next=/risk appended by api.ts:73). The e2e test 'demo-skip bypass navigates without auth' (audit/artifacts/e2e/tests/audit.spec.ts:54) clicks the first form button[type=button] and records the resulting URL. Source: LoginPage.tsx:53-55 continueDemo(){ navigate(landing,{replace:true}); }; api.ts:68-74 redirectToLogin() does window.location.replace(`/login?next=${...}`).
impact: A new evaluator who has no backend running clicks the most inviting alternative to logging in, the screen flickers, and they are returned to the same login form with no explanation. They cannot tell whether they mis-clicked, the app is broken, or login failed. The single most common 'kick the tyres' path on the entry screen is a confusing dead end.
reproduction: 1. Open /login (backend may be up or down — result is the same with no token). 2. Click 'Continue without backend (demo mode)'. 3. Observe the URL returns to /login?next=/risk with no toast or message (matches audit/artifacts/e2e/results/demo-bypass-url.txt). The user is back where they started.
resolution: Either (a) remove the CTA until a real offline/mock data mode exists, or (b) make the label honest about what happens and add feedback. If the button is meant only to preview the shell, relabel it to set the right expectation and show a toast explaining that live data needs the backend. Do not present a destination the global 401 handler will instantly reject.
references: NN/g: Microcopy and the principle of least astonishment
WCAG 2.1 SC 3.2.4 Consistent Identification (predictable component behaviour)

title: loginNetworkError exposes developer jargon and a localhost URL to end users
cvss: No direct security impact. UX-only: the only network-failure message a signed-out user can hit names 'the API' and prints http://localhost:8084, which is meaningless (and slightly alarming) to a non-developer and stays in the deployed build. Rated Medium as it is the primary error string on the entry screen, in both locales.
description: When login fails with anything other than a 401, LoginPage.tsx:46 shows t('loginNetworkError') = 'Cannot reach the API. Is the backend running on http://localhost:8084?'. This is a developer's debugging note, not a user-facing message: it uses the term 'the API' and 'the backend', and hard-codes a dev hostname/port that will be wrong in any real deployment. The Arabic string mirrors the same jargon and URL.
rootCause: A dev-time troubleshooting string was promoted to the user-facing default error. It conflates two distinct audiences (developer running locally vs. an end user whose connection dropped) and bakes the dev port into copy that ships to all environments.
evidence: en.ts:113 loginNetworkError: 'Cannot reach the API. Is the backend running on http://localhost:8084?'; ar.ts:113 loginNetworkError: 'تعذر الوصول إلى الواجهة الخلفية. هل تعمل على http://localhost:8084؟'. LoginPage.tsx:42-47 routes every non-401 error here (the catch block: ApiError 401 -> loginInvalid, else loginNetworkError; non-ApiError -> loginNetworkError). The good-pattern sibling loginInvalid (en.ts:112 'Invalid username or password.') shows the same file is capable of clean user copy, which makes this string an outlier.
impact: A real user on a flaky connection, or anyone on a deployed instance, is told to check whether 'the backend' is 'running on http://localhost:8084' — advice they cannot act on and that signals the product is unfinished. It is the wrong voice for the entry screen and undermines the polished impression set by the rest of the login copy.
reproduction: 1. Open /login with the backend stopped (or block requests to :8084). 2. Click Sign In. 3. The red .login-error banner shows 'Cannot reach the API. Is the backend running on http://localhost:8084?'. Switch to Arabic (lang toggle) and repeat — same jargon and localhost URL appear.
resolution: Rewrite to a calm, user-actionable message that does not name internal components or hard-code a dev URL: tell the user the app could not connect and what to do (check connection, try again). Keep any developer hint (the localhost reminder) to console.warn in DEV builds only.
references: NN/g: Error message guidelines (be specific, no jargon, suggest a next step)
Microsoft Writing Style Guide: error messages

title: Catastrophic Core Web Vitals on /login: FCP 37.4 s, LCP 72.3 s, Speed Index 37.4 s, TTI 72.3 s
cvss: Not a CVE. UX impact: every Core Web Vitals timing metric on /login scores 0 — FCP 37.4 s, LCP 72.3 s, Speed Index 37.4 s, Time-to-Interactive 72.3 s — driving the Performance category to 0.38. These are far beyond any usable threshold (good FCP < 1.8 s, good LCP < 2.5 s). High, with the caveat that absolute values are inflated by the Vite dev server (unbundled, on-demand compilation) and a local Kaspersky AV script injection; a production build will be dramatically faster, but the structural causes (LH-01/LH-02, 196 requests) are real.
description: All paint/interactivity metrics fail with score 0. FCP = 37,409 ms (37.4 s), LCP = 72,262 ms (72.3 s), Speed Index = 37,409 ms, Time-to-Interactive = 72,262 ms. The root cause is the combination of (a) 196 network requests on a single page navigation — 182 to localhost:5173, because the Vite dev server serves each TS/TSX module as a separate, on-demand-transpiled ESM request rather than a bundle; (b) the ~1.7 MiB of eager authenticated-module JS (LH-01) and ~1.9 MiB of dual-locale translations (LH-02) that load before first paint; and (c) a render-blocking third-party script injected by local Kaspersky AV (~2.1 s blocking, see LH-05). Notably Total Blocking Time is only 40 ms and main-thread work 1.2 s — the wall-clock latency is dominated by the request waterfall and dev-server compile latency, not CPU.
rootCause: Measured against the Vite dev server (no production bundle), so the metrics reflect on-demand module compilation plus an unbundled ESM request waterfall (182 localhost requests) amplified by the eager-import bloat (LH-01, LH-02) and an injected blocking AV script. Dev mode inflates the absolute numbers, but the eager-import/translation-bundle/request-count problems persist in any environment.
evidence: audit/raw/lighthouse-login.report.json: first-contentful-paint numericValue 37409.26 ms / displayValue '37.4 s' / score 0; largest-contentful-paint 72262.21 ms / '72.3 s' / score 0; speed-index 37409.26 ms / score 0; interactive 72262.21 ms / score 0; total-blocking-time 43.5 ms (score 1); mainthread-work-breakdown 1195.5 ms (score 1); network-requests count 196 (182 localhost). categories.performance.score 0.38.
impact: If these timings held in production, the login page would be effectively unusable (over a minute to interactivity). Even discounting the dev-server inflation, the 196-request waterfall and multi-MiB eager payload guarantee a slow first render for real users on mobile/slow networks.
reproduction: 1. Run Lighthouse (mobile, simulated throttling) against http://localhost:5173/login on the Vite dev server. 2. Read the metrics block. Captured verbatim in audit/raw/lighthouse-login.report.json. For a representative production number, build (`vite build`), serve the static output, and re-run.
resolution: Two-track. (1) Re-measure against a production build served statically — this alone removes the dev-server compile latency and collapses the 182-request module waterfall into a handful of hashed bundles, which will move FCP/LCP by an order of magnitude. (2) Land LH-01 and LH-02 so the production entry chunk for /login is minimal, and add `build.rollupOptions.output.manualChunks` to split vendor (react, react-router, lucide-react) from app code for better caching. Re-run Lighthouse to validate the Performance score recovers.

_verification.rationale: The cited metrics are exact in lighthouse-login.report.json: FCP 37,409 ms / LCP 72,262 ms / Speed Index 37,409 ms / TTI 72,262 ms, all score 0, performance 0.38, 196 network requests. BUT the report's own rootCause states these were 'Measured against the Vite dev server (no production bundle)' — the 37s/72s wall-clock is dominated by on-demand ESM transpilation and an unbundled 182-request waterfall, not the shipped artifact; Total Blocking Time is only 40 ms and main-thread work 1.2 s. The real, environment-independent defects (eager imports, dual-locale bundle) are already captured as High in LH-01/LH-02. The headline catastrophic CWV figures do not reflect a production build, so a standalone High is inflated — Medium.

title: Cumulative Layout Shift 0.344 on /login — 6 layout shifts during load
cvss: Not a CVE. UX impact: CLS = 0.344 fails Google's 'good' threshold (< 0.1) and even the 'needs improvement' ceiling (0.25); 6 discrete layout shifts occur while the login page loads. Medium because it degrades perceived stability and can cause mis-clicks on the login form, but it is visual rather than blocking.
description: Cumulative Layout Shift is 0.344 (score 0.32) and the layout-shifts audit reports '6 layout shifts found' (score 0). Content reflows as late chunks/fonts/translations resolve — consistent with the staggered arrival of the dual-locale translation dictionaries (LH-02) and the on-demand dev-server module waterfall, which let the login form render against incomplete strings/styles and then jump as resources land.
rootCause: Elements (login form, header/brand, localized text) render before their final content/dimensions are known, then shift when async resources (translations, fonts, late JS) resolve. No reserved space (explicit dimensions / min-height / skeleton) for the shifting regions, and locale strings swap in after first paint.
evidence: audit/raw/lighthouse-login.report.json: cumulative-layout-shift numericValue 0.34425702372849826 / displayValue '0.344' / score 0.32; layout-shifts displayValue '6 layout shifts found' / score 0; cls-culprits-insight score 0.
impact: Form fields and buttons move under the user during the multi-second load, risking accidental focus loss or mis-clicks on the credential fields and submit button; degrades the professional feel of the first screen users see.
reproduction: 1. Lighthouse /login run, open the CLS and 'Avoid large layout shifts' audits in audit/raw/lighthouse-login.report.json. 2. Observe CLS 0.344 and 6 shift events.
resolution: Reserve space for late-arriving content: give the login card/brand fixed dimensions or a min-height; preload the brand/logo image and set explicit width/height; show a skeleton matching final layout while translations resolve; ensure web fonts use `font-display: optional/swap` with size-adjust metrics to avoid reflow. Once LH-02 ships a base login-string namespace synchronously, the locale-swap shift disappears.

title: Topbar page title is crushed to 2–3 glyphs because the search box holds a fixed 320px width
cvss: Medium user impact: the single strongest wayfinding cue (the page title) is illegible on every module page at the captured 1366px viewport, harming orientation; no data loss or security impact.
description: On the inner module pages the topbar title block is squeezed to almost nothing — the captured screenshots show the page title rendered as only "إد...", "الا..." or "الإ..." with the eyebrow truncated to "...RM"/"...MA"/"تعدي...". The topbar lays out a fixed-width search box (320px), a context-pack selector, an environment pill, and five icon buttons, all in a flex-shrink:0 right group, while the title block (the only flex-shrinkable child) absorbs all the remaining-space deficit and collapses to ~30px. The title therefore conveys no information at this viewport.
rootCause: .topbar (shell.css:166) is a single flex row with overflow:hidden. .topbar-right (line 191) and .search-box (line 200, width:320px) are flex-shrink:0 / fixed-width, so the only element that can give up width is the title block (line 180 min-width:0). With ~8 right-side controls plus a 320px search field, on a 1366px-wide canvas minus the 280px sidebar there is no room left for the title, and its text-overflow:ellipsis (line 182) clips it to 2–3 characters.
evidence: shell.css:200 `.search-box { ... width: 320px; }`; shell.css:182 `.topbar-title { ... white-space: nowrap; overflow: hidden; text-overflow: ellipsis; }`. Captured renders: risk-register.png shows the heading "إدارة المخاطر المؤسسية" reduced to "إد..." and the eyebrow to "...RM"; the same crush appears in bcm.png, compliance.png and settings.png.
impact: Users cannot read which screen they are on from the topbar on any module page at common laptop widths. The page H1 inside the body still shows the full title, so the topbar title is pure redundant chrome that now actively misleads (it looks broken). The truncated eyebrow ("...RM", "...MA") looks like a rendering bug to auditors evaluating the product.
reproduction: Run the v2 UI (localhost:5173), log in as admin/Admin@12345, open any module (Risk Register / BCM / Compliance / Settings) in a ~1366px-wide window. The topbar title and eyebrow appear clipped to a few characters. Reproduced in the captured shots risk-register.png, bcm.png, compliance.png, settings.png.
resolution: Make the search box shrinkable and give the title priority: set `.search-box { width: clamp(160px, 22vw, 320px); min-width: 0; }` and collapse it to an icon-only button below ~1100px. Alternatively, since the page body already renders the full H1, drop the duplicate topbar title on inner pages (keep it only on the dashboard) and reallocate that width to the search box. Ensure the title block keeps `flex: 1 1 auto; min-width: 0;` so it wins remaining space over the controls.

title: Risk Register KPI tiles show a number and a stray arrow but no visible metric label
cvss: Medium user impact: the four headline risk metrics (19 / 4 / 2 / 51) are ambiguous because their labels are visually subordinated and one tile shows an arrow affordance with no apparent destination, slowing comprehension of the register's top-line numbers.
locations: audit/artifacts/e2e/results/shots/risk-register.png (four tiles: 19 مفتوحة, 4 مُعالجة, 2 المخاطر الحرجة, 51 إجمالي المخاطر)
description: The Risk Register KPI strip renders large numbers (19, 4, 2, 51) with a leading arrow icon in each tile's corner and a small grey label beneath the number. In the captured shot the arrow reads as a clickable CTA but its target is unclear, and the label sits below the giant number in --ink-3 grey at a much smaller size, so the eye lands on a bare number first ("19", "4") with the meaning ("Open", "Critical risks") demoted. Two of the four tiles have no icon-color/tone differentiation that ties the number to its severity, so "2 critical" does not read as more urgent than "19 open".
rootCause: The .kpi tile pushes the value to the bottom (`.kpi-value { margin-top: auto; }`, components.css:334) and the label is the smaller .kpi-label in --ink-3. The .kpi-clickable arrow (components.css:285-290) is shown on every tile but the affordance reads as decorative when the destination is the same register the user is already on, and tone classes (.kpi-tone-danger etc., lines 344-347) are only applied to some tiles, so the critical count is not visually escalated.
evidence: components.css:329-339 `.kpi-value { font: 800 var(--num-clamp)/1 ...; margin-top: auto; }`; components.css:285-290 define the per-tile `.kpi-arrow` hover affordance. risk-register.png shows the 4 tiles where the number dominates and the arabic label (مفتوحة / مُعالجة / المخاطر الحرجة / إجمالي المخاطر) is the smaller secondary line, and each tile carries a directional arrow.
impact: A first-time auditor reading the Risk Register cannot immediately tell what "19" and "4" count without reading the small grey caption; the arrow implies an action that may navigate nowhere new, eroding trust in the affordance. The most important number (critical risks) is not visually prioritised over the routine counts.
reproduction: Open the Risk Register page (risk-register.png). Observe the four KPI tiles: each shows a bold number, a corner arrow, and a small grey label. Hover a tile to see the arrow shift (components.css:287) even when the navigation target is ambiguous.
resolution: Lift the label to the top of the tile in --ink-2 (eyebrow style) and keep the number as the value, so the reading order is label → number, not number → caption. Only render the .kpi-arrow on tiles that genuinely navigate (and give them a tooltip/aria-label naming the destination, e.g. "View 2 critical risks"); make the rest non-clickable. Apply .kpi-tone-danger to the critical-risks tile so the number reads red.

title: Login error/feedback states are not visible; the only guidance is a literal credentials hint baked into the page
cvss: Medium user impact: the sign-in form gives no inline validation or error affordance in the captured state and instead displays raw demo credentials (admin/Admin@12345, riskmanager/Risk@12345) on the production-styled login page, which is both a UX and a credential-exposure concern.
description: The login screen pre-fills the username "admin" and a masked password, shows required-field asterisks, and a footer panel that prints two live demo credential pairs verbatim. There is no visible inline error region, no field-level validation styling, and no indication of how an invalid login is communicated. The credential hint is presented as ordinary page furniture, so a real deployment that forgets to strip it would leak working logins, and a user who mistypes has no feedback contract to rely on.
rootCause: A dev/demo affordance (printed credentials) is rendered unconditionally on the login page, and the form appears to rely on browser-native validation rather than a styled inline error/aria-live region for failed authentication.
evidence: login.png renders a footer card reading "تجريبي · admin / Admin@12345 · riskmanager / Risk@12345" directly beneath the sign-in button, plus a "الدخول بدون الواجهة الخلفية (وضع تجريبي)" link. The username field is pre-populated with "admin". No error/validation element is visible in the captured state.
impact: New users have no learnable feedback model for failed sign-in (was the password wrong? the account locked?). The printed credentials normalise insecure behaviour and would be a finding on their own in a banking-sector deployment; they also clutter the otherwise clean hero layout.
reproduction: Open login.html / the v2 login route. The credentials hint and "offline demo" link render below the submit button (login.png). Submitting bad credentials should surface a styled, screen-reader-announced error — verify whether one exists; none is present in the captured state.
resolution: Gate the demo-credentials block and the offline-mode link behind import.meta.env.DEV (or a feature flag) so they never ship to staging/prod. Add a persistent inline error region with role="alert"/aria-live="assertive" above the form that renders auth failures (wrong credentials, lockout, network) in --danger styling, and add aria-invalid + a field-level message on the offending input.
patchBefore:
{/* login form footer */}
تجريبي · admin / Admin@12345 · riskmanager / Risk@12345
الدخول بدون الواجهة الخلفية (وضع تجريبي)

title: Mobile Risk Register page title wraps to one word per line, consuming most of the first screen
cvss: Medium user impact: on a phone viewport the page header (eyebrow + title + 3-line subtitle) stacks vertically and the title breaks one Arabic word per line, pushing all actionable content below the fold and wasting the most valuable mobile real estate.
description: On the captured ~390px phone shot, the Risk Register header occupies roughly the top half of the screen: the eyebrow, title and subtitle compete with the floating "مباشر" live pill and the action buttons (تصفية / العروض) which overlap the eyebrow. The Arabic title and the long ISO 31000 / COSO ERM subtitle wrap aggressively (the subtitle breaks to ~9 short lines), so a user must scroll past a wall of descriptive text before reaching the records list or any KPI.
rootCause: .page-header (shell.css:257) keeps display:flex with justify-content:space-between and the actions on the same row even on small screens; there is no mobile rule to stack header + actions or to clamp/hide the descriptive .page-sub (line 262 caps max-width:600px but does not shorten it). breakpoints.css contains table/KPI/form mobile rules but nothing for .page-header density.
evidence: mobile/risk-register.png shows "سجل المخاطر" wrapped across two lines and the subtitle "دورة حياة المخاطر التشغيلية وفق ISO 31000 9 COSO ERM" broken into ~9 stacked tokens, with the تصفية/العروض buttons overlapping the eyebrow at the top. shell.css:257 `.page-header { display:flex; ... justify-content:space-between; }` has no max-width:767px override.
impact: First-screen mobile content is descriptive boilerplate rather than the risk records. The overlap between the floating live pill and the action buttons looks broken. Field users (the audience for mobile) have to scroll before they can act.
reproduction: Open the Risk Register on a ~390px viewport (mobile/risk-register.png). The header consumes the top portion of the screen; the subtitle wraps to many lines and the action buttons overlap the eyebrow.
resolution: Add a mobile rule that stacks the header (flex-direction:column), moves actions to their own row, clamps the title to two lines and hides or collapses the long .page-sub behind a tap-to-expand on small screens, so the records list rises toward the fold.

.page-sub { font-size: 13px; color: var(--ink-3); margin: 6px 0 0; max-width: 600px; line-height: var(--leading-normal); }

title: Mobile dashboard renders the gauge above its own title, leaving the headline number labelled by overlapping clipped text
cvss: Medium user impact: the dashboard's primary score widget is unreadable on mobile — the radial gauge overlaps the greeting and the score caption, so the headline governance number (50/100) sits on top of clipped Arabic text rather than a clear label.
locations: audit/artifacts/e2e/results/shots/mobile/dashboard.png (gauge overlaps "مساء الخير، أيمن" and "مؤشر الحوكمة الشامل")
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/styles/shell.css:270-281 (.dash-grid collapses but inner card not reflowed)

evidence: mobile/dashboard.png shows the gauge ring drawn across "مساء الخير، أيمن" and "مؤشر الحوكمة الشامل", with "50" and "100/" partially overlapping the caption; the export controls (ملف المجلس · PDF, ملف المجلس · PPTX, تصدير) are stacked full-width above it. shell.css:270 `.dash-grid { grid-template-columns: 1.4fr 1fr; }` → :279 collapses to 1fr but the card internals are unchanged.

title: Generic, non-actionable load-failure messages across modules ("Failed to load X" with no recovery path)
cvss: No security impact. UX-only: a repeated family of ~18 terse load errors tells users what broke but never what to do next (retry, contact admin), leaving a dead state on data-fetch failure. Low severity given they are recoverable on reload, but the pattern is system-wide.
description: There is a large, consistent family of fetch-failure strings of the form 'Failed to load <thing>' / 'Could not load <thing>.' — riskLoadError 'Could not load risks.', annexLoadFailed 'Failed to load annex data', comLoadFailed 'Failed to load committees', f4pLoadFailed 'Failed to load fourth-party register', and ~14 more. None offers a recovery action (no 'try again', no 'reload', no 'contact your administrator'). When a list fails to load the user is left on a terse red line with no obvious next step.
rootCause: Error copy was authored as a status label ('what failed') rather than as guidance ('what failed + what to do'). Each module added its own *LoadFailed key by copy-pasting the same terse template, so the missing call-to-action propagated to ~18 keys.
evidence: grep over en.ts: 18 keys match '/LoadFailed:/' plus riskLoadError (en.ts:455 'Could not load risks.'). Representative values: annexLoadFailed 'Failed to load annex data' (1656), comLoadFailed 'Failed to load committees' (5220), f4pLoadFailed 'Failed to load fourth-party register' (5556), srtLoadFailed 'Failed to load resilience tests' (5734). Contrast with the project's own strong empty-state copy that DOES give a next step, e.g. riskEmptySub 'Click "New Risk" to register the first one.' (en.ts:187) — proving the convention exists but was not applied to load errors.
impact: On any transient fetch failure the user sees a dead-end message and must guess that reloading might help. For a GRC tool where users may be screening alerts or controls under time pressure, the lack of a retry affordance/instruction adds friction and support tickets. Multiplied across ~18 registers it is a consistent quality gap.
reproduction: 1. Sign in. 2. Open a register whose API is briefly unavailable (e.g. throttle/kill the relevant endpoint) — Risk, Committees, Fourth-party, etc. 3. Observe the failure text is e.g. 'Failed to load committees' / 'Could not load risks.' with no retry button or guidance on what to do next.
resolution: Add a recovery clause to the load-failure copy and pair it with a Retry affordance in the shared error component. Standardise on one template ('We couldn’t load <thing>. Try again, or contact your administrator if it persists.') and reuse it across the *LoadFailed keys.

riskLoadError: 'Could not load risks.',
annexLoadFailed: 'Failed to load annex data',
comLoadFailed:   'Failed to load committees',
f4pLoadFailed:   'Failed to load fourth-party register',
references: NN/g: Error message guidelines (offer a constructive next step)

title: Inconsistent error voice across modules — "Failed to load" vs "Could not load" vs "Could not save"
cvss: No security impact. UX-only consistency defect: the same class of failure is phrased three different ways across modules, weakening the impression of a single, coherent product voice. Low severity, system-wide.
description: Failure copy mixes verb choice, capitalisation and punctuation between otherwise-identical situations. Across en.ts there are 20 strings beginning 'Failed to …' but only 7 beginning 'Could not …'; some end with a full stop ('Could not load risks.'), most do not ('Failed to load committees', 'Export failed'); some are noun-first labels ('Export failed') while others are sentence-style. The result is three competing voices for the same kind of event.
rootCause: No shared copy convention for failure messages; each module/author picked their own phrasing and punctuation, and there is no lint/style guide enforcing one error template, so divergence accumulated as modules were added.
evidence: grep counts over en.ts: 20 strings start with 'Failed to', 7 start with 'Could not'. Concrete clashes: riskLoadError 'Could not load risks.' (455, period) vs annexLoadFailed 'Failed to load annex data' (1656, no period); toastRiskFailed 'Could not save the risk' (485) vs sigSignFailedToast 'Could not record the signature' (877) vs exportFailed 'Export failed' (198, noun-first). Same product, three styles.
impact: Inconsistent failure voice makes the UI feel assembled by many hands and reduces perceived quality and trust — especially noticeable in a bilingual enterprise GRC tool where copy is part of the compliance/professionalism signal. It also complicates Arabic translation review since there is no single target phrasing to mirror.
reproduction: Static review: open tss-grc-ui-v2/src/translations/en.ts and compare lines 100, 198, 455, 485, 877, 1656 — note 'Failed to load …' (no period), 'Could not load …' (period), and 'Export failed' (noun-first) all coexist for the same class of failure.
resolution: Adopt one failure template and apply it everywhere: choose a single verb ('We couldn’t …' / 'Could not …'), consistent sentence case, and consistent terminal punctuation; document it in the UI style guide and sweep the existing keys. Keep EN and AR phrasing aligned to the chosen template.
patchBefore:
// en.ts — three voices for the same event
orgSwitchFailed: 'Could not switch organisation',
exportFailed:    'Export failed',
riskLoadError:   'Could not load risks.',
toastRiskFailed: 'Could not save the risk',
annexLoadFailed: 'Failed to load annex data',
patchAfter:
// en.ts — one template: "We couldn’t <verb> <thing>."
orgSwitchFailed: 'We couldn’t switch organisations. Try again.',
exportFailed:    'We couldn’t export the file. Try again.',
riskLoadError:   'We couldn’t load your risks. Try again.',
toastRiskFailed: 'We couldn’t save the risk. Try again.',
annexLoadFailed: 'We couldn’t load the annex data. Try again.',
// ar.ts mirrors the same single template: 'تعذّر … . حاول مرة أخرى.'
references: NN/g: Maintain consistency and standards (Nielsen heuristic #4)
Microsoft / Apple HIG writing style: consistent error phrasing

title: Insecure (HTTP) requests and render-blocking script from local Kaspersky AV injection on the login page
cvss: Not a CVE in the app. Best-Practices impact: is-on-https scores 0 ('6 insecure requests found') and the render-blocking-insight attributes ~2.1 s of blocking to an injected http:// script. All six insecure requests are to gc.kis.v2.scr.kaspersky-labs.com — a local Kaspersky antivirus extension man-in-the-middling the page, NOT app-served content. Low because it is an artifact of the test machine's AV, not the application; however it documents that the app is served over plain HTTP in this environment, which is a real prod-readiness concern.
description: The is-on-https audit lists 6 insecure (http://) requests, all to gc.kis.v2.scr.kaspersky-labs.com (Kaspersky's local web-shield injects scripts into pages). The render-blocking-insight audit (Est savings 1,050 ms) and unused-javascript both implicate the same injected main.js (~201 KB, 2,104 ms blocking). These are introduced by the auditor's machine, not the application bundle. Separately, the app itself is served over http://localhost:5173 in dev with no HTTPS, which is acceptable for local dev but must be HTTPS in staging/prod (CLAUDE.md notes prod uses SSL/PKCS12).
rootCause: Local Kaspersky antivirus browser integration injects its own HTTP scripts and beacons into every page it scans; Lighthouse counts them against the page. The underlying app is plain HTTP in the dev profile.
evidence: audit/raw/lighthouse-login.report.json is-on-https: score 0, displayValue '6 insecure requests found', all items url host = gc.kis.v2.scr.kaspersky-labs.com. render-blocking-insight: displayValue 'Est savings of 1,050 ms', top item url = http://gc.kis.v2.scr.kaspersky-labs.com/.../main.js, wastedMs 2104, totalBytes 201599. network-requests: 6 of 196 are kaspersky.
impact: On the audited machine the AV script blocks rendering for ~2.1 s and triggers the HTTPS failure, distorting the Best-Practices score (0.77) and the timing metrics. It does not affect end users who lack this AV, but it inflates the audit and masks the app's true numbers. The real, app-attributable point is that the app must be served over HTTPS outside dev.
reproduction: 1. Inspect is-on-https and render-blocking-insight in audit/raw/lighthouse-login.report.json; note every insecure/blocking third-party URL is kaspersky-labs.com. 2. Re-run Lighthouse on a machine without Kaspersky web-shield, or in an incognito profile with extensions disabled, and these 6 requests + the blocking script disappear.
resolution: Re-run the audit on a clean profile (no AV script injection, extensions disabled) to get representative Best-Practices/timing numbers. Confirm prod is served strictly over HTTPS (the prod profile already mandates SSL/PKCS12 per CLAUDE.md) and add a strict Content-Security-Policy + HSTS so injected http scripts are blocked in production. No change to the login page code is required for the AV artifact itself.
patchBefore: # Audited on a workstation with Kaspersky web-shield active; app served over http://localhost:5173 (dev).
patchAfter:
# Re-audit with `--chrome-flags="--disable-extensions"` on a clean profile;
# enforce HTTPS + HSTS + CSP in staging/prod (prod profile already uses PKCS12 SSL).

title: Console error on /login: favicon.ico returns 404 (errors-in-console audit fails)
cvss: Not a CVE. Best-Practices impact: the errors-in-console audit scores 0 because the browser logs a failed request — GET /favicon.ico returns 404 (Not Found). Low: cosmetic and a noisy console entry, but it contributes to the Best-Practices score (0.77) and signals a missing static asset / favicon link.
description: errors-in-console fails (score 0) with a single logged error: 'Failed to load resource: the server responded with a status of 404 (Not Found)' for http://localhost:5173/favicon.ico. index.html declares no <link rel="icon"> and there is no favicon.ico at the web root / public dir (public/ contains brand/ and sw.js but no favicon.ico), so the browser's default /favicon.ico probe 404s and logs an error.
rootCause: No favicon is provided at the default location and index.html does not declare an icon link, so the browser's implicit /favicon.ico request 404s. A brand/ directory exists under public/ but is not wired to a favicon link.
evidence: audit/raw/lighthouse-login.report.json errors-in-console: score 0, items[0] = {source: 'network', description: 'Failed to load resource: the server responded with a status of 404 (Not Found)', sourceLocation.url: 'http://localhost:5173/favicon.ico'}. tss-grc-ui-v2/index.html head contains <title>, charset, viewport, theme-color but no icon link. public/ listing: brand/, sw.js (no favicon.ico).
impact: Every page load logs a 404 error in the console (noise that hides real errors during debugging) and the tab shows no favicon. Counts against the Best-Practices category score.
reproduction: 1. Open audit/raw/lighthouse-login.report.json errors-in-console — note the /favicon.ico 404. 2. Load http://localhost:5173/login in a browser and check DevTools Console / Network for the 404 on favicon.ico.
resolution: Add a favicon asset (e.g. public/favicon.ico or an SVG from the existing public/brand/ set) and declare it in index.html with <link rel="icon">. This removes the 404 and the console error.
patchBefore:
<title>TSS GRC Platform</title>
    <!-- no icon link; browser probes /favicon.ico -> 404 -->
patchAfter:
<title>TSS GRC Platform</title>
    <link rel="icon" type="image/svg+xml" href="/brand/logo.svg" />
    <!-- or place a real /public/favicon.ico -->

title: Missing meta description on /login (SEO audit fails; SEO category 0.82)
cvss: Not a CVE. SEO impact: the meta-description audit scores 0 — index.html declares no <meta name="description">, so the SEO category sits at 0.82. Low for an authenticated GRC tool (the login page is not a public marketing surface), but trivially fixable and improves how the app is represented if ever linked/crawled.
description: meta-description scores 0: index.html's <head> contains charset, viewport, theme-color and <title>TSS GRC Platform</title> but no <meta name="description">. Lighthouse SEO category is 0.82, with meta-description (and the environmental robots-txt audit, which reports 27 errors but is not under app control on localhost) as the contributors.
rootCause: No description meta tag authored in the single static index.html shell.
evidence: audit/raw/lighthouse-login.report.json meta-description: score 0. categories.seo.score 0.82. tss-grc-ui-v2/index.html head (lines 3-9) has <title> and theme-color but no <meta name="description">.
impact: Search engines and link-preview unfurlers have no summary text for the app; minor for an internal/authenticated platform but it caps the SEO score and looks unfinished in any preview card.
reproduction: 1. Open audit/raw/lighthouse-login.report.json meta-description (score 0). 2. Inspect tss-grc-ui-v2/index.html and confirm no description meta tag.
resolution: Add a concise <meta name="description"> to index.html describing the platform.
patchBefore:
<meta name="theme-color" content="#0E5E5E" />
    <title>TSS GRC Platform</title>
patchAfter:
<meta name="theme-color" content="#0E5E5E" />
    <meta name="description" content="TSS GRC Platform — bilingual (Arabic/English) Governance, Risk & Compliance for Saudi Arabia and MENA." />
    <title>TSS GRC Platform</title>

title: Workflow "start" stage rail and action chip rows are dense undifferentiated chains with no clear primary next step
cvss: Low user impact: the lifecycle stage rail and the row of quick-action chips present 5–7 equally weighted pills with numeric badges, so a user cannot tell which step is the recommended next action; comprehension is slowed but no task is blocked.
locations: audit/artifacts/e2e/results/shots/risk-register.png ("ابدأ معالجاً" rail: 5 chevron pills; lower chip row with red !-badges)
audit/artifacts/e2e/results/shots/compliance.png (chip row with 6 chips, several red "!" badges)
description: Each module page shows an "ابدأ معالجاً" (start processing) rail of chevron-linked pills (e.g. تحديد وتقييم المخاطر 5 خ, خطة معالجة المخاطر 4 خ, قبول المخاطر 3 خ, إقرار دوري بالمخاطر 1 خ) and, below the KPIs, a second wrapping row of action chips with small red "!" count badges (e.g. "خطة معالجة المخاطر 4 !", "تصعيد تجاوز شهية المخاطر 1"). All pills share the same size, weight and border, so nothing signals which is the primary or most urgent next action; the red "!" badges indicate attention items but are visually identical in shape to the neutral count badges, and the chevrons imply sequence on a row that wraps.
rootCause: The stage rail and the quick-action chip row use a single uniform chip style with a trailing count; there is no primary/secondary hierarchy and no visual escalation tying the red "!" attention badges apart from neutral counters beyond color. With 5–7 items wrapping, the chevron "flow" metaphor breaks.
evidence: risk-register.png renders the rail "ابدأ معالجاً" with 5 chevron pills of equal weight, and a lower chip row where "خطة معالجة المخاطر" carries a red "4 !" and "الاستجابة لتجاوز عتبات المؤشرات" carries "3 !". compliance.png shows the same pattern with 6 chips, several bearing red "!" badges. bcm.png shows a 6-pill rail.
impact: A user landing on a module cannot quickly identify the single recommended next action or distinguish overdue/attention items from routine ones at a glance; this dilutes the value of the otherwise informative attention badges and adds cognitive load on every module entry.
reproduction: Open Risk Register / BCM / Compliance (respective shots). Observe the "ابدأ معالجاً" rail of equal-weight chevron pills and the lower wrapping chip row mixing red "!" attention badges with neutral counters in the same shape.
resolution: Promote one chip as the primary next action (filled --primary, larger), demote the rest to secondary outline chips, and give the red "!" attention badges a distinct shape/icon (e.g. a triangle warning glyph) plus an aria-label like "4 items need attention" so they are not confused with neutral counts. Cap the rail to the active stage plus next, with a "+N" overflow, rather than rendering all stages as equal pills.

title: Settings customizer applies theme/color changes immediately with no preview boundary or confirmation copy
cvss: Low user impact: the workspace customizer auto-applies and auto-saves every change to the device with only a one-line note and a single "restore defaults" escape, risking accidental, non-obvious changes (e.g. an unreadable color) with no undo of the last action.
locations: audit/artifacts/e2e/results/shots/settings.png (subtitle "التغييرات تُطبّق فورًا وتُحفظ على هذا الجهاز"; only control: استعادة الافتراضيات)
description: The "تخصيص مساحة العمل" page states that changes apply instantly and are saved to this device, and offers presets, a quick-colors row, font-size tiles, and sidebar/header sliders. The only safety control is "استعادة الافتراضيات" (restore defaults), which is an all-or-nothing reset. There is no per-change undo, no explicit Save/Cancel boundary, and no warning when a user picks a custom page-background/identity color that could reduce text contrast (the color swatches show raw hex like #F2EEE6 / #FAF8F4 with no contrast feedback).
rootCause: The customizer writes directly to CSS variables/localStorage on every interaction (tokens.css exposes --ui-scale and per-token overrides applied via inline style.setProperty per the comment at lines 234-257), so there is no staged/preview state to commit or discard, and no validation that a chosen color preserves legible contrast against ink tokens.
evidence: settings.png subtitle: "تعديل الألوان وحجم الخط والشريط الجانبي والتخطيط. التغييرات تُطبّق فورًا وتُحفظ على هذا الجهاز." with "استعادة الافتراضيات" as the sole non-content control. tokens.css:234-257 documents the live-applied --ui-scale and the per-token user overrides that "win because inline style.setProperty wins over stylesheet rules."
impact: A user can pick a near-white identity/background color and make text unreadable with no inline warning and no way to undo just that one change short of resetting everything. The lack of a Save/Cancel model also makes the customizer feel risky to explore on a shared/work device.
reproduction: Open Settings → تخصيص مساحة العمل (settings.png). Change a quick color or background swatch; the whole UI re-themes immediately with no confirmation and no single-step undo, only a global restore-defaults.
resolution: Add an inline contrast check on the page-background / identity color pickers that warns when the chosen color fails AA against --ink-1 (e.g. a small "تباين منخفض" badge), and add a lightweight per-change Undo (toast with "تراجع") alongside the existing restore-defaults so users can revert the last action without losing all customisation. Clarify the persistence copy to name where it is saved (this browser/device).
patchBefore:
// color picker change handler
onChange={(hex) => setToken('--bg', hex)} // applies + persists immediately

title: Recent-records list and KPI strip have no visible empty/zero-state treatment distinct from low real values
cvss: Low user impact: BCM shows a "0 بنود غير ممتثلة" tile and other modules can render zero counts that read identically to a still-loading or no-data state, creating brief ambiguity about whether data is absent or genuinely zero.
locations: audit/artifacts/e2e/results/shots/bcm.png (tile "0 بنود غير ممتثلة"; readiness index 31.7/100)
description: BCM renders a KPI tile with value "0" (بنود غير ممتثلة / non-compliant items). A zero in a KPI tile is visually indistinguishable from a tile that failed to load or has no underlying data — the same big-number layout is used. The codebase has both a full .placeholder empty state and a calibrated .empty-inline mini empty state (components.css:972-985), but KPI tiles render a literal 0 rather than choosing an explicit "no data" vs "genuinely zero" treatment, so a 0 could equally mean "clean" (good) or "not yet measured" (unknown).
rootCause: KPI tiles render the numeric value unconditionally; there is no branch that swaps a missing/uninitialised metric for the existing .empty-inline-compact treatment (components.css:985 is explicitly scoped "even denser for sidebars / KPI cells" but is not wired into the KPI render path here).
evidence: bcm.png shows the tile "0" with label "بنود غير ممتثلة" next to "2 أزمات نشطة", "5 فجوات مفتوحة", "1 تحليلات BIA معتمدة", and a readiness index of 31.7/100. components.css:972-985 defines `.empty-inline` and `.empty-inline-compact` ("even denser for sidebars / KPI cells") that exist for exactly this case but are not applied to the zero tiles.
impact: Users cannot tell at a glance whether "0 non-compliant items" means the program is clean or the metric has never been computed, which matters for a compliance audience where "zero findings" and "not assessed" have very different meanings.
reproduction: Open BCM (bcm.png). Note the "0" KPI tile; compare to the readiness index which is computed (31.7/100). There is no visual cue distinguishing a true zero from an unmeasured metric.
resolution: When a metric is genuinely zero, render the number with a subtle confirming cue (e.g. a small "✓ لا توجد" tone or success tint) and when a metric is unavailable/uninitialised render the existing .empty-inline-compact "—" treatment with a tooltip ("لم يُحتسب بعد"), so zero-good and no-data are unambiguous.
